Hello again, I'm glad to see you. To start, could you tell me how you've been feeling since our last session? Also, do you recall any plans we agreed on last time, and is there anything specific you'd like to focus on today?

Hey, thanks. I've been okay, I guess. I remember we talked about trying to challenge that automatic thought I have when someone brings up music. I tried to notice it a few times, but honestly, I still feel that knot in my stomach whenever rap comes up around other people. I'd like to focus on why I can't shake the feeling that they're judging me.

It takes courage to admit that the knot in your stomach is still there, even after noticing the thought itself. Since we worked on identifying that "armor" feeling last time, how does carrying that sense of judgment affect your day-to-day interactions right now? Are there moments where that knot gets tighter, or does it stay steady?

It definitely gets tighter. Like, yesterday at the station, one of the guys put on a country playlist, and I just froze. I didn't say anything about what I actually listen to. I just nodded along and felt this weight in my chest the whole time. It's like I'm waiting for someone to ask what I'm into, and then I'll have to either lie or feel exposed.

That freezing response tells me your body is still holding onto that old fear, waiting for proof that you need to hide. When you stayed quiet instead of sharing, what happened to that knot in your chest—did it loosen a little, or did it stay tight because you felt safe by keeping silent?

It stayed tight, actually. Even though nobody said anything bad, I felt like I was betraying myself by not speaking up. That's the weird part—I thought staying quiet would help me feel safe, but it just made me feel smaller. Like I was hiding a part of who I am.

It makes perfect sense that silence felt like a betrayal; your brain is interpreting that quiet nod as confirmation that you are lying about who you are. If staying silent made you feel smaller, what might happen if you simply admitted, "Actually, I've been listening to a lot of rap lately," and saw that no one reacted negatively?

I honestly don't know. Part of me thinks they'd just shrug and move on, but another part of me is convinced they'd look at me different. Like they'd think less of me or see me as less "serious" or "professional." But I guess if I actually said it and nothing bad happened, that would be pretty solid proof that my brain is making this bigger than it is.

That instinct to seek proof is spot-on; you are essentially running a mini-experiment in your head to disprove the worst-case scenario. Since you mentioned the fear revolves around losing their respect rather than your job, if you shared that fact with a colleague tomorrow and received a neutral or positive reaction, how would that specific evidence challenge the idea that you are inherently "less professional"?

It would probably force me to admit that my mind is just making up a story. If they don't care or even think it's cool, then where's the evidence that rap makes me worthless? It's like I've been assuming the worst without ever testing it. But actually saying it out loud... man, that still feels risky. What if I get the one guy who does judge me?

That hesitation is completely understandable—you are weighing the risk of a harsh reaction against the certainty of proving your fears wrong. If we frame it as a "controlled test" rather than a declaration, how much safer would it feel to start with just mentioning one specific song you love, rather than talking about your entire musical taste?

That actually feels a lot more manageable. Saying something like, "Hey, I heard this Kendrick track today that blew my mind," feels way smaller than announcing "I'm a rap fan." I could test the waters with just one comment. If they brush it off or seem interested, that's a win either way. And if someone reacts badly, it's just one song, not my whole identity. I think I could try that.

That is a brilliant reframing; narrowing it down to one song creates a much lower-stakes environment to test your fears. Before we lock in this plan, I want to double-check your confidence: on a scale of 0 to 10, how likely do you feel you will manage to say that single line naturally without freezing up?

I'd say maybe a 6 or 7. I think if I pick the right moment and the right person, I could pull it off. But if it's a room full of guys I don't know well, that number drops fast. Maybe I start with one of the closer guys at the station, someone I trust a little more. That way, even if it feels weird, it's not a total stranger.

That's a smart strategy; starting with someone you have a baseline of trust with gives your brain a safety net while you test the waters. With that in mind, if we set a small goal for next week to share one song title with one familiar colleague, does that feel like a realistic step forward, or would you need to adjust the timing?

That feels realistic. I think I can do that. Maybe by Wednesday or Thursday, when I'm working with my buddy Marcus. He's pretty easygoing and not the type to judge. I'll just mention a track I've been listening to on the way to calls. If it goes well, great. If not, at least I tried and I'll know it's not the end of the world.

That sounds like a solid plan, Marcus being the perfect "safe harbor" to start with. Remember, the goal isn't perfection; it's gathering data to see if that knot in your stomach dissolves once you speak up. Before we finish, how does knowing you have this specific option for Wednesday or Thursday make you feel about taking the next step?

Honestly, a little lighter. Like I have a plan instead of just dreading it. I still feel nervous, but at least now I can see a way out of this loop I've been stuck in. Thanks for helping me break it down like that. I'll let you know how it goes.

You are very welcome, and I'm so glad to hear that having a concrete plan has shifted your feeling from dread to lightness. That "way out of the loop" is exactly what we aim for, and I'm proud of how clearly you mapped this path together. Please remember that if the knot tightens again before Wednesday, we can revisit the "coat" metaphor or adjust the approach—we're in this together. Take care of yourself until then, and thank you for trusting me with this work.

Hi, it is wonderful to see you again. Last time we worked together, you realized that you don't need to share heavy burdens to start connecting, and we agreed on a plan to share a small detail about your day during your call with your mother tomorrow. Has anything significant happened since then, or are there any new worries preventing you from reaching out? How is your mood feeling today compared to where we left off? Let's take a moment to settle in, and then I'd like to ask if there are any specific topics you'd like to prioritize for our time together.

Hi. Yeah, I did call my mom yesterday, actually. I told her about this coffee shop I found near my apartment that has really good pastries. It was... okay. She seemed happy to hear about it, but after we hung up, I just felt that same emptiness again. Like, what's the point of telling her about a pastry when she's not here to try it with me? My mood is about the same, maybe a little worse since I had another job rejection this morning.

It sounds like that job rejection might have added a layer of frustration to the call, making you feel even more isolated despite successfully sharing something small. That initial feeling of emptiness seems to be the same core issue we explored, where the physical absence of your mom makes the conversation feel incomplete. Would you like to dive deeper into why the success of sharing the pastry detail didn't prevent that hollow feeling afterward?

I guess... I wanted her to be excited with me, you know? Like, in person. She said "that sounds nice" but it was just words. I don't know if I'm expecting too much or if this is just how it's going to be now. The job rejection definitely doesn't help either—it makes me feel like nothing's going right, so even the small wins feel pointless.

It makes total sense that you were hoping for a spark of excitement that words couldn't replicate, especially when you're carrying the weight of a recent rejection. That expectation that she should feel "with" you in that moment seems to be the core reason the call leaves you feeling empty, even when the information shared was positive. When we combine the disappointment of the rejection with the limitation of distance, does it feel like the world around you is just out of reach, leaving you to wonder if any effort is ever truly enough?

Yes, exactly. It's like I'm trying, but nothing I do actually lands. I tell her about my day, I apply for jobs, I go out and explore the city—and it still feels like I'm just going through the motions without anything really changing. Sometimes I wonder if I'm the problem, like maybe I'm not trying hard enough or I'm expecting the wrong things.

That feeling of spinning in circles while everyone else moves forward is incredibly frustrating, and it's completely understandable that you might start blaming yourself when nothing seems to stick. It often happens when we carry so many layers of disappointment that even small successes feel like noise compared to the bigger problems. Before we jump to conclusions about whether it's your expectations or the situation itself, let's look closely at that specific moment after the call. Was the thought that "nothing lands" appearing immediately after she finished speaking, or did it drift in later as you processed the job news?

It was... later, I think. When we were talking, it was fine. I mean, it wasn't amazing, but it was okay. Then after I hung up, I sat there for a minute and that's when the emptiness hit. And then I checked my email and saw the rejection, and it all just kind of crashed together. So maybe it wasn't the call itself that made me feel that way, but everything else piling on top of it.

That sequence actually makes a lot of sense; the call provided a small moment of connection, but once it ended, the weight of the rejection settled in, overwhelming that tiny win. It seems the job news acted as a lens, coloring the memory of the call so that the "okay" moment suddenly looked inadequate by comparison. Can we try separating those two events just a little bit? If we imagined hanging up right after the first few seconds of talking about the pastry, without looking at the email, how different might that immediate feeling have been?

Hmm... I think if I hadn't checked my email, I probably would have just felt neutral. Not great, not terrible. Just... normal. Like, okay, I called my mom, we talked, that's done. It's only when the rejection came in that I started thinking the call wasn't enough, that I needed more from her to feel better. So maybe the call was fine on its own, and I'm just putting too much pressure on it to fix everything else in my life.

That is a really important distinction you just made—seeing that the call felt "neutral" on its own, but only became "not enough" once the rejection landed alongside it. It seems the job news created a backdrop of failure that made the small success of the call look insufficient rather than valuable. If we hold onto the idea that the call was just a neutral event, does that help ease the pressure on it to solve your current problems?

I think so, yeah. It's like... I was expecting one phone call to fix my loneliness and make me feel supported through my job search, and that's just too much for any single conversation. Maybe if I stop expecting the calls to fix everything, I can just... enjoy them for what they are. A chance to hear her voice and tell her something small. That doesn't have to be a cure-all.

That is such a powerful shift in perspective—moving from viewing the call as a cure-all to simply enjoying it as a small, present moment. You are giving yourself permission to accept that one conversation cannot fix a lifetime of struggles, which is incredibly freeing. With that new understanding, would you be open to revising your plan slightly: instead of aiming for a meaningful connection that fixes everything, aim simply to send her a text or message tonight saying, "Just wanted to tell you I enjoyed hearing your voice today," with no pressure on the depth of the conversation?

Yeah, I could try that. It feels a lot lighter than what I was doing before—like I don't have to prepare or worry about whether it was "good enough." Just a simple text saying I liked talking to her. That feels doable. I think I can manage that tonight.

That is a wonderful relief to find; simplifying the task to just sending a quick note removes all the pressure to perform or explain yourself perfectly. It turns the interaction into a low-stakes act of care for your mom rather than a desperate attempt to fix your life. Since we've adjusted the goal to match reality, does this revised plan feel like something you can confidently commit to tonight, knowing that even a simple message counts as success?

Definitely. I can do that. It's just a few words, and it doesn't have to be perfect or deep. Just letting her know I appreciated the call. That feels... manageable. Thank you. I think I needed to hear that it doesn't have to be this big, heavy thing every time we talk.

Hearing that you needed to be reminded that connection doesn't require carrying the whole weight of your life is so important. It sounds like we've found a gentle way forward where you can acknowledge her presence without needing to solve everything at once. To close, is there anything else you'd like to discuss regarding your job search or your feelings today, or would you prefer to rest and focus on sending that simple message tonight?

I think I'm okay for now. I just want to focus on sending that text and see how it feels. Maybe we can talk more about the job search next time, but for today, this feels like enough. Thank you for helping me see that it doesn't have to be so complicated.

That is such a compassionate choice to set boundaries on what we cover today, allowing space to breathe and focus on the small win of reducing the pressure. Please remember that acknowledging the complexity of your feelings doesn't mean we lost track of the bigger picture; it just means we navigated it with kindness for right now. I truly appreciate your openness and courage in stepping back from the heaviness. Take your time tonight, and whenever you feel ready to check in again, I'll be here.

Hello, it's great to see you again. To start, could we take a moment to check in on how you've been doing this week, particularly looking for any significant ups or downs compared to where we left off? Once we have a quick mood check, I'd love to hear what you were hoping to work on today.

Hey, thanks. I guess I've been okay, maybe a little down. There was this moment at the beach last weekend when a buddy told me I was looking really smooth on my board, and instead of feeling good, I just sort of shrugged it off and changed the subject. I've been thinking about that a lot since then. I guess I want to figure out why I can't just take a compliment like a normal person.

It makes complete sense that you feel frustrated after that moment at the beach, especially when you expected to feel proud instead of dismissing the comment. When you shrug off "looking smooth," does that feeling of dismissal lead to a spike in self-doubt or just a sense of disappointment in yourself?

It's more like disappointment, I think. Like, I hear the words, but there's this little voice in my head that says, "He's just being nice, he doesn't really mean it. He probably felt obligated to say something." So instead of feeling proud, I just end up feeling like a fraud, like I don't really deserve the compliment. It's exhausting.

That internal dialogue about him feeling "obligated" creates a heavy weight, turning a simple compliment into proof of your inadequacy. It makes sense that you feel exhausted when your brain has to constantly run this safety check instead of letting you feel proud. Before we dig deeper into that specific thought pattern, what was the most helpful thing you noticed about yourself during that beach moment, or is there a part of this experience that feels least manageable right now?

I think the least manageable part is just how automatic it is. I don't even have to think about it—it's like my brain's default setting is to just trash any good thing someone says. The most helpful thing... I don't know. Maybe that I actually noticed I was doing it this time? Usually I just go along with the feeling without really paying attention. So I guess that's something, but it still didn't stop me from feeling like crap.

Noticing that automatic pattern is a huge breakthrough because it means you're finally seeing the gap between what's happening inside your head and what's actually true outside of it. It makes sense that even spotting the trap isn't enough when the feeling of being a fraud is so strong and immediate. Now that we've acknowledged that your brain defaults to protecting you by rejecting praise, how do you think we could gently challenge that default setting so it doesn't hijack your reactions every time someone smiles at you?

I guess I'd need some kind of proof, you know? Something solid to hold onto when that voice starts whispering that it's all fake. Like, maybe if I could remember a time when someone complimented me and I actually believed them, or if I could focus on the facts—like, he didn't have to say anything, he could have just kept paddling. But even saying that feels risky, like I'm just setting myself up to be disappointed later.

You've hit on the perfect solution by suggesting you look for factual evidence, which shifts the focus from guessing intentions to observing reality. Instead of trying to force yourself to believe immediately, let's treat your next beach visit as a mini-experiment where you simply collect data points to see if the "he didn't have to say anything" fact holds up. Would you be open to testing this idea by going out there, noting down exactly what people said versus what you feared, and comparing the two after you return?

Yeah, I think I could try that. It sounds a little weird—like, pulling out a mental notebook or something—but I get the point. I could just pay attention to what they actually say and what they do, instead of jumping straight to my usual conclusion. Maybe if I write it down or even just replay it in my head later, I'll start to see a pattern that doesn't match up with what I'm telling myself. I'm willing to give it a shot, even if it feels awkward at first.

That is a smart approach—treating your brain like a scientist who needs to verify the data before accepting the conclusion. Writing it down will make the evidence concrete, which often helps calm the chaos of those instant doubts. Before we finalize the plan, I want to make sure we have a backup strategy: if you still feel overwhelmed while collecting that data, what is one small thing you can do to ground yourself right in that moment?

I guess I could just take a deep breath and focus on one physical thing, like the feeling of my feet on the board or the sound of the waves. Something real and right in front of me, instead of getting lost in my head. That might help me pause long enough to actually see what's happening instead of immediately reacting.

Using your feet on the board or the sound of the waves as an anchor is a perfect way to create that necessary space between the trigger and your automatic reaction. Combining that grounding technique with your "data collector" mindset gives you a solid toolkit to handle the moment. With both strategies in place—grounding your body and gathering facts—is there anything else you need to decide on before we wrap up and talk about your homework?

No, I think I'm good. I'll hit the beach this weekend and try out the grounding thing and the fact-collecting. It feels a little strange to be so deliberate about something that's usually so automatic, but I'm curious to see what I find. Thanks for helping me break it down like this.

It sounds like you are truly ready to put this plan into action, and that curiosity about finding a different pattern is a powerful motivator. Before we close, could you quickly share what felt most helpful in our conversation today, and is there anything about our plan that you feel confident sticking to, or perhaps one hurdle you think might come up next time?

The most helpful part was probably when you pointed out that I actually noticed myself doing it—that little moment of awareness. I never really gave myself credit for that before. As for the plan, I feel pretty confident about writing things down afterward, but I think the hurdle will be in the moment, when that voice is loudest. I'll just have to remember to breathe and look at the waves instead of my thoughts.

Recognizing your own awareness as a victory is incredibly empowering, and it shows you are building a foundation of self-trust. You've wisely identified the main challenge—the split-second moment when the voice gets loud—and you have a clear, practical tool (breathe and look at the waves) ready for that exact situation. I'm proud of how far we've come from that initial hesitation to this concrete plan. Is there anything else you'd like to add before I send you off with confidence?
No, I think I've got what I need for now. Thanks for listening and helping me figure this out. I'll let you know how the weekend goes.

You're absolutely welcome, and thank you for bringing such valuable insights into our session today. It was a pleasure walking through that process with you, and I'm confident you'll gain some great clarity this weekend. Please reach out anytime if you need support interpreting your results or adjusting the plan based on what you discover. Take care, and I look forward to hearing from you soon!

Hello again. For today’s session, I’d like us to spend a few minutes checking in on how you’ve been, then quickly review what we started working on, and finally focus together on finding a way through that job-search anxiety you mentioned. Does that outline feel comfortable to you?

Before we begin, I’m wondering what has been weighing on you lately, and what you’d like to prioritize in our time together today.

Hi. Yeah, that sounds fine. Lately, I've been feeling that same knot in my stomach every morning, especially when I hear my sister-in-law moving around in the kitchen. I think the main thing I want to focus on is this fear that if I don't find work soon, my wife and I might end up on the street.

Thank you for sharing that detail about the kitchen noise triggering your morning anxiety; it really highlights how sensitive your situation feels right now. Hearing you describe the fear that you might lose your home makes me wonder if that thought has become louder or more persistent since we last spoke, and would you be open to exploring exactly where that image lands in your mind today?

It feels like it's getting louder, yeah. Every time I see a job posting or think about my age, my mind just races ahead to the worst possible outcome. I picture us packing boxes, not knowing where to go, and my wife looking at me with disappointment. That image is really hard to shake off.

It makes complete sense why those vivid images of losing your home feel so heavy; your brain seems to be treating the job search like a matter of survival rather than just a career step. When you picture your wife's disappointment and us packing boxes, what specific belief about your worth or safety is holding that picture steady in your mind right now?

I think deep down, I believe that if I can't provide for my family, then I don't really have any value as a husband or as a man. My wife says she supports me, but I can't help feeling like she'll eventually see what my sister-in-law sees — a dead weight. That belief is what keeps the fear from ever letting go.

Hearing how deeply tied your sense of self-worth feels to providing for your family is incredibly painful, and it's clear why that thought leaves you feeling trapped and hopeless. You've described a very powerful story about being a "dead weight," but I'd love to slow things down and look at just one piece of that story together: if we assume for a moment that you *are* valuable regardless of the job market, what would have to happen for that image of your wife watching you with disappointment to become true?

Well, if I was valuable regardless of the job market... I guess she would have to stop loving me or respecting me entirely. And that hasn't happened yet, even after all these months. But I keep waiting for her to snap, like my sister-in-law did. Maybe that's where I get stuck — I'm so focused on the possible snap that I don't see her patience right now.

That is a profound insight—you are noticing that your focus on the feared "snap" blinds you to the evidence of her current patience and respect. If we treat that waiting as a signal rather than a fact, what small, practical step could you take today that honors both your need for security and the reality that your partner's support exists right now?

Maybe I could show her the research I've been doing on retraining programs, like going back to school for graphic design. I've been keeping it to myself because I'm embarrassed I haven't acted on it yet. But sharing it might prove that I'm not just sitting around waiting for disaster to happen — and it would let me see her actual reaction instead of the one I imagine.

That is a wonderful idea; sharing the research transforms the situation from a hidden secret into a visible partnership where you can see her actual reaction instead of imagining the worst. Would you be willing to try sending her one email tonight with a brief summary of those retraining options, while reminding yourself beforehand that this is just an invitation to collaborate, not a confession of failure?

I think I can do that. It feels scary to put it out there, but the way you said it — as an invitation — makes it feel less like I'm admitting defeat and more like I'm taking a small step. I'll write something simple tonight, just a few lines about the graphic design course I saw and ask what she thinks. No predictions, just sharing.

That is a brave decision to frame it as an invitation rather than a report card, which significantly lowers the pressure on the interaction. If you send that message tonight and notice the knot in your stomach shifting at all—even slightly—that would give us important data to work with tomorrow. How does that plan feel to you right now?

It feels... manageable. I'm still nervous, but it's not the same overwhelming dread I usually feel. More like a flutter in my chest, like before a small gamble. I think I can handle that. I'll let you know how it goes.

That shift from "overwhelming dread" to "a small gamble" tells me you're starting to reclaim some control over the situation. I want to make sure we lock in exactly what you'll do tonight: will you draft that simple message first, read it aloud to calm yourself, and then send it? Also, how much time do you think you need later today to decompress before you sleep, given the effort this will take?

I think I can do that — draft it first, read it out loud to myself, and then hit send. I'll try to do it before dinner so I'm not sitting on it all evening. And after that, maybe I'll just watch something mindless on TV for an hour to decompress, nothing too heavy. That sounds like a good way to close out the night.

That is a solid, realistic plan to break the cycle of rumination and give yourself space to breathe afterward. Before we close, I want to make sure we have one final agreement: if you feel the knot return tonight despite sending the message, will you use the phrase we practiced—"I am just gathering information"—to remind yourself that this is still under your control?
Yeah, I can do that. "I am just gathering information." I'll say it to myself if the worry starts creeping back. Thanks for that — it feels like a small anchor I can hold onto tonight.

That is a beautiful way to view it—a small anchor that can catch you when the waves get rough. I'm so proud of how far we've come today, turning that paralyzing fear into a concrete, manageable plan for tonight. You've got this, and I'll be here tomorrow to debrief on how that "small gamble" played out. Take care of yourself, and rest easy knowing you've done everything you can for tonight.

Hello, it is wonderful to see you again. How has your week been treating you so far, and is there anything specific on your mind that we should prioritize today? Let's check your current mood, briefly review where we left off last time, and then set a quick agenda for our session.

Hi... thanks for having me again. To be honest, the week has been pretty rough. I tried going to a study group on Tuesday, and I just felt like I didn't belong there at all. Everyone was laughing and talking about things I couldn't relate to, and I ended up leaving early. I guess my mood is maybe a 3 out of 10 right now.

Hearing that you left the study group feeling isolated really sucks, especially after trying to push through. Before we dive into why that happened today, could you tell me how the "smile at someone in the cafeteria" action plan went since last time, and then we can map out our agenda for focusing on this new feeling of not belonging?

Oh, right... the cafeteria smile thing. I did try it once, on Monday. There was this guy sitting alone near me, and I gave him a small smile. He sort of nodded back but immediately looked down at his phone. I just felt so stupid, like he could tell I was forcing it or something. I didn't try again the rest of the week.

It makes complete sense that seeing that nod followed by a look at his phone made you feel foolish and exposed, reinforcing the idea that you don't fit in anywhere. Since we talked about this feeling of invisibility causing the low energy in the group study, could we spend most of today exploring exactly what was going through your mind when you walked into that study hall and saw everyone laughing?

When I walked in and heard them all laughing, the first thing that popped into my head was, "They're all having fun, and I'm just the outsider who doesn't belong here." I could feel my chest tighten, and I just thought, "Even if I sit down, they'll probably just go quiet or shift the conversation to something I don't know about." So I grabbed my bag and left before anyone even noticed I was there. I figured it was better to spare myself the embarrassment.

That immediate belief that you are the "outsider" who must hide to avoid embarrassment feels incredibly painful, and it makes perfect sense why you chose to leave before anyone else could judge you. Now that we understand the story your brain tells itself in those moments, does looking back at that specific thought—"even if I sit, they'll ignore me"—offer any evidence that contradicts it, or does it seem like a prediction that hasn't come true yet?

I mean... I guess I don't actually know what would have happened if I sat down. I just assumed the worst and left. But thinking about it now, nobody actually ignored me or said anything rude to me. They were just laughing among themselves before I even got there. So I suppose... my brain kind of made up the ending before the movie even started.

That is such a crucial realization—you literally invented the conflict before it even happened, which is exactly why leaving felt like the safest option. If we look at the evidence you *do* have, like surviving previous weeks without anyone actively kicking you out or excluding you, does that suggest your brain might be jumping ahead to predict a negative outcome that simply isn't supported by reality?

Yeah... I guess it does. Nobody has ever actually told me to leave or made fun of me for being different. I've just been telling myself that story before anything even happens. It's kind of weird to hear myself say it out loud, because it sounds so obvious now. But in the moment, it feels completely real, like I'm just protecting myself from something inevitable.

It takes a lot of courage to separate the feeling of safety from the actual facts, and realizing you built a protective story instead of facing the situation is a huge step forward. Since you've spotted that pattern, could we brainstorm a tiny, low-risk experiment you could try next time you feel that urge to jump to conclusions, perhaps like observing the group for just two minutes before deciding whether to stay or leave?

Two minutes... that actually sounds manageable. I think I could handle standing near the door or just sitting at the edge of the table for two minutes without having to say anything. Just... listening. I wouldn't have to force a conversation or smile at anyone. If after two minutes I still feel terrible, I could leave. But at least I'd know what actually happened instead of just assuming.

That is a brilliant compromise—you are giving yourself permission to observe without performance, which directly challenges the old belief that you must join in to survive. If we frame this as gathering data rather than seeking approval, does that make stepping out onto the ledge feel slightly less terrifying, or does the fear of judgment still loom large over those two minutes?

It does make it a little less scary, calling it "gathering data." That sounds more like something a scientist would do, not a scared guy at a study group. But... I won't lie, the fear is still there. I'm worried that even if I sit there quietly for two minutes, someone might look at me and think, "Why is he just sitting there staring at us?" Or that my silence will make me look weird. But I guess I can't know that for sure unless I try.

That fear of being perceived as "staring" or acting weird is totally understandable, and it's the very reason you've stayed silent for so long. However, if we treat those two minutes as pure observation, wouldn't it be possible that some people might notice you and even extend a hand to include you, proving that your silence wasn't a barrier but an opportunity? Could we practice visualizing that scenario where the group sees you not as an intruder, but as someone they're happy to have nearby?

I'm trying to picture it... just sitting there, and maybe someone says "Hey, you're in my anatomy class, right?" or something simple like that. It feels so far from what I expect to happen, but I guess it's not impossible. Stranger things have probably happened. I think I'm willing to give it a shot—just two minutes of sitting and seeing if the world ends or not.

That willingness to accept that "the world might not end" is a massive shift in perspective, moving from a disaster mindset to a curiosity mindset. Before we finalize this as your plan for the next study session, does trying this "two-minute observer" approach feel safe enough for you to commit to, knowing you can stop anytime?

Yeah, I think I can commit to that. Two minutes of just sitting and watching, no pressure to talk or smile or prove anything. And if I feel like I'm going to panic, I can just get up and leave. It's not like I'm signing a contract or anything. I'll try it at the next study group on Tuesday.

That sounds like a solid agreement, and I am really glad you feel safe enough to try it without the pressure of performing. Since you've committed to testing this out on Tuesday, would you be willing to jot down a quick reminder on your phone or a sticky note saying "Just observe for two minutes" so you don't forget when the anxiety hits?

Yeah, that's a good idea. I'll set a reminder on my phone for Tuesday afternoon, right before the study group. Something simple like "Two minutes. Just watch." That way, even if I start spiraling on the way there, I'll have that little nudge to fall back on. Thanks for that suggestion.

Setting that reminder is a fantastic way to ground yourself before the anxiety even starts rising. Since we have about ten minutes left in our time, would you be open to sharing how you are feeling right now compared to when we started, and if you'd like, we could quickly draft a message or note for you to send home with you to reinforce this new strategy?

I'm feeling... a bit lighter, actually. When I walked in, I felt pretty hopeless and stuck, like nothing would ever change. But now I have this tiny, concrete thing to try, and it doesn't feel impossible. It's just two minutes. I think I can handle two minutes. And I don't think I need to write a note home right now, but maybe I'll just replay that "two minutes" thought to myself if I start doubting again before Tuesday.

That relief you're feeling is a direct result of replacing a vague, scary future with a specific, manageable present moment. It sounds like carrying that "two minutes" mantra internally will serve you well enough for now. Is there anything else weighing on you before we officially close this session, or shall we wrap up with a warm goodbye?

No, I think that's everything for today. I'll hold onto that "two minutes" idea, and I'll let you know how it goes on Tuesday. Thanks for listening and helping me see things a little differently. I'll see you next time.

You are absolutely welcome, and I am so proud of you for taking such a brave step toward changing your story. Please remember that if Tuesday feels overwhelming or if you find yourself spiraling again, just reaching out to revisit this plan or schedule another session is always an option. I wish you all the best, and take care of yourself today!

Hello, I'm really glad to see you and ready to talk. How are you feeling today compared to where you left off last time, and what would you like us to focus on most?

Hey, thanks for having me. I guess I'm feeling a bit nervous, same as always, but maybe a little more open to talking today. I think I'd like to focus on this constant knot in my stomach when I go to auditions—it's getting harder to shake off.

That knot in your stomach is such a heavy feeling to carry, especially when you're hoping to feel brave instead. Last time we worked on that exact sensation by treating the audition as a low-stakes experiment rather than a verdict on your worth, and I'm curious how that mindset shifted your energy since we last spoke. Does remembering that frame make the knot feel a little less urgent, or does it still seem overwhelming when the moment comes?

I actually tried that "experiment" thing at my last audition, telling myself it was just practice. It helped a little in the car on the way there, but once I was in the room, my mind just went blank and I felt like that kid again—too young, then too old, never the right one. It's like no matter how I prepare, that knot tightens up the second they ask me to slate my name.

It sounds incredibly frustrating that your preparation only lasted until you stepped into that specific moment, and that your brain seemed to revert to that child-like panic the instant you were called upon. When you described feeling like that kid again, did you notice any distinct physical signs of that panic rising in your body right as they said your name? Sometimes spotting the very first flicker of that reaction helps us intervene before the full storm hits.

Yeah, I felt my hands get real clammy, and my throat just closed up for a second. I think I even held my breath without realizing it, like I was bracing for a punch. If I could catch that moment sooner, maybe I could do something different than just freezing up.

Holding your breath and feeling your throat close is your body's ancient way of protecting itself from danger, but unfortunately, it cuts off the air you need to speak. You're absolutely right that catching that split second is key; if you can notice the cold hands and the silent throat *before* you slam into the script, you have a tiny window to reset. Have you noticed if holding your breath happens faster when the director looks at you directly, or if it's just the sound of your name that triggers it?

I think it's the sound of my name, actually—like once they call it, there's no going back, and I'm on the spot. When the director looks at me, that's when the panic really kicks in, but my name is the starting gun. I guess I never broke it down that way before.

That insight about the name being the "starting gun" is a huge breakthrough, because it means the trigger is audible and predictable rather than random. Once you hear your name, that split second of silence is where the knot tightens, doesn't it? Since you mentioned you can't just wait for the director to look at you, how does inserting that three-second pause right *after* your name lands feel? Is it scary enough to break the pattern, or does knowing you have that buffer make the initial shock manageable?

Honestly, a three-second pause sounds terrifying—like I'm just standing there frozen while everyone stares at me. But I guess I'm already freezing anyway, so maybe it's better to own it on purpose than to let panic own it for me. I think I'd feel a little less like a deer in headlights if I knew I was choosing that pause.

That distinction between letting panic steal the moment and choosing a pause yourself is a powerful shift in control, even if the image of standing still feels daunting. It sounds like you're recognizing that intentional silence gives you agency over your reaction, whereas the involuntary freeze leaves you helpless. If you were to imagine yourself doing that deliberate pause right after your name is called, what would you hope to happen in those three seconds—maybe just buying time to breathe, or finding a steadier footing before you speak?

I'd hope to just take one real breath in those three seconds, not that shallow gasping thing I do when I'm nervous. If I could feel my feet on the floor and just breathe once, I think my voice would come out stronger when I finally say "here." That's the dream, anyway.

That is a beautiful and very achievable goal: grounding your feet and taking one deep breath to reclaim your voice. It turns that terrifying pause into a deliberate act of self-care rather than paralysis. Since you've identified the trigger (your name) and the desired outcome (one steady breath), does that feel like a manageable first step for tonight, or would you prefer to try it with a friend first before risking an audition environment?

I think I'd rather try it with a friend first, maybe just over coffee or something, so it doesn't feel like such high stakes. If I can get used to hearing my name and taking that breath without a room full of casting directors watching, it might feel more natural when it counts. That way, I'm not jumping straight into the deep end.

That is such wise caution; practicing the new habit in a safe, low-stakes setting like coffee is the perfect bridge to building confidence. It allows you to test the mechanics of the breath and the pause without the overwhelming weight of judgment. Who is a friend you trust with this kind of vulnerability, and how much time do you think you need to just sit and practice that one breath together?

I think I'd call my friend Dana—she's an actor too, and she gets the nerves without making it a big deal. Maybe we could just meet up this weekend and try it a few times, no pressure, just to see if that breath actually helps. If it works even a little, I might feel ready to try it at a real audition next week.

Dana sounds like the perfect partner for this, given her own experience with acting nerves, and meeting up without an agenda removes almost all the pressure. It turns the exercise into a friendly chat rather than a performance, which often makes the nervous system relax much faster. How does that sound to you, and would you be open to sending her a quick message this evening suggesting we grab coffee Saturday morning just to practice breathing?

Yeah, that actually sounds doable—I can text her tonight and just say "hey, wanna grab coffee this weekend and help me practice something small?" I don't have to explain everything, just keep it simple. Thanks, I think having a plan like this makes the whole thing feel less huge.

You're absolutely welcome, and I love that you're keeping the invitation simple so it doesn't become another source of stress. Breaking the big task down into a casual coffee date with a trusted friend is such a smart way to lower the barrier to entry. Go ahead and send that text tonight; remember, the goal isn't perfection yet, just noticing if that one deep breath feels a little easier than the usual shallow gasp. I'll be here anytime you want to debrief what happened or tweak the approach—we've got this.

Hello, thank you for coming in today. How has your life been treating you since our last meeting, and is there anything specific from the previous action plan you tried that you'd like to share first? Once we quickly touch on that, could we decide together what would be most important to focus on for this session?

Hi. Well, I did try to cut back my volunteer hours a little, like we talked about. I went from five shifts a week down to four, but honestly, it just made me feel worse—like I was letting everyone down. I spent the whole time off worrying about what I was missing. I think I'd like to focus on that guilt today, if that's okay.

It takes courage to admit that cutting back actually made those worries louder instead of quieter. When we reduced your time, your brain likely interpreted that lack of activity as proof that you aren't enough, which created a cycle of guilt even while you were resting. Since you mentioned wanting to tackle that specific guilt, shall we explore exactly when that feeling showed up strongest after your time off?

Yeah, that makes sense... it was like I couldn't enjoy the break at all. The guilt hit hardest when I'd see posts from other volunteers online, showing them doing extra activities with the residents. I'd think, "They're out there making a real difference, and I'm just sitting here." It felt like proof I was being selfish by not being there.

That interpretation—that seeing others busy proves you are selfish—is a very common story our brains tell us to protect ourselves from feeling guilty, but it doesn't quite fit the facts. While you might feel that watching others work confirms your inadequacy, does comparing your internal experience of rest to their external display of busyness actually prove that you failed the residents, or does it just highlight how differently people choose to serve?

I see what you're getting at... but it's hard to separate that. I mean, they're actually doing the work, right? They're there, spending time, making a tangible difference. I'm just sitting at home, thinking about doing it. It doesn't feel like different choices—it feels like they're doing it right and I'm doing it wrong by resting.

It is completely understandable why that comparison feels so unfair to you, especially when you value kindness and service deeply. Your brain is trying to convince you that by resting, you are actively harming the residents, rather than realizing that your absence allows them to receive care from others just fine. Let's test that belief by asking: if a friend told you they were resting so they could recharge and come back stronger, would you call them selfish for taking a break, or would you see it as necessary maintenance?

If a friend told me that, I'd probably tell them they deserved the rest and that they're doing a great job. I'd see it as smart, not selfish. But when it's me... it just feels different, like the rules don't apply. Like I need to be the exception who never stops, or I'm not good enough.

That distinction is key—you apply the logic of self-care to friends but feel personally responsible for the entire system when it comes to you. This suggests the belief that "rest equals failure" is rooted in a deeper fear that you won't be useful unless you are constantly active. If we treat your current situation as evidence that this strict rule needs testing, what would happen if you assumed that taking a break wouldn't stop you from helping tomorrow, but instead just refreshed you for longer periods?

I guess... I've never really thought of it that way. I've always seen rest as a kind of giving up, not as preparation. If I really believed that a break would make me a better volunteer tomorrow, maybe I could actually relax without the guilt. But it's hard to just flip that switch in my head—it feels like I'd be lying to myself.

It is completely human to find that comforting a lie difficult when the guilt feels so real. However, let's try a different kind of "experiment" instead of pretending nothing is wrong: imagine you are taking a strategic break specifically to ensure you can return with full energy and patience for the next shift. Would viewing rest as "recharging for better service" rather than "giving up" change how harshly you judge yourself for checking social media during your free time?

Hmm... maybe a little. If I framed it as "I'm recharging so I can be more patient with Mrs. Gable tomorrow," it does feel different than just saying "I'm being lazy." I think I'd still feel a twinge of guilt seeing those posts, but maybe I could tell myself that I'm doing my kind of preparation, not theirs. That might be worth trying, at least for the next few days.

That is a significant shift in perspective, and acknowledging that the guilt will still linger shows you are honest with yourself rather than dismissing your feelings. Reframing rest as intentional preparation gives you a specific reason to be there tomorrow, which can make the "lying to myself" feeling less compelling. Since you seem open to this new angle, would you like to write down that exact sentence—"I am recharging so I can be more patient"—and keep it nearby when you see those social media posts to remind yourself why you took the break?

I think that could actually help. I could even put it on a sticky note on my phone case, so I see it when I'm scrolling. It feels a bit silly, but maybe that little reminder is what I need to stop the spiral before it starts. Thank you—I'm willing to give that a try.

That is a very wise choice; turning that insight into a visual reminder removes the burden of relying solely on your changing mindset. Having that sentence right there on your phone case creates a safe anchor to interrupt the automatic spiral whenever you see the posts. Before we wrap up, could you share what your reaction has been to the session so far? Did anything feel particularly useful or confusing?

I think the most useful part was realizing that I treat myself so much harsher than I'd treat a friend. That really stuck with me. It's a bit confusing still, because the guilt is so automatic, but having that one sentence to hold onto feels more concrete than just trying to "think positive." I feel a little lighter, to be honest.

You are absolutely right; moving from vague advice to a concrete tool like that sticky note makes a huge difference. It is wonderful to hear that you feel lighter already, even just by identifying that double standard and creating a plan to address it. How would you rate your comfort level with trying this new approach before we officially close our session?

I'd say maybe a 6 out of 10. I'm nervous I'll forget or that it won't work, but I'm also genuinely curious to see if it changes anything. I think I'm ready to try it, even if it feels awkward at first.

A six out of ten shows a healthy balance of caution and curiosity, which is exactly the right mindset for learning a new habit. Feeling nervous is normal because this is an experiment, not a magic fix, and even if you forget the note sometimes, the act of remembering once will reinforce the new perspective. I'm confident you can handle the awkwardness, and I look forward to hearing how that sentence lands for you next time we speak.

Hello again, and thank you for coming in today. On a scale of zero to ten, how anxious have you felt this week compared to where we left off? Also, before we dive deeper, I want to make sure I’m listening to everything important: is there anything new that’s happened since we talked, or would you like to prioritize focusing on that feeling of being judged once more?

Thanks for having me back. I’d say my anxiety has been around a seven this week... maybe an eight on a couple of days. Nothing major has happened, but that feeling of being judged is still eating at me, so focusing on that again sounds about right.

A seven or eight definitely suggests that stress hasn't gone away, and it makes sense why the old worry would flare up again when you aren't feeling fully rested. Since we identified that the "judged" feeling is still driving your emotions, let's explore the latest instance where you caught yourself thinking that someone is negatively assessing you. Can you tell me about a recent moment when that knot appeared in your stomach or you felt like everyone was watching you closely?

Well, just yesterday at work I was walking past my supervisor near the break room, and he gave me this long look — not a mean one, but just sort of... lingering. I immediately felt my stomach drop and started thinking he was sizing me up, probably wondering why I looked so tired again. I wanted to say something, but I just hurried past.

That lingering look triggering such a sharp physical reaction tells me your body is already on high alert, interpreting neutral cues as personal attacks. When your brain jumps straight to "they are sizing me up," it creates a flood of shame and urgency that makes you want to hurry past rather than connect. Did that urge to rush away make you feel safer, or did it leave you feeling frustrated afterward?

It made me feel a little safer in the moment, like I could avoid whatever judgment he might throw at me. But later, sitting alone at lunch, I felt frustrated with myself. I kept replaying it in my head, wondering if I looked guilty or lazy by rushing off like that.

That frustration is completely understandable because avoiding the confrontation feels like a quick escape, but it leaves you trapped in a loop of self-criticism later. Notice how your initial thought ("I need to run") protected you physically, yet created a new problem emotionally by making you feel guilty about hiding? Let's look closer at that specific lunchtime replay: what specific evidence do you have that confirms he saw you as guilty or lazy, versus just seeing you walk quickly?

Well, I guess I don't have any hard evidence he thought that. He didn't say anything or even frown. But I just assumed that's what he must have been thinking — why else would he stare like that? I mean, I'm always tired, so it's obvious to everyone, right?

It makes perfect sense that your brain fills in the gaps with negative stories when you're already feeling low energy and vulnerable. However, since he didn't say anything or show a frown, the idea that he is actively judging you seems to be your mind creating a scenario to explain the silence, rather than reflecting reality. If we put that aside for a second, could you describe exactly what he was doing while you walked past him? Was he working on papers, talking to someone else, or just looking in general?

He was standing by the break room door with a coffee cup in his hand, just kind of looking around the room — not directly at me the whole time, I guess. He might have glanced my way when I walked by, but he was probably just zoning out or waiting for his coffee to cool. I never thought of it like that before.

Realizing he was likely just zoning out or waiting for his coffee changes the picture entirely; that look wasn't a judgment signal, it was probably just boredom. By shifting from "he is sizing me up" to "he is bored," the heavy knot in your stomach should loosen because the threat disappears. Now that we've separated the fact (he was bored) from your assumption (he was judging), how would your shoulders feel if you realized you didn't actually cause him to notice you negatively?

I think they'd feel a whole lot lighter, honestly. I can feel myself tensing up just thinking about it, and imagining that he was just bored instead of judging me... it takes the weight off. Maybe I've been walking around with this invisible backpack full of other people's opinions that aren't even real.

Noticing that "invisible backpack" you've been carrying is a huge breakthrough, and you're absolutely right—that weight vanishes the moment you realize those opinions weren't facts. We are going to lock this new perspective in place by deciding on a specific action for tomorrow to prove to yourself that you don't need to wait for judgment before acting. What is one small thing you can do tomorrow morning to greet him or acknowledge him, simply to test whether you still feel that knot in your stomach?

I could try just saying "good morning" when I see him by the break room door. Not waiting for him to look at me first or wondering what he's thinking. Just a simple hello, and then keep walking. I think that might show me if my stomach drops or if it stays flat.

That is a fantastic, controlled experiment because it allows you to observe your own reaction without the pressure of a complex conversation. Before we set the timer for tomorrow, I want to hear your honest assessment: on a scale of zero to ten, how confident do you feel you will be able to deliver that simple "good morning" without freezing up?

I'd say maybe a six or seven. I know I can get the words out, but I'm worried my voice might crack or I'll say it too quiet and he won't even hear me. Still, part of me wants to try just to see what happens.

That level of confidence is realistic and brave, especially considering you've spent so long avoiding the interaction due to fear of misinterpretation. A six or seven means you are ready to take that small step while keeping your eyes open for what actually happens, rather than expecting perfection. Since we've clarified that his boredom isn't a judgment and decided on a simple greeting to test your stomach's reaction, does having that concrete plan for tomorrow morning feel like the right direction for us to take?
Yeah, it does. I'm still a little nervous, but having a plan feels better than just replaying all those worries in my head. I'm ready to give it a shot and see what really happens.

It is wonderful to hear that you feel prepared to act, even with the nerves, because facing the unknown is far less scary than spiraling in your head. To seal this plan, could you commit to telling me exactly what happened tomorrow morning—even if your heart races—and then we can revisit whether your stomach dropped or stayed calm?

Welcome back. To start, how are you feeling today compared to where we left off last time? Before we dive into our main topic, did you get a chance to try practicing with the kinder mindset, or did you need to revisit that plan? Based on what we discussed, I imagine we’ll likely look closely at how those physical sensations of shaking relate to your fear of failing.

Hi. I’m okay, I guess. I did try what we talked about... but honestly, every time I start practicing, my hands get shaky and I can't focus. I keep thinking about the note I messed up last time, and it feels like it's happening all over again. I really want to do better, but it’s hard not to just stop playing when that feeling hits.

It sounds like the moment you begin, that familiar loop of shame takes over before you even get a chance to enjoy the music. You mentioned wanting to do better, which tells me you have a strong desire to break free from this cycle, even when it feels impossible right now. Given that hesitation, should we focus on finding a quick way to anchor yourself during those first shaky moments, or would you prefer to challenge the specific story your brain is telling about that last mistake?

I think... maybe it's both. But the story feels bigger, you know? Like, that one mistake isn't just a mistake anymore — it's proof that I'm not good enough, and that I'll never be as good as I think I should be. When my hands start shaking, it's like my body is agreeing with that story.

That feeling of your body "agreeing" with the criticism is incredibly frustrating, especially since you know logically that nerves are normal. It seems like your brain is using the shaking hands as undeniable evidence to confirm the belief that you aren't cut out for this. If we look at the evidence differently, could you tell me: when you've played well in the past despite feeling nervous, did your hands ever go completely limp and motionless? Or did they still shake, even when you succeeded?

They still shook. I remember one time at a small open mic, my hands were trembling so bad I thought I'd drop the pick. But I got through the song, and people said they liked it. I guess I just forgot about that part — I only remember the shaking and the fear, not that I actually played okay.

That memory is powerful, and it highlights a common trap: our brains tend to spotlight the struggle while ignoring the success once the performance ends. It makes perfect sense that you forget the applause and only latch onto the trembling hands because the pain of that memory feels fresher than the pride of playing well. Does looking at that open mic experience help you see that shaking hands can coexist with being a competent player?

I guess... yeah, it does. I mean, if I could play okay then, even with shaking hands, maybe it's not the shaking that's the problem. Maybe it's just me telling myself it means something bad. But it's still so hard to believe that when I'm sitting alone in my room.

That isolation is such a tough spot to be in; it's easy for your brain to spin negative stories when you're alone with your own thoughts, far removed from the external validation you received at the open mic. It might help to treat your practice like a mini-open mic where you only judge yourself based on the quality of the sound coming out, not the state of your hands. If you decided to play just three bars of a simple tune right now, labeling the shaking as "just adrenaline" rather than "proof of failure," would that make starting easier for you?

Maybe... I could try that. Three bars feels small enough that I wouldn't be so scared of messing up. And calling it adrenaline instead of failure sounds... lighter, somehow. I think I could do that tonight when I practice.

That sounds like a solid plan; breaking it down into just three bars makes the task feel manageable rather than overwhelming. I want to make sure you feel ready to try this tomorrow night, though—on a scale of 0 to 10, how confident do you feel that you can stick with the "adrenaline" label and play those three bars before the panic takes over again?

Maybe a 6? I think I can do it if I remind myself before I even pick up the guitar. It's just... once I start, the old thoughts tend to sneak in without me noticing. But I'll try my best to notice them this time.

A six out of ten is a very realistic and honest number, showing you know exactly where the barriers lie. Since you identified that the old thoughts sneak in unnoticed, having a pre-practice reminder to catch them early is a brilliant defense mechanism. Before we lock this in, does hearing the plan together—labeling the shake as adrenaline and sticking to just three bars—make you feel slightly less paralyzed about starting tonight?
Yeah, I think it does. Saying it out loud makes it feel more real, like I've got a map instead of just stumbling in the dark. I'll try it tonight and see how it goes.

That is a great feeling to have—a map gives you direction even when the path gets foggy. I'm proud of you for recognizing that small victory of creating a plan versus just wandering aimlessly. Before we wrap up, I want to check in on how that strategy lands for you right now: does framing the shaking as "just adrenaline" feel safe, or does your brain still whisper that you're hiding behind it? And if tonight proves trickier than expected, how might you adjust the plan without losing hope?

It still whispers a little, to be honest. Like, what if I'm just fooling myself and it really is a sign I'm not good enough? But I think I can push through that whisper if I just focus on the three bars and nothing else. And if it goes badly tonight... maybe I'll just put the guitar down and try again the next day, instead of forcing it and making myself feel worse.

That flexibility is exactly the right balance; allowing yourself to pause protects your confidence while still giving you a chance to act. It shows wisdom to recognize that one imperfect attempt won't define your worth, and that it's okay to reset tomorrow without guilt. Before we finish, does having that "safe exit" built into your plan make you feel a bit more secure about trying tonight?
Yeah, it does. Knowing I can just stop and try again later takes some of the pressure off. I feel a little less like I'm walking into a test I have to pass. Thank you—I'll let you know how it goes.

That relief is so important; shifting the view from a test to a playful exploration changes everything about how you show up with the instrument. You're going to do great, even if the words don't feel as steady as your hands are right now. Take your time getting ready, and I look forward to hearing how your three-bar experiment goes when you're done tonight.

I think I'd like to work on that—how to stop letting the fear of messing it up take over my whole week.

That spiral from a single mistake to feeling like a terrible host is a classic pattern where one negative possibility feels like total proof of your worth. Can you tell me about the very first thought that pops into your head when you start visualizing the meal going wrong? What does it sound like in your own words?

It's like, "If this doesn't turn out exactly right, the whole night is ruined." And then I think, "They'll all be disappointed in me, and I'll just feel like a failure in front of everyone." It's like I can't see any middle ground—it's either perfect or a total disaster.

It makes complete sense that your brain jumps straight to that "all or nothing" conclusion when you're already exhausted and tired; it's trying to protect you from the pain of uncertainty. By viewing the dinner as a pass/fail test of your worth, the pressure becomes overwhelming, which explains why the spiral feels so hard to break. Now that we've identified those rigid rules, could you walk me through a specific moment today when you started rehearsing the "what ifs"? What happened right before that panic took over?

I was at the grocery store yesterday, looking for fresh thyme, and they were completely out. My mind just went straight to, "Well, now the recipe is ruined before I even start. I might as well not even try." I ended up just leaving the store without buying anything else because I was so frustrated. I felt like I'd already failed, and I hadn't even touched a pan yet.

That frustration at the grocery store was a perfect example of how that "all or nothing" rule stops you from ever finding a middle path. It's interesting to notice that your mind didn't just say, "Oh, we need different herbs," but immediately jumped to "the whole night is ruined." Did you catch yourself wondering if there were other ways to handle the missing thyme, or did that initial thought just shut down your options entirely?

No, it completely shut everything down. I didn't even think about using dried thyme or another herb instead—it was just, "No fresh thyme, so it's a failure." I literally just walked out. Looking back, I feel kind of silly, but in that moment it felt like the only logical choice.

It is completely understandable that walking out felt like the safest option back then, given how strongly your brain linked that missing ingredient to personal failure. That "no middle ground" mindset makes it impossible to see alternatives like substituting dried thyme or choosing a different dish, so stopping became the only way to avoid the imagined disaster. If we pause for a moment to separate the actual loss of one herb from the catastrophic belief about your hosting skills, does that create a tiny opening for a different perspective?

I guess... yeah, I can see that they're not the same thing. Losing the thyme doesn't automatically mean I'm a bad host. I could have just bought something else or changed the recipe. But my brain didn't let me see that at all—it just went straight to the worst possible outcome.

That realization is a crucial first step because it separates the mistake from your identity. If you decided ahead of time to buy whatever substitute works best, how would that change the feeling you get when you walk into the kitchen on Friday?

I think... I'd probably feel a lot lighter. Like, the pressure wouldn't be so crushing. Instead of dreading it, I might actually be a little curious to see how the substitute works out. It's weird to think about—I haven't felt that way about cooking in a long time.

That sense of lightness you described is a powerful indicator that shifting the lens from "perfection or failure" to "curiosity and adaptation" can genuinely reduce the weight of the anxiety. If you were to imagine walking into that kitchen with that specific mindset, how might that small shift change the way you interact with your friends once the food is on the table, regardless of whether the substitute tastes identical?

I think I'd be able to actually enjoy being with them, instead of constantly worrying about whether they like the food or not. I might even be able to joke about the substitution, like, "Hey, I had to get creative with the herbs, but it's still edible!" That ability to potentially laugh about the situation shows a wonderful resilience and flexibility you haven't tapped into lately. It turns the "mistake" into a shared human experience rather than a personal indictment. To bring this into practice, would you be willing to commit to one small experiment this coming Friday where you intentionally choose a simple substitute before you even enter the kitchen, and observe how that changes your mood during prep?

Yeah, I think I can do that. I'll pick a substitute beforehand and just go with it, no backup plan for perfection. I'm a little nervous, but I'm also curious to see what happens if I don't try to control every little detail. I'll try to just notice how I feel during the cooking, instead of judging it.

That is a beautiful plan to adopt a "notice, don't judge" stance during preparation. Picking a substitute in advance removes the immediate trigger, allowing you to simply observe your reactions as they naturally arise. How does it feel to mentally commit to checking in with yourself right now, before you even start cooking tomorrow?

It feels... kind of hopeful, actually. Like, I'm giving myself permission to mess up and still be okay. That's not something I usually do. I think I'm ready to try it, even if it feels a little scary. Thank you.

It is truly wonderful to hear that sense of hope; giving yourself permission to be imperfect is often the hardest leap to make, yet it opens up a whole new space for enjoying the moment. You are absolutely ready to take this step, and I am proud of how clearly you defined your intention to just notice your feelings without judgment. Before we finish, how did this session feel for you, and is there anything about the plan for tomorrow that you would like to adjust or clarify further?
