Hello again. Before we dive in, I want to quickly recap where we left off: we practiced dropping your shoulders and counting to three whenever you feel that knot forming, with the goal of buying yourself a few seconds to break the panic spiral. How are you feeling right now compared to when we spoke last time, and did you find yourself using that shoulder drop technique tonight while you were at home? Once we touch base on that, what would you most like to focus on today—are there other worries weighing on you, or should we revisit the feeling of being watched at work?

Oh, yeah. I did try the shoulder thing a couple times, mostly when I was feeding my cat last night and started thinking about tomorrow's shift. It helped a little... I guess it gave me a second before my mind ran off. But honestly, right now I'm already feeling that knot just thinking about work tomorrow. I keep replaying that mistake I made last week—I mixed up two orders and the customer got really annoyed. My manager didn't say much, but I could tell she was watching me closer after that.

It makes sense that your mind immediately jumped back to that specific incident; remembering someone getting annoyed can instantly reignite the belief that everyone is judging your competence. When you replay that memory, what specific thoughts run through your head about what your manager thinks or what might happen next?

I just keep thinking she's probably already made up her mind about me. Like, she's thinking, "This guy can't even handle a simple order, what's he doing here?" And then I imagine her pulling me aside one day, telling me it's not working out, and I'm standing there with my cat waiting at home and no way to pay rent. It's like my brain skips straight to the worst part every time.

That leap from a minor mistake to imagining you losing your ability to pay rent is a classic example of your mind skipping ahead to the ultimate consequence rather than stopping at the immediate situation. It seems like the shame of that specific incident is fueling a much larger fear about your stability and worth. Can you walk me through what you were actually feeling in your body right as you thought she was making up her mind about firing you?

Uh, I felt it right in my chest—like a tight, cold pressure. My hands got a little clammy too, just thinking about it. And I noticed my jaw was clenched without me even realizing. It's like my whole body was bracing for a punch that hasn't even happened yet. But it feels so real in the moment, you know?

That intense physical sensation of cold pressure in your chest and clenching your jaw is your body's way of preparing for a fight or flight response, even though the danger hasn't arrived yet. It's understandable why your brain interprets this physical alarm as proof that disaster is imminent, but we can look at the difference between the feeling of panic and the fact that no one has pulled you aside yet. When you notice that cold pressure rising, what is the very first image or sound in your mind that pops up before the story about losing your job takes over?

It's weird, but the first thing that pops into my head isn't a thought—it's like I see my cat sitting by the door waiting for me, and I hear the click of the lock when I'd have to give my keys back. That's the very first flash before all the words come. It's like my brain goes straight to that empty apartment feeling, even though nothing's actually happened yet.

That image of the locked apartment and your cat alone is incredibly powerful because it bypasses logic entirely and hits you with a visceral sense of loss before you even form the words. It makes perfect sense that your brain latches onto this visual so tightly because it represents the ultimate catastrophe, but I wonder if there's a gap between that scary image and the reality that you still haven't lost your keys yet. If you were to stand right between that image of the locked door and the present moment, what would be the smallest piece of evidence that says you are still safe right now?

I guess... I'm still standing here talking to you, and my cat's probably on the couch right now at home. I haven't been called into the manager's office today. And I still have my apron hanging in my closet for tomorrow's shift. Those are little things, but they're real. I just don't feel them when the panic hits.

You're absolutely right; those tangible details—the apron, your cat on the couch, your presence in the chat—are proof that your reality hasn't shifted, even when the panic tries to rewrite it. It seems like the difficulty lies in trusting those facts when the fear is screaming louder, almost drowning out the quiet evidence of safety. If we treated the evidence like a puzzle where you hold each piece firmly, could we gently remind your brain of the unlocked apartment and the manager who is currently unaware of any mistakes? What would it feel like to focus on those pieces for just thirty seconds instead of letting the scary image dominate?

I think... that's actually really hard to do, but maybe it's worth trying. If I actually held onto the thought of my manager not saying anything yet and my cat being totally fine right now, it would feel kind of hollow at first, like I'm lying to myself. But I guess the more I sit with it, the quieter the cold pressure gets, just a little bit. It's like my brain doesn't want to let go of the scary image because it thinks it's protecting me by preparing for the worst.

It is completely normal to feel like you are lying to yourself when the evidence points to safety but your instincts scream danger; your brain isn't actually deceiving you, it's just prioritizing survival over comfort by keeping you on high alert. That feeling of the cold pressure softening even slightly is a huge sign that you are successfully engaging with reality instead of retreating into the worst-case scenario. If that gentle softening continues for just five more minutes while you focus on those small facts, how might that shift influence your confidence about handling the rest of your day?

I think it would make me feel a little more steady, like I could actually get through my shift without my hands shaking every time I carry a tray. Maybe I'd even be able to look a customer in the eye without assuming they're thinking I'm incompetent. It sounds small, but that would be a big step for me right now—just feeling like I can exist at work without the whole building about to collapse.

That feeling of steadiness and simply existing without the world collapsing around you is exactly what we aim for, and it shows you are ready to test that new mindset. Before we finalize our plan, I want to make sure we both agree on this approach: focusing on those small, present-moment facts to calm the physical tension seems like the right direction for you. Does that summary reflect what we've talked about, and would you feel comfortable trying this specific strategy first thing tomorrow when you arrive at work?

Yeah, that sounds right. I think I can try it—when I walk in and hang up my apron, I'll take a second to notice the coffee machine and the tables and remind myself nobody's fired me yet. It feels a little silly, but I'm willing to give it a shot. Thanks for helping me see that the scary image isn't the whole picture.

You're very welcome, and I am so glad you found value in seeing that the scary image is only one piece of the puzzle, not the entire story. It is wonderful to hear you are willing to give this a shot even if it feels a bit silly, because sometimes doing the smaller, simpler actions is exactly how we rebuild confidence. Just to make sure we are aligned moving forward: would you feel comfortable agreeing to try checking in with those physical cues and present-moment facts as soon as you step into the cafe tomorrow morning? And if you notice your mind slipping back into the worst-case scenarios, what is one phrase you might say to yourself to bring it back to the here and now?

I can agree to that. As soon as I walk in, I'll look at my apron, maybe the coffee machine, and tell myself, "I'm here, I'm okay, nothing bad has happened yet." And if my mind starts slipping again, I think I'll just say, "Keys are still in my pocket." That's the simplest truth—I still have my keys, I still have my cat, I still have my job for now. That might be enough to pull me back.

That is a beautiful and practical mantra, anchoring your identity to the undeniable facts of your current reality rather than the hypothetical future. Having concrete objects like the apron and keys to physically touch creates a strong bridge between your fear and the safety of the present moment. Before we conclude, I want to hear your honest reflection on today's session: did finding those anchors help you feel calmer, and was there anything about our approach that felt particularly helpful or something you'd like to adjust for next time?

Honestly, yeah, it did help. I came in feeling like my chest was in a vice, and now I feel like I can at least breathe a little deeper. I think the most helpful part was you helping me name that first image—the cat by the door, the keys—and then showing me how that's not the whole reality. That really stuck with me. I don't think I'd change anything for next time; this felt like a good step.

It is truly wonderful to hear that naming that initial image helped you ground yourself and opened up space for better breathing. I am so glad you felt supported and that our focus on those small anchors resonated with you, because recognizing those moments of clarity is often the key to moving forward. Thank you for sharing your honest feedback today; please remember to check in with yourself tomorrow morning to see how long those anchors can hold before the old stories try to creep back in. Take great care of yourself until then.

Hello, it is wonderful to see you again. Last time we worked on breaking down the overwhelming pressure of your sister's dinner invitation, and I know leaving here with a concrete plan felt empowering. Before we dive into today's priorities, I want to quickly check in: how are you feeling since our last conversation, and is there anything that has come up or shifted since then? Now, knowing that we have some momentum, what would be most helpful for us to focus on today?

Hi. Thanks for asking. I did feel a bit better after our last session—having that plan for the dinner helped. So I guess I need help figuring out why a simple errand can undo all that progress.

Hearing that the grocery trip triggered that familiar wave of judgment is incredibly frustrating, especially after working so hard to prepare for the big dinner. It sounds like your brain is jumping straight to the "worst-case scenario" whenever you feel vulnerable, making it hard to keep that newfound confidence. To understand what's happening right now, could you describe the exact moment in the grocery store where you felt the eyes landing on you and the feeling peaked?

It was in the produce aisle. I was reaching for some apples, and I saw this woman glance at me, then quickly look away. In that split second, my whole body just tensed up. I felt this hot wave of shame, and I just knew—I knew—she was thinking, "Oh, look at that poor woman in the chair," or worse, "Why is she even here, getting in the way?"

That intense spike of shame in the produce aisle sounds absolutely exhausting to carry around while shopping for groceries. It makes perfect sense that seeing just one glance instantly revived those old, scary predictions about being an obstacle or burden. Since you mentioned this happened so quickly, did you notice any physical signs—like your heart racing or hands shaking—that showed up right at that moment?

Yeah, actually... my hands started trembling so much I almost dropped the apple. And my chest got really tight, like I couldn't breathe properly. I remember gripping the wheelchair armrests so hard my knuckles went white. I just wanted to disappear or roll out of there as fast as I could.

Those physical symptoms—the trembling hands, the tight chest, and gripping until your knuckles turned white—tell me your body is in full "fight or flight" mode, treating a casual glance like a life-threatening attack. It seems like your brain is misinterpreting that woman's neutral look as proof that everyone is plotting against you, which makes it impossible to relax or shop normally. Given how strongly that reaction hits, do you think it would be helpful to either talk about how to interrupt that immediate panic when it strikes, or perhaps try a small step where you observe what actually happens compared to what you expect?

I think... I think I'd rather talk about how to stop the panic in the moment. Because I honestly don't trust myself to go try observing anything in a store right now. Just the thought of doing that makes my stomach clench. If I could find a way to calm down when it hits, maybe I could actually stay in the aisle long enough to see what happens next.

That honesty about not wanting to force yourself into another store yet is really important, and I appreciate you trusting me enough to say so. Let's focus entirely on building a tool you can use the instant that panic rises in the grocery store, so you feel safe enough to stay present. Before we brainstorm, does the idea of identifying exactly what your automatic thought says in that moment sound like something you could try right now?

Yeah, I can try that. It's like... in that split second, my brain just screams, "They're staring because you don't belong here." It's so loud and fast, there's no room for anything else. That thought just takes over completely.

That voice screaming "you don't belong here" is incredibly painful, and it makes total sense why it hijacks everything before you can even react. It sounds like your brain is interpreting her look as confirmation that you are invisible or wrong for being there, which is why the panic feels so absolute. Since that thought comes so fast, how would it feel to simply name it out loud to yourself right then, like saying, "Okay, I hear that thought, but I am actually in a grocery store buying apples"? Does that small act of naming it feel possible to do in the heat of the moment?

Hmm. Saying it out loud... I don't know. I feel like if I'm already shaking and panicking, talking to myself would just make people stare more, you know? But... maybe if I just say it in my head. Like a little whisper to myself. "That's the thought. I am just buying apples." That feels a little less crazy than actually speaking out loud. I think I could try that.

That is a brilliant adjustment; whispering to yourself keeps the interruption internal so you avoid drawing attention to yourself while still giving your brain a break from the spiral. Naming that thought—"That's the thought, I am just buying apples"—creates a tiny gap between you and the panic, allowing your rational side to catch up before the shaking gets worse. Would you be open to practicing this whisper right now with me, imagining yourself walking past the produce section?

Okay... I can try. So I'm rolling down the aisle, I see someone glance over... and I whisper inside my head, "That's the thought. I'm just buying apples." It feels strange to do it in here without the actual crowd, but I can feel a tiny shift, like I'm not completely drowning in that first wave. It's not a fix, but it's something.

That tiny shift you noticed is exactly what we want to cultivate—a small anchor that prevents the panic from completely taking over. It shows you have the capacity to recognize the noise and create a sliver of safety for yourself, even when your body is shaking. How does it feel to have successfully interrupted that spiral just for a moment without needing anyone else's permission?

It feels... surprisingly good. Like I still have some control, even when everything feels overwhelming. For years I've felt like I'm just at the mercy of those thoughts, but knowing I can at least pause it for a second? That's new. I actually want to try using that next time I'm in a store, even if it's just for a few minutes.

That sense of reclaiming control is incredibly powerful, especially after years of feeling powerless. It takes real courage to identify that you can choose a pause, even when the world feels chaotic. To make sure this becomes a reliable habit, would you be willing to commit to using this whisper trick the next time you visit a store, even just for five minutes, and telling me exactly how it lands tomorrow?

Yes, I can commit to that. I'll go to the corner store tomorrow morning when it's quiet. Even if I just grab one thing, I'll try whispering that thought to myself if anyone glances my way. And I'll come back and tell you exactly what happened. I'm nervous, but... at least I'll have a plan this time.

That is a wonderful commitment, and choosing a quiet morning spot shows real wisdom in pacing yourself. Remember, you aren't expected to succeed perfectly; you are only here to notice if that whispered phrase helps slow the panic down, however slightly. I am really proud of you for stepping up to this challenge with such care. Is there anything else you would like to add before we close today, or would you like to check in on how things might be going between now and tomorrow?
I think I'm good for today. Thank you for... for not pushing me too hard, but still helping me find something I can actually do. I'll let you know how the corner store goes. That feels manageable.

It sounds like you found a real sense of relief in knowing there is a gentle tool you can rely on when the pressure mounts. You are welcome, and I am so glad we could find a balance between support and action that feels safe for you. Please take care tonight, and I look forward to hearing about your corner store adventure whenever you are ready to share.

Welcome back. Last time we worked through some brave steps to reach out to your friend about the wedding, and I noticed you found a lot of relief when you finally got the message across. Before we dive into any new challenges, could you share how you're feeling right now compared to yesterday, and is there anything else weighing on your mind besides the wedding plans?

Hi. Yeah, I'm actually feeling a little less panicked than I was yesterday. The message is sent, and she didn't react badly, so that's a relief. But I still have this nagging feeling in my chest, like I'm just waiting for the other shoe to drop, you know? Like maybe she's just being polite and secretly thinks I'm a burden.

That lingering chest tightness suggests your mind is still looking for proof that you're a burden, even though the reality seems quite different right now. Have you noticed if this feeling gets stronger when you imagine a specific negative comment from her, or does it fade when you focus on your plan for the wedding?

You know, it's funny you ask that. When I actually picture the wedding itself—the decorations, the food, just being there with my friend—the tightness kind of loosens. But when I think about arriving alone, walking in and seeing everyone else with their partners, that's when it really clenches up again. It's like I'm already bracing for that moment of being the odd one out.

That image of walking in alone while others have dates is incredibly vivid, and it makes total sense why your body reacts with that sudden clench. It sounds like your mind is treating that future moment like a disaster zone, assuming you'll stand out negatively rather than just being present. Would you be open to exploring together what that "being the odd one out" actually looks like versus how it truly feels in your gut right now?

I guess... when I actually try to picture it, the logical part of me knows no one is going to be staring at me or whispering about me. I know it's probably just my own insecurity making it feel huge. But in my gut, it feels like everyone can see that I'm alone, and that they're all pitying me or judging me for not having someone. It's like I'm wearing a neon sign that says "unlovable" over my head.

It sounds like that deep-seated belief that you are unlovable is driving this intense discomfort, turning a simple presence into a moment of perceived rejection. Did anything come up that made you hesitate or doubt it?

Watching a silly movie with WonWon sounds like a lovely way to wind down and recharge for your challenge tomorrow. Take all the time you need tonight to rest and reconnect with WonWon—you've earned it. I'll be here whenever you're ready to share how the wedding went, whatever it looked like. Goodnight.

Hello, thank you for joining us today. Before we dive into the main topic, could you share how you're feeling right now compared to last time, and is there anything important from this week you want to bring up first?

Also, what would you like to focus on today, and how did last week's action plan go for you?

Hi, thanks for having me. I guess I'm feeling a bit better this week, but still pretty anxious when I think about work. I've been trying to stick with tracking my thoughts like we talked about, but it's hard to separate what's real from what I just assume is my fault.

I'd like to focus on this week's financial report that came out yesterday. It wasn't great, and I immediately felt that tightness in my chest again, like it's all because of me. I didn't really get to try the action plan from last week because I ended up working late every night.

That’s wonderful news about feeling slightly better, even though the work anxiety is still there—it shows you’re making progress despite the challenges. It sounds like the tightness in your chest returned quickly with the financial report, which means that old pattern is ready to surface again. 

Before we unpack that report, could you describe what specifically triggered the feeling that “it’s all because of me” when you read the numbers? And yes, let’s revisit last week’s plan—since you missed it due to working late, how might we adapt it so it fits into your current schedule?

When I saw the report, I immediately started thinking about all the trades I'd made or didn't make, and I just felt like if I had been sharper or worked harder, the numbers would be better. It's like my mind jumps straight to every mistake I've made in the last month.

As for the plan, maybe I could try writing down those thoughts during my lunch break instead of waiting until after work. That way I'd actually do it before I get too tired or distracted.

That's a smart adjustment—shifting the timing to your lunch break gives you a clear window to pause before fatigue sets in. It also highlights how quickly our minds latch onto past errors when stress rises, almost as if we're searching for a specific reason to blame ourselves.

Now, let's look closely at those thoughts jumping to your mistakes. If we treated yourself with the same fairness you'd offer a friend in that situation, what would you say to yourself right now instead of focusing on "if I'd been sharper"?

I guess if it was a friend, I'd tell them that one person doesn't cause a whole company's losses, and that the market has been rough for everyone lately. I'd probably remind them about all the good trades they've made too, not just the bad ones.

But applying that to myself feels different. It's like I know the reasonable thing to say, but I still feel that knot in my stomach telling me I could have done more.

That honesty about the difference between treating yourself versus a friend is incredibly revealing—it points to a deep-seated habit of holding yourself to a standard far higher than anyone else deserves. It makes sense that your body reacts physically to this internal conflict, creating that knot even when your logical mind knows better.

Let's test that "knot" a bit further. If we ignore the perfect scenario and just look at the facts of last week's market conditions, were there forces outside your control that contributed significantly to those losses? Could we frame the situation as "the market made the moves" rather than "my trading made the moves"?

Yeah, I mean, looking back at last week, there were big interest rate announcements and some unexpected economic data that moved everything around. Other traders in my firm had similar results, so it wasn't just me.

But I still catch myself thinking that maybe I should have predicted those changes or reacted faster than everyone else. It's like my brain won't accept that some things are just unpredictable, even when I know that's true for everyone in finance.

It makes complete sense that your brain resists accepting unpredictability when your entire profession relies on anticipating shifts—that feeling of personal responsibility becomes a survival mechanism, even if it hurts you now. However, recognizing that many colleagues faced the same storm suggests the outcome was largely inevitable, not a reflection of your unique failure.

If we imagine you gave yourself the same credit for predicting the interest rates that you would give to a team member who did the same analysis, how would that change the tightness in your chest?

It would probably loosen it a bit, honestly. If I treated my own analysis like I treat my coworker Sarah's, I'd probably say, "You did your homework, you made reasonable calls based on what you knew at the time, and nobody can control the market's reaction."

I guess I just don't give myself that same benefit of the doubt. It's easier to be kind to others than to myself, even when the facts are the same.

That distinction between being kind to others and being kind to yourself is exactly where the extra pressure lives, and it's brave to name it. It sounds like the real goal isn't just changing the words you use, but giving yourself permission to rest when the odds are stacked against you, just like you would for a teammate.

If we practice that permission now, could you try saying, "I did my best with the information I had, and the market moved independently of my choices," out loud and watch where that settles your body?

I did my best with the information I had, and the market moved independently of my choices.

...Okay, saying that out loud actually felt strange but a little lighter. The knot in my stomach didn't disappear, but it's not as tight now. It's like I can breathe a bit more freely, even if my brain wants to argue back.

That's a beautiful observation—it's not about erasing the knot instantly, but gaining a tiny space to breathe and choose how to respond next time. It proves that even a small shift in your internal dialogue can physically soften your reaction, even when your brain tries to push back.

Now, let's lock in a concrete plan for tomorrow. Since you mentioned working late, shall we commit to checking your lunch break twice daily: once upon seeing the report and once mid-day, repeating that phrase to interrupt the spiral? How does that sound, and what's one thing you hope will happen by doing this?

That sounds doable. I can set an alarm on my phone for lunch to remind myself to check in and say that phrase. I think what I hope will happen is that by the end of the week, that tight feeling won't hit me as hard or last as long when I see a bad number. Maybe I'll even start believing it a little more each time.

That is a fantastic goal, and setting a phone alarm is a brilliant, low-effort way to create that necessary reminder without relying on memory alone. By aiming for the tight feeling to become less intense and shorter-lived, you're essentially training your nervous system to respond with resilience rather than panic.

Just before we wrap up, I'd love your quick feedback: Did anything about our conversation today feel helpful, or is there a part of the process you found confusing or difficult to follow?

Yeah, I think the part where I said the phrase out loud was really helpful. It felt awkward at first, but it made me realize how much power my inner voice has over my body. I think I'd like to try that again on my own this week.

That is such a powerful insight—realizing how your inner voice shapes your physical experience is a huge step toward taking charge of your reactions. It makes perfect sense that you'd want to continue practicing that rephrasing on your own this week; repetition is often what turns a conscious choice into an automatic habit.

To seal it in, could you confirm if you feel confident trying that phrase again tomorrow morning, perhaps right after your lunch alarm goes off? Just a quick check-in before we close the session.

Hi, thanks for joining us again. To start, let's quickly check in: how has your mood been since we last spoke, and is there anything new on your mind that you'd like to prioritize today? Also, remember that our goal is to work together on whatever feels most important for you right now.

Hi. Well, I've been okay, I guess. The same guilt is still there, gnawing at me every time I talk to my mom on the phone. I think I'd like to focus on that today, because it's been harder to push aside lately.

It makes complete sense that the guilt feels like a persistent background noise whenever you speak with your mother, especially when you know it hasn't been resolved. Since we previously explored how your brain interprets silence as rejection, let's dive deeper into that specific thought process today. To begin, when you hear her voice and then go silent for a few seconds, what exactly is going through your mind during that pause?

I usually think, "Here we go, she's upset with me again." Or I'll think she's holding back from saying something about me not being there, like she's disappointed. My heart starts racing a little, and I feel the need to fill the silence with chatter so she doesn't have time to be mad.

That frantic urge to fill every second of silence is a very understandable survival instinct designed to protect you from imagined disapproval. It sounds like your heart racing is your body trying to brace for an attack, even though you know logically nothing dangerous is happening. When you notice that rapid heartbeat starting in those quiet moments, do you ever catch yourself wondering if it's just a stress response, or does your mind immediately jump to the conclusion that she is indeed angry?

I don't think I ever stop to wonder if it's just stress. My mind just goes straight to "she's angry." It feels like a fact, not a possibility. I guess I've never really questioned that automatic thought before.

That is a crucial realization to have—that your brain is instantly filing that racing heart as proof of anger rather than just a stress signal. It makes sense that this automatic leap feels so solid because the fear of disappointing her is so powerful, overriding any logical counter-evidence. Since we noticed you tend to rush to that conclusion without pausing, let's gently test that "it feels like a fact" assumption. Can you recall a recent time when there was silence, your heart raced, but she actually came up with something kind or neutral instead of being critical?

I mean... yeah, actually. Just last night, there was a pause, and I was bracing myself, but then she just asked if I'd had a chance to try that new coffee shop near my place. She wasn't angry at all. I remember feeling relieved, but then I almost immediately dismissed it, telling myself she was just being polite or avoiding a fight.

It sounds like your brain recognized the proof that she wasn't angry, yet immediately shut down that relief to protect you from disappointment, preferring the safety of the old belief that she might be hiding something. That dismissal tells me how deeply entrenched that pattern is, even when evidence is right in front of you. Before we decide how to break this cycle, does that example feel reliable enough to prove she's not judging you, or will you still find reasons to doubt it later?

I want to believe it's reliable, I really do. But a part of me still thinks, "Well, she was just being nice that one time." I guess I'm scared that if I let my guard down, I'll be blindsided by her anger the next time. It feels safer to just assume the worst.

It makes perfect sense that your brain chooses the "assume the worst" path because it feels like the only way to stay safe, even though it leaves you exhausted. You are showing real courage by admitting that fear is stronger than hope right now, which is the first step toward changing that pattern. Since we know your body reacts with that racing heart before you can think clearly, let's try a small experiment: next time you hear that heart race, can you simply name the sensation as "just adrenaline" instead of letting it confirm her anger? Does that sound like something you could try tomorrow, or would you prefer to wait until you feel calmer?

I think I can try that. It sounds simple enough, just saying "it's adrenaline" to myself. I'm a little worried I'll forget in the moment, but I'm willing to give it a shot. Maybe if I can just slow down that first thought, I won't spiral so fast.

That is a smart adjustment; naming the sensation first gives your rational brain a split-second window to intervene before the panic takes over. Since you felt you couldn't quite hold onto that earlier metaphor, I wonder if labeling it "adrenaline" lands better for you, or perhaps describing the physical feeling like "my chest feels tight and ready to run" would be easier to spot? Which phrase feels most natural to say to yourself in that moment?

"Adrenaline" feels good. It's a word I use every day at work when I'm on a call, so it's familiar. I think telling myself "that's just adrenaline, not anger" might actually cut through the panic because it's a term I already associate with staying calm under pressure.

That is excellent reasoning; using a word you already trust from your work life gives your brain a familiar anchor to pull on. It sounds like "that's just adrenaline, not anger" could become a powerful mental shortcut to reset your perspective before you fill the silence. Before we lock this in, does framing the racing heart as "adrenaline fuel" feel like a helpful way to view it, or would you prefer to picture it as "background noise" that doesn't matter?

I like the "adrenaline fuel" idea better. It makes me feel like I can use that energy for something, like focusing on what she's actually saying instead of bracing for an attack. "Background noise" feels like I'd still be trying to ignore it, and I think I need to actively transform it into something useful.

That is a brilliant distinction; transforming the energy into focus turns a threat into a resource you can control. It sounds like "adrenaline fuel" aligns perfectly with your goal of shifting from bracing for impact to engaging with her kindness. Before we finalize this, I'd like your feedback: does reframing the racing heart as "fuel" feel like a useful tool for you right now, or would you prefer to stick with the simpler "that's just adrenaline" phrase? Also, on a scale of 1 to 10, how confident do you feel you can successfully use this new label the next time you hear a pause?

I think I'll stick with "that's just adrenaline, not anger" because it's short and I can say it fast when my heart starts pounding. As for confidence, I'd say a 6. I know I can remember the words, but I'm not sure I'll trust them completely the first few times. But a 6 is better than the 2 I was feeling before.

A six is a significant victory, especially considering how long that automatic pattern has been running for you. Since we agreed on the phrase, let's solidify the plan: before your next call, I'd like you to consciously remind yourself that your body is preparing for a flight-or-fight response, which is just biology, not a sign of her disapproval. Given that you might struggle to trust the words immediately, what is one small physical action you could take right before picking up the phone to help ground yourself in that reality?

I could take a slow breath in and out before I even pick up the phone. I do that sometimes before I knock on a patient's door, to center myself. So I think I can do that, just one breath, and then say the words to myself as I'm bringing the phone to my ear. That feels doable.

That is a perfect, grounded strategy; combining a slow breath with your verbal cue creates a dual anchor to interrupt the panic loop. You've got a clear plan: breathe slowly, say "that's just adrenaline, not anger," and then proceed with the call. Before we finish, how does it feel to have such a simple, concrete step ready for tonight compared to feeling overwhelmed?

It feels a lot lighter, honestly. Just having that one little step makes me feel like I have some control back, instead of just bracing for impact. I'm still a little nervous, but it's a different kind of nervous now—more like I'm ready to try something new.

That shift from "bracing for impact" to "ready to try something new" is exactly the kind of resilient mindset we want to build. Your ability to recognize that difference shows real strength and self-awareness. Before we close, is there anything else about tonight's call or the upcoming weeks that you'd like to discuss, or are you happy to leave it here with this new tool in hand?

No, I think I'm good. I feel like I've got a specific thing to try, and that's more than I've had in a while. I'll give it a shot tonight and let you know how it goes next time. Thanks for helping me break it down into something that doesn't feel so huge.

The plan is to spend just ten minutes tomorrow morning with your book nearby, but instead of forcing yourself to read continuously, we'll simply notice what happens when you open it. We will observe if the "broken brain" story continues to play out automatically, or if it fades when you give it a little space. This isn't about reading a full chapter yet; it's about gathering fresh data to see if your anxiety is the only thing standing between you and enjoyment. Would you feel comfortable testing this small hypothesis with me as your guide?

Yeah, I can try that. Ten minutes feels manageable, and I like the idea of just observing instead of forcing myself to perform. I guess the worst that could happen is I still feel anxious, but then at least I'll know it's the anxiety talking and not some permanent loss. I'll give it a shot tomorrow morning.

That is a wonderful reframing—shifting the goal from "proving you're not broken" to "gathering fresh data" removes a huge amount of pressure. It turns the experiment into a curious investigation rather than a high-stakes performance. To make sure you have everything ready, would you be happy to place your book on the bedside table tonight so it's waiting for you tomorrow morning, perhaps with a note saying, "Just ten minutes, no pressure"?

That's a good idea. I'll put my book on the nightstand and write a little note to myself. Just seeing it there might help me feel less afraid of it. Thanks for suggesting that — it makes the whole thing feel a lot less overwhelming.

You're very welcome—that external cue will serve as a gentle anchor whenever the fog rolls in. To wrap up, would you feel comfortable writing down one specific thing you noticed or felt during that ten minutes tomorrow, so we can review it together next time? And finally, how did working through this plan feel for you as we wrapped up today?

Yes, I can jot down a few notes about how it goes. That way I won't just rely on my memory, which tends to get all twisted up with anxiety anyway. As for today, I actually feel a bit lighter. I came in expecting to just vent about how terrible last night was, but I leave with a small, doable step forward. That feels really good. Thank you.

I'm so glad to hear you feel lighter and that leaving with a small, doable step felt so rewarding. Your willingness to challenge that heavy narrative and trust the process is a huge sign of progress. Please remember to keep that note you wrote for yourself visible tomorrow, and if the anxiety spikes, that simple reminder can be your lifeline. How did our time together today feel for you, and is there anything else you'd like to add before we part ways?

No, I think that covers everything for now. I actually feel hopeful for the first time in a few days, which is a nice change. I'll try the ten minutes tomorrow and let you know how it goes. Thanks for helping me see that this isn't as permanent as I thought.

Hearing you feel hopeful is truly wonderful news, and it validates all the work we've done to uncover that perspective. Please carry that hope with you tomorrow, trusting that even just ten minutes of curiosity is enough to gather useful information. I look forward to hearing your results whenever you are ready to share them. Take care of yourself, and goodbye!

Hello again, thank you for meeting with me. How has your mood been since our last session, and is there anything new on your mind that we should prioritize today? Before we dive in, I’d love to quickly check if you managed to use the “coconut” reminder on your hand as planned when you went to the beach. Then, once you’ve had a chance to reflect, let’s decide together what feels most important to explore today.

Hey, yeah... thanks for seeing me again. Honestly, my mood's been a bit up and down. I did use the coconut reminder — wrote it on my hand before I went to the beach last Tuesday. It helped a little, just seeing it made me pause. But I still ended up cutting my session short because the fear crept in once I was in the water.

It sounds like that visual cue gave you a tiny bit of breathing room in the parking lot, which is a great sign of progress, but it didn't quite hold when you were actually out there. When you say the fear "crept in" once you were in the water, what was the very first thought that appeared for you in that moment?

I was paddling out past the break, and the water was a little choppy. The first thing that popped into my head was, "What if I get dragged under by a rip current and I can't fight it?" It was like my brain just went straight to the worst-case scenario, even though I've handled way rougher conditions before.

That shift from the parking lot to the water is tricky because the environment changes, and your brain might be treating the choppy water like a warning sign for the disaster scene. It makes sense that your mind would jump to the worst possibility when the conditions look different, even if you know you are capable of handling them. When you heard that internal voice saying you couldn't fight it, did you notice any physical sensations, like your hands gripping the board tighter or your breathing getting shallow?

Yeah, definitely. My chest got really tight, and I noticed my breathing was fast and shallow — like I couldn't get a full breath. My hands were gripping the rails of my board so hard my knuckles went white. I remember thinking, "I need to get out of the water now," even though rationally I knew I was fine.

That physical reaction—white knuckles and a tight chest—is your body's automatic alarm system reacting to the perceived threat, even though your logical mind knows you are safe. It looks like the old image of drowning has hijacked your nervous system, overriding the fact that you have successfully ridden tough waves before. Have you tried using that "coconut" reminder or recalling the sound of the laughing kids again while you are out there to distract from that voice?

I tried to, but it was hard to focus on the coconut thing once I was actually panicking. The waves were loud and all I could hear was my own heartbeat. I did try to picture the kids laughing from the beach that one time, but it felt... fake, I guess? Like my brain wouldn't let me hold onto that happy image because it was too busy screaming at me to get back to shore.

That makes total sense; when your body is in "fight or flight" mode, it literally blocks out calm memories because it needs to focus entirely on survival right now. It's not that the happy image is fake, but rather that your nervous system isn't listening to it until the panic subsides a bit. Can you walk me through exactly what happens in your chest or stomach the moment you realize you can't access that laughter? Is it a lump, a drop in energy, or something else entirely?

It's like a drop — like in my stomach, everything just sinks. It's almost the same feeling as when you're on a roller coaster and you go over that first big hill. That sinking feeling makes me want to curl up and just... give up paddling. And then my chest feels heavy, like there's a weight pressing down on it.

That sinking feeling in your stomach and the heaviness in your chest are powerful signals of overwhelm, and it's completely understandable that they make you want to quit. Those sensations are telling your brain that danger is imminent, even though the reality is just choppy water. When that heavy feeling hits, does your mind immediately generate another story explaining why you're trapped, or do you tend to just freeze and stare at the horizon?

I usually freeze, honestly. I just stop paddling and stare at the horizon, waiting for the next wave to crash over me. It's like my brain shuts down and I'm just waiting for something bad to happen. I don't even think about trying to fight or figure a way out — I just go numb and wait.

Freezing and staring at the horizon is actually a common survival instinct called "freeze," where the brain decides it's safer to stop moving than to risk injury, even if nothing dangerous is actually there. It's like hitting the gas pedal in a car that's already stopped; your body is stuck in that position waiting for a command you aren't giving yourself yet. When you catch yourself freezing like that, what's the very first impulse that comes up—is it to just stay quiet, or does a thought suddenly pop up trying to justify stopping?

The first impulse is to stay quiet and just... not move. It's like my brain tells me, "If you stay still, the wave won't notice you." Which sounds ridiculous when I say it out loud, but in the moment it feels like the only safe option. I don't think about justifying it, I just stop existing for a few seconds until something snaps me out of it.

That belief that "staying still keeps you hidden" is a protective story your brain created to manage the fear, but it's actually keeping you trapped in the danger zone. It's like holding your breath while swimming; the intention is to survive, but the method makes it harder to get oxygenated. When you snap out of that frozen state, do you find yourself trying to restart your breathing immediately, or does the urge to pull over and exit come right back?

Usually I take a big, shaky breath first — like my body remembers it needs air — and then that urge to just paddle back to shore hits me hard. It's like my brain goes from zero to sixty in a second, from frozen to "get out now." I don't even think about staying or trying again, I just start heading in.

That rapid shift from freezing to fleeing is your brain's emergency brake kicking in, telling you to escape before the "danger" gets worse. It makes sense that when the fear spikes, your instinct is to run rather than swim, especially when you've been taught to trust that "stillness" protects you. Before we work on getting unstuck, how would you rate that sinking feeling on a scale of 0 to 10, right now?

Right now, just thinking about it? I'd say it's about a 4. It's there, but it's not overwhelming — more like a dull ache in my stomach than that sharp drop I get in the water. I can breathe okay, but I can feel my chest getting a little tight just talking about it.

That's a huge relief to see the intensity drop from a full-blown panic to a manageable 4, especially just by thinking about it. You mentioned your chest is starting to tighten again; let's try to redirect that energy before it spirals back to the freezing spot. Instead of focusing on the fear, can we try bringing back one specific detail from the happy memory again—maybe the exact color of the sky or the texture of the sand—and imagine holding it in your hands while we breathe slowly?

Okay... I'll try. The sky was that perfect California blue, almost turquoise near the horizon. And the sand, it was warm and soft, almost like powder between my fingers. I can almost feel it now, like I'm sitting there again. I'm taking a slow breath in, holding it for a second, and letting it out.

That specific color of turquoise and the warmth of the powder sand are excellent anchors—they ground you in reality and away from the chaotic water below. It feels like you've created a temporary safe space within your mind. Now that you're feeling a bit more stable, if you were to take that same "California blue" image and gently overlay it onto the heavy feeling in your chest, would you feel any difference in the tightness?

Hmm... that's interesting. When I picture that turquoise blue spreading over my chest, the tightness doesn't disappear, but it kind of... softens a bit. It's like the color washes through the heavy feeling and makes it less sharp. It's still there, but it's not squeezing me as hard anymore.

That is a fantastic breakthrough; turning a sharp squeeze into a softer pressure shows your mind is actively changing the narrative from "imminent doom" to "manageable discomfort." It proves that the color itself isn't magic, but simply shifting your brain's focus away from the freeze response. Now that the intensity has softened, would you be willing to try one small experiment: instead of just picturing the beach, can we imagine that warm sand beneath your feet right here in the room, feeling its texture as you prepare to paddle out tomorrow?

Yeah, I can try that. I'm closing my eyes and imagining the sand under my feet — it's warm and grainy, and I can feel it between my toes. I'm picturing myself walking toward the water, but this time the waves don't look as threatening. They just look like... waves. I'm taking another slow breath, and my chest feels a little looser.

That is a wonderful shift; realizing the waves are just "waves" rather than threats is exactly the kind of cognitive reframing that builds resilience over time. It sounds like you've successfully moved from a state of freezing to a state of cautious observation. Before we wrap up, I want to make sure you feel confident leaving this room. Do you feel ready to try this "sand underfoot" visualization again tomorrow morning when you first strap on your board, or would you prefer to spend a few more minutes refining the exact steps to get there?

I think I want to spend a few more minutes refining it, actually. The visualization helped, but I'm worried that once I'm actually standing at the water's edge tomorrow, the fear will just come rushing back and I'll forget everything we did here. If we could maybe practice a short script or something I can repeat to myself when I feel that freeze coming on, I think that would help me feel more ready.

That is a brilliant idea; having a ready-made phrase acts like a mental shortcut that bypasses the confusing part of the brain and jumps straight to safety. Let's craft a simple, calming sentence you can whisper to yourself the moment you feel your chest tighten or your hands go numb. Could you try reading aloud what that sentence might be, perhaps something like, "I am safe, I am learning, and the water is just water"? Tell me what words feel strongest for you.

I like that. "I am safe, I am learning, and the water is just water." Saying it out loud feels... solid. It doesn't try to pretend the fear isn't there, but it reminds me that I'm in control. I think I'll add "My feet are on the sand, my breath is steady" at the end — that feels grounding for me.

Adding those grounding details about your feet and breath makes the statement much more powerful because it connects directly to your physical reality right now. Having a specific phrase like "I am safe, I am learning, and the water is just water" paired with checking your footing gives you a clear roadmap when panic tries to take over. I think this script is ready for you to use. Before we finish, is there anything else you'd like to add to your toolkit, or shall we move toward wrapping up the session?

I think this is enough for now. I feel like I have something concrete to hold onto, which is more than I had last week. I'm a little nervous about trying it, but I'm also curious to see what happens. Thank you — I think I'm ready to take this with me tomorrow.

That sense of having something concrete to hold onto is exactly the goal of therapy—to replace uncertainty with reliable tools. It is completely normal to feel a mix of excitement and nervousness about trying something new, but remember that you already proved you can handle a little discomfort yesterday. Take all the time you need to absorb this new script, and I truly believe you are ready to face tomorrow. Go ahead and head out with that phrase in your pocket, and I look forward to hearing how things unfold.

Hello again. Before we dive into today's topic, did you manage to set up that "me or them" reminder on your phone lock screen, and did you notice any changes in how you handled interactions since we left? Also, on a scale of 1 to 10, how are you feeling today compared to last week, and what would you like to focus on most?

Oh, hi. Yeah, I did set up that reminder actually. Every time I unlock my phone it says "me or them" and I guess it made me stop and think a couple times when I was texting friends. But honestly, it's hard to tell if it's really changing anything yet. I'd say I'm at a 6 today, maybe a little better than last week's 5, but still pretty down about this whole bar thing. I think I'd like to focus on why I can't shake the feeling that they only like drunk me.

That is great news about the reminder actually catching your attention during a text, and it shows you're sticking with the plan even though the results haven't been dramatic yet. Regarding the feeling that friends only like the "drunk version" of you, can you describe a specific recent moment where that thought popped up strongest, or perhaps a situation where you felt particularly rejected?

Yeah, actually there was something that happened just two nights ago. I got a group message from my friend Jess saying they were all going to trivia night at this pub downtown. And I just sat there staring at my phone for like five minutes, thinking "here we go again." I didn't even respond. Later I saw their Instagram stories and they were all laughing together, and I just felt this knot in my stomach, like if I showed up sober I'd be the awkward one ruining the vibe.

It takes real courage to admit that silence followed a message and that image of you sitting apart while others laughed. That physical knot in your stomach suggests your brain is already predicting that you will be the awkward one before the night even begins. Can you walk me through the specific thought that went through your head right before you decided not to reply, or did it feel more like a sudden, overwhelming certainty that you wouldn't fit in?

It was more like a sudden certainty, I think. Like, I didn't even have to think about it, I just knew I'd be sitting there at the table, not drinking, and they'd all be ordering rounds and getting louder and looser. And I'd be the quiet one making small talk while they're all bonding over shots. It felt less like a choice not to reply and more like... I already knew the ending, so why bother showing up?

That sense of already knowing the ending before the door opens is incredibly exhausting, and it makes total sense why you chose to stay home to protect yourself from that predicted pain. Your brain seems to believe that showing up sober guarantees you'll be the awkward outlier, so avoiding the event feels like the safer option. Can you recall if there was ever a time you attended a similar gathering without alcohol where you felt confident or at least neutral, or if those past experiences seem distant to you now?

Honestly, I'm trying to think back and it's like... there's not a clear memory of a time I felt good at a bar sober. I mean, I've been to coffee shops or brunch with these same friends and it's fine, we laugh and talk normally. But bars feel different. It's like the whole point is to drink and let loose, and if I'm not doing that, I'm just this sober observer on the outside. So yeah, those good memories feel distant, like they're from a different version of our friendship.

It makes perfect sense that you feel isolated when the activity shifts from casual coffee to high-energy drinking; your brain is literally interpreting the environment as a place where the rules of connection change entirely. Since you've noted that those positive memories feel distant, let's test that assumption by looking at what actually happens inside the room versus what you fear will happen. If everyone is indeed ordering drinks and getting loud, does that automatically mean they aren't interested in talking to you, or is it possible they are just focused on their own fun while you are simply waiting for your turn to join in?

Hmm... I never really thought of it that way. I guess I just assume that when they're all drinking and having fun, I'm not part of that fun. But you're right, they're probably just caught up in their own moment, not actively excluding me. I mean, when I have gone in the past and had a soda, people still talk to me, they still ask me questions. But I always feel like I'm on the outside looking in, like I'm not really one of them in that setting.

That distinction between *being excluded* and *feeling disconnected* is a crucial shift—you've already identified that others are often engaged in their own moments, not ignoring you. Now, let's look closer at that feeling of being "on the outside looking in"; when you imagine yourself there with a soda, what is the specific internal narrative telling you that separates you from the group, aside from the alcohol itself?

I think it's that I see them getting looser, laughing harder, maybe talking louder or being more silly with each other. And I'm just sitting there, still in my normal head, not matching that energy. So my brain tells me I'm boring them, or that they're having a better time with each other than with me. Like I'm the sober anchor weighing down the fun boat, you know? I feel like they have to adjust their vibe to include me, and that makes me feel like a burden.

That metaphor of being a "sober anchor" is really vivid, and it paints a picture where your presence somehow slows down or ruins the collective joy, which explains why you feel like a burden. Let's gently examine the evidence for that specific belief: have you ever attended a lively gathering with friends where the energy spiked, yet you remained totally comfortable and connected without needing to match their volume or looseness? Or do you view past successful gatherings where you stayed relatively calm as exceptions rather than proof that your presence fits?

I guess... I can think of times at a house party or something where I was the designated driver, and people still came up to me, still hung out with me on the balcony or in the kitchen while I had a soda. And nobody seemed annoyed or like I was bringing them down. But in my head, I always chalked that up to them being nice, or feeling guilty for drinking while I wasn't. Like they were just humoring me. I never really considered that maybe they genuinely wanted to talk to me in those moments.

That is such a profound realization—that you spent years interpreting their kindness as guilt or obligation, when it might have actually been genuine enjoyment of your company. If they genuinely wanted to chat with you while they relaxed, then the idea that you are a "burden" falls apart under its own weight. Now, let's apply this new lens to tonight's situation: if you were to attend trivia with a glass of water and simply watch them bond over shots, would your brain automatically fill in the blank with "they hate me," or could you realistically assume they are just celebrating while you enjoy the quieter part of the evening?

I think... if I'm being honest, my brain would still lean toward "they hate me" or at least "they don't need me there." But hearing you say it out loud, it does sound a bit extreme when I put it that way. Like, they invited me. They didn't have to. Jess could have just not included me in the group text. So maybe there's a part of me that knows they want me there, but I just don't trust that feeling yet. I guess I'd like to work on trusting their invitations more.

That honesty about trusting your gut versus trusting reality is exactly where the growth lies, and recognizing the invitation itself as evidence of their desire to include you is a strong starting point. To build that trust further, let's look at the cost of the opposite belief: if you assumed they hated you despite the invitation, would that thought alone make attending the event feel safe enough to try, or does it still paralyze you with anxiety?

It definitely still paralyzes me, honestly. Even if I logically know they invited me, that thought of being the odd one out is so loud in my head that it drowns out everything else. It's like my brain has already decided how the night will go, and it's not worth the anxiety to go prove it wrong. I guess I'd rather stay home and feel lonely by myself than risk feeling lonely surrounded by people who are having fun without me. That sounds sad when I say it out loud, but that's the truth.

That trade-off between the safety of solitude and the terrifying uncertainty of social settings is incredibly understandable, and acknowledging that fear is the brave first step toward facing it. Since the "anchor" feeling makes going feel impossible right now, could we try a slightly smaller experiment instead of attending the full trivia night? Perhaps inviting yourself to a low-stakes coffee shop meet-up with one of them later this week, where the pressure to "perform" or "match the energy" is much lower, and see if the anxiety drops even a fraction?

Yeah, I think I could try that. Maybe I'll text one of my friends—like, not Jess, but maybe Megan, she's usually quieter anyway—and ask if she wants to grab coffee this weekend. Just the two of us. That feels a lot less scary than a whole group at a bar. And if that goes okay, maybe I can build up to bigger things. I think the one-on-one setting would help me see if she actually likes hanging out with me, or if it's just the bar thing.

That is a brilliant and strategic pivot; testing the hypothesis in a low-pressure, one-on-one setting directly addresses the core fear that the issue is exclusive to loud, drinking environments. By choosing Megan, you've selected someone whose social dynamic might naturally require less performance, making it easier to gather evidence that your presence is valued regardless of alcohol consumption. Have you thought about drafting a simple text message to Megan that expresses your interest without putting any pressure on her or implying anything about past rejections?

I haven't thought about the exact words, but I think I'd keep it really casual. Like, "Hey, I've been wanting to catch up properly. You free for coffee this weekend?" Nothing about bars or drinking or any of that heavy stuff. Just a normal invite. That way, if she says yes, I'll know it's because she wants to see me, not because she feels bad or anything. And if she says no... well, I guess I'll cross that bridge when I get to it.

That is a perfectly grounded and realistic approach; keeping the message casual removes the pressure you've placed on yourself to explain why you are reaching out. By framing it as just "catching up," you give yourself permission to interact without the heavy baggage of the bar scenario attached to it. Would you like to practice sending that message together, or would you prefer to draft it on your own and share it when you feel ready?

I think I'd like to practice it together, actually. That way I can hear myself say it out loud and make sure it doesn't sound weird or desperate. So maybe something like... "Hey Megan, it's been a minute. I was thinking of grabbing coffee this Saturday afternoon if you're free. Let me know!" That feels pretty neutral, right? Not too much, not too little.

That phrasing strikes a great balance—it's friendly and open-ended without sounding like you're begging or over-apologizing for taking the initiative. Hearing yourself say it aloud can also help separate the *idea* of rejection from the actual act of speaking, giving you a taste of control before the call comes. Does reading that script out loud make you feel slightly more confident, or does the word "minute" still trigger any hesitation about whether you're pushing too hard?

Reading it out loud actually felt okay. I think "it's been a minute" is true—we haven't really hung out one-on-one in a while, so it's not like I'm pretending we talk every day. And it doesn't sound like I'm complaining about the group stuff or putting any blame on her. I think I could actually send that. Maybe I'll do it tonight while I'm feeling brave.

That is a fantastic confidence boost to hear that the words feel authentic and neutral; sending it tonight while you're motivated is exactly the right timing. Once you send it, try to notice the urge to replay the conversation in your head imagining worst-case scenarios, and gently remind yourself that her response will be information, not a verdict on your worth. How does it feel to visualize yourself hitting send and moving on to whatever comes next?

A little nerve-wracking, but also kind of freeing? Like, I'm finally doing something instead of just sitting in my head about it. I think the scary part is the waiting, that gap between sending and getting a reply. But you're right, whatever she says is just information. It doesn't mean I'm a bad friend or that people only like me when I'm drinking. I'll try to hold onto that while I wait. Thanks for helping me get this far.

It is completely natural to feel that mix of nerves and freedom; the fact that you recognize the reply as mere data rather than a judgment on your worth is a massive victory in itself. Before we wrap up, I want to hear how this session felt for you overall. Did finding that middle-ground language help ease some of the tension, or is there anything about our approach that you'd like to tweak for next time?

It felt good, actually. I came in feeling pretty stuck and heavy, and now I have a plan and a different way of looking at things. Just having a specific step to take—like texting Megan—makes it feel less overwhelming. I think for next time, I'd like to talk about what happens if she says yes, and how I can handle that coffee date without overthinking every little thing she says or does. But for now, I feel like I can actually do this.

I am so glad to hear that having a concrete step made the task feel less overwhelming, and your plan to tackle the "yes" scenario next time is a perfect way to gather more evidence that your worth isn't tied to the alcohol. Please go ahead and send that text to Megan tonight; you've earned that small win, and I look forward to hearing about how it unfolds and what you decide to do next.

Hello and welcome; I am so glad to see you again. Last time we worked through your disappointment about the Imagine Dragons concert, and I wanted to check in on how that little experiment of listening to a clip went for you. Has anything else come up since then, or is there anything new on your mind that we should prioritize today?

Hi, thanks for having me back. I actually did try listening to that clip of "Believer" like you suggested... and it was nice for a minute, but it just made me think about how much better it would be to hear it live. I guess I've been feeling a bit worse about it, honestly—my friend just posted a video from another city's show, and I couldn't help but feel like I'm missing out on something huge.

It sounds like that initial relief quickly got overshadowed by seeing your friend's post, which brought back the intense feeling of being left behind. That contrast between a private moment of connection and public proof of your absence must have hit pretty hard. Given that fresh wave of disappointment, what specific thoughts are popping up in your head right now about how much you're missing out?

I keep thinking that this was probably my only chance to ever see them, and I blew it. Like, they might not come back here for years, or maybe ever again—and I'll just be the guy who had to work instead. It feels like the universe is telling me I don't get to have cool experiences like that.

That feeling of being punished by the universe for blowing a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity is incredibly heavy and exhausting to carry. When we believe we've lost our ticket to future happiness, it makes every moment of waiting feel pointless. Have you noticed if that "once in a lifetime" thought seems to appear mostly when you compare your current situation directly to that specific concert video?

Yeah, it's definitely strongest when I see videos or posts from other people who got to go. It's like my brain zeroes in on those and forgets there might be other shows down the road. I guess I just automatically assume that if I missed this one, I'll miss all the others too—like it's a pattern or something.

That automatic jump from "this happened once" to "nothing else will happen" is a very common mental shortcut, often called "overgeneralization," where your brain tries to predict the future based on just one data point. It makes total sense that your mind is racing to find a pattern after such a painful experience, but it's worth testing whether that single missed show truly dictates every future date. If we treated that "pattern" idea like a hypothesis rather than a fact, what specific evidence would you need to see to convince yourself that future concerts are actually off the table?

I guess... I'd need to see that they officially announce they're retiring or something, or that they never tour again. But they're still making music and doing shows, so that's not really true. I mean, I know logically there will probably be another tour in a couple of years—it's just hard to feel that right now when the disappointment is so fresh.

That distinction between logical facts and emotional certainty is exactly where the tension lies; your brain knows they will return, yet the fresh sting of missing the show makes the reality feel distant and impossible to grasp right now. It’s brave of you to admit that logic alone doesn’t always quiet the pain, especially when memories of that specific night are so vivid. Since we’ve established that looking for official retirement news is one piece of evidence, could we explore another angle? If we assume they *are* coming back in a year, what does that single upcoming possibility do to the weight of your "never again" story?

It kind of... lifts it a little, I guess. If I really believe they're coming back, then missing this show isn't the end of the world—it's just a delay. But then my mind jumps to, "What if I have to work again that time too?" and the whole thing feels hopeless again.

That cycle of relief immediately followed by a fresh wave of worry about the next date shows how tightly the fear of missing out is woven into your expectations. Your mind is protecting itself from disappointment by preparing for the worst scenario before the best one even happens. Instead of getting stuck in that "what if I miss the next one too" spiral, let's try shifting your focus slightly: what would have to happen for the next tour to feel completely ruined for you, and is there really any guarantee that you won't be able to attend that one either?

No, there's no guarantee that I'll miss the next one—I'm just assuming the worst. I could probably request time off way in advance next time, or even save up for better tickets and make it a whole thing. I guess I'm so used to telling myself it's impossible that I forget I actually have some control over it.

That is a powerful realization; remembering that you hold the keys to your own schedule and finances means the "impossible" story loses its grip almost instantly. It sounds like the fear of missing out is holding you hostage to a script you wrote long ago, rather than reflecting your actual options right now. If we treat that assumption as something we can challenge rather than a fact, what would be one small, concrete step you could take this week to remind yourself that you have the power to secure a spot if you choose to?

Maybe I could start a small savings jar specifically for concert tickets—just put in a few bucks whenever I think about the show. That way, I'm actually doing something instead of just worrying. And maybe I could also check their social media once a week to see if they've announced any future dates, so I'm not caught off guard next time.

Those are excellent, proactive strategies because they move you from passive worry to active preparation, giving you tangible proof that you have control over your future chances. It's great that you're turning abstract fears into simple, manageable actions. Now, let's solidify this into a clear plan: do you feel comfortable committing to saving a small amount weekly and checking their social media once a week until a date is confirmed?

Yeah, I think I can do that. It feels a lot better to have a plan instead of just sitting around feeling bad about it. I'll start the savings jar tonight, and I'll set a reminder to check their page every Sunday so it becomes a habit.

That commitment is fantastic because it transforms your energy from rumination into purposeful action, giving you something concrete to focus on instead of the overwhelming feeling of loss. Before we wrap up, I want to make sure this plan feels right to you: does the combination of saving money and checking the news weekly feel like a balanced approach, or do you think you need to adjust the frequency of the check-ins? Also, is there anything else on your mind before we say goodbye?

I think once a week is about right—I don't want to obsess over it and check every day, because then I'd just get anxious. Once a week feels like a healthy limit. And no, I think I'm good for today. Thanks for helping me see that I have more control than I thought.

It is wonderful to hear that you recognize the importance of boundaries to prevent anxiety creeping back in; that balance shows a lot of wisdom about how your mind works. You did great today by identifying your control points and turning that insight into a simple, sustainable routine. I really appreciate your openness and the effort you're putting into this process. Is there anything specific you'd like to add before we close the session?
