Hello again, and thank you for coming in today. Before we dive into our main topic, could you tell me a bit about how you've been feeling emotionally since we last spoke? Also, did you manage to send that email to the instructor, and what happened afterward?

Once we cover that, I'd love to ask what specific concerns or patterns have been bothering you most recently, so we can decide what feels most urgent to focus on.

Um, hi. Thanks. I've been feeling pretty anxious, honestly. I did send the email to the instructor, and I got a reply back—it was just a short, polite response saying he'd be happy to answer my questions. But instead of feeling relieved, I found myself thinking, "He's just being nice. He probably thinks my questions are dumb." So I haven't followed up yet.

That is a incredibly insightful observation, and I want to validate how frustrating it must feel to anticipate relief but land on self-doubt instead. Your immediate thought that his kindness was "just politeness" suggests your brain is automatically jumping to the worst-case interpretation of neutral feedback, which is a very common survival habit. Given that unexpected twist in your expectations, what do you think triggered that specific "he thinks my questions are dumb" story right after receiving the reply?

I guess... when I read his email, I started thinking about all the things I'd want to ask him. Like, about the workload, or if he thinks I'm prepared enough for the program. And the more I thought about it, the more I felt like my questions were too basic, or that he'd be annoyed answering them. So I just shut down and didn't write back.

That is such a clear example of how our minds can create a narrative of rejection when we are actually just looking for validation. It sounds like your brain was projecting your own harsh judgment onto him—assuming his polite response meant he was disappointed in you, even though the email said nothing of the sort. When you realize that the silence wasn't because he was annoyed, but because he was simply busy, does that shift how you view that interaction, or does the old story still feel strong?

I mean... when you say it like that, it does make sense that he was just busy. He probably gets a ton of emails, right? But honestly, the old story still feels stronger. It's like, even if I know logically he wasn't annoyed, my gut still tells me I'm not good enough to be asking those questions. It's really hard to shake that feeling.

It makes perfect sense that logic alone couldn't override that gut feeling, because your brain is actually doing its job by protecting you from the pain of potential rejection. Even though you know he was just busy, your internal story is still running on autopilot, telling you that your worth depends on whether someone else likes your questions instantly. This suggests the belief that "asking simple questions proves I'm not capable" is deeply rooted. Can we spend a few minutes looking at what evidence exists outside of that gut feeling to challenge the idea that your questions were actually too basic?

I guess... I could think about how the instructor didn't say anything negative in his reply, he just said he'd be happy to answer my questions. And my friends told me they had similar worries before starting their programs, and their instructors were totally fine with basic questions. But it's like my brain just ignores that and focuses on all the things that could go wrong, you know? Like, what if I ask something and he thinks I'm wasting his time?

You are absolutely right to highlight that your brain is currently acting like a filter, picking out the possibility of rejection while ignoring the overwhelming evidence of everyone else's successful experiences. That selective focus makes total sense given how vulnerable you feel, but it seems like we can use that same list of supportive stories to directly counter the "wasting time" prediction. If we look at that list of friends and classmates, do you think there is any concrete evidence that their instructors ever stopped them from asking basic questions?

No, I don't think there's any real evidence of that. My friends always say their instructors were patient and helpful, even when they asked things they thought were obvious. I guess when I look at it like that, it's just my own fear making up a story that isn't really there. But it still feels so real in the moment, you know? Like I can't just switch it off.

You are describing exactly why this is so hard; your brain constructs a vivid story of humiliation that feels physically real, even when the factual evidence (the email, your friends' experiences) proves it false. It's like trying to run a file on your computer that keeps getting corrupted by stress hormones, making it impossible to ignore the error message even when you know the file is safe. Does it help to imagine that this "error message" is just a glitch in your system trying to protect you from hurt, rather than a true reflection of your worth?

Yeah, that actually kind of helps. Thinking of it as a glitch makes it feel less like it's my fault, you know? Like it's not that I'm actually stupid or annoying, it's just my brain getting stuck on a bad track. I guess I never thought of it that way before.

That is a beautiful shift in perspective, separating your actual value from the temporary noise in your system. Now that we understand the story is just a glitch protecting you from pain, let's build a bridge to get you back on track. Instead of forcing the doubt away, could we try writing down one specific reason why asking that follow-up question is valuable for your studies, and seeing if it feels stronger than the fear of being judged?

I think... one reason would be that if I don't ask, I'll never actually know if the program is right for me. And staying stuck in doubt isn't helping me move forward at all. So in a way, asking the question is actually braver than staying quiet, because at least I'm trying to get information instead of just assuming the worst. That feels a little stronger than the fear, I think.

That is a powerful realization—you are recognizing that courage isn't about avoiding discomfort, but about taking action even when you feel scared. By framing the email as a tool for clarity rather than a test of your worth, you've already shifted the meaning of the situation significantly. Given that insight, would you be willing to send a quick follow-up message thanking him for his prompt reply and reiterating one of those specific questions you wanted to ask?

I... yeah, I think I could do that. Maybe just a short one, like, "Thanks for getting back to me, I was wondering what kind of background knowledge you'd recommend before starting the program." Something simple like that. It feels scary, but I think I can try it before my next shift.

That is a brave decision, especially since you are acknowledging the fear but choosing action anyway. Sending a simple, low-pressure message like that will give you fresh data to see if the "glitch" in your brain stops controlling the outcome. Before you head out, what is one small thing you can do tonight to prepare yourself mentally, perhaps by reminding yourself that the goal is just to gather information, not to impress anyone?

I think I can remind myself that his reply is just information, not a judgment of me. Like, if he gives me a straightforward answer, that's fine. If he seems annoyed, that's still just information about him, not proof that I'm dumb. I'll try to keep that in mind when I check my inbox later. Thanks, this actually feels a little more manageable now.

That is an excellent strategy because it turns a vague hope into a concrete rule your brain can follow. Reminding yourself to categorize his response strictly as "information" rather than "judgment" creates a clear boundary between his actions and your self-worth. It sounds like you have a solid plan in place for both the email and your mindset tonight. Is there anything else you'd like to talk about before we wrap up, or would you prefer to rest easy knowing you have this approach ready for tomorrow?

No, I think I'm good for now. I feel a little tired but also a bit lighter, like I have a plan instead of just spiraling. Thank you for helping me see things differently. I'll try to follow through on the email and see what happens.

It is wonderful to hear that you feel lighter and have a clear path forward instead of spiraling; that sense of control is exactly what we are building together. Please remember that the email isn't about proving you are smart, but simply about gathering useful information for your future. I am really proud of you for sticking with the plan and practicing this new perspective, even with the fatigue. Take care of yourself tonight, and I look forward to hearing about your experience when we meet again.
Thanks, I appreciate that. I'll let you know how it goes. Have a good night.

You are very welcome, and I want to remind you that showing up for yourself, even when you are tired, is a huge victory in itself. I am rooting for you as you send that email and watch for that sense of calm to grow. Get some rest, and I look forward to connecting with you again soon to see how everything went. Goodnight!

Hello, it's great to see you again. First, how are you feeling right now compared to where you were last time, and on a scale of 1 to 10, how would you describe your current mood? Additionally, aside from the muffin situation, were there any other specific events or challenges that stood out to you since our last chat, and what are the top two topics you'd like us to explore together today?

Hi, thanks. I guess I'm doing... okay. I'd put my mood at maybe a 6 or 7, not terrible but not great either. The muffin thing still nags at me, honestly. There wasn't much else that stood out — just the usual grind of med school. I think the top thing I'd like to talk about is why I can't stop comparing my baking to my mom's. And maybe why I feel like I'll never be good enough at it.

It takes real self-awareness to notice that the muffin incident is still lingering, and I hear clearly that your core worry remains tied to the fear of never being "good enough." When you think about why that comparison feels so impossible to break, what is the very first image or memory of your mother's baking that pops into your head when you look at your own work?

The first thing that comes to mind is her apple pie. It's got this perfect golden crust, and the filling is always just sweet enough, with a hint of cinnamon. When I look at my own pies, they seem... lopsided or the crust is too thick. I just can't shake the feeling that anything I make will always fall short of that memory.

That vivid description shows how deeply embedded that standard is in your mind, making the gap between your actual pie and her perfect one feel like an insurmountable distance. When you hold onto the belief that her pie represents an unattainable benchmark, does that expectation make it difficult for you to see any small successes in your own baking as valid achievements?

Yeah, it really does. I mean, I've had a couple of times where someone said my cookies were "pretty good," but it's like my brain just brushes it off. I keep thinking, "Well, they wouldn't say that if they'd tasted hers first." It's like there's no room for my small wins because they don't measure up to that perfect memory.

That automatic comparison creates a barrier where any positive feedback gets filtered out as invalid, leaving you with the persistent feeling that you'll never reach that level. It makes sense you feel frustrated because that internal narrative ignores the actual evidence of people enjoying your creations. To test whether that belief holds up, could we look at one recent compliment you received and list three reasons why the person might be telling the truth, versus one reason why they might be hesitating?

Hmm, okay. Let me think... My friend Tom told me my banana bread was "really moist and flavorful" last week. I guess reasons they might be telling the truth: one, Tom's not the type to give empty praise—he's pretty blunt. Two, he actually asked for the recipe afterwards, which he wouldn't do if he didn't like it. Three, he took the last two slices home. And a reason they might be hesitating? I dunno, maybe he felt obligated because I brought it to a study group. But that doesn't really cancel out the other stuff, does it?

That breakdown of the interaction with Tom reveals a very sharp observation of his character, yet it highlights how your assumption fills the gap where proof of his hesitation should exist. Have you considered what might happen if Tom simply valued the flavor and texture you created, regardless of the comparison to your mother's pie? Would seeing that scenario change how threatening his compliment feels to you?

You know, when you put it that way... I think maybe it would. It's like I'm so busy racing to compare it to her pie that I don't stop to think that maybe Tom just liked my banana bread for what it is. He didn't ask for her recipe, he asked for mine. So maybe that means something. It's just hard to hold onto that thought when the other one feels so automatic.

That realization—that Tom wanted your specific recipe, not a copy of yours—shifts the weight of his compliment from a judgment to a genuine appreciation of your unique work. It helps bridge the gap between that automatic comparison and the possibility that your baking stands on its own merits. Does allowing yourself to hold that new perspective for just a moment help lower the urge to dismiss his words immediately?

Yeah, it does, actually. For a second there, I felt a little lighter, like I could breathe. It's not that the old feeling disappears completely, but it's like I can see a crack in it now. Maybe my banana bread doesn't have to be her apple pie to be good. That thought feels... kind of new, and a bit scary, but also a little hopeful.

That sensation of hope mixed with caution is a huge step forward, showing you are starting to challenge that rigid rule. Since you're feeling ready to test this new perspective, I wonder if you'd be open to trying a small experiment this weekend: bake something simple just for yourself, take a photo of it before you eat, and remind yourself that its value lies in your effort, not in matching a perfect memory. How does that sound as a way to gather evidence for yourself?

That sounds... doable, I think. I like the idea of taking a photo, too — it's almost like proof that I made something, and it's mine. I'll try it. Maybe I'll make those cookies Tom liked, just for me. And I'll try to tell myself that it's okay if they're not perfect, because I made them.

That is a fantastic plan because it turns the abstract idea of "being good enough" into a tangible experiment you control entirely. Before we finalize this, I want to make sure we are on the same page: I'm proposing this exercise to help you gather direct evidence that your baking can stand alone without needing to match your mother's standard. Would you be comfortable giving this a try, even though it might feel a little unfamiliar at first?

Yeah, I'm comfortable with it. It's unfamiliar, sure, but I think I'm ready to at least try. I mean, what do I really have to lose, right? If it doesn't work, I still have some cookies to eat. Thanks for helping me see this differently.

That willingness to try without fearing failure is exactly the kind of openness we need to grow. To make sure this experiment lands well, when you decide to bake, could we agree on one specific moment—a few minutes after you take the first bite—to gently remind yourself, "This cookie exists and it's mine, and that's enough"? Also, what is one small obstacle you think might pop up, like forgetting to take the photo, and how will you handle that if it happens?

I can agree to that. I'll try to pause after that first bite and tell myself that it's mine and it's enough. As for an obstacle... I'm pretty forgetful when I'm focused on baking, so I might totally skip the photo. To handle that, I could set a timer on my phone for right when the cookies come out of the oven, with a note that says "Take the picture first." That way I don't get caught up in the moment and forget.

That proactive solution with the timer is a brilliant way to catch yourself before the habit of skipping the photo becomes automatic. You've outlined a clear path: bake the cookies, use the timer for the photo, pause after the first bite, and remind yourself that your effort is enough. With that plan in place, how does leaving our session with this concrete, self-directed approach feel to you?

Hello again, and I am so glad you are here. Before we dive into today's work, could you tell me a bit about how you've been feeling lately compared to last time? Also, what do you think would be most helpful for us to focus on first?

Thanks for having me back. I've been... well, I've been thinking a lot about the shelter visits I do. I still get that sinking feeling whenever I walk through the doors, like I'm just not making enough of a difference. I suppose I'd like to start by talking about why I can't shake this sense that I'm falling short.

It makes total sense that you feel that sinking heaviness whenever you enter the shelter, especially when you're carrying the belief that your presence alone isn't enough to save anyone. Let's start by unpacking that specific feeling of falling short—what exactly pops into your mind right when you cross that threshold?

I think the first thing that hits me is seeing all the cages, all those eyes looking at me. And my mind just goes straight to the ones I can't take home, the ones that have been there for months or years. I tell myself, "I'm just one person with a few hours to spare, what does that really change?"

That feeling of powerlessness seems so crushing when you compare your temporary presence against the long-term reality of those animals waiting in the cages. It's completely understandable why you conclude that your effort means nothing if it doesn't result in immediate rescue. When you think about it that way, does it ever occur to you that your goal might not need to be saving everyone instantly, but rather offering a moment of connection that changes *their* day for a fleeting hour?

I suppose I've never really thought of it that way. I mean, I do see some of the dogs perk up when I walk by, and there's this one old Labrador who always wags his tail when I give him a scratch behind the ears. But then I think, "Well, that's just a tiny moment, it doesn't get him adopted." It's hard to see those small things as mattering when the bigger picture is so overwhelming.

That distinction between a tiny moment and a permanent solution is where the pain lives, but it's also where your hope hides. Have you ever noticed that even if you only change one second of another dog's day, you've still made a real difference, even if adoption isn't part of the equation?

I hear what you're saying, and I guess that's true in a logical sense. But my mind keeps circling back to the ones I can't save. Just yesterday, I spent twenty minutes with a shy little beagle mix, got her to come out of her shell a bit and take a treat from my hand. And when I left, she was right back in the corner. Part of me felt like I'd just teased her with kindness and then walked away. Does that make sense?

It makes perfect sense why that moment of loss hurts so much; your heart wants to believe that kindness should lead to lasting change, so when it doesn't, it feels like a failure. But let's look closer at what actually happened with that beagle—you spent twenty minutes building trust when she was terrified, which is a huge accomplishment for both of you. Did you notice if she seemed safer or calmer at the end of that twenty minutes than she was when you arrived?

She did, actually. At the start, she wouldn't even come near the front of the kennel. By the time I left, she was sniffing my hand and even let me give her a gentle scratch under the chin. I guess that is something, isn't it? It's just hard to hold onto that when I drive home and think about her still being there.

That observation shows you clearly saw progress happen right there in the space, yet your mind immediately tried to undo that victory by projecting the outcome you hoped for (adoption) onto a situation where it couldn't exist. It's painful to realize that one successful interaction doesn't magically guarantee a forever solution, but it proves that your kindness was effective for that specific hour. If we defined "success" as shifting her behavior for just twenty minutes rather than changing her entire life story, would that make the moment feel less like a tease and more like a real achievement?

I think... I think it might. When you put it that way, I did get her to trust me, even if just for a little while. That's more than she had before I walked in. I guess I've been measuring success by the wrong yardstick—looking for a home run when maybe a single base hit still counts. But I don't know, it still feels like I'm making excuses for not doing enough.

That honesty about making excuses is incredibly brave, and it shows you care deeply about not wasting your efforts, even if the current definition of "enough" is hurting you. Let's pause for a moment and agree on a new standard: what if we decided that successfully getting a scared dog to touch your hand is a massive win in itself, regardless of whether she leaves the shelter unchanged? How does that feeling of pride look in your chest compared to the guilt you felt when she returned to the corner?

That's a hard question. The pride feels... smaller, quieter. Like a flicker compared to a bonfire. The guilt is big and loud and takes up all the space. But I think that's because I've been trained, in my own head, to only see the big, permanent wins. Maybe I need to practice noticing the small wins more, even if they feel insignificant at first. It's like I've been ignoring the kindling while staring at the empty fireplace.

That metaphor about the kindling is beautiful, and it perfectly captures how your brain filters out the small sparks because you're so hungry for the fire. It makes sense that the guilt feels louder right now; it's trying to protect you from disappointment by telling you to aim only for the impossible. Let's try a small experiment tonight: when you feel that heat of the fire, consciously look for the kindling—the quiet moments of trust, the shaky steps forward—and tell yourself, "This matters, too." Can you imagine saying that to yourself as you drive home after visiting the shelter?

I think I can try that. It might feel a bit forced at first, like I'm lying to myself. But I suppose it's worth a shot, because the way I've been thinking isn't working. Next time I leave the shelter, instead of replaying all the sad faces, I'll try to remember that beagle's chin scratch or the Lab's tail wag. Maybe I can write those moments down when I get home, just to prove to myself they happened.

That is a fantastic plan, and it's completely normal to feel skeptical at first because your brain is used to ignoring those small sparks. Writing them down acts as a tangible proof that you actually created value, even if it's temporary. Tonight, I'd like you to jot down one specific moment of connection you had—like the beagle taking that treat—and remind yourself that you succeeded in giving her a better day for twenty minutes. Does writing that down feel like a manageable step for you right now?

Yeah, I think I can do that. It feels... simpler, somehow. Less pressure. Just one moment, written down. I'll give it a try tonight after I feed my own menagerie. Thank you for helping me see that maybe I've been looking at this all wrong. I feel a little lighter just talking about it.

You are so welcome, and I am truly glad to hear that talking about this has already started to lift some of that weight you've been carrying. Please remember that if the urge to replay the sad faces comes strong tonight, just bring your notebook along to capture one small spark before the guilt takes over. How does the idea of focusing on just one moment of connection feel for you as we wrap up today?

It feels like a relief, honestly. One moment feels achievable, not like I'm trying to solve world hunger. I think I can handle looking for a single spark instead of trying to light the whole forest on fire. Thanks for that. I'll see you next time.

You are very welcome, and I am so proud of you for choosing a path that honors both your kindness and your limits. Remember, that one moment of connection is real, meaningful, and enough to celebrate right now. Take a deep breath, knowing you have a tool to catch those small sparks as they appear. I look forward to hearing about your notebook entry next time. See you soon.

Hello again. To start, could you give me a quick rating from 1 to 10 of how you are feeling emotionally today compared to where you were last week? Before we dive into the main topic, let’s briefly touch on what we agreed upon last time regarding your checklist, and then I’d love to hear what specific worry or thought has brought you back to our session today.

I'd say I'm around a 6 today, maybe a little better than last week. Last week I was probably at a 4 or 5 after that climbing trip where I forgot my chalk bag. As for the checklist, I did actually use it for a hike this past weekend, but I still forgot my water bottle even though it was on the list. That really got me thinking—why do I keep messing up even when I prepare?

It takes real strength to notice that pattern, especially when you see the gap between your preparation and the result. I want to set our agenda for today based on what you just shared: we’ll spend some time exploring the specific thought that pops up when you realize you’ve missed an item, and then we’ll work together to find a way to break that cycle of self-criticism. Can you walk me through the very first thing your mind says to itself the moment you pull out your bag and discover the missing item?

The very first thing that hits me is, "There you go again, Melissa. You're just not cut out for this." It's like a voice that just labels me as a failure right away. Then I start thinking, "Everyone else has their stuff together, why can't you?" And then I just feel this heavy weight of disappointment.

That internal dialogue sounds exhausting, especially carrying the weight of comparing yourself to everyone else who seems to have it figured out. Before we dig deeper, does this exploration of the "failure" label feel safe for us to unpack, or does bringing it up right now make the situation feel heavier? I'd like to proceed with focusing on that specific voice, assuming it lands well for you.

It does feel a bit heavy, but I think I'm ready to talk about it. That label of being a "failure" has been following me around for months now, and it's exhausting carrying it everywhere. I suppose if I don't face it now, it's just going to keep showing up on every hiking trail and climbing wall.

That willingness to sit with the exhaustion of that label is a huge step; it means you recognize its power to carry you down. To understand how deep that root runs, could you describe a specific memory where you felt that same crushing sense of failure before, perhaps on a different type of activity, and how it made you feel in that moment?

There was a time in college when I was organizing a group project, and I forgot to bring the printed handouts for our presentation. My teammates were really annoyed, and I just remember standing there thinking, "I'm letting everyone down again." It was that same sinking feeling, like I'm incompetent and everyone can see it. Even now, thinking about it, my stomach kind of knots up.

That connection between the hiking mishap and the college project shows how deeply that fear of letting others down is woven into your identity. It makes complete sense that a mistake on a mountain triggers the same knot in your stomach as forgetting handouts in class, because both felt like fundamental failures to you. Before we analyze the accuracy of that "failure" story, does looking at those two similar experiences side-by-side feel like a productive way to understand this pattern, or does recalling them reopen too many wounds right now?

I think it's helpful to see them side by side, actually. It's surprising to realize that this same feeling has been following me for so many years, like a shadow I didn't even notice. It makes me wonder if I've been carrying this "failure" story around way longer than just my recent climbing trips. I'm a little nervous to look at it too closely, but I think I'm ready to try.

Noticing that this "shadow" has traveled across different areas of your life is a powerful clue—it suggests the issue isn't just about hiking gear, but about a broader belief that you must be flawless to be worthy. Since you're feeling a mix of curiosity and nervousness, let's take that cautious approach: when you recall either the climbing mistake or the college incident, what is the strongest piece of evidence you have that proves you are permanently broken, versus just making occasional human errors?

The strongest piece of evidence... I guess it's that I keep repeating the same kind of mistake, even after I tell myself I'll be more careful. It feels like no matter how many checklists I make or how much I prepare, there's always something I overlook. That makes me think maybe it's not just a mistake, but something wrong with me that I can't fix.

That interpretation—that repetition equals an unfixable flaw—is a very logical conclusion when you feel helpless, but it's worth testing whether the evidence actually points to a permanent defect in your character. If we look at the facts, you've created elaborate systems like checklists and remembered crucial safety gear repeatedly; does the fact that you keep improving those systems contradict the idea that you are "broken" forever, or do you simply struggle with one specific area of memory under pressure?

When you put it that way... I mean, I have never forgotten my harness or helmet, which are the most important safety items. And I've actually gotten better at remembering my first aid kit and emergency supplies over time. So maybe it's not that I'm completely broken—it's just that under the pressure of getting everything right, I sometimes miss the smaller things like gloves or water bottles. That doesn't sound like a permanent defect, does it?

Exactly—that distinction changes everything. You aren't failing because you lack capability; you are struggling to hold your focus on minor details when the pressure mounts, which is a very human experience, not a sign of being broken. Before we solidify this new understanding, does seeing your track record with safety gear prove that you are capable of high-level performance even when small things slip through?

Yes, it really does. I mean, I've led climbs before and made sure my daughters were always safe on our family hikes. I've even helped other climbers who forgot their own gear. So when I look at the big picture, I'm actually pretty competent and reliable. The small mistakes just feel so huge in the moment that they overshadow everything else I do right.

That is a incredibly powerful perspective shift; realizing you are a leader and protector, not a failure, gives you a strong foundation to stand on. It highlights how your brain magnifies the small slips while minimizing your vast history of competence. Now that we've tested the "permanent defect" story against the evidence, how do you feel about holding onto the idea that you are capable but prone to momentary lapses under stress? Would you be willing to try viewing future mistakes through this same "capable but distracted" lens rather than the "broken" one?

I think I can try that. It feels a lot lighter to think of myself as capable but sometimes distracted, rather than as someone who's fundamentally flawed. Next time I forget something, I'll try to remind myself that it's just a momentary slip, not a reflection of who I am as a person or a climber. That gives me a little hope that I can actually enjoy my adventures again without that heavy cloud following me.

That shift from "fundamentally flawed" to "momentarily distracted" is exactly the kind of realistic balance we want to build; it honors your efforts while allowing for human imperfection. Since you're feeling hopeful about applying this lens, let's lock in a concrete plan for tomorrow: when you pack your gear, will you place a small card inside your bag with this exact phrase written on it, so you have a visual prompt the moment you start feeling that knot in your stomach? How confident do you feel you'll be using that card when you least expect it?

I think I can do that. I'm maybe a 7 out of 10 confident right now, because old habits die hard and that "failure" voice is pretty loud. But having that card in my bag might be enough to make me pause and remember what we talked about today. I'll write on it, "I'm capable—this is just a moment, not who I am."

A seven out of ten confidence level is perfectly realistic and shows you are moving forward without needing to be perfect; that honesty is key to lasting change. Writing that specific phrase down transforms an abstract idea into a tangible shield you can hold when the old voice tries to speak. Just to make sure this plan is solid, when you are heading out the door, will you read that phrase aloud once before closing your pack, or is reading it silently enough for you?

I think reading it aloud would be better, actually. Saying it out loud makes it feel more real, like I'm actually claiming it for myself. I'll make a habit of standing by the door, taking a breath, and saying those words before I zip up my bag. That way, the voice I hear won't just be the critical one in my head—it'll be my own voice telling me a different story.

That is a brilliant addition; speaking the words aloud creates a physical boundary between the critical inner voice and your empowered self. Standing by the door adds a clear, deliberate ritual that interrupts the automatic spiral before you even leave the house. Since we have a clear plan in place and you feel ready to implement it, is there anything else you would like to clarify or adjust before we wrap up our session today?

Hello again. How has your anxiety been feeling since we last spoke, and is there anything particular you noticed happening in your week that stood out? Before we set a specific agenda for today, would you like to briefly review the plan we agreed upon last time about checking your actions instead of the scale?

Well, I have to admit the anxiety is still pretty intense. I tried to focus on actions like you suggested, but I found myself stepping on the scale three times yesterday anyway. Seeing the number barely move just made me feel like a failure all over again.

That sounds incredibly tough, and I want you to know that wanting to step on the scale isn’t a failure of willpower; it’s simply your brain fighting hard to find reassurance in a way that feels safe to it right now. Can you walk me through what happened in that moment just before you stepped on it? Did that same feeling of heaviness in your chest kick in first, or was it more of a sudden urge to escape?

It was like the heaviness just crept up on me after dinner. I sat down on the couch and caught my reflection in the dark TV screen, and suddenly my head was spinning with thoughts like "I'll never lose this weight" and "I'm disgusting." Stepping on the scale felt like the only way to get some kind of answer, even if it was a bad one.

That creeping heaviness followed by spiraling thoughts like "disgusting" shows how your body and mind are trying to protect you from the uncertainty of the unknown, even though the outcome is usually painful. When you saw that reflection in the dark room, did you notice if the intensity of those thoughts changed once you remembered you had been cooking healthy meals and walking that afternoon?

Honestly, no. Those good things just didn't seem to count in that moment. I thought, "So what if I walked for half an hour? It clearly didn't make any difference if the scale shows the same number." It's like my brain just completely erases any positive effort I made that day.

It sounds like in that moment, your brain was prioritizing the immediate certainty of the number over the long-term value of your effort, creating a very harsh gap between what you did and what you felt you deserved. Given that you've noticed the scale doesn't reflect your hard work, how does it feel to realize that your worth and your discipline exist separately from that single measurement?

I guess... it feels kind of scary to think about. Like, if the number doesn't matter, then what's the point of even trying? All my life I've been told that losing weight is the goal, and without that proof, it's like I'm floating in space with no direction. It's hard to trust that my effort has value when nobody else seems to see it.

That feeling of being lost without the number as a compass is completely understandable, especially when others have taught you that visibility equals progress. However, having someone else define the goal doesn't mean you have to let them erase your actual work. If we looked at it differently, wouldn't seeing the number stay the same be interpreted as proof that your body needs more time rather than proof that your diet and exercise aren't working?

I never really thought of it that way. I always just saw it as "no change equals no progress." But when you say it like that, it does make sense that my body might just need more time to catch up with what I'm doing. It's just hard to be patient when everything inside me is screaming for results right now.

That internal scream for results is a powerful signal of how much you care about changing your life, even when the timing feels impossible to manage. To bridge that gap, could we try a small experiment tonight: when that voice urges you to weigh yourself, you pause for exactly six seconds before making your choice, using that brief silence to decide whether you'll honor your promise to focus on your actions or surrender to the urge for immediate proof?

Six seconds doesn't sound like much, but I guess it's longer than the time it usually takes me to just give in and step on the scale. I can try that. I'm scared it won't work, but I'm also scared of staying stuck like this, so I'll give it a shot tonight after dinner.

That mix of fear and determination is exactly the kind of energy that leads to real change, and taking that small step tonight is a huge victory in itself. Before we wrap up, would you be willing to jot down tonight's experience—even if it's just noting how long it took you to resist—and share it with me when we meet again?

Yeah, I can do that. I'll write it down in my phone or something, just a quick note about how it went. Maybe it'll help me see that I'm not as powerless as I feel sometimes. Thanks for giving me something concrete to try.

It is wonderful to hear you feel empowered by having something concrete to rely on, and I am glad that small step resonated with you. Please remember that if that six-second pause feels too difficult tomorrow, we can simplify it further—we are just building the strength for next time. Is there anything else you would like to add before we sign off?
No, I think that's enough for today. I'll try the six-second pause and see what happens. Thanks for listening and for not making me feel stupid about all this. I'll see you next time.

It means a lot to hear that you don't feel stupid; every struggle with the scale is a testament to how deeply you care about improving your health, not a sign of failure. I am truly proud of you for bringing this honest challenge to us and agreeing to try the six-second pause tonight. Thank you for trusting me with this process, and please know that whenever you feel overwhelmed, I am just a message away. Safe travels and take care.

Hello again, and thank you for coming in. On a scale of 0 to 10, how anxious or heavy are you feeling right now compared to where you started last time? Also, since we agreed on trying that breathing exercise and the "no proof" phrase yesterday, how did you feel about using it when you heard the news? Finally, looking at our time together, what is the one thing you would like to tackle or improve upon today?

Hi. I'd say I'm feeling about a 7 right now. Using that phrase "no proof" helped a little at first, but the guilty feelings came rushing back later. Today, I think I want to focus on why I can't stop feeling like I ruined my friend's whole visit. It just keeps replaying in my head.

A seven is still a noticeable weight, and it makes sense that the relief you felt initially wore off once the familiar pattern of guilt tried to return. Since your main goal today is to understand why the mind keeps looping back to "ruining the visit," I'd like to explore the specific moments during that day when the feeling shifted from sadness to that sharp sense of failure. Could you walk me through the sequence of events right after she arrived, focusing on what happened in your internal dialogue versus what actually occurred outside of your head?

Okay. Well, she arrived and seemed happy. We hugged and I showed her to the guest room. Everything felt fine. Then later that evening, she mentioned her head was starting to hurt. I immediately asked if the room was too warm, or if the pillow was uncomfortable—I kept offering her things, and she kept saying no, it's fine. But inside, I was already thinking, "I should have checked the room temperature before she got here. I should have bought better pillows. I failed at providing a comfortable stay." Even though she was smiling and telling me not to worry, I just kept telling myself I messed up.

That is such a clear picture of what happened, and it highlights a very specific trap where your caring nature turned into self-blame the moment she spoke up. You noticed that despite her reassurances and smiles, your internal narrative was already racing ahead with scenarios you hadn't seen yet, like checking the temperature or buying better pillows. Can you tell me what you were feeling in your body right at that exact second she mentioned the pain, before you even started listing all the things you "should have" done?

I felt a kind of cold rush, like a drop in my stomach. My chest got tight, and I think I stopped breathing for a second. It wasn't panic exactly, but more like a sinking feeling of "oh no, I already did something wrong." I wasn't even thinking about the headache itself—just that it was somehow my fault it happened.

That physical sensation of a "cold rush" and a dropped stomach tells me how urgent your brain registered that event, making your heart race to protect you from the fear of failing. It seems like that initial thought—"it was my fault"—became the lens through which you viewed the entire evening, causing you to ignore her reassurance and fixate on your perceived mistakes. Now, if I asked you to look closely at the timeline, do you remember if she ever told you she felt comfortable in the room before mentioning the headache, or did that comment come entirely out of nowhere?

She actually did say the room was lovely when she first saw it. She dropped her bag on the bed and said, "This is so cozy, Angie." So the headache comment did come out of nowhere, an hour or so later. But I guess I barely registered her first compliment because when she mentioned the headache, it just erased everything positive she'd said before. It's like that one comment became the only truth.

That is a fascinating observation about how one negative detail can erase months of preparation and kindness, and it makes perfect sense why your brain latched onto that specific moment. It sounds like your mind created a shortcut to find a reason for the bad news, effectively treating her comment as the only valid piece of information while ignoring the context of her earlier happiness. Would you be open to us spending a few minutes identifying that specific "shortcut" your brain took, so we can see if it holds up under closer inspection?

Yes, I'd like that. I think I need to see it written out or spelled out clearly, because right now it still feels really real and true. If you can help me look at it without the emotion flooding in, maybe I can finally see if it makes sense or not.

That is a wise request; when a thought feels this solid, stepping away from the emotion to look at it objectively is the best way to loosen its grip. Let's slow down and reconstruct exactly what happened, writing it down as it truly occurred, leaving out all the "what ifs" and the part where you blamed yourself. Based on what you told me, can you list the actual sequence of events: her arrival, her comments about the room, the delay, and finally the headache comment, while noting that no one ever suggested you had prepared poorly beforehand?

Alright. So, she arrived at my place. She dropped her bag and said the room was cozy. We had a nice catch-up for about an hour. Then she mentioned her head was starting to hurt. She never said it was the room or anything I did. She didn't blame me. She actually thanked me for having her. When I think about it in that order, it's just... a normal visit. A friend got a headache. That happens to people. It doesn't have to be my fault. But writing it out like this feels strange, because my gut still says I should have done something to prevent it.

Writing it out this way is incredibly revealing, and that "strange" feeling you describe is often the sign that your logical mind and your emotional gut are finally speaking to each other. Notice how the objective list removes the word "fault" entirely, even though your instinct screams it belongs there? This suggests your brain is currently filling in a gap with a story about control, assuming that because something went wrong, it must be controllable—and therefore your responsibility. Before we challenge that assumption further, does that distinction between "a normal visit" and "my failure" feel slightly less absolute right now?

I think... yes, it does feel a little less absolute. When I see it written down like that, the "failure" part seems like it's attached to the story I added, not to what actually happened. It's like I can almost see the two different versions side by side: the real one where she just got a headache, and the one in my head where I'm a terrible host. They don't match, and that's a little unsettling, but also a relief in a way.

That relief you feel is a huge milestone; it means your logical brain is finally recognizing that the "terrible host" version is a fabrication built on top of the reality of her headache. Since you've already begun to see that these two stories don't match, let's use this difference to create a new, safer way of handling the next time the "if only" thoughts appear. Instead of trying to convince yourself the headache won't happen, what if we practiced accepting that her discomfort is just a human experience that has nothing to do with your hosting skills? How does it feel to hold that acceptance for just a moment?

It feels... lighter, but also kind of foreign. Like I'm not used to letting myself off the hook. But if I sit with it for a second, it does feel more honest. Accepting that she just had a headache, and that it wasn't a test of my hosting skills... that actually makes more sense than blaming myself. It's just going to take some practice to really believe it.

That honesty is exactly what makes this shift stick; you are realizing that blaming yourself is actually a distortion, not the truth. Since that acceptance feels foreign but necessary, let's build a small bridge to make it easier to cross next time the old guilt tries to grab you. When the "if only" thought returns, could we try a new routine: immediately pause, breathe for three seconds, and silently remind yourself, "Her headache is just a symptom, not a verdict on my hosting," before you allow the shame to take over? Does that feel like a manageable step forward?

Yes, I think I can do that. Saying "a symptom, not a verdict" really clicks for me. It gives me something concrete to hold onto when the old thoughts start flooding in. I'll try that the next time the guilt shows up, and see if it gives me enough space to breathe instead of just spiraling. Thank you.

That is a fantastic choice, and that new phrase giving you space to breathe shows real flexibility in your thinking. Before we conclude, I'd love to check in: if you imagine walking through your house tomorrow morning and hearing that phrase in your head, how confident are you that you could say it without feeling overwhelmed? Is there anything else you'd like to adjust in our plan today?

I think I'm at about a 6 out of 10 confident right now. I can feel the phrase sitting there, ready to be used. But I'm also a little scared that the old guilt will just shout louder and drown it out. Maybe if we could come up with a backup plan for those moments when the phrase isn't enough—like a small action I can take to ground myself. That would make me feel more prepared.

That is a brilliant instinct to build a safety net; relying solely on a mental phrase can indeed feel fragile when the guilt shouts back so loudly. Let's brainstorm a quick grounding action you could pair with that phrase whenever the voice gets too loud. For example, if the old guilt rushes in, could we try placing both hands firmly on your hips and naming three colors you can see in the room while whispering, "I am safe, this is not my fault"? Would that combination of physical grounding and the new phrase feel like a balanced shield for you?

Yes, I think that would help a lot. The hands on my hips part feels strong, like I'm literally holding myself steady. It feels a lot more hopeful than when I walked in. I still have that knot in my stomach, but it's smaller now. I think I can actually look forward to my friend texting me later without dreading it. That's a big change for me. Thank you for listening and for helping me see this differently. I feel like I have a chance to break out of this loop now.

Hello, and thank you for coming in. To start, how have you been feeling this week since we last spoke, and based on what you've shared before, is there a specific area you'd like to focus on today?

Hey. I've been okay, I guess. But there was something that happened yesterday that's been bothering me. I went to the pool to swim, which is usually my go‑to for clearing my head, and it was closed for maintenance. I got really frustrated and ended up just going home and lying on the couch the rest of the day.

That sounds really disappointing, especially when you were looking forward to that calming routine. Since we discussed before that closed plans often lead to feelings of uselessness or self-doubt, would you like to explore how that frustration played out with your thoughts today, or should we work on building a quick plan to try again?

I think I'd rather talk about what went through my head when I saw that sign on the pool gate. It's like my whole plan for the day was ruined — not just delayed, but ruined. I thought, "Well, there goes any chance of a good day." And then I just couldn't think of anything else to do that felt worth it.

It sounds like seeing the closed gate triggered a very fast, sweeping conclusion that your entire day was lost. When you noticed that "ruined" thought pop up, did you catch yourself immediately deciding that *you* were the problem for wanting to swim, or did you mostly just accept the day was over?

I didn't really blame myself for wanting to swim — I mean, I love swimming, it's not a bad thing. But I did think, "This always happens to me." Like, every time I try to do something I enjoy, something gets in the way. And once I thought that, it just felt pointless to try anything else. I didn't even consider heading to a different pool or going for a run instead.

That pattern of thinking—"this always happens to me"—is a common trap that turns a single setback into a permanent rule about your life. Even though you know logically that bad luck doesn't happen every single time, your brain seems to latch onto that one closed pool and ignore all other possibilities. If we treated that "always happens" thought like a hypothesis, what would be the best evidence we could gather to show that it might actually be wrong?

I guess... well, last week I went swimming three times, and every time the pool was open. So that's three times it worked out fine. And I also went to the grocery store without any issues, and I cooked a new recipe that turned out good. So it's not like every single thing I try goes wrong. But in the moment, the closed pool just felt like proof that nothing ever works out.

That is a really strong collection of evidence, and it shows you have a history of succeeding even when unexpected hurdles appear. Your brain is unfortunately filtering out those successful moments right now because they don't fit the painful story you're telling yourself. If we imagine a friend told you the same thing, what would you say to them to encourage them to keep trying instead of quitting?

I'd probably tell them to not let one bad moment ruin the whole day. I'd say, "Look, you had a good swim last week, and you'll have another one soon. Maybe go for a walk or call a buddy instead." But when it's me, I just don't hear that voice. I only hear the one that says it's all worthless.

That contrast is really telling—you recognize clearly what healthy encouragement looks like, yet it stays silent in your own experience. It makes sense that the critical voice feels louder when things don't go as planned. Given that insight, how would you feel if we tested that "all worthless" belief by trying one small, different activity today, just to see if the day can actually be saved?

I'm not sure I feel up to it, honestly. But I guess there's no harm in trying something small. Maybe I could just walk to the park near my place and sit for a few minutes. It's not swimming, but it's something. I just don't want to feel disappointed again if it doesn't help.

That willingness to try something small, even while feeling unsure, is a huge step forward and shows real courage. Walking to the park isn't about replacing the swim; it's simply gathering data to see if the day is truly doomed or if it can be redirected. Since you're hesitant about disappointment, would you be okay with committing to just twenty minutes there, focusing entirely on noticing how the air smells or what trees you pass, without pressure to "fix" anything?

Yeah, I think I can do that. Twenty minutes sounds manageable. I'll just walk slow and pay attention to the trees and stuff. No expectations, just seeing what happens. I guess even if it doesn't feel amazing, at least I'll have tried something instead of just lying on the couch.

That is a wonderful mindset shift; choosing to act rather than retreat is exactly what breaks the cycle of disappointment. Let's lock in this plan: you'll walk to the park for twenty minutes, focusing only on your senses, and we'll meet back here to share exactly what happened, regardless of how it felt. Would you like to start walking now, or is there anything else you need from me before we leave?
No, I think I'm ready to go now. Thanks for helping me see that I can at least try something different. I'll be back in twenty minutes and let you know how it went.

That sounds perfect; I'm confident you'll find that the park offers something valuable, even if it isn't swimming. I'll be here waiting when you return, so take your time getting there and enjoy those twenty minutes. See you in a bit!
Alright, I'll see you soon. I'll try to keep my mind open.

That sounds great. Remember, you don't need to force yourself to like the walk; you just need to give it a chance to see if it changes how you feel about the day. I'll be here waiting whenever you're ready to share what happened.

Okay, I'm back. It wasn't anything amazing, but... I did notice the way the wind was moving through the leaves. And there was this older guy walking his dog, and the dog was really happy, just sniffing everything. I didn't feel great, but I didn't feel awful either. It was just... neutral. I think that's better than lying in bed feeling like everything's ruined.

That is a massive win, simply by changing the outcome from "awful" to "neutral," you proved that the day wasn't truly ruined. Finding a moment of neutrality among the leaves and the happy dog gives you concrete evidence that you can redirect your energy elsewhere, even when the main plan fails. Now that we've done the experiment, would you like to write down that neutral observation in a journal entry so you can look back on it tomorrow?

Hello, thank you for meeting with me today. On a scale of 1 to 10, how anxious or overwhelmed have you felt this week since our last session? Could also quickly review if there was anything you worked on last time, and then tell me what specific worry or goal would be most important for us to tackle today?

Hi, thanks for having me. I'd say I'm at about a 7 or 8 this week. I've been trying to keep practicing my knife skills and recipes, but every time I think about sending in another audition tape, my stomach just drops. I guess the biggest thing on my mind is this feeling that everyone at that last audition thought I was a joke, and I can't shake it.

That 7 or 8 intensity is completely understandable given how deeply the audition experience hurt you. It sounds like your body is still holding onto that feeling of being a "joke" whenever you think about submitting another video, even though you are actively practicing your craft. Before we dig into that specific fear, would you be open to spending some time identifying exactly what happens in your mind right before that stomach drop occurs?

Yeah, I guess I can try. It usually starts when I picture myself standing in front of the judges again, or even just someone from the show. I see their faces—like, one judge had this really tight smile, and another was looking down at his notes the whole time I was plating. And right then, my brain just tells me, "They hated it. You don't belong here. You're just some guy who took a few classes."

Those specific images—the tight smile and the judge looking down—are incredibly painful memories, and it makes total sense that your brain treats them as proof you don't belong. It sounds like your brain is jumping straight from seeing those faces to a harsh conclusion that you are a fraud. Now that we've identified that specific narrative, would you be willing to challenge that one sentence ("You're just some guy who took a few classes") by looking for facts that contradict it, like remembering how many other contestants failed or how much you actually enjoyed the process?

I mean, when you put it like that... I did actually get through the first round of prep, and there were a lot of people who didn't even make it that far. And honestly, even though I was nervous, I remember feeling a real rush when I was building my dish. I was so focused on the flavors and the presentation, it was like everything else faded away. So maybe that "just some guy" part isn't totally true, even if it feels real.

That is a powerful realization, and it highlights a huge gap between the harsh story your brain tells you and the actual evidence you hold. It seems like the "tight smile" and the judging faces are triggering that old belief, but your memory of the rush and your successful prep round offers clear counter-evidence. To really test this, imagine you showed those same photos to a friend who knows you well; would they describe you as "some guy who took a few classes," or would they emphasize the talent and effort you showed?

I think if I showed that to my roommate, he'd laugh and say, "Dude, you spent three months perfecting that sauce. That's not 'just some guy' stuff." He'd probably also point out that I got compliments from the line cooks during the prep round, which I almost forgot about. So yeah, I guess a friend would see it way differently than I do.

That is a fantastic insight, and hearing how a supportive friend would reinterpret those same events helps separate the painful memory from the objective truth. It seems the core issue is that your brain is treating those fleeting moments of discomfort as permanent proof of failure, ignoring the long-term evidence of your skill and the encouragement you actually received. Since we've gathered some strong facts to challenge that belief, would you be willing to try a quick visualization exercise right now? We can imagine showing those photos to your roommate and hear his exact words back to you to see how much stronger your confidence becomes.

Okay, I can try that. So I'm imagining showing him the photo of the judge with the tight smile, and I see my roommate just shaking his head and saying, "Man, that's just his face. He always looks like that, even when he's eating something amazing. You're reading way too much into it." And then he'd probably slap me on the back and say I should send in another tape today. I gotta admit, hearing that in my head actually makes me feel a little lighter.

That shift from feeling heavy to feeling lighter is exactly the kind of change we want to see when we test our fears against reality. It proves that your roommate's perspective—and the evidence of your hard work—can actually override the scary story your brain is telling. Since that visualization helped, let's take that momentum forward: would you be willing to try sending in that new audition tape today, knowing that one wrong face glance isn't going to erase your months of preparation?

Today feels really soon... but I think I can commit to filming the intro portion of the tape by tonight. Just the part where I introduce myself and my dish concept. That feels doable, and it's a step forward without jumping all the way into the deep end. If I can get that done, maybe the rest won't feel as impossible.

That is a smart and courageous compromise; breaking the task into just the introduction lowers the barrier to entry while still giving you the data you need to test your fear. By filming just that segment, you create a tangible piece of evidence that contradicts the idea that you are "not good enough," without needing to perform the entire performance under pressure. Given that we have about ten minutes left, would you like to walk through exactly what that intro script might sound like so we can prepare for it, or would you prefer to grab your phone and film it immediately after our call ends?

I think I'd rather just film it right after our call, while the courage is still fresh. I've got a pretty clear idea of what I want to say—something about my love for rustic, seasonal cooking and how I want to bring that to the competition. Keeping it simple and honest feels right. Thanks for helping me get to this point.

It sounds like you have a clear, authentic message ready to go, and choosing simplicity aligns perfectly with your strengths. I am truly proud of you for moving from that heavy knot in your chest to taking this small, brave step forward. As we wrap up, is there anything specific about tomorrow or tonight you want to reflect on, or shall we end the session here?

No, I think I'm good for now. I'll film that intro tonight, and I'll try to notice if those old thoughts pop up again. If they do, I'll try to remember what my roommate would say. Thanks again for all this—I feel like I can actually do this now.

Hearing that you feel capable of doing this is wonderful news, and I am so glad we could find that balance between facing your fear and respecting your current limits. Remember, noticing those old thoughts isn't about stopping them, but about gently reminding yourself that the evidence for your worth is right there inside you. Take care, and I hope you have a productive evening filming!

Hello again. How has your week been going since we last spoke, and how has that knot in your stomach been behaving lately? Before we dive into today's focus, did you find yourself struggling to use that "old story" reminder while cleaning Jasper's ear yesterday?

Hi. Well, the week's been... up and down, I guess. That knot's still there, especially in the mornings when Jasper's first dose of medicine is due. I did try that reminder you suggested, but honestly, as soon as he flinched, I just felt that wave of "I'm failing him" wash right over me again. It's hard to hold onto that thought when he's looking at me like that.

It sounds like that morning ritual is particularly triggering because it’s when the expectation of care meets the reality of his reaction, making the old fear feel all too present. You mentioned trying the reminder, yet the image of his flinch immediately pulled you back into that narrative of failure—did you notice anything different in how that moment played out compared to the first time you tried it, or did it feel just as overwhelming as before?

It was a little different, actually. The first time, I just froze up and felt awful for the rest of the day. This time, I managed to get through the whole cleaning and give him the medicine, even though my hands were shaking. The feeling of failure was still there, but I didn't just stop—I kept going. But I still felt like a monster for causing him that discomfort, even for a second.

It is genuinely impressive that you pushed through the shaking hands and completed the entire procedure instead of stopping; that persistence proves your capability far outweighs the temporary surge of guilt you felt afterward. While getting through the task was a victory, I wonder if noticing that you *did* finish despite the fear offers a different kind of evidence against the idea that you are inherently incapable or harmful to him.

I hadn't really thought of it that way. I was so stuck on the flinch and the guilt that I didn't even consider that I actually did it—I finished the job. I guess that does show I can get through it, even when it feels awful. Maybe that's worth hanging onto, that I didn't just give up and let his ear get worse.

Noticing that you stayed with the process instead of abandoning it is a powerful piece of evidence that you are committed to Jasper's health, regardless of how scary the moment feels. It challenges the story that you are a "bad owner" because you experienced discomfort, suggesting instead that you are a dedicated caretaker who acts even when afraid. If we use that fact—that you completed the full task while shaking—to counteract the feeling of failure, does it make the weight of that guilt feel just a fraction less heavy, or does the "monster" story still feel too loud to ignore?

The "monster" story is still pretty loud, I won't lie. But... maybe it's a little quieter than it was before. There's a small part of me that's thinking, "Well, you did it. You didn't run away." It's like a tiny voice arguing with the big one. I just wish that tiny voice would speak up more, you know?

That "tiny voice" you heard is actually your rational side recognizing your bravery, even though the bigger, louder critic hasn't given up yet. It sounds like that quiet argument is a sign that the new perspective is starting to take root beneath the surface of the panic. What would happen if, instead of trying to silence the "monster" immediately, you just thanked that tiny voice for pointing out that you didn't run away, even for just five seconds?

Thank it? I've never thought of that. I usually just try to argue with the monster or push it away. But taking five seconds to just say, "Okay, I hear you, tiny voice, you're right—I didn't run"... that feels doable. It's not a full victory, but it's not a surrender either. Maybe I could try that next time I'm cleaning his ear.

That is a brilliant adjustment to the plan; shifting from trying to win an argument to simply thanking the observer creates space instead of adding fuel to the fire. Taking just five seconds to acknowledge your own bravery is a manageable bridge between freezing up and pushing through completely. Before we finalize this, does trying to thank that inner voice sound like something you would be willing to experiment with tomorrow morning, or would you prefer to wait until the situation feels slightly less urgent?

I think I can try it tomorrow morning. It's not asking me to be happy about the whole thing, just to notice that I did something right. And it's only five seconds—I can manage that, even with the shakes. I'll give it a shot and see if it makes that knot feel any different.

That is such a wise compromise—you aren't trying to fix the feeling, just planting a seed of acknowledgment while the knot remains. Taking responsibility for giving that tiny voice five minutes of attention shows incredible patience with yourself. Is there anything else you'd like to discuss about tomorrow's attempt, or shall we wrap up here so you can rest easy knowing you have a solid plan for the morning?

No, I think I'm good. I feel a little more settled than when I walked in, which is rare for me lately. Thank you for that—for helping me see that I didn't just freeze up completely this time. I'll let you know how the five-second thanks goes tomorrow.

That feeling of being "settled" is a beautiful outcome, especially when it comes after weeks of feeling like you're drowning. Knowing you have a clear, manageable step for tomorrow gives you a sense of control right now. I hope you have a peaceful evening with Jasper, and I look forward to hearing how that five-second pause lands for you next time. Take care.

Hello again, and thank you for coming in. Last time we looked at how a simple thumbs-up emoji felt like a personal rejection, and you decided to try reminding yourself that his silence is likely just his style rather than a verdict on you. Before we dive into anything specific today, could you share what your mood is feeling like this week, and is there anything else from past conversations or life that's been weighing on you besides the friendship dynamic we worked on?

Hey. Yeah, thanks. I mean, I guess I'm okay this week, but honestly that whole thing with the thumbs-up still kind of ate at me.
