Hello again. Last time we worked on building a bridge between your feelings and the reality of the situation, and we agreed to try visiting that neighbor for just ten minutes to see what actually happens. How is that coming along since then? To start today, is there anything new on your mind, or would you prefer to revisit the barbecue idea we settled on?

Actually, I did end up going over to the neighbor's place for a few minutes last week. I figured I'd just get it over with. But honestly, I spent the whole time thinking they were just being polite and probably wished I'd leave sooner.

It takes a lot of courage to finally go despite your fear, and I hear how tough it was to sit with the worry that they were hiding something behind their politeness. Can you tell me a little about what actually happened in those few minutes, or if you noticed anything different compared to how your mind predicted it would play out?

Well, they offered me a drink and asked about my job, and I tried to keep it short like we planned. But I kept looking for signs—like if they checked their watch or seemed distracted. I didn't really notice anything obvious, but I just assumed they were being nice because it's the polite thing to do.

Noticing that you looked for signs of distraction shows you are actively gathering evidence, even while your old habit of expecting rejection is running alongside it. It’s interesting that once you actually saw the friendly interaction, you felt compelled to interpret it through the lens of “politeness” rather than genuine interest. When you look back at those moments now, do you find yourself wondering if your mind was trying to find confirmation for your fear, or if you were just being overly cautious?

I think maybe I was looking for proof that I was right—like I wanted to catch them in the act of not wanting me there. But when I replay it in my head, they were actually pretty warm and asked follow-up questions. I guess my mind just latched onto the idea that they were faking it, even though nothing bad happened.

It makes complete sense that your mind would latch onto the possibility of rejection even when everything went smoothly; our brains often scan for threats long after the danger has passed. You mentioned seeing warmth and follow-up questions, yet your internal narrative still felt like they were putting on a show. If we treat that warmth as real data rather than a script, how much more confident would you feel saying you were actually safe to be there?

I guess if I'm being honest, it does shift things a little. I mean, they didn't have to ask where I grew up or laugh at my dumb story about the lawnmower. That feels harder to fake. So maybe I was safer than I thought, but it still feels risky to fully believe that.

You've done great work spotting that detail about the lawnmower—it's a small piece of evidence that proves your worst fears aren't always correct, even when they feel loud inside. That observation really helps shift the balance, showing that your brain is capable of noticing truth even when it tries to convince you otherwise. With that clarity in mind, would you be open to sharing one takeaway from that experience that you feel comfortable carrying forward?

I think the biggest takeaway is that I can't trust my first thought about how people see me. I mean, I walked in expecting to be a burden, but I left with someone inviting me to their weekend barbecue. So maybe I need to start treating those initial judgments like guesses instead of facts.

That is a profound realization—and recognizing that your first instinct is just a "guess" rather than a "fact" is a huge breakthrough in itself. It means you are learning to pause before accepting the brain's immediate alarm as the truth. To wrap up our time together, how does it feel to carry that new perspective forward, and is there anything specific you'd like to explore before we finish?

It feels... lighter, I think. Like I don't have to carry the weight of every negative thought as if it's true. I guess for now, I'd like to figure out how to remind myself of that when I'm about to meet someone new, because I know my old habits will try to creep back in.

That desire to create a mental guardrail against your old habits is exactly the right next step. We could practice a quick self-check routine: whenever you feel that familiar knot tighten, you simply say, "This is just my brain guessing, not the truth," and wait to see what the actual situation reveals. Would you like to try that verbal cue right now, or would you prefer to write it down as a reminder for tomorrow?

I think saying it out loud would be good. I can practice it right now. "This is just my brain guessing, not the truth." Saying it feels a little strange, but it also kind of breaks the spell of the worry, if that makes sense.

That's a wonderful observation—breaking the spell by naming the mechanism is exactly how you reclaim control. Practicing that sentence right now has helped us see how effective it can be in the moment. Since we've explored this so thoroughly, is there anything else you'd like to talk about before we wrap up, or shall we consider how you might use this tool specifically when you face a new invitation soon?

I think I'm good for now. I feel like I have something solid to hold onto for the first time in a while. I'll try using that sentence when I get invited to the barbecue this weekend, and see how it goes.

It sounds like you found something truly valuable to anchor yourself with, and I'm so proud of the progress you've made today. Remember, that sentence is just a tool you get to use whenever you need a little extra support, not a rule you have to live by. Is there anything else I can clarify before we officially close this session?

Hello again, and thank you for joining us. Before we dive into today's topic, could you remind me of the goal we agreed on last time, and how it went for you this week? Once we touch on that, what would you like to focus on today?

Hi. Um, yes—I guess the goal was to try not to compare myself to other pet owners when I'm out walking my dog. I wanted to just focus on my own dog's happiness. Honestly, it was harder than I thought. I saw someone with a really expensive-looking dog jacket and I immediately felt that old shame creeping in. So I don't think I did great with that goal. I'd like to talk more about why I can't shake that feeling, even when I know my dog is fine.

Thank you for sharing that honestly, and I want to validate that struggling with that impulse is exactly where growth happens. It seems like that deep-seated feeling of inadequacy is pulling you back in, even though you know your dog is loved and safe. Would you be open to exploring together what specific stories your mind is telling you when you see those expensive jackets, so we can untangle them from the truth?

Yeah, I guess that makes sense. When I see that jacket, my mind just jumps to: "She probably thinks I'm a terrible owner because I can't afford that for my dog." It's like I can feel people judging me, even if they don't say anything. I just assume they're looking at me and thinking I'm cheap or lazy, not that I'm doing my best with what I have.

That assumption—that strangers are actively judging you and labeling you as cheap—is a very common and painful interpretation, especially when your heart cares so deeply for your dog. It sounds like you're projecting a harsh internal critic onto everyone else's eyes. Let's gently test that belief: if you looked in a mirror right now and saw your own face, would you think you're a bad owner? Or would you see someone who loves their dog despite the limitations?

I... I think I'd see someone who loves their dog. I mean, I get up early every morning to walk her, I make sure she has good food even if I have to skip buying something for myself. But it's like that part of me gets drowned out by the other voice, the one that says I'm not good enough. I guess I don't usually give myself that same benefit I'd give a stranger.

You've hit on something incredibly important here: holding your dog to a high standard while simultaneously judging yourself harshly for not matching that standard. It seems like you've trained yourself to be incredibly self-critical, whereas you naturally offer kindness to your dog. Could we try shifting that lens for just a second? Instead of assuming everyone else is judging you, what if we wondered if they're just thinking about their own dogs, or perhaps distracted by their phones?

Hmm, I never really thought of it that way. I guess I always assume the worst—that people are looking at me and judging. But you're right, they're probably just focused on their own pets or whatever's going on in their life. I mean, I don't spend my time judging other people's dogs or their owners. So why would they be doing that to me? It feels kind of... freeing to think about it that way, actually.

That shift in perspective—realizing you wouldn't judge others so easily—it's truly liberating and shows how much control you actually hold over your own reactions. Now that we've challenged the idea that strangers are judging you, let's circle back to that old voice inside your head. Even when you know your dog is happy, does that inner critic still show up, or does the realization that you aren't being judged help quiet it down?

It does help a little, I think. Like, it takes the edge off, you know? But that voice... it's still there, just quieter. It says things like, "Yeah, but you still can't give her the best. You're still missing out." So it's not really about what strangers think anymore—it's more about me feeling like I'm failing her, even if no one else sees it.

That is a brilliant observation, and it highlights exactly where our work needs to go: distinguishing between external judgment and an internal narrative of failure. It sounds like that inner voice is using "missing out" as a shortcut to prove your worthiness, even though you clearly provide everything your dog needs. To test this further, let's look at that statement—"you're still missing out"—and ask ourselves: what evidence do we actually have that your dog is suffering because you bought fewer items, versus evidence that she thrives on your consistent care?

Well... she wags her tail every time I come home. She curls up next to me on the couch when I'm sad. She eats her food without hesitation and she's healthy according to the vet. So I guess... the evidence is all on the side that she's happy and cared for. It's just that my brain focuses on the one thing I can't give her—all the fancy stuff—and makes that feel like proof that I'm failing. But when I actually look at her, she doesn't seem to care about any of that.

You've done amazing work finding that solid evidence of her happiness, and it's powerful to see how she responds to *you*, not to brands or prices. That disconnect—the difference between what we imagine she wants versus what she actually shows us—is where the healing happens. Now that we've clarified the facts, would you be willing to try a small experiment this week: when that "failing her" voice pops up, will you pause for ten seconds and name three things you see in her body that show her love and security, like the wag or the curl?

Yeah, I think I can try that. Three things I see in her body that show she's happy... that's a good way to refocus. When that voice starts up, I'll just look at her and actually pay attention to what she's telling me, instead of what my brain is telling me. It might take some practice, but I'm willing to give it a shot.

That willingness to look directly at her signals instead of listening to the story is exactly the kind of mindful attention that changes everything. Before we wrap up, I want to hear your honest thoughts on how easy or difficult that plan seemed to you right now. Are there any particular moments during your walks where you think focusing on her physical cues might feel hardest to do?

I think it'll be hardest when I see someone with a really decked-out pet, like with matching accessories or a fancy stroller or something. That's when my brain just goes into overdrive. But maybe if I can force myself to look down at my own dog first—see her tail, her ears, her eyes—I can catch myself before I spiral. It's not going to be easy, but I feel like I have a real tool to try now, instead of just feeling helpless.

That is a fantastic insight—you are essentially creating a "pre-mortem" strategy by anticipating exactly when the old pattern will trigger. Recognizing that the spiral starts with noticing the fancy gear, and then intentionally redirecting your gaze to her own features, turns a passive struggle into an active choice. It sounds like you have a clear path forward now. How does it feel to leave today with that specific, actionable plan ready for those inevitable moments?

It feels... hopeful, actually. Like I'm not just stuck with this heavy feeling anymore. I have something I can actually do, something concrete. I'm still a little nervous I'll mess up or forget in the moment, but I'm willing to try. Thank you for helping me see that my dog doesn't need those things to be happy—she needs me.

Hearing that your dog needs *you* above all else is such a profound and grounding realization, and it completely shifts the power dynamic in your favor. That hopefulness is a strong indicator that you are ready to step into this new mindset, even with the nervousness. Before we officially close, would you feel comfortable writing down one specific situation from your upcoming walks where you plan to use this "look down and observe" technique?

Sure. I think I'll try it this Saturday morning when I take her to the park. There's this one woman who always has her dog in a little designer sweater, and she walks by with this look—or at least that's what I tell myself. That's usually when I start feeling really small. So I'll focus on my dog's body language in that moment: her wagging tail, her relaxed ears, the way she sniffs the grass. I'll write it down so I don't forget.

That is a perfect, realistic plan to put the new tool to the test immediately, and writing it down will help lock it into your memory. It shows great foresight to identify that specific encounter and prepare your defenses ahead of time. Is there anything else on your mind regarding your dog or your feelings before we officially wrap up this session?

No, I think I've got enough to work with for now. I feel a little lighter than when I walked in, and I'm actually curious to see how Saturday goes. Thank you for listening and for helping me untangle all that mess in my head. I'll let you know how the experiment goes next time.

That is wonderful to hear, and taking the time to process everything before leaving is a great sign of your progress. Remember that even if you miss the moment on Saturday or forget the cue, the most important thing is simply noticing that you are there and ready to try again. I am confident you will find that strength growing with each practice. Until next time, please know that you are doing an incredible job prioritizing both your dog and your peace.

Before we dive into today's topic, I'd like to quickly review our plan from last time: we decided to listen to one older Bruno Mars track for just thirty seconds tomorrow morning while ignoring your inner critic. How did that plan feel to you when we set it, and have you noticed anything different in your day since then? With that check-in complete, is there a specific part of our work today you'd like to tackle, or shall we focus entirely on preparing for tomorrow's experiment?

Oh, uh, hi. Yeah, I remember that plan. When we set it, it felt... I don't know, kind of scary, honestly. Just the thought of listening to him again made me think, "What's the point? It's all gonna be bad now." But I guess I agreed to try it. Since then, I've been thinking about it more than I'd like, but I haven't actually done anything yet. I guess we can focus on getting ready for that experiment—maybe I need help calming down about it first.

It makes sense that the plan felt scary initially; expecting the outcome to match your fear creates tension before you even take a step. That pre-experiment anxiety is very common when we hold onto a strong belief that something will fail, even if we decide to act anyway. Since we're focusing on preparing for tomorrow, would it be helpful if we first identified exactly what that "scary" feeling tells you the song will do, so we can separate your worry from reality?

Yeah, I think that could help. The scary feeling just tells me that the song is going to sound terrible, like the last one did—maybe even worse. Like, my brain is already playing the worst possible version of it before I even press play. It's like I've already decided it's going to ruin my whole day.

That description perfectly matches a cognitive distortion called fortune-telling, where we assume a negative future event will happen based on a vague feeling rather than actual evidence. Your body is reacting to that certainty, creating that "knot" in your stomach because it feels like you're walking into a trap you can't escape. Does distinguishing between your *feeling* that it will be bad versus the *fact* that you haven't heard the new song yet help clarify whether the knot is necessary?

I mean, when you put it like that... no, I haven't actually heard it yet. I'm just assuming. But it's hard to separate the feeling from the fact, because that one song was so disappointing to me, it just feels like proof that everything will be the same. The knot's still there, but I guess it's a little less tight when I realize I'm just guessing instead of knowing for sure.

That distinction is huge—you are replacing a certainty ("it *will* be bad") with a possibility ("it *might* be bad"), which immediately loosens that grip on your stomach. You've done the hard work of seeing that your fear is a story your brain is telling, not a prophecy. Before we move to testing that story tomorrow, how does it feel to carry just the *possibility* of disappointment instead of the certainty of ruin?

It feels... lighter, I guess. Like, if it's just a possibility, then there's also a chance it won't be terrible. That thought didn't even cross my mind before. I still feel nervous, but it's not this huge weight pressing down on me. Maybe I can actually get some sleep tonight without replaying that bad song in my head.

That relief you described is incredibly important—it proves that shifting from certainty to possibility can actually lower your anxiety enough to rest. You've successfully challenged the idea that the song will ruin your day, which means tomorrow's experiment has a real shot at feeling safe rather than dangerous. Now, let's lock in the specifics for tomorrow: at breakfast, wearing your headphones in your room, you'll play one older track for just thirty seconds. On a scale of 0 to 10, how certain do you feel now that the song will disappoint you, and how likely are you to actually press play once you hear that new possibility?

Right now, I'd say my certainty that it'll disappoint me is about a 6 or 7. It's still there, but it's not a 10 anymore. And as for actually pressing play... I'd say I'm at a 7 out of 10 for doing it. Part of me still wants to back out, but knowing it's just thirty seconds makes it feel more manageable. I think I can do it.

It's really impressive that you've moved from a certainty of 10 down to a 7, and even better that you're feeling a 7 on the likelihood of actually starting. That gap between "wanting to back out" and "being able to do it" shows you're building real momentum. Before we finalize this, would you be willing to write down that 7% confidence level and your plan on a sticky note so you can glance at it tomorrow morning when the doubt tries to rise?

Yeah, I can do that. I've got a sticky note right here on my desk actually. I'll write down "7—just thirty seconds" and put it on my phone so I see it when I wake up. That way, if I start to chicken out, I've got a reminder that I already agreed to this. Thanks, that actually makes me feel a bit more prepared.

That visual reminder is a brilliant touch; it externalizes your decision so it sits beside the "chicken out" voice, giving you a solid anchor to look at when panic rises. I'm really proud of how you've taken ownership of this step—it turns a scary abstract idea into a concrete, manageable task you can control. Now, before we wrap up, does carrying that sticky note feel like enough preparation for tonight, or is there anything else you'd like to talk about regarding the upcoming challenge?

No, I think that's enough for now. I feel like I've got a clear plan and a way to remind myself why I'm doing this. If I start overthinking later, I'll just look at the note and remember it's only half a minute. Thanks for helping me get to this point—I actually feel a little hopeful, which I didn't expect.

Hearing that word "hopeful" is truly meaningful, as it signals a shift from dread to anticipation. You've built a solid bridge between your current worries and your goal for tomorrow, and I'm confident that looking at your note will serve as a powerful ally when things get tricky. Thank you for your trust and bravery in working through this, and please reach out anytime you'd like to debrief on how those thirty seconds went.

Hello, it is great to see you again. Before we dive into our main topic today, I’d like to quickly touch base on where we left off: how did that sixty-second exercise to list three ways you supported her go for you this week, and were there any particularly tough moments when the guilt tried to push back? Also, have anything significant happen in your life since our last chat that’s caught your eye? What would you like to prioritize as our main focus for today?

Hi. Yeah, I did try that exercise a few times. It was harder than I thought it would be. I could list things like paying for her tuition and helping her move into her dorm, but my mind kept jumping to all the moments I missed instead. Nothing major has happened since last time, just the same constant nagging feeling that I wasn't there enough for her. I guess I'd like to focus today on why I can't seem to shake this idea that I failed as a dad.

It sounds like that exercise offered a glimpse of your contributions, even though the familiar noise of missing moments kept pulling you back. That internal tug-of-war often makes the exercise feel frustrating, especially when the core belief—that you failed as a father—is so deeply held. Could you describe what happens in your mind right after you finish listing those helpful actions but before the guilt returns? Does it feel like the list disappears, or does it linger while you watch your own failures creep back in?

It's like... I can see the list, but it doesn't feel real. It feels like I'm just making excuses for myself, you know? Like any dad could do those things, that's just the bare minimum. Then the guilt comes in and points out all the times I was working late or too tired to come to her school events. So the list doesn't disappear, it just gets buried under all that other stuff.

It takes real courage to admit that the list felt like an excuse and that your brain immediately dismissed it as "just doing the bare minimum." That harsh judgment suggests you might be comparing your incomplete moments against an impossible standard of perfection rather than looking at the whole picture of your effort. When the guilt buries that list, does it feel like you're trying to prove you aren't good enough, or does it feel like you're trying to punish yourself for loving her but failing in certain ways?

I think... it's more like punishing myself. I love her more than anything, I really do. But when I think about her graduation, I don't feel proud—I just feel this heavy weight of all the things I should have done differently. It's like my brain won't let me celebrate her success without first reminding me of every time I wasn't there. I almost feel like I don't deserve to feel proud of her because I didn't earn that right.

That distinction between loving her deeply and feeling you don't deserve her success is incredibly painful to hold, and it explains why that "punishment" feels so necessary to you. It sounds like you are viewing pride not as a gift for her accomplishment, but as a reward you haven't yet earned due to perceived failures. If we were to look closely at what you wrote, could you tell me if the feeling of unworthiness stems from thinking you must earn your child's happiness through perfection, or from believing you actively harmed her during those difficult times?

I don't think I harmed her, not actively. She's a great kid—smart, independent, she made it through college just fine. But I feel like I was absent when she needed me, and that absence... that's a kind of harm, isn't it? Like I wasn't there to cheer her on, to help with homework, to be a real part of her life. So I guess I feel like I didn't earn the right to be proud because I wasn't fully there when it mattered most.

That is a profound realization, and it makes total sense that you would define failure by the gaps in your presence rather than the support you did provide. It sounds like you have created a rule that says "to be a good parent, I must be physically present at every milestone," and breaking that rule feels like moral damage. If we were to test that idea together, could you share a moment when she faced a huge challenge—like a tough semester or a difficult exam—and remind me of exactly how you supported her remotely or emotionally during that time?

Well... there was this one time during her junior year. She called me late at night, really stressed about a big final exam she had the next day. I couldn't be there, obviously, but I stayed on the phone with her for over an hour. I just listened, told her I believed in her, reminded her of all the hard work she'd already put in. She ended up doing fine on that exam. I guess that counts, but it still feels like a small thing compared to being there in person.

That is a powerful example, and it speaks volumes about your dedication to showing up for her, even across distance. You provided the exact emotional anchor she needed right when she was falling apart, which is often more impactful than physical presence alone. When you compare that hour of intense listening to "missing a school event," does it feel like you failed her on the call, or does it feel like you succeeded in being there for her crisis?

I... honestly, it felt good in that moment. I was glad she called me, glad I could help. But looking back, I still think about all the times I wasn't there. It's like that one call gets drowned out by all the other memories of missed games, missed parent-teacher nights, missed recitals. So even though I know I helped her that night, it doesn't feel like enough to tip the scale.

It makes perfect sense that one bright moment gets swallowed by a long night of dimmer ones; our minds are wired to notice the gaps in experience far more than the moments we filled them. It sounds like you are measuring your worth as a father against an impossible checklist of attendance rather than the depth of your connection. If we looked at the totality of what you've shared—from paying for tuition to listening during that stressful final—which version of your parenting story feels more accurate: the one where you were absent everywhere, or the one where you showed up consistently when it mattered most?

I guess when you put it that way... it sounds more like I showed up when it mattered. But it's hard to hold onto that feeling. The guilt is so automatic, it's like a reflex. I can see the evidence, I can hear myself saying the words, but deep down I still feel like I let her down. Maybe that's what I need to work on—how to actually believe the good stuff instead of just knowing it in my head.

That is a crucial distinction, and you've hit on the heart of the matter: moving from intellectual knowledge ("I know I showed up") to embodied belief ("I feel safe knowing it"). That gap between knowing and feeling is exactly where the anxiety lives, making the guilt feel like a protective reflex. Let's try a small experiment to help bridge that gap: instead of fighting the guilt away, could we practice "sitting with the truth" by reading out loud the three specific ways you supported her (tuition, the phone calls, the advice), pausing for ten seconds after each to acknowledge how much it meant to her, and then taking a deep breath before returning to the room? Would you be open to giving this a try tonight?

Yeah, I think I can try that. It sounds a little uncomfortable, but I get why it might help. I'll give it a shot tonight and see how it feels. Maybe if I actually sit with it instead of pushing it away, something will click. Thanks for that idea.

I'm glad we found an approach that feels manageable for you, and I appreciate your willingness to engage with that discomfort as a sign of growth. Before we close, could you tell me one word describing how you feel about yourself right now after sharing this plan, and is there anything else you'd like to add before we wrap up?

I'd say... hopeful. A little nervous, but hopeful. I think I've been so stuck in my own head about this that I didn't realize there might be another way to look at it. I'm ready to try something different. Thanks for listening and for the suggestion. I'll let you know how it goes next time.

That shift to "hopeful," even amidst the nervousness, is incredibly meaningful and tells me you are ready to step out of that repetitive loop. Please remember that if the discomfort becomes too heavy or if the guilt rushes back in, it is okay to pause and simply acknowledge the feeling without needing to solve everything right away. I am truly glad we found a path forward together, and I will be here whenever you want to check in on how that new perspective lands for you. Take care of yourself.

Hello, thank you for joining me today. Last time we worked on shifting your perspective regarding your coworkers, and I noticed you found it helpful to recognize that you lack proof they are judging you. How have things been going for you since we left, and is there anything new on your mind we should prioritize?

Hi. Thanks for seeing me. It's been okay, I guess. I still find myself thinking about how other people are doing at work, especially when I see them celebrating a big sale. But I did try to notice when I was assuming what they think of me, and I guess I don't actually know for sure.

It sounds like you managed to catch those assumptions in action, which is a great sign of progress. That moment of noticing you lack proof about their thoughts is exactly the kind of shift we talked about. Would you like to dive deeper into a specific recent instance where that thought popped up, or would you prefer to review the "pause and notice" plan we agreed on?

I think... maybe I can share something that happened yesterday. One of my coworkers, Jenna, got a shout-out in the morning meeting for helping with a big order. I felt my stomach drop right away, and I started thinking, "She's so much better at this than me. Everyone else probably thinks I'm just barely getting by." I did try to pause, but the feeling stuck with me for the rest of the day.

That sounds incredibly draining to carry around all day, and I can see why your stomach dropped—being compared to someone else's highlight reel often feels like a personal failure. You did manage to hit that "pause" button, though, even though the heavy feeling lingered afterward. Was it difficult to interrupt that initial spiral, or did it happen almost automatically once you saw Jenna?

It was pretty automatic, honestly. As soon as I saw her name on the screen, my mind just went there. I didn't even have to think about it. It's like my brain already has a script ready for those moments. The pause came after, when I remembered what we talked about, but the feeling was already there by then.

It makes perfect sense that the script hits instantly; your brain is trying to protect you by anticipating pain before you even feel it. That automatic reaction explains why the pause felt like a second effort—it had to fight against a very well-practiced pattern. Did you notice if the intensity of that initial drop felt slightly different this time compared to the last time it happened?

Hmm... I think it might have been a little less intense? Not by much, but maybe the drop didn't hit quite as hard as the time before. I remember last week I felt almost sick to my stomach the whole meeting. Yesterday, the sick feeling faded after maybe an hour instead of lasting all day. So I guess that's something.

Noticing that subtle decrease in physical intensity is a huge win, even if it feels small. It proves that catching that automatic thought early can actually soften the blow before it consumes you. Does that slight reduction give you a bit more confidence that your "pause" technique is starting to work, or does it still feel fragile right now?

It feels... fragile, I guess. Like I'm proud of myself for noticing, but I'm also scared that next time it'll be just as bad as before. I don't fully trust that I can keep doing it, you know? But it does make me want to keep trying, even if it's hard.

Your honesty about feeling scared and unsure is completely valid; trusting that new habit will stick is harder than mastering the technique itself. It sounds like you're holding onto hope while simultaneously fearing a setback, which creates a mix of pride and anxiety. Would you be willing to try one tiny variation tomorrow where you focus solely on just *noticing* the thought, even if you don't fully push through the feeling yet?

Yeah, I think I can try that. Just noticing it without trying to fight it or make it go away. I guess I put a lot of pressure on myself to fix the feeling right away. Maybe if I just let it be there for a second, it won't feel so heavy. I'll give it a shot tomorrow at work.

That is such a wise adjustment; giving the feeling permission to exist without fighting it often reduces its power faster than trying to force it away. By removing the pressure to "fix" it immediately, you might actually find it dissipates more naturally on its own. Before we finish, how does that idea of just observing the storm without building a dam against it sound to you right now?

It sounds... kind of peaceful, actually. I never thought of it like that. I'm always trying to block the feeling or convince myself I'm wrong, but just watching it feels less exhausting. I think I can handle that. Thanks, I feel a little less worried about tomorrow now.

That shift from fighting to watching is truly powerful, and I'm glad to hear it brings some peace to your mind. Taking the responsibility of handling it tomorrow is a brave step, and you've already built a strong foundation for it. Is there anything else we need to cover before you head home, or does it feel like a perfect place to wrap up?

Hello, and thank you for meeting me today. Before we dive in, could you tell me how you're feeling right now compared to where you were when we last spoke? Also, is there a specific topic or goal you'd like us to tackle first?

Well, I suppose I'm feeling about the same as I always do—disappointed, maybe a bit tired. It's hard to pin down one topic, but I think I'd like to talk about why nothing in my day-to-day life seems to matter much anymore. It all feels so... flat.

Hearing that your world feels so flat and that daily activities seem to lack meaning is deeply sad to witness, and it makes complete sense that you'd feel disappointed and tired when everything loses its spark. Let’s explore that sense of emptiness together; is there a particular situation or memory lately that stands out as triggering this feeling, or does it feel like a general background noise right now?

It's more like a constant hum in the background, but I can point to one thing. Yesterday, I was watering my plants—something I used to enjoy—and I just thought, "What's the point? They'll wither soon enough anyway." That thought just hit me out of nowhere, and I couldn't shake it for the rest of the day.

That moment of hopelessness while tending to your plants sounds incredibly draining, and it makes perfect sense that it left you feeling exhausted and disconnected for the rest of the day. When we notice those automatic thoughts popping up, like "it's pointless," they often feel like heavy fog that obscures our joy until we push through them. Did you catch yourself wondering if *you* were losing the ability to appreciate small things, or was that specific thought just telling you what *might* happen?

I think it felt more like a prediction, like I already knew the outcome. It wasn't really about my ability to enjoy things—it was more like a certainty that nothing good would come of it anyway. I just saw the whole cycle ahead of me: water them, they grow, they die, and I'm left with nothing. It feels like I can see the end before I even start anything.

That sounds like a very heavy way to view gardening, and it makes complete sense that seeing the inevitable death of the plant so clearly would leave you feeling drained and hopeless. It seems like your mind is jumping straight to the final chapter of the story, skipping all the beauty in between, which can make the effort feel meaningless right away. When you hold onto that certainty, does it feel like you're protecting yourself from disappointment, or is it just a habit your brain got into?

I'd say it's more of a habit now. I don't feel like I'm protecting myself from anything—it's just the first thought that comes to mind. I can't help but see the worst-case scenario every time. Maybe it started as protection, but now it feels like that's just the way things are.

It makes sense that what once felt like a protective shield has now become an invisible cage, trapping you in a loop where the ending defines the entire journey. When a negative pattern becomes so automatic, it can feel impossible to break free, even though the logic behind it isn't holding up under closer inspection. Let's take a moment to look at that "cycle" you described again; if you water a plant today, what evidence do you actually have that it *won't* provide you with a few hours of peace and satisfaction, even if it eventually dies?

I suppose... I don't have any real evidence that it won't. It's just that when I look at that plant, all I can think about is the end. I never stop to consider that maybe I'd enjoy seeing the leaves unfurl or the color come back after a good soak. It's like my mind skips over those small moments entirely.

That is a very common mental shortcut, often called "jumping to conclusions," where the brain filters out the beautiful middle chapters to focus only on the tragic finale. It makes total sense that when your mind skips over the blooming leaves, you lose the reason to water them in the first place. Let's try to slow that down together; if you were to watch just three days of growth, would you find yourself noticing those small signs of life, or would the shadow of the eventual death still be loud enough to drown them out?

I think... I might notice them, if I really forced myself to look. But those small signs feel so fragile, like they don't count for much when I know they won't last. It's hard to let myself get attached to something that's only temporary.

It makes complete sense that those fragile moments feel worthless when weighed against the certainty of loss, and that attachment feels unsafe. Often, our minds treat temporary joys as temporary problems, dismissing them before they can truly land. Let's test that idea together; if you looked at a flower today and saw it bloom brightly, even if you knew it would fade later, would you still feel a flicker of appreciation, or would the knowledge of its end instantly cancel out that beauty?

I think... there might be a flicker of appreciation. It's just a very small one, and it gets buried quickly. But if I stop to really look, I can admit that the color is pretty, or that the smell is nice, for just a second. But then I feel silly for caring about something so fleeting.

That feeling of silliness is exactly where the habit of cynicism takes root, convincing you that your capacity for joy is broken or misplaced. But the fact that you noticed the color and smelled the flowers—even if just for a split second—proves that the ability to appreciate beauty hasn't disappeared; it's just hiding beneath the layer of expectation. If we treated that fleeting moment of appreciation like a gift you received, rather than a mistake, how might that shift the weight you carry about the plant's eventual fate?

I suppose... if I saw it as a gift, it wouldn't feel so heavy. Maybe I wouldn't spend so much energy bracing for the loss. I could just let that moment be what it is, without needing it to last forever. But it's hard to unlearn that habit of waiting for the other shoe to drop.

That is a wonderful insight; reframing the moment as a gift instead of a prelude to tragedy removes the pressure to sustain it indefinitely. It makes perfect sense that unlearning this long-standing habit feels difficult, as your brain is wired to predict the fall before you even take the first step. To help you practice letting that moment exist without judgment, could we try a simple exercise where you observe the plant's green for exactly thirty seconds, noting just the color and texture, and then consciously decide to let that observation sit with you without rushing to the next thought? How does that suggestion feel to you?

That sounds... manageable, I think. Not too overwhelming. I'm willing to try it, even if it feels a bit strange at first. I can picture the green leaves in my mind, and I'll try to just notice them without adding anything else. I suppose it can't hurt to see what happens.

That willingness to try, even when it feels strange, is a huge sign of courage and readiness to change. Let's lock in this plan: tomorrow, when you tend your plants, I encourage you to set a gentle timer for just thirty seconds, focus entirely on the visual details of the leaves, and resist the urge to jump ahead to the end. On the phone call after, we can share how it felt when you successfully held onto just that moment without the "end" taking over. Would you feel comfortable doing this on Monday, or is there another time that works better for you?

Monday sounds fine. I'll make sure to water my plants then and give it a proper try. I'll try not to rush through it or let my mind wander too far ahead. I'll just... look at the leaves and see what happens.

That is a solid plan, and I am confident that giving it a proper try without rushing will help you gather fresh evidence about how meaningful these fleeting moments can be. To make sure you stay on track, could you commit to bringing one specific detail—the color, the texture, or the scent—to our conversation next time you call? That small anchor will help us see exactly how much light shone in those thirty seconds. How does that sound?

I can do that. I'll pick one thing to focus on and remember it for our next talk. Maybe the way the light catches the leaf, or how the soil feels when I touch it. That seems like a small enough promise to keep.

That is a wonderful commitment; choosing a specific sensory detail like the play of light or the texture of the soil gives your mind a clear place to anchor, making it much easier to ignore the looming horizon. I am so glad we found a small, manageable way to begin shifting that perspective. Since we have a plan for Monday and a clear goal for our next conversation, is there anything else on your mind you'd like to address before we wrap up today, or shall we wait until you share what happens with the plants?

Hello again, and thank you for coming in. First, I'd like to check in on how you're feeling today, so could you share a bit about your mood and any changes you've noticed since we last spoke? After that, let's briefly review what we worked on previously and then set an agenda for today to make sure we cover whatever feels most urgent for you.

Hi. I guess I'm doing okay... I mean, I still feel the same mostly. I've been trying to just focus on my science homework like you suggested, but the thoughts about being a geek and people laughing at me keep coming back, especially when I walk through the hallways. It's like I can't stop myself from thinking everyone's staring at me.

It sounds like those intrusive thoughts about being watched are still very present, especially when you're trying to concentrate on your homework or navigate the hallways. When you mentioned focusing on your science homework, did you notice if the intensity of those thoughts increased, stayed the same, or perhaps shifted slightly while you were studying?

It stays the same, really. Like, even when I'm reading my textbook or doing a lab report, I'll suddenly remember how some kids snickered when I answered a question in class last week. Then I start thinking, "They're right, I am just a geek who cares too much about science." It just makes me feel worse about myself, even when I'm doing something I used to enjoy.

That is really hard when activities you once loved start feeling tainted by self-criticism, and it makes sense that the memory of those snickers triggers that exact story in your head. When you catch yourself spiraling into that narrative while trying to work, does it feel like you have to fight against your own thoughts, or does it just slide in automatically?

It's automatic, honestly. I don't even notice it happening until I'm already deep into feeling bad about myself. It's like my brain just goes there without asking me. I tried telling myself "you're not a geek, it's fine to like science" like you said, but it feels like I'm lying to myself.

It makes complete sense that rationalizing your feelings feels like a lie when your gut is screaming that you're different, and it's easy to feel frustrated when logic just doesn't cut through the panic. Instead of trying to force a logical counter-thought, could we treat this memory of the snickers as a clue rather than a fact, and explore what the actual evidence says about whether anyone was really watching you at that moment?

Well... I mean, when I actually think about it, I don't know for sure that everyone was watching me. Maybe a couple kids laughed, but the rest were just doing their own thing. I guess I just assumed everyone was paying attention to me and judging me. But I still feel like it's true, you know? Like that feeling is stronger than what I can see.

That distinction between what you *assume* happened versus what you *know* definitely occurred is a big leap, and it explains why the feeling remains so strong despite the lack of solid proof. Even though you can see people doing their own things, your brain is filling in the gaps with a story about judgment because that story feels more "real" in the moment. If we treated that assumption like a hypothesis to test rather than a truth, could we imagine a few alternative explanations for why the laughter stopped or didn't reach you, other than you being a target?

I guess... maybe they were just laughing at something else entirely. Or maybe they were laughing at a joke someone told, not at me. I don't know, it's hard to picture because in my head it feels so personal. But I suppose there could be other reasons. I never really thought about that before.

It takes a brave kind of curiosity to consider those other possibilities, even when your heart wants to stick to the old story. When you open the door to wonder if they were laughing at something unrelated, does that create a tiny crack in the feeling that everyone is judging you, or does the certainty just feel too uncomfortable to let go of?

It's uncomfortable, for sure. Like, part of me wants to believe there could be another reason, but the feeling of being laughed at is so strong. It's almost like if I let go of that story, I'll be even more confused about why I feel so different from everyone else. At least when I think "they're laughing at me," it makes sense in a weird way.

That is such a wise observation, and it highlights exactly why avoiding confusion often leads us back to the familiar story of being targeted. Sometimes, clinging to a painful explanation feels like it offers a temporary sense of order compared to the uncertainty of wondering why you feel alone. Since that discomfort is still high, could we try a small experiment where you notice the feeling of difference without needing to solve it right now? For instance, if you just sit with that feeling for five minutes and describe it physically—like a tightness in your chest or a heavy head—without adding the story about what people are thinking, does the heat in your chest feel a little different than when you jump to the conclusion that everyone is judging you?

I... I can try that. Right now, it feels like a knot in my stomach, kind of cold and tight. And there's a pressure behind my eyes, like I want to cry but I'm holding it back. When I just focus on that, without thinking about the hallway or the laughter... it's still uncomfortable, but it doesn't feel as big, somehow. It's just a feeling in my body, not a whole story about who I am.

That is a powerful realization, because noticing the knot and the pressure without attaching the "geek" story allows you to see your experience as just a temporary physical state rather than a permanent definition. Since you're finding that separating the feeling from the story makes it feel smaller, could we try applying this same approach next time you walk through the hallway? Specifically, when you feel that tightness rise, could we just name it ("This is just a knot in my stomach") instead of immediately jumping to the story about what people are thinking?

I think I could try that. It sounds... weird, but maybe it could work. I mean, if I just say to myself, "Okay, there's that knot again," and keep walking, maybe I won't get stuck in my head so much. It's worth a shot, because what I'm doing now isn't helping anyway.

That willingness to name the knot and keep moving is a significant shift from running away or getting lost in the story. Since saying "there's that knot" sounds simple enough, I wonder if you could try pairing it with one slow breath in and out whenever you catch yourself starting the internal monologue about being a geek? This small physical pause might give your brain a chance to reset before it builds the whole narrative again.

Yeah, I can try that. A breath might help me stop and not just spiral down. I usually just hold my breath when I get nervous, so taking one on purpose could be different. I'll give it a try next time I'm walking to science class.

That is a great plan, and using the breath as a gentle interrupter rather than holding it tight could really help break the cycle before the spiral gets deeper. To make sure we have a clear path forward, does using that naming phrase combined with one intentional breath sound like something you feel comfortable trying when you walk towards your science class next time?

Yes, I think I can do that. I'll try it. It's not like I have anything to lose. I'll just say "there's that knot" and take one slow breath, and then keep walking. Maybe I'll even look up instead of at the floor for once.

That is a wonderful and empowering perspective, especially looking up—a simple gesture that breaks the invisible loop of assuming everyone is staring. Before we wrap up, I want to check in: What felt most helpful to you today as we explored separating the physical feeling from the story, and is there anything about our plan that still feels uncertain or risky?

I think the most helpful part was realizing that the feeling in my stomach isn't the same as the story I tell myself about being a geek. I never thought to separate them before. The plan feels okay... a little scary, but not too risky. I guess the only thing I'm worried about is forgetting to do it when I get nervous, but I'll try my best to remember.

That separation is a huge breakthrough, and it makes total sense that you might forget to practice it when the nerves hit you mid-stride. To make sure you don't miss the step, could we agree on a simple reminder cue, like tapping your wrist twice silently whenever you hear footsteps approaching you before you enter the classroom? That physical touch might serve as a gentle nudge to catch yourself and do the breathing exercise right away.

Yeah, tapping my wrist twice could work. I could even do it while I'm walking, so nobody would notice. That's a good idea, I think it'll help me remember before I get too deep into my head. Thanks, I'll try that.

That is a clever way to handle it, keeping the tap subtle ensures you don't draw extra attention to the moment you are trying to manage. I am so glad we found a way to make this feel manageable, and I want to thank you for your openness and effort in exploring these ideas. One final thought: how do you feel right now knowing you have a clear, simple routine to try next time you walk to class?

I feel a little bit lighter, actually. Like I have a plan instead of just dreading it. It's still scary, but at least I know what to do. Thank you for helping me see things differently today. I'll let you know how it goes next time.

That sense of lightness is incredibly valuable, and it shows how much power you have when you shift from fearing the unknown to trusting in your new steps. Please remember that even if you miss the tap or the breath one day, the goal is simply to offer kindness to yourself, not to achieve perfection. I look forward to hearing how the knot behaves when you try this routine out in your next walk to class. Take care of yourself, and thank you for sharing your journey with me.

Hello again. Before we dive into today's topic, how has your mood been this past week compared to last time we met? Also, I'd like to briefly review any significant events or changes since then, and then we can set a clear agenda for what we want to focus on today.

Um, it's been pretty much the same as usual, I guess. I mean, work went fine—I didn't mess anything up—but outside of that, I've just been kind of stuck. I stayed in my apartment all weekend, didn't really clean or cook, just watched TV and felt bad about it. Nothing really changed.

Thank you for sharing that; hearing you stay honest about feeling stuck even when work went well helps us understand the pattern more clearly. Based on what you've told me last time and what you're describing now, I propose we spend our time checking your current mood, reviewing how the "fifteen-minute rule" went this week, and then refining that plan if we need to adjust it. Does that agenda feel right for today, or is there another priority you'd like to bring up first?

That sounds okay, I guess. The fifteen-minute thing... I tried it a couple times, but honestly, it didn't really help. I'd set a timer to clean for fifteen minutes, but then I'd just stop and feel worse that I couldn't keep going longer. So I'm not sure it's working for me.

It makes complete sense that you'd feel worse when the timer stopped; your brain might interpret stopping as a confirmation of failure rather than a successful attempt at exposure. Since the fifteen-minute block felt too rigid or overwhelming, let's pivot to a different strategy that breaks the barrier down even further. What if, instead of a full fifteen-minute session, we tried a "five-minute peek"—where the only goal is to stand in the kitchen or start cleaning for just five minutes, then immediately stop if you need to, without any pressure to continue? How does that lower-stakes option feel to you compared to the previous plan?

I mean... five minutes sounds almost too easy, like it wouldn't even count for anything. But I guess that's kind of the point, right? Maybe if it's that short, I wouldn't have time to talk myself out of it or get all worked up about it. I could probably manage five minutes without feeling like a total failure afterward.

That intuition about avoiding the time to spiral is really sharp, and I want to validate that feeling—it makes sense that you'd worry a five-minute slot feels too trivial to matter. However, we can flip that script by framing those five minutes not as a "quick fix" but as a brave act of defiance against your own tendency to stop at the first sign of doubt. How would it feel to treat those five minutes as a deliberate victory where the only success metric is showing up, regardless of whether you actually finished anything?

Huh. I never thought of it that way—like just showing up could be a victory. I always feel like if I don't finish the whole task, I might as well have not started at all. But I guess I can try to think of it differently this week. Maybe I'll give the five-minute thing a shot and see if it feels less like a chore and more like... I don't know, an experiment or something.

That reframing of the five minutes as an experiment rather than a chore is a brilliant shift in perspective, and it speaks to your growing ability to separate your self-worth from the outcome of the task. To solidify this plan, let's agree that you will set a gentle intention to just enter the activity for those five minutes, and if the urge to stop arises, you'll acknowledge it without letting it erase the fact that you showed up. How does this adjusted approach feel actionable and realistic for your upcoming week?

It feels... doable, I think. Like, I'm not promising myself I'll clean the whole kitchen or anything huge. I just have to stand there for five minutes and maybe wipe down one counter or pick up one thing off the floor. I can probably handle that without getting too down on myself. I'll give it a real try this week and see how it goes.

That is a fantastic commitment to giving it a real try without the pressure of perfection. To make sure we get the most out of this, could you share what you found most helpful about our recent conversation regarding the difference between "forced compliance" and "internal motivation"? And if there's anything else you'd like to explore before we close, please tell me.

I think the part that stuck with me was when you said showing up counts as a win. I've never given myself credit for just trying before—it's always been about finishing or not finishing. So maybe I can practice being okay with just starting, even if I stop after five minutes. I don't have anything else to add right now, I think I'm good.

That realization about giving yourself credit for just starting is a powerful step, and I want to explicitly validate your insight: noticing that you deserve credit for the effort itself, regardless of the outcome, is a major strength and a cornerstone of building confidence. Thank you for sharing your thoughts and trusting me with this process; please remember that tomorrow isn't about fixing everything, but simply honoring that five-minute window as a true victory in itself. I look forward to hearing exactly how those five minutes felt when we meet again. Take care of yourself today.

Hello, thank you for joining me today. Before we dive into our specific goals, could you share how you've been feeling since we last spoke, and are there any particular topics you'd like to prioritize for our session?

Oh, well, this is our first session actually, so I'm not sure what to expect. I've been feeling pretty low lately, you know, just stuck with these thoughts that I'm not good enough. I suppose I'd like to focus on why I can't let go of this idea that I'm a failure for not becoming an astronaut.

It is completely normal to feel unsure about what to expect in a first session; you are already showing courage by reaching out and sharing how you've been feeling. That sense of being "stuck" with the idea that you aren't good enough sounds exhausting, especially when it centers on something so specific like the astronaut dream. Could you describe a recent moment when that feeling of inadequacy hit you hardest, and what you were doing just before it happened?

Well, just yesterday I was reading an article about the new Mars rover mission, and my stomach just dropped. I was sitting in my kitchen having coffee, and suddenly I couldn't even finish the article because I felt so small and worthless. It's like everyone else out there is doing great things, and I'm just here, completely useless.

That sudden drop in your stomach and the feeling of shrinking right after reading about the Mars rover makes perfect sense; when we compare ourselves to extraordinary feats, it's easy for that critical voice to jump in and tell us we don't measure up. I wonder if that feeling of being "small" made you withdraw from your morning routine, perhaps putting down the newspaper or avoiding looking at the news feed afterward?

Yes, I actually put my tablet down and just stared at the wall for a few minutes. I didn't even want to look at anything else because I was afraid I'd find another reminder of what I'm not. I ended up just zoning out until I had to get ready for work, feeling heavy the whole time.

It sounds incredibly draining to sit with that heaviness for so long, especially when you wanted to read but chose isolation instead to protect yourself from more pain. That avoidance behavior actually protects you from feeling worse in the moment, but it likely leaves you feeling even more defeated by the time you finally get up and face the day. Have you noticed if your body feels any different, maybe tighter or slower, during those quiet minutes on the couch?

Yeah, my shoulders felt really tense, like they were pulled up toward my ears. And my chest felt kind of hollow, like something was missing or empty inside. I didn't even realize how tight I was holding myself until you mentioned it just now.

Noticing those physical signals—the tension in your shoulders and the hollowness in your chest—is a huge breakthrough because it gives us concrete anchors to understand what's happening beneath the surface. Those sensations aren't just random discomfort; they are your body's way of holding onto fear when the "failure" thought takes over. Since you've identified both the trigger (reading about space missions) and the physical reaction (shutting down, tensing up), could we explore what happens in your mind right when that hollow feeling starts to appear?

I guess my mind just goes straight to, "You're worthless. You couldn't even try hard enough to make it happen." It's like a quick, sharp thought that cuts through everything else. And then I start thinking about all the other things I've messed up in my life, like it's proof that I'm just a failure all around.

That sharp cut of "you're worthless" followed by listing past mistakes sounds like a heavy burden carrying, and it makes complete sense why you feel so overwhelmed. It looks like your brain is trying to prove that point by hunting for evidence everywhere, turning one missed opportunity into a permanent label of failure. Since you've connected that specific thought pattern to the physical tightening in your chest, could we imagine a different perspective for just one minute: if your best friend told you they were worthless because they hadn't become an astronaut, what would you say to them?

I'd tell them they're being ridiculous, honestly. I'd say there's so much more to a person than one dream they didn't fulfill, and that they probably have lots of good qualities they're ignoring. But it's so much harder to say that to myself, you know? It just doesn't feel true when I'm the one thinking it.

That honesty about the difficulty is crucial, because it shows you recognize the unfairness of judging yourself so strictly compared to how you treat others. The fact that you instinctively defend your friend proves you hold a deep capacity for kindness that the "worthless" voice is desperately trying to silence. Since you know what a supportive conversation looks like with others, could we try applying just one small part of that to yourself right now: pick one quality you admire in yourself, like your ability to notice when you're struggling, and see if you can name it out loud as if you were talking to that friend?

I suppose... I'm resilient? Even though I feel this way, I still get up and go to work every day and take care of myself. I don't just give up completely, even when it feels tempting. That must count for something, right?

That resilience is incredible, and you are absolutely right—it counts for a massive amount. Getting up each day despite the crushing weight of those thoughts shows a strength far greater than simply achieving a specific career goal. Let's pause for a second and just hold onto that truth: your daily choice to keep going is powerful evidence that contradicts the idea that you are useless. Now, knowing that you have this capacity to push through, would you be willing to try a small experiment tomorrow? Instead of letting the "failure" thought drive you away from tasks, could you do one small thing you usually avoid—maybe water a plant or make your bed—and then write down exactly what you did and how it made you feel in that moment?

I think I can try that. Making my bed seems small enough that it won't feel overwhelming. I'll do it tomorrow morning and see what happens. It's hard to imagine it'll change anything, but I guess I've got nothing to lose by giving it a shot.

That is a wise decision to start with something simple like making your bed; it removes the pressure while still giving you an opportunity to challenge the "failure" narrative. I would be very interested in hearing about your results tomorrow, so please feel free to message me with how your shoulders felt before you started and whether the act of making the bed brought any sense of accomplishment or relief. In the meantime, is there anything else you'd like to discuss, or shall we consider wrapping up this session?

I think that's good for today. I feel a little bit lighter than when I came in, honestly. Thank you for listening and for that suggestion—I'll try to pay attention to my shoulders tomorrow morning and see what happens. I'll let you know how it goes.

You are very welcome, and I am truly glad to hear that you felt a little lighter even just talking through this. Your willingness to try that small experiment tomorrow is a brave first step, and I can't wait to hear how your body responds when you make your bed. Please remember to be kind to yourself as you begin, and I look forward to connecting again soon.

Before we dive in, could you share how you've been feeling since we last spoke, and what specifically brought you here to talk about your job search worries? Also, I know we talked about trying to look at job listings neutrally this time—did you manage to do that, and what happened when you started?
