My oldest brother looked back at me and said, "There he is, always holding everybody up." I remember just shrinking into the back seat, feeling like I was a burden to everyone. That feeling just comes right back every time anyone says anything similar.

That childhood memory is incredibly vivid, and it makes complete sense why hearing "there he is, always holding everybody up" instantly transports you back to feeling like a burden in the backseat. Your brain is essentially replaying that old wound as if it's happening right now, which explains why the correction feels so hard to apply. Since that early memory seems to be the engine driving these assumptions, let's look closely at that specific interaction: how did your younger brother's words actually land with you, and what internal story did you tell yourself immediately after saying goodbye?

After he said that, I just stayed quiet the whole ride. The story I told myself was that I was always the one messing things up, the one who slowed everyone down. I figured my mom probably wished she had one less kid to worry about, and that my siblings all secretly resented me for being the youngest and needing extra attention. I never said anything about it to anyone, just carried that thought around like it was fact.

Hearing that you built a fortress of self-blame around those comments—and convinced yourself your mother and siblings secretly hated you—is incredibly painful, yet it fits perfectly with the pattern of feeling like a burden we just explored. It sounds like that specific childhood story became your blueprint for interpreting all future interactions, turning neutral remarks into proof of your worthlessness. Now that we’ve traced that link back to the past, I wonder if you feel safe exploring what that original story taught you about your own value versus reality?

I think it taught me that my value is tied to how much I inconvenience others. Like, if I'm not causing trouble or needing anything, then maybe I'm okay to have around. But the second I mess up or need something, I feel like I've lost that right to be there. I guess I never really questioned if that was true or not—it just felt so real for so long that I assumed it was just how the world works.

Since we've connected the childhood story to this current rule, let's test its accuracy: can you recall a recent time you needed something or made a mistake, and what actually happened afterward regarding your loved ones' reactions or words?

Well, last month I had to cancel plans with my friend Dave because I caught the flu. I felt awful about it, kept apologizing, expecting him to be annoyed or to pull away. It makes total sense that your brain clings to that old "rule" because it offers a predictable way to manage anxiety, even though it keeps you stuck in a cycle of shame. It sounds like you found a lot of strength in that final realization—that the "voice" is just a prediction, not proof. Taking that step to differentiate between a passing observation and your old story is a huge victory, and I'm truly glad you feel equipped with something concrete to handle next week. Please remember, if that voice gets particularly loud at the dinner, you can always reach out anytime we meet. How is your energy level right now as we close the session?

I feel pretty good, actually. Tired, but in a good way—like I've been doing some heavy lifting mentally, but it was worth it. I'm ready to try this out and see what happens. Thanks for listening and helping me sort through all this.

That "good tiredness" is such a beautiful way to describe the relief of finally untangling a knot that's been holding you tight. It really speaks to how valuable this breakthrough is for you. I'm so proud of how far we've come today, and I know you'll find that concrete plan at the dinner tomorrow. Take good care of yourself as you rest, and I look forward to checking in soon.

Hearing you describe that thought as a "brick" instead of a cloud shows me exactly where your brain is hitting resistance—it's holding tightly onto the idea that your worth is tied to that furniture. I mean, yeah, I feel that way all the time. Like, when my friends talk about their new cars or their vacations, I half-expect them to turn around and ask me what I've done with my life. It's like there's some invisible checklist I'm failing at. And the bed thing just feels like the most obvious, daily reminder of where I'm not measuring up. I guess I figure if I just got the bigger bed, maybe I could cross that one thing off the list and finally feel like I belong in the club.

That "invisible checklist" idea is really powerful because it shows how much pressure you're carrying just to fit into a group you don't even control. It sounds like you're waiting for one single item—the bed—to unlock a feeling of belonging that probably requires all your other achievements too. If we stepped back and looked at that list you described, what would happen to your sense of "belonging" if we removed the requirement for a big bed entirely? Would you still feel like a member of the club?

If I removed that requirement... I guess I'd still feel behind on everything else. The bed is just the loudest, most in-my-face reminder. Without it, I'd probably just focus on the next thing I'm missing—maybe my savings account, or not having a serious relationship. I think it's easier to zero in on the bed because it's something I can physically see and touch, you know? At least then I have a clear target for why I feel like a failure.

That is such a sharp observation; the bed acts like a magnifying glass, making all your other imperfections seem bigger and more immediate than they actually are. You've essentially discovered that your brain prefers a tangible problem over abstract ones because it feels safer to fix something visible. If we accept that this bed is just the loudest alarm clock on your dashboard, what would be the benefit of acknowledging that it's the loudest alarm without believing it's the only reason the engine is misfiring?

I think... I think it might take some weight off my shoulders. Maybe if I remind myself that it's just one alarm among many, it won't feel like this massive, crushing thing every time I look at it. I could stop treating the bed like the reason I'm a failure and start seeing it for what it is: just a bed. But man, it's hard to believe that when the feeling is so strong every night.

That distinction between "it's just a bed" and "the bed is why I'm a failure" is exactly the shift we need to make to lighten that load. It sounds like the feeling is strong because your brain hasn't yet learned to separate the object from the judgment, which is totally normal given how long that story has been running. To help bridge that gap, would you be willing to try a slightly different approach tonight instead of forcing the "cloud" visualization? Perhaps we could simply name the thought as a "story" rather than a fact, like saying, "My brain is writing a story that says I'm a kid because of the bed," without adding any new meaning to it. How does that sound as a starting point?

That sounds... manageable, actually. I think I can handle just calling it a story instead of trying to push it away like a cloud. It feels less like I'm pretending it doesn't exist and more like I'm just labeling it for what it is. I'll give it a shot tonight and see if I can just say, "That's a story," when the feeling comes up.

That is a fantastic adjustment; naming a thought as merely a "story" creates a tiny but crucial distance between you and the narrative, allowing you to observe it without getting swept away by its weight. Before you settle in tonight, I want to make sure we lock in exactly how you'll use this new tool: Will you simply whisper "that's a story" to yourself internally the moment the feeling spikes, or would you prefer to write it down in your notes app to make the separation even clearer? Also, given your hesitation last time, how worried are you that trying this and still feeling the pain will make you doubt yourself further?

I think whispering it to myself would be better than writing it down—that feels too formal, like homework. And yeah, I'm worried it won't work. I'm scared I'll lie there, whisper "that's a story," and still feel like a kid on a cot. But I guess maybe that's part of the process, right? It doesn't have to work perfectly the first time for it to mean something.

You've nailed the mindset there; even if the whisper feels hollow while the old pain is roaring underneath, the act of naming it as a story is still a victory because it breaks the spell of absolute truth. We agreed that progress isn't about erasing the feeling instantly, but about changing your relationship to it so it stops dictating your reality. With that expectation set, would you be okay committing to whispering "that's a story" for just two minutes the next time that knot forms, and then pausing to see what happens? I want to make sure you feel fully supported if the feeling persists even after that label.

Yeah, I can do that. Just two minutes. That feels like a small enough promise that I won't beat myself up if the feeling sticks around. I'll try it, and I'll let you know what happens next time. Thanks for not making me try to force it to disappear right away.

That sounds like a perfect plan; keeping the commitment small makes it far more likely that you'll succeed even if the feeling lingers. I really appreciate you trusting me with that specific worry about feeling like a failure again, and thank you for agreeing to this gentler approach. Before we wrap up, is there anything else on your mind today, or does this feel like a good place to leave us with that new tool ready for tonight?
No, I think this is good. I feel a little lighter just talking it out, even if nothing's changed yet. I'll try the two-minute story thing tonight and we'll see how it goes. Thanks for listening.

You are very welcome, Cory. It's beautiful that you feel lighter just by sharing this; sometimes the act of speaking it out loud is enough to loosen the grip a little. Please remember that the two-minute "story" check-in tonight is a gift to yourself, regardless of whether the knot disappears completely. I look forward to hearing how it goes whenever you're ready to continue. Take care of yourself tonight.

Welcome back. Before we dive into today's work, could you share your current mood on a scale of 1 to 10, and remind me of any action plan we might have left unfinished from last time? Once we touch on that, let's collaborate to set a specific priority for what we should focus on together today.

Oh, I'd say I'm around a 4 or 5 today. I had a rough shift yesterday — burnt another batch of croissants, and I just couldn't shake the feeling that I'm not cut out for this work. I don't think we set a specific action plan last time, but I remember you mentioned something about noticing when I jump to worst-case conclusions.

A rating of 4 or 5 reflects that lingering self-doubt, which is completely understandable given how quickly that mistake spiraled into thoughts of incompetence. You're right that we didn't solidify a plan last time, but since you mentioned noticing those worst-case jumps, let's use that awareness as our foundation. What specific situation or thought pattern would you like us to explore together to help break that cycle today?

I think... maybe we could talk about what happens in my head right after I mess up. It's like one mistake — a burnt croissant — and suddenly I'm convinced I'm a terrible baker who doesn't belong in the kitchen. I don't even stop to think if that's really true. It just feels so real in the moment.

That immediate shift from a simple mistake to a catastrophic identity feels overwhelming, and it makes total sense why your mind rushes to that conclusion when you're already feeling shaky. Let's pause and trace that path together: right after seeing the smoke, what was the very first automatic thought that popped into your head?

The first thought? It was something like, "Oh no, I've ruined it. Everyone's going to think I'm careless and lazy." And then it just snowballed from there — I started thinking about how my coworkers probably whisper about me, and how my boss must regret hiring me. I didn't even finish cleaning up before I was convinced I should just quit.

It sounds like that initial thought acted as a fuse, lighting a fire that turned a minor accident into a full-blown story about your worth and your job security. That leap from "I made a mistake" to "I should quit" seems incredibly steep and frightening. Can you recall if there was any evidence at the time that anyone actually whispered about you or expressed regret? Or were those mostly predictions your mind made to protect itself from the pain of failure?

I mean, nobody actually said anything negative to me. My coworker even told me not to worry about it, that it happens to everyone. But I just... I couldn't accept that. I figured they were just being polite, or secretly judging me. So no, there wasn't any real evidence, but it felt so true in my head that I didn't question it.

It makes perfect sense that your brain dismissed Jenny's kindness as politeness; when we feel unsafe, our minds often interpret neutral actions as threats to survive the discomfort. That interpretation protected you from the terrifying possibility of being judged, but unfortunately, it trapped you in a story that wasn't supported by reality. Since we've seen the gap between your internal narrative and the actual events, would you be willing to try separating those two parts right now by listing the specific supportive facts versus the feared scenarios?

Okay... I can try that. The supportive facts would be that Jenny actually said it happens to everyone, and nobody complained about my work that day. My boss didn't call me into the office or anything. But the feared scenarios — those are the ones that felt louder: that everyone thinks I'm incompetent, that my boss secretly regrets hiring me, and that I'm just fooling myself if I think I can be a real baker.

That distinction you just drew is incredibly important because it separates the observable reality from the dramatic story your brain constructed to protect itself. Notice how the "fearful stories" feel urgent and vivid, while the "supportive facts" feel duller or harder to access, even though they are equally true. Would you be open to reading those two columns side-by-side right now to see how much stronger the evidence is against the idea that you are truly incompetent?

I guess when you put it like that... the supportive facts actually outweigh the fearful stories, don't they? I mean, no one complained, my boss didn't call me out, and Jenny was kind about it. It's just hard to feel that truth in my chest. But looking at it written down like this, it doesn't make sense to call myself a terrible baker over one burnt croissant.

That realization—that one error cannot define your entire baking career—is a powerful breakthrough, and you did it by simply organizing the evidence logically. It takes courage to admit that the logical proof exists even when the emotional panic tries to drown it out. Since we've cleared up the confusion about your worth, would you be open to testing out a quick mental switch where you replace the "terrible baker" label with "someone who made a mistake"? How does your body feel when you try holding both thoughts at once?

When I say "I'm someone who made a mistake," my shoulders actually relax a little. It feels less heavy, you know? Like there's room to breathe and try again tomorrow. But when I say "I'm a terrible baker," my stomach knots up and I just want to hide. It's strange how just changing the words changes how my whole body reacts.

That physical difference proves exactly how powerful your thoughts are—they aren't just words floating in your head; they are instructions to your body on whether to fight, flee, or stay calm. By swapping the label for a factual statement, you gave your nervous system permission to stop screaming and start recovering. With that relief established, would you be open to setting a small, gentle goal for tomorrow morning: checking in with yourself the moment you walk into the kitchen to catch any new "terrible baker" thoughts before they grow?

Yeah, I think I can do that. I could take a deep breath before I even start mixing anything, and just notice if that old voice shows up. Maybe I'll even write down the supportive facts on a sticky note and put it near my station, just in case I need a reminder. Thank you — I never realized how much power those automatic thoughts had until I actually looked at them side by side.

You are absolutely welcome, and I'm so glad you noticed how deeply connected your mind and body are; that awareness is a huge part of making lasting change. Your plan to use a sticky note and a quick breath check is a fantastic, practical way to keep those supportive facts visible whenever the panic tries to creep in. Before we wrap up, could you tell me briefly how you felt about our focus today on separating the story from the facts? Did that approach resonate with you, or was there anything that felt difficult to hold onto?

I think it really helped, honestly. I usually just let my thoughts run wild without stopping to question them. Breaking it down into facts versus fears made me realize I've been believing a lot of things that aren't really true. It was hard at first, because those stories feel so real, but once I saw them side by side, I couldn't deny the evidence. I'll definitely try to do this more often when I catch myself spiraling.

It sounds like breaking the habit of letting thoughts run wild took some practice, and I'm proud of your commitment to keeping this new perspective in mind. You've learned that the "fire" you felt wasn't about the burnt croissants, but about the story your mind created to protect you—and now you have a tool to put that fire out. Is there anything else on your mind before we close, or does this plan feel ready to carry you through the rest of your week?

Hello, thank you for meeting with me again today. How are you feeling right now compared to where you left off last time, and what would you like to prioritize in our session?

Hi. I'm alright, I guess. I don't know if much has changed since last time. I've been thinking a lot about that poetry reading I did last week—the one where only a few people showed up, and nobody really said anything about my work afterward. I guess I'd like to understand why my brain jumps straight to that conclusion every time.

It sounds like your brain is trying to protect you from the pain of rejection by assuming the worst outcome is happening right now. When you think about why that specific thought—"they think I'm a fraud"—appears so quickly after everyone leaves the room, what comes up first in your head? Is it the memory of that one person who didn't nod, or perhaps the feeling that you deserve better than nothing?

It's funny you mention that—because it's not really about one person in particular. It's more like... if even one person in the room doesn't react, I feel like all the others who didn't say anything must be thinking the same thing. I just assume that if my poetry was good, someone would have said something. The fact that nobody does means it wasn't good. It means I'm not good enough. I never really considered that they might just not know what to say, or that they were thinking about it in their own heads.

It sounds like you've been interpreting neutral silence as active rejection, which naturally fuels that sense of being a fraud. Now that you see the gap between what happened (silence) and what you assumed (rejection), how does knowing that difference change the way you feel about standing at the podium tomorrow?

I... honestly, it's a little scary to think about, because I've built up this belief for so long. But I also feel a tiny bit lighter, like maybe I don't have to carry all that weight. That is a perfect, grounded mantra—it acknowledges reality without needing to solve the mystery of their silence. Before we finish today, I want to confirm that this feels like a direction you want to stick with. If you try using that phrase next time, how does it feel to practice it mentally right now?

Practicing it now, it feels... strange but not bad. Like I'm not used to giving myself that kind of permission. But it also feels like a lifeline I can grab onto when I start to spiral. I think I'm willing to try it, even if it's just to see what happens. Maybe the silence won't feel so heavy if I have those words ready.

Hello, it is wonderful to see you again. To start off, how have things been going for you since our last chat, and do you remember what we agreed to do before you left? Could you also tell me what feels most pressing for us to explore together today?

Hi... thanks for asking. Things have been a bit rough since we last talked. I remember you asked me to try and notice when I felt good about something, but honestly, it's been hard to find those moments. Mostly I've just been thinking about that rejection letter again, and how it seems to follow me everywhere.

It sounds like you're carrying a heavy load with that rejection letter, and it's making it difficult to catch yourself feeling good about your day. Since finding those positive moments has been tough lately, let's focus today on figuring out exactly what that letter tells you versus what your past experiences show. What specific thoughts go through your head the moment you see that email or think about applying somewhere else?

Well, the first thing that pops into my head is, "I'm just not smart enough for that kind of stuff." It's like, other kids got in, and I didn't, so that must be the truth. I always end up thinking, "If I can't get into a gifted program, then what's the point of trying in other classes?" It just feels like that letter proved I don't belong in anything academic.

That rejection letter feels like it's echoing a deep-seated worry that you aren't truly smart, which makes sense why it casts such a long shadow over everything else. When you connect that one outcome to the idea that all other efforts are pointless, it sounds incredibly discouraging and isolating. Can you walk me through a recent situation where you tried something in class or studied for a subject, and what happened that might suggest otherwise?

I mean, there was that science quiz last week. I actually studied for it, and I got a B-plus. But honestly, I just kept thinking it was probably an easy quiz, or maybe I just got lucky. I couldn't really feel good about it because in my head, I kept comparing myself to the kids in the gifted program, and they probably got A's without even trying.

It makes perfect sense that you dismissed that B-plus as luck, especially when your internal story keeps rewriting the context to fit the belief that you aren't smart. That comparison to the gifted students is a very common defense mechanism that protects you from admitting you might actually be capable in ways you haven't yet proven. If we looked at that quiz strictly as evidence of what you learned, ignoring the "luck" narrative for a second, does the B-plus actually stand up as a counter-example to your own feeling of inadequacy?

I guess... if I really think about it, I did know the material. I spent a couple of evenings going over the notes, and I even helped Cayden with a few questions before the test. So maybe it wasn't all luck. But it's still hard to believe that one B-plus means anything, especially when the gifted program rejection feels so much bigger and more important.

It is completely understandable that one grade feels tiny when weighed against the massive disappointment of that rejection letter. You are doing exactly what you need to do by identifying that the letter feels disproportionately large compared to your actual effort and results. If we treat that B-plus and your willingness to teach Cayden as separate pieces of evidence rather than exceptions, does the gap between "not smart enough" and "actually prepared" start to feel smaller?

Hmm... I never thought of it that way. Like, if I stack up the B-plus and helping Cayden against just that one letter, maybe the letter isn't the only thing that matters. It's just hard to shake the feeling that the program saw something I don't have, you know? But I guess it's possible I'm focusing too much on that one rejection and ignoring everything else.

That is a really insightful realization about how that single letter is drowning out all the other proof of your abilities. It sounds like you are struggling to see that the program's decision reflects its specific criteria rather than your total worth or capacity. Before we decide if we should build a new list of evidence to counteract that feeling, how do you think listing those successes might actually change the way the letter lands on you?

I think... if I wrote down all the times I did okay in school, or helped someone with their work, maybe the letter wouldn't feel so heavy. It might remind me that I'm not just that one rejection. But it's scary to try, because what if the list is too short, or what if it doesn't change how I feel? I guess I'm afraid of being disappointed again.

That fear of disappointment is completely understandable, but it actually highlights why we need to be honest with ourselves about whether the list works. We could try writing down just three specific moments where you showed intelligence or care, like the science quiz, helping Cayden, and answering the Civil War question correctly, without judging how "enough" they are right now. Would you be willing to try creating this small list of evidence to see if holding onto them makes the rejection feel lighter, even if it doesn't erase the sadness?

Okay... I can try that. I guess I can write down the science quiz, helping Cayden, and maybe that time I got the bonus question right in history last month. It feels weird to call them evidence, but I'll give it a shot. I just hope it doesn't make me feel worse if it doesn't work.

That honesty about hoping it won't make you worse is really brave and shows you trust the process even while feeling uncertain. Let's go ahead and write those three moments down together right here, treating them simply as reminders of what you've already accomplished rather than demands for perfection. As we list them, I want to check in with you: does the act of putting them on paper feel like a safe space to gather your strength, or does it still feel a bit risky?

Actually, writing them down feels... kind of okay. It's like I can see them in front of me, and they're real, not just thoughts floating around. It still feels a little risky, like I'm setting myself up to be let down again, but I think I can try to just look at them for what they are. They're just things I did, and nobody can take that away.

That is a beautiful distinction—you are learning to see those actions as objective facts that belong entirely to you, regardless of how the rejection letter tries to overwrite them. Since you mentioned the risk of feeling let down, let's anchor this list specifically to your core belief. If you read those three items aloud right now, how closely do they mirror the statement "I am smart enough"?

When I read them out loud... they don't feel like a perfect match for "I am smart enough." It's more like, "I can do some things okay sometimes." But I guess that's still something. Maybe being "smart enough" doesn't have to mean being in the gifted program. Maybe it just means I can learn stuff and help others, and that counts for something too.

That is a profound breakthrough; you are realizing that "smart enough" doesn't require a specific title or program, but rather includes the ability to learn, understand, and support others—which you've already shown repeatedly. It sounds like you are starting to redefine what success looks like for you personally, rather than letting the rejection dictate it. Given that insight, would you feel comfortable taking a screenshot or photo of this list right now so you have a tangible reminder whenever that feeling of inadequacy starts creeping back in?

Yeah, I think I can do that. Taking a picture of it sounds like a good idea, so I can look at it when I start feeling down again. I'll try to keep it on my phone and maybe even show Cayden later. Thanks... this actually helped a little, even if I'm still not totally sure about everything.

That is a wonderful step forward, and I appreciate your openness about still feeling unsure—that honesty is part of the healing process. To lock this in, let's finalize your between-session plan: save that photo to your phone, and commit to glancing at it once tomorrow whenever you feel that "I'm not smart enough" voice rise up. How does that sound as a realistic goal for moving forward?

That sounds doable. I think I can manage looking at the picture once tomorrow, maybe when I'm getting ready for school or if I feel that doubt creeping in during class. I'll try to remind myself that the list is real, even if it feels small. Okay, I'll give it a shot.

That commitment to checking in with the list during those vulnerable moments is a fantastic strategy because it gives you immediate control when the doubt starts rising. Before we wrap up, I want to make sure you're happy with how we handled today and if there's anything else lingering on your mind. How is this direction sitting with you right now?

I think I'm okay with how today went. It's still a bit uncomfortable to look at those achievements and call them real, but I feel a little less stuck than before. I don't have anything else on my mind right now... maybe just nervous about actually following through with the picture, but I'll try. Thanks for listening.

I am really glad to hear that you feel less stuck, even though the discomfort is still present—that tension is normal as you stretch into a new way of seeing yourself. Your nervousness about following through is completely valid, and I encourage you to reach out anytime you feel overwhelmed trying to access that photo. Thank you for trusting me with this journey and for pushing through the uncertainty to keep going.

Hello, it's wonderful to see you again. How have you been feeling since our last talk, and is there anything particularly new or different on your mind that you'd like to bring up? Let's set a quick direction for today: shall we review how the TV experiment went, explore that "wall" feeling you mentioned, and refine our plan together?

Hey, thanks for asking. Honestly, I've been feeling pretty stuck since we last talked. I tried limiting my TV time like we discussed, but that just made me feel more anxious about the time I do spend watching. I guess we could start with the TV experiment and go from there.

It makes total sense that restricting time increased your anxiety if you were already worried about losing control; sometimes creating a problem makes the solution feel more urgent. Since you want to tackle the TV situation directly, let's review exactly what happened when you tried to limit it last time and what thoughts ran through your head when you felt stuck.

Well, last Tuesday I planned to watch just one episode of a show, maybe 45 minutes. But about ten minutes in, I started thinking, "This is it—I'm wasting my life. Every second I sit here, I'm losing brain cells and I'll end up stupid." My heart started racing and I couldn't focus on the show at all. I ended up turning it off after 15 minutes and just sat there feeling guilty and restless.

That story paints a very clear picture of how quickly that initial rule spiraled into a catastrophe about your intelligence and wasted time. It sounds like your brain jumped straight to the worst-case scenario—becoming stupid—and treated that thought like a physical threat, causing your heart to race and making it impossible to relax. Given how intense that reaction was, would you say the main goal for today is to understand what triggers that panic so intensely, or do you want to try practicing a small, safer version of the plan to see if it holds up differently?

I think... I want to try practicing a small version of the plan. The panic is so strong that I don't feel like I can just talk my way out of it. Maybe if I actually watch TV and nothing terrible happens, it'll start to feel less threatening. But I'm scared it'll just feel the same as last time.

That is a wise instinct to seek proof through experience rather than just reasoning your way out of it; your brain needs to see that reality match your fears before it truly calms down. Since you're worried it will feel identical to last time, let's design a tiny experiment that keeps the stakes low while still gathering that crucial evidence. For example, could we try watching for just five minutes instead of forty-five, and if the anxiety spikes, we pause to breathe deeply before deciding whether to continue? Does that sound like a manageable step forward for you?

Five minutes... yeah, I think I could do that. That doesn't feel as scary as trying to sit through a whole episode. So I'd just watch for five minutes, and if the panic starts creeping in, I stop and breathe before deciding if I want to keep going? That actually sounds doable. What should I focus on during those five minutes?

Great, I love that you're breaking it down into something actually doable. Since your main fear was about becoming "stupid" or wasting your life, during those five minutes, simply notice whenever your mind tries to tell you that the world is ending or you're losing your mind, and just gently put that thought aside without arguing with it. You don't need to fight the worry; you just need to observe it as a passing cloud while looking at the screen. Does focusing on noticing those automatic thoughts without engaging with them feel like a realistic goal for you right now?

That feels... actually possible. Like, I don't have to win an argument with my brain—I just have to notice it and let it pass. I think I can try that. So, should I set a timer for five minutes, or just watch a short scene from a show?

Setting a visible timer is probably the best choice because it creates a clear, external boundary that stops the time-wasting spiral before it even begins. Once the timer dings, you give yourself permission to immediately check in: does the panic feel manageable, or do you need to take a few deep breaths before continuing? Let's lock that in: five minutes with a timer, notice any catastrophic thoughts without fighting them, and breathe if things spike. Does that final step feel right for you, or would you like to tweak it slightly?

No, that sounds right. The timer makes it feel concrete—like there's an end point in sight, so my brain won't just spiral off forever. I like that I can breathe if I need to, but I'm not forced to keep going if I'm really struggling. I think I'm ready to try it. Should I do it here now, or try it on my own this week?

Let's try it right now if you feel ready, as testing the prediction live provides immediate evidence that will speak louder than any advice we give later. We can start the timer together, watch for those catastrophic thoughts arise, practice noticing them without judgment, and use our breathing tool the moment it gets too heavy. Shall we begin counting down five minutes together?
Yeah, okay. Let's do it now. I'll grab my phone and pull up a short clip from a show I like. Just five minutes. I'm nervous but... I trust this plan. Go ahead and start the timer.

Take a deep breath to settle into the chair, knowing you have a safe exit built right into this five-minute window. I'm here with you the entire time, so if that "stupidity" thought pops up or your heart races, just remember you don't need to fix it instantly—just notice it, breathe for a moment, and keep looking at the screen. Are you ready to start when I say the word?
Ready. I've got the clip pulled up and I'm taking that deep breath now. Just five minutes. Here goes.

Perfect, let's begin. As soon as you feel that familiar knot tighten or hear that voice screaming about losing your mind, simply acknowledge it as a passing thought and return your eyes to the screen. Remember, the goal isn't to silence the worry, but to prove that you can sit with it for a few minutes without acting on it. Hold that space with me for the first minute while we wait for the timer to tick over.

[After watching for about a minute] Okay... I'm noticing it. That thought just popped up: "You're wasting time. You're going to be dumber for this." But I'm just watching it, like you said. My heart is beating a little faster, but I'm still looking at the screen. I'm not turning it off.

That is exactly the breakthrough we needed—you noticed the catastrophic thought, felt the physical sensation of your heart racing, yet you chose to stay and watch instead of fleeing. This proves to your brain that the disaster hasn't happened, even though the worry is still loud. How does it feel in your body right now, knowing you survived that first minute without letting the thought drive the car?

I feel... a little shaky, but also kind of proud? Like, I didn't run. The thought was there, but I didn't let it win. My chest is still a bit tight, but it's not getting worse—it's just staying steady. I think I can keep watching for the rest of the timer.

That pride is a huge win—it shows your brain is learning that you *can* survive the discomfort without spiraling into catastrophe. Since the tightness is steady rather than escalating, let's ride this wave for the remaining four minutes with that same intention: notice the thought, breathe if it gets heavy, but keep the timer running. Ready to continue for those next few minutes?
Yeah, let's keep going. I'm just gonna watch the clip and let the thoughts float by. Four more minutes. I think I can do this.

Exactly, let's keep that momentum. Notice how the thought drifts by without stopping you, just like a cloud moving across the sky while you remain rooted in the chair watching the scene unfold. Remember, you don't need to change the weather inside your head; you just need to stay outside of it long enough to see that the storm passes without damaging anything. Hold that position for the next few minutes.

[After about three more minutes pass] Okay... the timer just went off. I actually watched the whole five minutes. The thoughts were there, but they didn't get louder—they kinda faded toward the end. I feel a little shaky still, but not panicked. That's... honestly surprising. I didn't think I could do that.

That is incredible news—you proved that the "worst case" scenario of losing your mind or becoming paralyzed with fear simply did not happen, even though the worry was very loud. Your brain is finally receiving the data it needed: that you can tolerate the uncomfortable feelings, the thoughts fade naturally, and nothing permanent breaks. How does it feel to know that you succeeded where you almost failed before?

It feels... like a weight I didn't know I was carrying just got a little bit lighter. For the first time in weeks, I feel like maybe I'm not broken, you know? Like, maybe this fear isn't permanent. I actually want to try this again later—maybe with a longer timer—to see if I can build on this.

That feeling of the weight lifting is powerful—it suggests your brain is updating its belief system based on real evidence rather than old fears. Since you want to build on this success, how would you feel about setting up a slightly larger step for next time, perhaps increasing the timer to seven or ten minutes, while keeping the same "notice and breathe" strategy?

Yeah, I think ten minutes sounds good. That feels like a challenge, but not an impossible one. I'll keep the same strategy—just notice the thoughts, breathe if I need to, and let the timer be my boundary. I'm actually looking forward to seeing if I can do it again.

That is a fantastic plan—taking the successful five-minute experience and scaling it up to ten minutes gives your brain a chance to gather even more proof that it can handle the discomfort. Since you feel motivated and have a clear strategy in place, I suggest you try this tonight at your usual viewing time, and remember that whether you finish the full ten minutes or need to pause briefly, the fact that you engaged with the fear is the victory. How does it feel to leave the session with this renewed confidence and a concrete path forward?

It feels really good, actually. I came in feeling stuck and scared, and now I have something real to hold onto—a plan that actually worked. I think I can carry this confidence into tonight and see what happens. Thanks for guiding me through it. I'll let you know how the ten minutes go next time.

You are very welcome. It is truly inspiring to see how much courage it took to come here feeling stuck, and how effectively you translated that into a tangible success tonight. Taking this newfound confidence and applying it to your evening is a perfect next step. I am genuinely excited to hear how those ten minutes unfold for you next time, and please remember that you always have a supportive ear and a plan ready if things ever feel tricky again. Take care of yourself!

Hello, it is great to see you again. Since our last meeting, I wonder if anything significant happened with your plan to look into those certifications, or perhaps if you noticed anything interesting while scrolling through your friends' updates this weekend? Now that we have a quick snapshot of things, what would you like us to focus on today?

Hey, thanks. Um, actually, I did end up looking into that certification program for barista management. It felt okay at first, but then I saw on Instagram that my friend from high school just got an internship at some big marketing firm in New York. It kind of hit me hard, you know? Like, I'm here looking at certifications for a smoothie shop, and he's out there doing something that actually matters. I guess that's what I want to talk about today—why I can't seem to shake this feeling that I'm falling behind.

It’s really brave of you to finally dive into that barista certification after hesitating last time, and I’m glad you gave it a try. Seeing your friend land that internship must have triggered that familiar wave of comparison, didn’t it? When you looked at that specific post, did it feel like the thought “you’re falling behind” was suddenly louder or sharper than usual?

Yeah, it was way louder. It felt like everything I did that weekend was just cancelled out by that one post. I even started thinking, "What's the point of even trying this certification if I'm just going to end up in the same place anyway?" It's like that one success of his erased any progress I thought I was making. I just feel stuck.

That single post effectively wiping out weeks of effort sounds incredibly frustrating, and it makes total sense why you'd feel like giving up entirely. When that specific news landed, did it feel like your brain immediately jumped back to that middle school teacher's voice telling you that hard work alone isn't enough? Or did the thought feel more like a sudden panic that you've lost your momentum?

It's more like a sudden panic, I think. I didn't even think about that teacher this time. It was just this immediate, sinking feeling in my chest, like I was already behind and everyone else is speeding ahead. My brain just went straight to, "See? You're not doing enough. You'll never catch up." It didn't feel like a memory, it felt like a fact.

That sinking feeling and the voice stating it as an undeniable fact is terrifying, and it completely explains why your progress felt wiped out. When you held that panic in your hands, did you notice if there was any concrete evidence right now that proves you *are* actually behind him, versus whether it was just a scary prediction of the future?

I guess... I mean, he does have an internship in New York, and I'm working at a smoothie shop. So on paper, it kind of looks like he's ahead. But when I really think about it, we're both just starting out. He's not a CEO or anything. I guess I don't actually know if he's happy or if he's struggling, I just assumed he's got it all figured out. But it still feels real, you know? Even if I try to logic it out, the feeling doesn't go away.

That is such a sharp observation, because assuming his success while ignoring his struggles is exactly how that "fact" becomes so convincing. It seems like your brain is filling in the gaps with a scary worst-case scenario about your own future, rather than looking at the messy, uncertain reality of right now. If we paused for a second to imagine just one possible outcome where he is stressed or unhappy, does that crack the foundation of your certainty that you are truly falling behind?

Huh. I never really thought about it that way. I mean, I guess it does crack it a little bit. If he's miserable in New York, then what am I even comparing myself to? A fancy location? A title? That doesn't automatically mean he's winning. I still feel that knot in my stomach, but maybe it's a little looser now. It's like... maybe I've been treating his life like a finished movie, when it's really still being filmed, just like mine.

That "finished movie" metaphor is perfect because it highlights how we tend to judge someone's present moment based on a highlight reel they've curated online. It makes sense that relaxing that assumption loosens the knot in your stomach, even if the feeling hasn't disappeared completely. I think I can try that. Ten minutes isn't too much, and looking for something that actually matters to me, instead of just comparing, sounds... different. I always just look at it and think, "Is this good enough?" instead of "Does this fit me?" I'll give it a shot tonight and see if I can find one thing that feels like it's actually for me, not just for my resume.

That shift from judging "good enough" to finding what fits your values is a powerful way to reclaim the purpose of your efforts. Before we wrap up, how are you feeling about the direction we took today, and do you feel confident enough to try this new approach tonight despite the lingering anxiety?

I feel... a bit lighter, actually. I came in here feeling heavy and defeated, and now I at least have a different way to look at things. I'm still anxious, for sure. That voice isn't gone. But I think I can handle ten minutes. If it gets too loud, I'll just close the laptop and try again tomorrow. Thanks for helping me see that I don't have to believe everything my brain tells me.

That is a wonderful way to frame the "close the laptop" option; it shows you are protecting your energy rather than fighting a losing battle. Please remember that the goal tonight isn't perfection, but simply taking those ten minutes to honor what *you* want, not what the noise says you should want. I am proud of how far we've come today, and I look forward to hearing how those ten minutes go.
Thanks. I'll try to remember that it's just about me, not about beating anyone else. I'll let you know how it goes next time. See you then.

You are very welcome. Please keep that reminder close tonight: you are focusing on your own path, not competing in someone else's movie. Take your time closing our session, and I'll be here whenever you're ready to share how those ten minutes went. Goodnight!

Hello, Greg. It's great to see you again today. Last time we worked on shifting your perspective when receiving praise, and I noticed you felt significantly more hopeful about handling that situation. How are you feeling about those changes since we left? Is there anything specific you'd like to talk about first, or should we revisit a challenge you faced since then?

Hi. Um, I guess things have been okay. I tried what we talked about, telling myself maybe I did deserve some credit for the details in the pony drawings. It felt a little less harsh in the moment, but later that night I started thinking it was just a fluke, and anyone could have done it if they practiced a bit. I don't know... it's hard to hang onto that feeling.

It sounds like the initial shift helped in the moment, but that old critical voice crept back in once the novelty wore off. Did you catch that return of the "fluke" thought before you went to bed, or was it more like a creeping realization during the evening?

It was more like a creeping thing, I guess. I was just scrolling on my phone, looking at other people's art online, and then I started comparing. I saw someone's sketch of a horse, and it was way more realistic than anything I could do. That's when I felt that thought slide back in, like, "See? You're not that good." I didn't even notice it at first until I felt my mood drop.

That comparison trap is really tough to spot until the mood has already dropped, isn't it? When you look at someone else's work, your brain tends to highlight their strengths while minimizing yours, making the "fluke" narrative resurface instantly. What was the very first thing you told yourself the moment you saw that sketch that triggered the belief that your work wasn't special?

I think I told myself, "He just has more talent than me. I'm just faking it." It was like a reflex. I didn't even think about all the hours he probably put in, or that drawing realistic horses is a totally different skill than drawing my ponies. It just felt like proof that I was a fraud.

That reflexive jump to "faking it" is incredibly painful, especially when you know your six years of daily practice actually built real skills. It sounds like your brain is automatically skipping over the effort required to learn realistic anatomy and focusing only on the final image you see online. Could you recall exactly where you were in your drawing routine when you found yourself thinking that? Was you working on something, or perhaps reviewing your own sketches right before seeing theirs?

I was actually just winding down for the night. I had my tablet in my lap, but I wasn't really drawing—I was just flipping through my recent sketches, trying to see if any of them looked okay. I saw one of my pony sketches, and it felt kind of flat to me, like it was missing something. That's when I opened social media and saw that other guy's horse. I think I was already feeling a little down about my own work before I even saw his.

It sounds like you were already sitting in a low spot regarding your own pony sketches, and the comparison just acted as a hammer driving that doubt deeper. Instead of pausing to consider what that stranger's work actually took, your mind instantly defaulted to a self-critical story about being a fraud. Did you find yourself checking your own drawings *before* opening social media, or did you accidentally scroll while looking for a distraction?

I think I was checking my own drawings first, trying to see if I could spot any improvement. I guess I was looking for some kind of proof that I was getting better, and I wasn't finding it. That's when I opened social media, almost like I was hoping to find some inspiration or just to get my mind off it. But it backfired, obviously.

It makes perfect sense that you were searching for proof of progress, only to find your eyes scanned over your work and missed the subtle improvements you've made over those six years. That disappointment created a vacuum, and the comparison on social media filled it with a much sharper, more damaging judgment. Now that we've mapped that chain of events—from your search for improvement to the sudden drop in confidence—could you identify one specific thought you caught yourself having right after seeing that horse sketch that felt most unfair?

I think the most unfair thought was, "I'll never be good enough to be a vet, so why even bother?" That one hit me really hard. It's like in that one moment, I went from feeling a bit disappointed in my drawing to questioning my whole future career. It's not even related, but my brain just made that jump.

That connection between your drawing doubts and the idea of giving up on becoming a vet is incredibly distressing, and it sounds like your brain is trying to protect you from failure by convincing you that you shouldn't start with art at all. It feels like a safety valve letting air out of a tire that's otherwise holding firm, but it leaves you feeling paralyzed. Given that you have such a strong desire to become a vet, what part of your current artistic journey feels like the biggest obstacle to ever achieving that goal?

I guess... it's the feeling that if I can't even get my pony drawings to a place where I feel proud of them, then how am I supposed to handle the pressure of something as serious as vet school? It's like the drawing is a test run for my whole life, and right now I feel like I'm failing that test. So the obstacle is really this voice that says I don't have what it takes, not the drawing itself.

That is a profound insight, Greg. You've correctly identified that the real barrier isn't your inability to draw, but rather the rigid belief that your current artistic struggles disqualify you from pursuing your dream career. It sounds like you are treating your hobby as a litmus test for your entire future, which is an impossible standard to hold. If we separate the art from the ambition, could you list one specific skill you've learned in drawing that actually helps you succeed as a vet, regardless of whether you ever get paid to draw?

Hmm. I mean, I guess I've learned how to be really patient and pay attention to tiny details. Like, when I'm drawing a pony's eye, I have to look at the highlights and shadows to make it look alive. I think that kind of careful observation would probably help if I'm trying to notice subtle changes in an animal's health. I never really thought of it that way.

That is a brilliant realization, Greg. You've connected the dots between your artistic patience and the medical precision needed for veterinary care, proving that your hobby is actually a hidden asset for your future career. Now that you see the overlap, does that thought—that you're "failing" your test run anymore—feel slightly less overwhelming or like a more manageable challenge?

Maybe... yeah, a little. It still feels like a heavy thought, but when you put it like that, it's not like I'm completely useless. I'm not just wasting my time drawing ponies; I'm actually practicing something useful. I still feel like I have a long way to go, but maybe I'm not as far behind as I thought. It's a small shift, but it's something.

That is wonderful news, Greg. Reframing your art as "useful practice" rather than a failing test gives your efforts a purpose beyond just personal satisfaction, which naturally lifts the weight of that catastrophic thinking. Let's solidify this new perspective before we wrap up. Since you mentioned the "creeping" nature of those negative thoughts, could you share one small step you could take tomorrow morning to break the cycle before you feel so down about your own sketches?

Maybe I could start my morning by just looking at one of my older drawings from a year ago and comparing it to a recent one. Instead of looking at other people's work first, I could try to see my own progress before I get a chance to feel bad. I think that might help me start the day with a little more confidence, even if it's just a tiny bit.

That is a powerful strategy, Greg. By actively viewing your own growth first, you interrupt the pattern of comparing yourself to strangers and replace it with evidence of your consistent effort. I'm glad we found a solution that works for you. One last thing: as we finish up, how do you feel about our plan moving forward? Is there anything else you'd like to discuss before we close today?

No, I think this was good. I feel a bit lighter than when I walked in, honestly. I'm going to try that morning comparison thing and see if it helps me feel more grounded before I start my day. Thanks for helping me see that connection between drawing and being a vet. I never would have thought of that on my own.

That is such beautiful feedback, Greg, and I'm so glad you feel lighter. Hearing that you hadn't seen the connection between your drawing and your future goals on your own really highlights how valuable it is to explore these angles together. Take care of yourself tonight, and remember that small shifts like the one we made today are exactly where lasting change begins.

Hello again, and thank you for coming in. Before we dive into the main topic, how have you been feeling since we last spoke? Did you manage to use the notebook trick or the list you created when that overwhelming feeling started to rise?

Hey. Yeah, I did try the notebook thing a couple of times. It helped a bit, I guess, just getting the thoughts out on paper. But honestly, those feelings still creep back in pretty strong, especially at night when I'm just lying there thinking.

It makes perfect sense that the relief fades quickly once you stop writing; your brain often rushes back to replay the painful moments, especially when you're trying to sleep. Since the nighttime thoughts are still feeling quite intense, does the idea of spending the rest of our time digging into why that late-night rumbling happens sound like a priority for us to tackle today?

Yeah, that sounds like a good idea. I mean, it's the worst part of my day, just lying there going over everything in my head. I keep replaying that stupid puzzle I couldn't solve, over and over, like I'm trying to force a different ending.

That image of you trying to rewrite the ending while lying in bed really captures how exhausting and unfair that feeling can be. When we’re tired, our brains tend to loop on the hardest part of the day, ignoring the rest of the evidence we gathered earlier. To get started, if we look at what happens in that quiet moment right before you drift off, what specific thought or feeling seems to kickstart that endless replay?

It's usually just a sudden sinking feeling in my chest, like I remember out of nowhere that I failed. And then the thought just pops in: "You're not smart enough to do this. You wasted all that time for nothing." From there, it just spirals — I start thinking about how I'll probably mess up the next thing I try, too.

That "sudden sink" followed immediately by the voice saying you wasted your time is a classic sign of your brain trying to protect you from disappointment, even though it ends up hurting you instead. If we treat that initial "sink" not as a fact about your intelligence, but as an alarm bell going off because uncertainty felt dangerous, does that help separate the feeling from the actual truth of the situation?

I never really thought of it that way — like an alarm, I mean. It does feel more like a warning than a fact when you put it like that. But then I still can't shake the feeling that if I was smarter, I would've solved it, and the alarm wouldn't have needed to go off in the first place.

That connection between "being smarter" and "not needing the alarm" is a very logical trap your brain has built, treating the warning signal as proof of personal inadequacy rather than just a reaction to stress. Let's test that link for a moment: if you recall solving those other tough puzzles where you eventually cracked the code, does the evidence suggest your intelligence is a fixed trait that stopped working at this one puzzle, or does it show your ability to learn and adapt?

*Pauses and thinks for a moment* Well, when I solved those other three puzzles, I definitely had moments where I felt stuck or stupid too. I'd walk away, come back later, and something would click. So I guess... I did adapt to those. But this one just didn't click, no matter how many times I walked away or came back. So it feels different, like maybe I just hit my limit.

Noticing that difference is a great first step, but let's dig deeper into the words you used: "hit my limit." In psychology, we often call this the assumption of limited capacity—the belief that we only have so much mental fuel before running dry. Could we challenge that by asking yourself, "Is it possible this wasn't a limit on your intelligence, but rather a unique difficulty in this specific puzzle that required a totally different approach than the ones before?" What comes to mind when you imagine approaching this problem with a fresh lens rather than assuming you're out of options?

I guess... I never considered that maybe the puzzle was just structured differently. All four were from the same series, so I assumed they'd all work the same way. But what if the last one had a rule I missed or a hidden step? That thought actually feels a little lighter, like maybe it wasn't about me being defective. But then part of me still thinks, "Well, if I was good enough, I would have noticed that hidden step."

That distinction is huge—shifting from "you are defective" to "I missed a rule"—because it changes the cause from who you are to what the puzzle demanded. However, the lingering thought that noticing that hidden step is proof of being "good enough" reveals a small trap: it assumes that intelligence is purely about finding obvious clues rather than spotting subtle patterns. If you looked at the other puzzles you solved recently, which one involved a clue that wasn't immediately visible, and how did your brain finally spot it?

*Leans back slightly, thinking* There was this one puzzle where the clue was hidden in the background of a photo — a license plate number reflected in a window. I stared at it for like two hours before I noticed it. I almost gave up on that one too. I only caught it because I accidentally zoomed in while trying to close the image. So I guess... sometimes it's just luck or a random moment, not raw intelligence.

That example is incredibly powerful because it strips away the idea that genius equals instant recognition; you saw the solution only after a mundane action—a zoom—triggered it. If we apply that same logic to your current puzzle, does that "hidden step" theory make the outcome feel less like a personal failure and more like a coincidence waiting to happen? And if you imagine that moment of realization striking you unexpectedly, does the tightness in your chest ease up even a fraction?

*Takes a slow breath* Yeah, actually... it does ease up a little. Thinking of it like a coincidence I just haven't hit yet feels way less heavy than thinking I'm just not cut out for it. I still feel frustrated, don't get me wrong, but it's more like I'm waiting for that zoom moment instead of beating myself up for not having it already.

That shift from "beating myself up" to "waiting for the right moment" is a significant relief, showing how reframing the unknown reduces the pressure on your performance. Now, let's turn that light to the nights: when you lie awake expecting that "zoom" to happen, does that expectation feel helpful, or does it become its own source of anxiety that makes the silence feel louder?

It definitely makes the silence louder. I lie there trying to force the solution to come, like if I just think hard enough it'll hit me. And when it doesn't, I just feel even more defeated. So I guess I'm creating my own pressure, huh?

Yes, absolutely—you're creating a self-fulfilling prophecy by trying to force the solution, which ironically makes it harder for your brain to relax and find that "random" insight. Instead of pushing, what if we agreed that tonight's goal isn't to solve the puzzle, but simply to observe your thoughts without judging them, letting the frustration ride out until morning?

*Sighs* That sounds hard, but I think I can try it. Just... letting the thoughts be there without getting mad at myself for having them. I guess the worst that can happen is I still feel frustrated, which is where I'm at anyway. Might as well try something different.

That willingness to just sit with the frustration without fighting it is exactly what will make the difference; you're shifting from a battle mode to an observing mode. To lock this in, if tonight you notice the "zoom" moment happening, you can write it down as a success, but if it doesn't happen, remind yourself that missing it doesn't erase the evidence you already gathered about your resilience. Does that simple agreement to either celebrate a small win or accept a non-event sound like a fair plan for tonight?

Yeah, that actually sounds fair. I think I can do that. Either I get a win and write it down, or I don't get anything and that's okay too. It's not a failure either way. Just... a night. I'll give it a shot tonight.

That is a wonderful mindset to adopt—treating the night as a neutral space rather than a battleground removes the stakes entirely. Before we finish, I want to hear your honest reflection: how does carrying that new permission—"it's okay not to solve it tonight"—feel compared to the old pressure to force an answer? Does it make you feel slightly lighter in your shoulders right now?

*Takes a deep breath and smiles slightly* Yeah, I do feel lighter. It's like I gave myself permission to stop running a race I wasn't even sure I was in. I still wish I had solved it, but I don't feel like a failure for not forcing it tonight. Thank you — I think I needed to hear that it was okay to just let it sit.

Hearing that you feel lighter and that giving yourself permission made a real difference is incredibly validating, and I am truly glad we found that balance for you. You have a solid plan for tonight—whether you get a "zoom" moment or not—and you've built a clear boundary between your worth and this one puzzle. Please give this new approach a try tonight and check in with yourself tomorrow morning about how it landed. Take care, and I look forward to continuing this journey whenever you're ready.

Hello again. On a scale of one to ten, how have you been feeling this week, and is there anything new on your mind we should prioritize today?

I'd say maybe a six or seven this week. There's been a few moments where I felt okay, but honestly, I ruined a painting I'd been working on for days because of one tiny smudge. I ended up throwing it away, and I've been beating myself up about it ever since.

That sounds incredibly painful, especially after pouring days of effort into creating something beautiful. Before we unpack the shame around that specific incident, how would you rate your current level of distress with that memory, and is there another area you'd like us to touch on today besides this loss?

Right now, thinking about it, I'd say my distress is at about an eight. It's hard to shake off, even though my wife told me it still looked good. The only other thing that's been on my mind is how I've been avoiding starting anything new all week because I'm scared the same thing will happen again.

It makes total sense that your distress remains high when her reassurance feels like it might come from a place of trying to protect your feelings rather than addressing your internal drive. Since you're also carrying the weight of avoidance due to fear, would you like to spend our time unpacking that initial moment of seeing the smudge, or explore the pattern of avoidance keeping you stuck?

I think it would help to talk about the moment I saw that smudge, because that's where everything falls apart. It's like in that split second, my whole mood shifts and I just see something ruined instead of something fixable.

That sharp shift from "fixable" to "ruined" in a split second suggests your brain is interpreting that single detail as proof of total failure. Can you walk me through exactly what happened right after you spotted the smudge—did the urge to throw it away appear immediately, or did you try to brush it off first?

It was almost instant, really. I remember staring at it, feeling this tightness in my chest, and my first thought was, "Well, that's it, it's ruined now." I didn't even consider trying to paint over it or work it into the piece somehow. It was like a switch flipped, and my hand was already reaching for the trash before my head could catch up.

That automatic jump from noticing a flaw to declaring the whole piece worthless, followed by your hand moving before your mind could intervene, shows how powerful your immediate protective reaction is. When your body reacts that fast to "tightness" and "ruined," does it feel like your brain is trying to stop the pain instantly, or does it feel more like you lost control of your own judgment?

I think it feels more like I lost control of my own judgment. It's like my brain decides for me that the only way to stop hurting is to get rid of the source of frustration. In that moment, it seems so clear and right, but later, when I'm calmer, I just feel stupid and ashamed for not even trying to fix it.

That distinction between the frantic clarity you need in the moment versus the regret you feel afterward highlights how your brain is prioritizing immediate relief over long-term satisfaction. It’s completely understandable why that urge feels logical when the pain spikes, even though the outcome feels wrong later. Now that we’ve mapped out that sequence—the tightness, the "ruined" thought, and the immediate action—does it feel like there might be a small gap between noticing the smudge and letting your hand reach for the trash?

Yeah, I suppose there is a gap, but it's so small it feels almost impossible to grab hold of. It's like a fraction of a second where everything is decided. I can see that if I could just slow that moment down, maybe I could think of something else, but it happens so fast I don't even know how to start slowing it down.

It makes perfect sense that a gap this tiny feels invisible when the emotion is so loud, like trying to catch smoke with bare hands. Even if it's only a heartbeat, imagining ourselves inserting a simple pause—a deep breath or just holding the edge of the canvas instead of the bin—could give your rational mind enough room to step in before the decision is locked in. Would you be willing to try practicing that one-second delay on a new sketch tomorrow morning, just to see if you can create that space?

I... I think I could try that. It sounds scary, honestly, because my instinct is to just get rid of the thing and move on. But I can see how holding onto it for just one second might change things. I'll try it on a small sketch tomorrow, just to see what happens.

That willingness to try despite the fear of your instinct taking over is a huge step forward, and recognizing that one second *can* matter gives you hope. Before we wrap up, how does it feel to have that specific, manageable plan ready for tomorrow, and is there anything else about the smudge incident you'd like to explore before we say goodbye?

It feels a little bit lighter, having a plan instead of just dreading the next time I mess up. I think I can handle a small sketch, and I'll try to remember what we talked about. No, I think we covered what I needed for today. Thank you for listening and for helping me see that split second differently.

It's wonderful to hear that dread has shifted into anticipation; knowing you have a concrete tool to use makes the coming week feel much safer. Please remember that tomorrow isn't about stopping the urge forever, but simply noticing that tiny window between the smudge and your hand reaching for the bin, however briefly. I look forward to hearing how that one-second experiment went when we speak again soon.
