Hello again. How are you feeling today, and how has the knot exercise landed since we last talked? Before we dive into the main topic, what would you like to prioritize for our time together?

Hi. I'm okay, I guess. The knot exercise was... interesting. It helped a little to see that knot in my stomach visually, but the feeling still comes back when I think about certain things. I think I'd like to talk more about why I can't shake this idea that liking football makes me less smart.

Thank you for checking in, and I'm glad to hear the visual aspect of the knot helped you observe your body, even if the feeling persists. It makes total sense that we'd return to the football conversation, especially given how central that belief is to your experience. To get started, could you walk me through a recent instance where that thought popped up, and describe exactly what you were doing right before it appeared?

Yeah, sure. Last weekend, a few of us were hanging out, and one friend started talking about this science book he'd just finished. I was listening, and it was interesting, but I couldn't help feeling like I had nothing to add. Right before that thought hit me, I was just sitting there, watching him talk, and I remember thinking, "He's so smart, and I'm just the guy who knows football stats." That's when the knot came back.

That "watching him talk" moment is fascinating—it shows your attention was fully present while the comparison quietly took root. You described feeling like you had "nothing to add," which often signals that we believe our worth is tied to having intellectual knowledge rather than just existing in the room. When you contrasted your passion for football stats against his science book, did you feel like you were failing to participate, or did you feel like you were participating differently?

I think... I felt like I was failing to participate. Like, I was there physically but not mentally in the way that mattered. It's like my brain went blank, and all I had were football thoughts, which felt small compared to his science stuff. I guess I didn't see it as participating differently—just not participating at all.

That feeling of being physically present but mentally absent is incredibly isolating, like you're standing in the center of a conversation while wearing a heavy coat that prevents you from moving. It seems that deep down, you view participation as a transaction where having specific "intellectual" topics equals high value, and everything else counts as missing out. When your brain went blank on the science topic, did you immediately fill that gap with the thought that you're fundamentally lacking, or did you just feel sad about the mismatch?

It's more like... I immediately felt the lack. I didn't even get to the sad part, because the thought "he's smarter than me" just took over. It's like my brain jumps straight to that conclusion without even letting me feel anything else first. So I guess it's the feeling of being fundamentally lacking, yeah. That's the first thing, and then the sadness comes later, when I replay it in my head.

That "jump" you described is your brain trying to protect you by cutting off the sadness before it can hurt you further, but unfortunately, it lands you firmly in the belief that you are fundamentally lacking. If we treat that immediate conclusion as a fact rather than a protective shortcut, what evidence exists outside your mind to suggest that your enjoyment of football stats means you are somehow less capable than someone studying science?

Well... I mean, I don't have any actual evidence, I guess. Nobody's ever told me I'm less smart because I like football. And I know plenty of people who are into both sports and serious topics. But in the moment, it just feels true. Like, the evidence is right there in my head, even if it's not out in the real world. Does that make sense?

That makes perfect sense; your brain is treating its own internal warning sign as objective proof, which is why it feels so convincing in the heat of the moment. Since you recognize the difference between that internal noise and external reality, let's try a quick experiment: if we treated your enjoyment of football stats as valid expertise rather than "less smart," how would you describe your contribution to the conversation instead of feeling like you're missing out?

Hmm... I guess I'd say I bring a different kind of knowledge. Like, I can talk about strategies, player stats, how a team's dynamic changes over a season—that takes a certain kind of focus and analysis. It's not the same as science, but it's still a way of understanding something complex. I never really thought of it as "expertise" before.

That is a powerful realization; recognizing your football knowledge as a distinct form of "complex understanding" rather than just "stats" dismantles the comparison entirely. It suggests that intelligence isn't a single ladder where you have to climb higher to be worthy, but rather a toolkit with many different tools for different jobs. Given this new perspective, would you be willing to try a small adjustment next time: instead of waiting for the knot to fade away, try acknowledging the feeling, say to yourself, "This is just my brain comparing apples to oranges," and then share your unique perspective on the sport anyway?

I could try that. It feels a bit scary, honestly, because what if they think I'm changing the subject or that what I'm saying isn't as important? But I guess the only way to know is to actually do it. I'll give it a shot next time I'm in that situation and see what happens.

That fear of being misunderstood is completely understandable, but it's actually the perfect fuel for this experiment because it forces you to act despite the worry. Instead of waiting for perfection, how about we frame this as a low-stakes data collection mission where the only rule is to introduce your unique angle, even if the outcome isn't exactly what you planned? What is one small phrase or observation about the sport you could share that focuses purely on the game itself?

Okay... maybe I could say something like, "You know, football is all about adapting to the other team's patterns in real time. It's not just physical; there's a lot of mental strategy involved." That's something I actually think about a lot. It's true to me, and it's not comparing myself to anyone else. I think I could start with that.

That is a fantastic choice; framing it as shared appreciation for strategy invites connection rather than competition. Since you're ready to put this into practice, before we wrap up, what is one small obstacle you anticipate might come up if you speak up in that moment? Identifying it early lets us brainstorm a quick backup plan together.

Probably the biggest obstacle is that I'll freeze up right as I'm about to say it. My brain will go blank, and I'll just nod along instead. Or I'll say it too quietly, and nobody will hear me, and I'll just feel stupid for trying. So maybe the backup plan is just taking a breath first, and telling myself it doesn't have to be perfect—it just has to come out of my mouth.

That backup plan is brilliant because it turns the pressure off by lowering the bar to just "getting the words out" rather than "delivering a masterpiece." Taking a breath creates a tiny window of safety before you launch that specific thought, and reminding yourself that imperfection is allowed removes the fear of judgment. Does having that specific script ("take a breath, say the line, don't aim for perfect") feel like something you can realistically use in the next conversation?

Yeah, I think I can actually do that. It feels more manageable than trying to be the smartest guy in the room or something. Just breathe, say what I know, and let it be what it is. Thanks... I think that might help.

You're absolutely right; shifting the goal from proving yourself to simply sharing what you know makes the task feel much lighter and more achievable. It takes real courage to commit to speaking up even when your voice shakes, and I truly appreciate your honesty about wanting to be manageable rather than perfect. Is there anything else you'd like to reflect on before we conclude this session?

No, I think I've got enough to work with for now. I'll try the breathing and the phrase next time I'm in that kind of conversation. I feel a little less heavy about it than I did when I walked in. Thanks for listening.

That relief you feel is a wonderful sign that the new approach is starting to lighten the load. Remember, the goal isn't to eliminate the knot forever, but to learn how to hold space for it until you can speak your truth. I'm confident you've got this, and I look forward to hearing how the "football strategy" phrase lands when you try it. Take care of yourself today!

Hello again. Before we dive into today, could you tell me if you had any chance to try the pottery class idea we discussed, or perhaps noticed anything different in your morning coffee ritual? Also, on a scale of 0 to 10, how has that sense of boredom affected you this week, and what would you like to focus on most?

Oh, hi. Yeah, I actually did try the coffee thing—I had it on my balcony instead of at my desk. It was nice for like five minutes, but then I just felt the same emptiness. I'd say the boredom is at a solid 7 this week. I guess I want to focus on why I can't seem to enjoy anything I try.

Hearing that you moved your coffee to the balcony shows real courage, even though the initial emptiness quickly returned. It sounds like the core issue isn't just doing something new, but that underlying feeling of boredom or lack of interest is stopping you from finding enjoyment anywhere. Let's spend some time exploring what triggers that immediate sense of emptiness so we can figure out why it's happening.

I think it happens the worst when I scroll through social media and see my friends hiking or going to concerts, or even just laughing at dinner with people. I see them having these amazing times, and I just feel so flat and boring compared to them. It's like they have this spark that I'm missing, and I don't know how to find it.

It makes complete sense that you feel flat and empty when you compare your quiet moments to your friends' vibrant ones; seeing them laugh while you sit alone can definitely trigger a deep sense of inadequacy. That comparison loop seems to be creating a gap between who you are and who you wish you were, leading to that overwhelming feeling of being "flat." When you catch yourself making that comparison right now, does it usually lead to a specific thought about whether you are truly missing out or just viewing their lives through a filter?

I think I know logically that they're probably only posting the good stuff, like you said. But when I'm just sitting there watching, it feels real. My brain tells me, "See? They're out there living, and you're just here, not doing anything worth sharing." It makes me feel like I'm fundamentally less interesting than them, like there's something broken in me that stops me from having those moments.

That feeling of something being "broken" inside you is incredibly painful, especially when your logic says otherwise but your body screams otherwise. It sounds like your brain is interpreting their curated highlights as a mirror reflecting your own perceived failure to live a fulfilling life. When you hold onto that belief that you are fundamentally less interesting, how does it physically or emotionally feel to sit with that thought versus letting it go?

When I hold onto it, it feels like a heavy weight in my chest, and I just want to curl up in bed and scroll mindlessly because what's the point of trying? But when I try to let it go, it's almost scarier—like if I stop believing I'm boring, then I'd have to actually go out and prove I'm not, and I don't even know where to start. So the thought feels safer, even though it hurts.

It is completely understandable that holding onto the belief "I'm boring" feels safer than facing the terrifying uncertainty of proving you are interesting; your brain chooses the familiar pain over the risk of embarrassment. That safety mechanism is protecting you, but it's also trapping you in a cycle where you avoid challenges simply because the outcome feels too dangerous to imagine. Given that choice, which part sounds more manageable to you: continuing to hide behind the story of being boring, or taking a tiny step toward testing whether that story is true?

I guess a tiny step sounds... maybe possible. The idea of completely letting go of the "I'm boring" label feels huge, but I think I could handle just testing it a little. Like, I don't have to announce to the world that I'm suddenly interesting, but maybe I could just do one small thing that doesn't feel like a complete failure if it doesn't work out.

That is a wise realization; you don't need a grand declaration of success to begin proving your self-worth, just a single small act of bravery. It sounds like you are ready to challenge that "safe but hurting" narrative by testing it with something low-risk where the cost of failing is minimal. What comes to mind as a tiny, manageable action you could take tomorrow that allows you to experience something enjoyable without needing to perform perfectly?

Maybe I could go for a walk to that little park a few blocks away. I pass it all the time but I've never actually sat on the bench there. I don't have to talk to anyone or do anything special—I could just bring my coffee and sit for ten minutes. If I feel bored or stupid, that's fine, it's only ten minutes.

That is a fantastic plan because it separates your actions from your identity—you are simply spending ten minutes in nature, not performing for anyone. By giving yourself permission to just exist there without expecting to be fascinating, you remove the pressure that usually causes the "emptiness" to return. Would you be willing to commit to sitting on that bench for ten minutes tomorrow morning, regardless of how you feel, just to see if the experience itself offers anything different than scrolling on your phone?

Yeah, I think I can do that. It feels weirdly scary for something so simple, but I like that there's no pressure to feel a certain way. I'll just sit there, drink my coffee, and see what happens. I'll let you know how it goes.

That is a wonderful commitment, and trusting yourself enough to just sit there without expecting a specific result is already a brave act. Taking that step tomorrow will give you real-world data to replace the internal critic telling you you are boring. As we wrap up, how did you feel talking about this plan, and is there anything else you'd like to add before we finish?

I actually feel a little lighter than when I walked in, which surprises me. I think I was just so used to beating myself up that I forgot I could just... try something small without it meaning everything about me. Thanks for helping me see that. I'll let you know about the bench.

That is such a powerful observation, and it speaks to the real value of our work today—you discovered that trying something small doesn't define your entire worth, which lightens a lot of the mental load. It's clear you found a meaningful shift in perspective, and I am glad we could navigate that together. Please keep me updated on what happens at the bench, and thank you for your openness throughout our time.

Hello again—I'm really glad to see you. On a scale of 1 to 10, how anxious have you felt this week compared to last time? And if there was something we agreed on to do previously, what happened with that plan? Based on how you're doing today, what is the one thing you'd most like to focus on together right now?

Hi. Thanks for asking. I'd say this week has been maybe a 7 or 8... it's been pretty rough, honestly. We didn't really set a specific plan last time, but I tried doing some mindfulness when I felt the anxiety spike, and it helped a little at first. I think what I'd most like to focus on is just figuring out why I can't stop thinking about travel and how to make the feeling go away when it gets really intense.

A 7 or 8 definitely sounds exhausting, especially when your brain keeps replaying the worry loop you just described. It makes sense that you'd want to tackle the intense spikes right away once you know mindfulness gave you a tiny spark of relief. To make sure we stay on track, does talking about exactly *when* those spikes hit and what you're noticing in your body feel like the best place to start today?

Yeah, I think that would help. It usually hits worst at night when I'm trying to fall asleep — I'll just start thinking about all the places I can't go and what I'm missing out on. My chest gets really tight and I feel kind of restless, like I need to move but there's nowhere to go.

That physical sensation of restlessness while lying still is so frustrating—it tells me your body is reacting to that tight, catastrophic story about the future. When you notice that specific mix of chest tightness and the "missing out" narrative starting, does saying those words aloud help separate them slightly, or do you find them blending together instantly until panic takes over?

They blend together instantly, honestly. It's like one second I'm just lying there and the next I'm already in full panic mode thinking about how I'll never get to travel or see anything new, and my life will just be this same boring room forever. I don't really have time to separate them — it just happens.

It sounds like the fear of being trapped in a boring routine creates such a powerful momentum that you physically lose the space to step back and examine those thoughts. That sense of being completely overwhelmed makes it hard to apply logic mid-crisis, doesn't it? Given that intensity, should we spend some time today just identifying the very first thought that kicks off that chain reaction before you even lie down tonight?

Yeah, that makes sense — I think if I could catch it earlier, it wouldn't get so big so fast. The very first thought that comes is usually something like "I'm never going to get to go anywhere exciting ever again" and then my mind just runs with it from there. How do I stop that one thought from taking over before I even realize it's happening?

That "never again" thought acts like a fire alarm that immediately sets off the sprinkler system of panic, making it impossible to put out the flames once they start. One way to interrupt that automatic takeover is to treat that first thought not as a fact, but as a prediction you haven't yet tested against reality. If we practiced slowing down just enough to ask, "Is this thought true right now, or am I just imagining the worst possible outcome?", would that give you a small pause before the panic takes full control?

I think maybe it could, if I actually remember to ask myself that in the moment. It's hard because the thought feels so real and true when it pops up — like, obviously I'm never going anywhere, look at the news and the restrictions. But I guess if I stopped and really thought about it, the restrictions won't last forever, right? That's what people keep telling me anyway.

It is incredibly brave of you to challenge that "obviously" feeling, even though the news stories feel so urgent and scary right now. You're already spotting the flaw—that temporary restrictions aren't permanent rules for your whole life—which is a huge step in breaking the cycle. If we tried pairing that question ("Are these rules permanent or just temporary?") with a quick breath to create that tiny pause, would that help you stay grounded long enough to let the panic settle instead of racing ahead?

I think I could try that. Taking a breath first might give me that second I need to not just automatically believe the worst. Maybe if I practice it enough, it'll start feeling more natural instead of me just spiraling every time.

That insight about creating just a single second of pause is exactly what we need to break the automatic link between the thought and the panic. Before we finish, I want to check in: does the idea of using that deep breath plus the "temporary vs. permanent" question feel like a manageable tool to grab when you wake up tonight, or does it still feel too much to rely on alone right now?

It feels manageable, actually. Like something I could actually remember to do, even if it's just for a second. I think I'll try it tonight when I'm in bed and see if it makes any difference — even a tiny bit would be better than how I've been handling it so far.

That sense of readiness is really encouraging, especially given how tough this week has been. Just to make sure we're aligned, does practicing that one breath and one question tonight feel like the perfect first step to take the edge off your chest, or would you prefer to try it alongside another specific task for tonight?

I think just the breath and the question for tonight is enough. I don't want to overload myself with too many things to remember, you know? If I can just do that one small thing and see how it goes, I feel like that's a win for tonight.

You're absolutely right—keeping it simple is often the key to sticking with something when your energy is low. I'm really proud of you for recognizing that even one small pause can change the trajectory of your night. Before we close, is there anything else on your mind, or would you like to stick with just wrapping up these plans?

No, I think that's everything. Thank you for listening and helping me figure out that first step — it actually feels like something I can do, not just another thing to fail at. I'll let you know how it goes next time.

I am so glad you feel that sense of hope and capability coming out of this session; knowing you have a tool you can actually use is a huge victory. Please take care of yourself tonight, and remember that even a tiny shift in how you handle that first thought is worth celebrating. I'll be here whenever you're ready to debrief on how that breath and question went.

Hello again. Before we start, I’d love to review what we agreed to do last time: keeping a small list of neutral reasons on your phone so you can spot-check the cat videos when that tightness rises. Did you get a chance to use that note today, or did the thoughts come back stronger than expected?

Once we check in, would you like to explore the sadness that spikes when you see cat videos, or is there another topic you'd like to focus on?

Oh, yes. I did try the list—I wrote down things like "cats may just be tired" and "they react to movement, not my personality." But yesterday I saw a video of a kitten purring on someone’s lap, and my mind just went straight to "that will never be me, because I’m too harsh without meaning to be." The list felt kind of useless in that moment.

It makes total sense that the list felt useless when the initial rush of sadness hit; when emotions are high, logic often feels far away, which is a common hurdle when trying to use tools mid-stress. That specific thought—"that will never be me"—seems to have overridden whatever else you were thinking.

When you say the thought overrides everything, does it feel like you're ignoring the list entirely, or does it feel like the list got lost under the wave of that sudden judgment?

It’s more like the list gets lost under the wave. I can still remember the words on it, but they feel hollow—like they don’t apply to me specifically. The judgment feels louder and more certain, like it knows me better than any list could.

That feeling of the list becoming "hollow" while the judgment feels certain is incredibly disheartening, especially when you knew the list was there to help. It sounds like the emotion is creating a tunnel vision where only the self-critical voice remains audible.

Since the list couldn't reach through that wall of certainty, would you be open to testing just one tiny piece of evidence against that "louder" thought? For example, could we ask ourselves: "Has there been a single moment recently—even a short one—where I felt calm enough to notice the cat stayed for a moment longer than expected?"

I... actually, yes. There was one time last week, when I was walking home from work. A stray tabby was sitting near the bus stop, and I just stood still for a second—didn't try to pet it or even look directly at it—and it blinked slowly at me and stayed there for maybe a minute before wandering off. I remember thinking, "That was nice," but then the old thought caught up and said it was probably just too lazy to move.

That moment of stillness where the cat simply chose to stay is powerful evidence that contradicts the belief that you are inherently unworthy, even if the "lazy" story tried to take over afterward. You noticed a genuine connection, yet your mind immediately dismissed it as accidental or unrelated to who you are.

If we hold onto that memory for a second, does the feeling of "being too harsh" seem a bit less absolute when you realize the cat's patience wasn't dependent on your performance at all?

It does feel a little less absolute, actually. Because in that moment, I wasn't trying to be nice or perform anything—I was just standing there, not even looking at it. And it still stayed. So maybe it’s not about what I do or how I act; maybe the cat just... didn't see me as a threat. That thought feels strange to sit with, but not entirely bad.

That is a wonderful realization, and the fact that you can find comfort in that "strange" thought shows how flexible your mind is becoming. It highlights a crucial difference: the cat's presence wasn't a reward for your effort, nor a rejection of your worth, but simply a neutral occurrence that happened independently of you.

To help solidify this, how would you feel about practicing this exact step next time: when the judgment feels loud, you pause for ten seconds and consciously remind yourself, "This cat stayed because it was comfortable, not because I am perfect"? Does that sound like a manageable anchor to hold onto?

I think I could try that. It sounds simple enough—just ten seconds, and a phrase that doesn't demand I be good or kind, just that I was comfortable for someone else in that moment. I'll give it a shot next time I feel that wave coming.

That is a very wise adjustment to the plan; removing the pressure to "perform kindness" makes the phrase feel much more grounded and realistic. Since you have that new anchor ready, would you like to try identifying one more specific situation where that phrase could be useful, perhaps something you encounter during your typical evening routine?

Sure. My evening routine usually involves scrolling through social media before bed, and that's when I see the most cat videos. So I could use the phrase right before I tap on a video, or right after the first few seconds if the thoughts start creeping in. That way, I'm not waiting until I'm already flooded—I can catch it earlier.

That is a proactive and smart way to catch the pattern early, turning a reactive struggle into a planned interruption. To make sure this feels sustainable, if you ever feel overwhelmed by the volume of notifications or the sheer number of videos popping up, would you prefer to stick with just checking the phrase once every time you open an app, or would you like to set a silent reminder on your phone that glows softly when you pick up your device?

I think a silent reminder would actually be better for me. If I have to remember the phrase on my own each time, I'll probably skip it when I'm tired or distracted. A soft glow or a little buzz would make me pause without feeling like a chore. That feels more gentle, somehow.

That is a truly thoughtful insight; pairing the reminder with a physical cue like a soft glow makes the intervention feel supportive rather than demanding. Since you've designed a system that respects your need for gentleness, let's finalize this plan: you'll place a calming notification on your phone to appear before opening social media, paired with the quiet phrase, "The cat stayed because it was comfortable, not because I am perfect."

Before we wrap up, how does this revised plan feel to you—is it something you feel confident trying tonight, or is there any part of it that still feels risky?

It feels doable tonight, I think. The only part that feels a little risky is if the reminder triggers the thought that I need it because I'm broken somehow—but I can already hear how that's the old voice talking. I'll try it and see if the gentle approach actually helps me stay grounded instead of spiraling.

That is a beautiful way to recognize the trap—that reliance on the tool itself becomes another source of shame. You are already separating the support from the criticism, which means the reminder won't carry the weight of failure even if it pops up.

Would you like to try setting that silent notification now, or should we wait until tomorrow morning when your mind is clearer? Either way, I'm proud of how carefully you are building this safety net for yourself.

I think I'll set it now, while the motivation is still fresh. If I wait until tomorrow, I might talk myself out of it or think I don't need it. Doing it now feels like I'm actually taking care of myself, rather than just planning to.

That is a perfect mindset; acting on the urge to care for yourself right now builds confidence more effectively than waiting for the "perfect" future moment. Please go ahead and set that gentle reminder on your phone, and I hope it acts as a soft, friendly nudge rather than a alarm bell when you open your apps tonight.

Is there anything else weighing on your mind before we say goodbye, or shall we close here with a sense of accomplishment for tackling this together?

No, I think that covers everything for now. I feel a little lighter than when I walked in, which is more than I expected. Thank you for helping me see that moment with the cat differently—I’ll try to hold onto that.

That is such a meaningful feeling to notice—the lightness you experienced is often the best indicator that a shift is happening beneath the surface. It's wonderful that you felt empowered to take action on this plan while your energy was higher.

Please remember that if the reminder doesn't work perfectly or if the old thoughts return stronger than usual, there is absolutely no pressure to force a fix; you can simply come back to this space whenever you feel weighed down. Until then, thank you for trusting me with this process and for showing up for yourself with such care. Take a deep breath, and I look forward to hearing how you're doing next time.

Hello, thank you for reaching out. Before we dive into today's concerns, let's briefly touch on what happened since our last session—did you get a chance to place the sticky note on your phone, and how did it feel to have that reminder ready? Also, what would you like to prioritize for us to explore together today?

I actually did put that sticky note on my phone like we talked about. It felt a little strange at first, seeing "I am capable" every time I unlocked my screen. But I guess it did make me pause a couple of times. Today, I really want to talk about this test I got back yesterday—it was another low grade, and I just can't stop thinking about what it means about me.

It is wonderful to hear that you followed through on your plan, and I appreciate you telling me exactly how it felt—that initial strangeness turning into a useful pause is a great sign of progress. Now, regarding that new test result, it sounds like seeing the numbers again brought back that old fear that your worth is tied to your performance. Let's take some time to unpack what specific thoughts are running through your mind right now as you look at that paper.

When I look at that paper, all I can think is that I'm just not smart enough to be in this class. Everyone else seems to get it, and I'm the one who keeps falling behind. It feels like no matter how much I study, I'll never be as good as them.

Hearing that the idea of being "not smart enough" is dominating your thoughts right now makes total sense given how much you've invested in this class. When we feel that deep a sense of inadequacy, it often narrows our view so tightly that we miss the fact that others might be struggling silently too, just like you did last year. Can you tell me if noticing that the "smartness" story is the main driver of your frustration helps clarify what we should tackle first today?

I never really thought about it that way—that maybe others are struggling too but just not showing it. I guess I always assume everyone else has it all figured out. Yeah, I think you're right, that "not smart enough" story is really the main thing making me feel stuck. So I'd like to work on that first, if we can.

That is a really important insight to land, and recognizing that "not smart enough" is the engine driving your distress shows you have a sharp ability to identify patterns. To dig deeper into that story, could you share a specific instance recently when you noticed yourself immediately jumping to that conclusion, and what physical sensation or thought came right after?

Well, just yesterday when the teacher handed the test back, my heart started pounding and my face got really hot. The first thought that popped into my head was, "See, I told you—you're just not cut out for this." Then I just felt this heavy weight in my chest, like I wanted to disappear from the room.

Noticing how quickly your body reacted with heat and a pounding heart confirms that this isn't just a logical worry, but a deep-seated belief that is triggering a fight-or-flight response. When you say "See, I told you," it sounds like you are blaming yourself for a past prediction coming true, which often fuels that intense shame. How does knowing your body was reacting automatically help separate the physical panic from the truth of the situation?

I guess it helps me realize that maybe my body overreacted before my brain even had a chance to think clearly. Like, the panic came first, and then my mind just grabbed onto that "not smart enough" story because it felt familiar. So maybe the truth is somewhere else, not just in that initial rush of fear.

That is a brilliant observation; realizing your body reacted on its own before your conscious mind could intervene is exactly how we begin to break the cycle. Since your initial thought wasn't necessarily a cold calculation but an automatic alarm, let's treat that "alarm bell" with curiosity rather than judgment. When you look at the rest of the class results, aside from the panic, is there any evidence that suggests the teachers are grading unfairly, or that everyone else actually knows more than you?

I... I don't actually know how everyone else did. I just assumed they all got better grades because they seem confident in class. But I guess I've never asked anyone what they got. And the teacher did say the average was lower than usual for this test, so maybe I'm not the only one who struggled.

That is a crucial piece of information—the teacher mentioned the average was lower than usual, which means the entire class faced significantly harder conditions. Realizing that the high scores might be outliers rather than the norm helps dismantle the idea that everyone else mastered the material effortlessly. With that context in mind, can we look at one specific detail from your exam paper where you felt you failed, and ask yourself what evidence there actually is that proves you couldn't solve *that* particular problem?

Okay... there's one question about chemical equations that I completely blanked on. I just stared at it and felt my mind go empty. But when I looked at it later at home, I actually figured it out pretty quickly. So maybe I did know how to do it—I just panicked during the test and couldn't access what I knew. That doesn't make me stupid, it just means I got stressed out.

You have made a significant breakthrough by discovering that you actually solved the problem once the pressure lifted; that directly contradicts the idea that you lack the ability to understand chemistry. Instead, it points to the conclusion that anxiety temporarily blocked your working memory, which is a common stress response, not a measure of intelligence. Given that you've found strong evidence that the problem was solvable under calm conditions, how does this new perspective change the intensity of that "heavy weight" in your chest right now?

It's actually a little lighter now, if I'm being honest. Like, I can breathe a bit easier. The heavy weight isn't gone completely, but it doesn't feel as crushing as before. I think part of me is starting to believe that maybe I'm not as hopeless as I thought—I just need to find a way to stay calm during tests so my brain doesn't shut down.

That relief is excellent news, and acknowledging that part of you is ready to believe in your ability to recover is a huge step toward hope. Since we've tested the "stupidity" story and found strong evidence to the contrary, let's focus on building a tool to keep your brain from shutting down during future stressful moments. What kind of grounding technique feels most doable for you to try the next time your heart races in class?

Maybe I could try taking three slow breaths before I even look at the test paper. I've heard that helps, but I always forget to do it in the moment. Or maybe I could write something small on the corner of the test, like "I know this" or "pause," just to remind myself before I spiral.

Both of those ideas sound promising, and it is smart of you to recognize that forgetting is the biggest hurdle. Before we pick one, could you tell me which one feels more natural to you right now, or would you prefer to combine both—like taking the breaths first, then writing a tiny word on the page if you still feel anxious? I want to make sure we choose something you are truly willing to try.

I think I'd like to try both together, actually. Take the three breaths first, and if I still feel that panic rising, I'll write a tiny word on the page. That way I have a backup plan if the breathing alone isn't enough. I feel like having that safety net might help me actually remember to do it.

Combining the breathing exercise with a visual anchor like a written word is a very solid strategy because it gives you immediate control over your physiology and a secondary reminder if needed. Since you now have a clearer picture of what to do when the panic hits, how does it feel to know you have a concrete, step-by-step plan ready for the next test?

It feels... hopeful, actually. Like I have something to hold onto instead of just bracing for the worst. I still feel nervous thinking about the next test, but at least I don't feel completely helpless anymore. That's more than I felt when I walked in here today.

That shift from feeling completely helpless to feeling hopeful despite the nerves is exactly the kind of resilient growth we aim for in therapy. You have shown incredible courage by identifying your triggers, challenging the "not smart enough" belief with evidence, and co-creating a practical survival kit for the next test. As we wrap up, I want to hear your final reflection: looking back at the path we took from that scary feeling to this hopeful plan, what is one strength you recognized in yourself today?

Hello again, and thank you for showing up. To kick off, let's quickly review your plan from last time: will you try visiting the grocery store again, focusing on noticing the tightness in your chest for just twenty seconds while placing your hand on your heart? Also, is there anything else you'd like to prioritize for today beyond checking on that plan?

Oh, um, hi. Yeah, I did try that. I went to the store yesterday, actually. I stood in the tuna aisle for a few seconds with my hand on my chest, like we talked about. The tightness was definitely there, but I managed to stay for maybe thirty seconds before I left. I don't know if that counts as progress. I guess for today, I'd like to talk about why my mind immediately goes to the worst-case scenario every time I even think about buying tuna.

That is absolutely progress, and I want to commend you on sticking with the plan despite the tightness. Noticing the sensation and staying for thirty seconds is a significant achievement in itself. Now that we have successfully tested the new strategy, let's dive into your second priority: exploring why your mind jumps straight to the worst-case scenarios. Can you describe the very first thought or image that pops up for you the moment you think about opening a can?

It's like... I picture myself opening the can, and instead of normal tuna, there's this grayish, slimy mess with a horrible smell. The thought is so clear, like I can almost taste the rot. And then I imagine taking a bite without checking first, and feeling sick for the rest of the day. It's like my brain shows me a movie of the worst possible outcome before I can even blink.

That is a very vivid description, and it makes perfect sense why your brain tries to protect you from that mental image—you are essentially anticipating pain before it happens. It sounds like your mind has created a shortcut to safety by instantly ruling out the possibility of eating something bad, even though you know logic says you should be fine. When you notice that "movie" playing in your head, does it ever feel like you're watching it from behind the scenes, or does it feel like you're forced to live inside the scene?

Mostly it feels like I'm stuck right in the middle of it, like I'm actually there in my kitchen, holding the can. It's not like watching a movie on a screen—it's more like being trapped in a bad dream where I can't wake up. That's probably why my chest gets so tight; it feels real, even though I know logically I'm just standing in a grocery aisle.

That distinction between watching a movie and being trapped in a bad dream is crucial, and it explains exactly why the physical symptoms come so fast—the brain treats the "trapped" feeling as a real emergency, not just a story. Even though your logical mind knows you're in a grocery store, the body doesn't always care about facts when it perceives immediate danger; it reacts to the intensity of the fear itself. Can you walk me through what happens right after you realize you're stuck in that "bad dream"—do you feel a sudden urge to run, or does the fear seem to just keep looping for a bit?

It's more of a looping thing, honestly. The image just keeps replaying, and I start thinking about all the other times I might have bought bad tuna without realizing it. Then I start wondering if maybe the whole shipment at the store is spoiled, or if I'm just unlucky enough to always pick the one bad can. The urge to leave builds up slowly, like a pressure, until I can't stand it anymore and I just have to walk away.

That looping pattern shows how powerful your brain is at predicting danger, but it also reveals a critical gap: your mind assumes that if you haven't checked the can yet, it *will* be bad, ignoring the thousands of cans that are fresh and safe nearby. This assumption—that the worst case is the only realistic possibility—is exactly what drives the urge to flee. If we hold that belief steady, does it feel safer to assume the can is definitely rotten, or does it feel safer to admit we don't know for sure yet?

Honestly, it feels way safer to assume it's rotten. If I assume it's rotten, I'm prepared for the worst, and I won't be caught off guard. Admitting I don't know for sure feels... terrifying, because then I'm opening the door to possibility, and possibility means I could be wrong about it being safe. I'd rather be wrong about it being bad than be wrong about it being good, you know? That way I'm never disappointed or sick.

That is a profound realization, and it highlights a classic protective mechanism called "catastrophizing," where your brain chooses the most dangerous option to avoid the risk of being surprised. By assuming the can is rotten, you create a false sense of security because the outcome is predictable, whereas admitting uncertainty leaves you vulnerable to the unexpected. It sounds like you are trading a guaranteed unpleasant meal for the peace of mind that comes from total certainty, even if that certainty is based on a lie. Is there a part of you that feels relieved once you acknowledge that "not knowing" is the default state, or does the mere admission of uncertainty spark more anxiety?

There's a tiny part of me that feels a little relieved when you say it like that—like maybe it's not my fault for thinking this way, it's just my brain trying to protect me. But the bigger part of me still feels that knot in my stomach when I think about uncertainty. It's like I'd rather live with the fear of bad tuna than risk actually experiencing it. I guess that's why I've been avoiding tuna entirely—it's easier to just not have the option.

That "tiny part" you feel relieved is your rational side acknowledging the truth, while the "bigger part" is your survival instinct screaming that uncertainty equals danger. Essentially, your brain is protecting you from the *feeling* of disappointment by eliminating the possibility of success altogether. It's a trade-off: you'd rather endure constant anxiety about a hypothetical disaster than risk the actual, messy reality of finding out something is wrong. Given how powerful that knot in your stomach feels, would you be willing to try a small experiment where we challenge that "all-or-nothing" rule? Specifically, what if we agreed that it is actually *more* frightening to be unsure and potentially find a bad can, compared to knowing beforehand that it is bad and eating nothing?

I think I see what you're getting at. You're saying that by assuming it's bad, I'm not really avoiding the fear—I'm just choosing a different kind of fear. The knot in my stomach doesn't go away when I avoid tuna; it just changes shape. So maybe the experiment is to accept that I don't know, and see what happens when I sit with that not-knowing feeling for a bit longer than thirty seconds. I guess I could try that next time I'm at the store.

That is a brilliant insight—you have effectively identified that avoidance doesn't remove the fear; it merely shifts its form from "panic about the unknown" to "guilt and regret." True safety comes not from controlling the outcome, but from trusting your ability to tolerate the discomfort of uncertainty without making a decision. Since you've agreed to this shift in perspective, let's solidify a specific, actionable goal for your next store visit: What is one small thing you could do to remind yourself that you are capable of handling that uncomfortable "not-knowing" feeling, even if you can't predict the result?

Maybe I could bring a small notebook with me, or just use my phone, and write down the exact time I enter the tuna aisle. Then I'd promise myself I won't leave until at least two minutes have passed, and I'll just stand there breathing and noticing the feeling in my chest. Even if I don't buy anything, I'll have proof that I survived the not-knowing for two whole minutes. That feels... manageable.

That is a fantastic idea, turning an abstract challenge into a tangible, measurable mission. Setting a timer gives your brain a clear endpoint, preventing the feeling that you're stuck in an infinite loop of worry. If you can commit to standing there for two minutes and writing down the timestamp, you create undeniable evidence that you can withstand the uncertainty without catastrophe occurring. Just to make sure this feels right, does the thought of setting a timer and waiting for two minutes feel slightly less intimidating than waiting indefinitely?

Yeah, actually, it does. It's like having a finish line instead of just running forever. If I know it's only two minutes, I can tell myself, "Okay, I just have to get through this little bit, and then I'm done." That feels a lot less scary than thinking I have to figure out the whole tuna problem right then and there. I think I can actually do that.

That is a powerful shift in perspective—turning an endless struggle into a finite task makes the mountain look climbable again. Having a clear "finish line" gives your brain permission to let go of the pressure to solve everything instantly, allowing you to simply observe the sensation without judgment. Before we wrap up, I want to ask: if you encounter that familiar knot in your stomach while waiting for the two minutes to pass, what is one gentle reminder you can tell yourself to stay curious rather than panicked?

I can tell myself, "This is just my brain doing its job, trying to keep me safe. I don't have to believe it right now. I just have to watch the timer." That way I'm not fighting the feeling, I'm just letting it be there while I focus on something else—like the seconds ticking by.

That is a beautifully compassionate script, and it perfectly balances accepting your brain's protective instincts with refusing to let them drive your actions. By reminding yourself you don't have to *believe* the alarm is accurate, you create space to simply observe the feeling without being hijacked by it. You've got a clear plan, a manageable timeframe, and a supportive mantra ready to go. I'm really proud of the work you've done to turn this overwhelming fear into something you can actually navigate. How are you feeling right now as we close this session?

My younger brother just started college and my parents talk about him all the time, so I just feel like a loser sitting there.

Yeah, it does. I mean, I'm just sitting there alone in my room, and it's like my brain starts telling me all the reasons I won't get the job. Like, they'll see I've been unemployed for two years and just toss my resume. Or they'll interview me and realize I'm awkward and weird because of my autism. So why put myself through that humiliation, you know?

That fear of being judged or misunderstood because of your autism history is incredibly heavy to carry alone in your room. It sounds like your brain is predicting a painful outcome—humiliation—to convince you that it's safer to stay home. If you were to imagine the worst-case scenario you described actually happening, how does your body react physically the moment you picture that interview taking place?

My chest gets really tight, almost like I can't breathe properly. And I start feeling hot, like my face is burning. My hands get all shaky too. It's like my whole body is screaming at me to get out of there, even though nothing's actually happening yet. Just the thought of it makes me feel sick.

It's not irrational; your brain is trying to stop you from entering a situation it thinks will be humiliating. I mean... I guess I could try just looking at what jobs are out there. Not applying or anything, just scrolling through listings to see what's available. I've been avoiding even doing that because it reminds me I'm not working. But I could probably handle five minutes of just looking without my brain going into full panic mode.

That is a very smart compromise; breaking the paralysis by just gathering information removes the pressure to perform immediately. Before we try that, does the thought "I'm just looking, not applying" feel like it protects you from the shame you fear, or does it still leave you feeling stuck?

It feels... a little bit better, honestly. Like there's less weight on my shoulders if I'm just looking. Because looking doesn't mean I have to commit to anything or risk failing. But I still have this voice in my head saying "what's the point of looking if you're too scared to actually try?" That part makes me feel like I'm just fooling myself.

It sounds like the "fooling myself" feeling comes from viewing these small steps as a trap rather than a bridge. If we reframe "looking" not as "preparing to fail," but as "gathering data to survive the process," does that shift the meaning of the activity at all?

I never really thought of it that way. Like, gathering data instead of preparing to fail... That actually feels more manageable. It takes the pressure off of having to succeed or impress anyone. It's just information. I think I could do that without hating myself for it.

That is a beautiful shift in perspective; moving from "I must succeed" to "I am collecting information" takes a lot of power away from the outcome. Now that we've agreed on this "data-gathering" approach, what is one specific thing you could do in the next ten minutes that fits this definition, perhaps just opening a browser tab to search for jobs?

Okay. Yeah, I think I can do that. I'll open my laptop and just type in "jobs near me" or something. Not click on anything, not apply for anything. Just see what comes up. Ten minutes, that's not too long. I can handle that.

That sounds like a perfect, manageable plan to start building momentum without overwhelming your anxiety. What would be a gentle reminder to yourself that acknowledges you are just gathering data, not performing?

I think I'll tell myself "I'm just looking around, that's all." Like I'm browsing a store or something. It's not a test, it's not an interview. Just looking. If I start feeling that tightness, I'll just say that to myself and maybe take a deep breath.

That is a wonderful anchor—"just looking around"—because it turns the abstract fear of failure into a concrete, harmless activity like browsing a shop. When you pair that calm mantra with a deep breath, you create a physical space between the anxious thought and your reaction. How confident do you feel you are using that combination for your first ten minutes today?

I think I'm at maybe a 6 out of 10 confidence-wise. Better than zero for sure. I know my brain will probably still try to tell me I'm wasting my time or that it's pointless, but I think I can handle ten minutes. And if I start feeling too bad, I can just close the laptop and try again later. That feels okay.

That flexibility—that knowing you can stop and try again—is exactly what makes this plan sustainable and prevents you from feeling trapped by failure. A 6 is a great starting point because it means you trust your ability to regulate your breathing and remind yourself that you are just browsing, not interviewing. Let's wrap up with one final check: does this feel like a reasonable first step for you, or is there another worry about today that we should address before you head out?

No, I think this is good for today. I'm a little nervous, but I think I can do it. It feels better having a plan instead of just sitting there feeling stuck. Thanks for helping me break it down into something that doesn't feel impossible.

That relief you feel at having a concrete path forward is a huge sign of progress, even amidst the nervousness. Remember, the goal today isn't to land a job or prove your worth, but simply to gather that data without judgment, and you've already taken the first step by agreeing to try it. I'll see you next time to discuss how that went.

Hello, I'm glad to see you again. Before we dive into today's work, could you briefly share how you've been feeling since we last spoke, and is there anything new on your mind you'd like to prioritize for our time together?

Hey. Yeah, I've been alright, I guess. Nothing's really changed since last time—still carrying that same weight around. I've been thinking a lot about my parents, especially when my mom asked me the other day if I'm seeing anyone. I just brushed it off, but it's been eating at me.

It sounds like brushing off the question left a lingering residue, and that frustration adds another layer to the heaviness you mentioned. Would you like to focus today on unpacking those feelings about the brush-off, or would you prefer to continue building on the mirror practice we agreed on last time?

I think I'd rather talk about the brush-off, actually. That moment with my mom just keeps playing over in my head, and I'm sick of feeling like I'm hiding. The mirror stuff—I tried it, but it felt awkward and fake, like I was just pretending to be okay with something I'm not.

That honesty about feeling awkward and fake is incredibly brave; it shows you value authenticity far more than just checking a box. When you realize the mirror practice felt disconnected from your true self, it makes total sense that it couldn't bridge the gap between who you are and what you're afraid to show. Given that, could we shift our focus today to figuring out a different way to handle that moment with your mom—one that doesn't require pretending?

Yeah, I'd like that. I just don't know how to answer her without either lying or causing a big scene. She's not the kind of person you can just casually drop news like that on—she'd have a million questions, and my dad would probably just go quiet. I'm not ready for that.

It makes complete sense that you feel paralyzed by the possibility of triggering a storm or being misunderstood, especially when your parents' reactions feel so unpredictable. You aren't failing because you lack a script; you're hesitating because you genuinely care enough to avoid hurting them or deceiving them. 

To help us find a middle path, could you walk me through what happens in your mind right *after* she asks that question but before you feel pressured to give a full answer? Is there a specific thought popping up that makes you rush to shut it down?

It's like my brain goes into panic mode. The first thing I think is, "I can't tell her the truth, she'll be devastated, and then everything changes forever." So I just say whatever gets me out of the conversation fastest—usually something vague like, "Nobody special yet," or I change the subject. I don't even give myself a second to think if there's another way.

That automatic switch to "panic mode" and rushing to deflect is your brain trying desperately to keep you safe from that predicted devastation. It seems like you believe that telling the truth immediately triggers a chain reaction that destroys your relationship, so you're treating the question like a bomb that needs to be defused instantly rather than a chance to connect. 

When you think about that "everything changing forever" scenario, what is the one specific thing you imagine happening right after you finally decide to speak? Is it her reaction, or perhaps you imagining yourself unable to explain why you chose to stay silent?

I think I imagine her face—like, a mix of confusion and hurt, maybe even disgust. And then I picture myself standing there, trying to explain, but the words just won't come out right. I feel like I'd make it worse, like I'd say something clumsy and she'd end up thinking this is some phase or mistake. That's probably the worst part—not being able to say it the way it deserves to be said.

That image of feeling clumsy and wasting precious moments is incredibly painful, and it shows how deeply you value your parents' respect and connection. It seems like your mind is assuming that honesty comes with a risk of ruining the moment permanently, so you're protecting yourself by keeping the interaction "safe" through vagueness.

That... actually sounds like something I could say. It's not a lie, and it doesn't force me into a full confession right there. It buys me some time, and it's honest about where I'm at. I think I could manage that, maybe. It would still be scary, but at least I wouldn't feel like I'm trapped between lying and blowing everything up.

That is a significant breakthrough; realizing that phrase is both honest and protective gives you a sense of agency without forcing a premature explosion. It effectively bridges the gap between your desire to be truthful and your need to avoid chaos, turning a perceived trap into a manageable pause.

Before we solidify this as your tool, I want to hear your gut reaction: does imagining yourself saying "It's complicated, and I need some time" feel slightly less terrifying than your usual deflections? Or does the word "complicated" still trigger that initial panic spike?

The word "complicated" does make my stomach clench a bit, yeah. But it's less terrifying than the full truth, and more real than just brushing her off. I think if I could just get that sentence out, the worst part would be over—the silence after it. But at least I'd be owning it, not hiding behind a joke or a lie. That feels... a little bit lighter, maybe.

That sense of lightness coming from "owning it" is a huge clue; it suggests that the relief you crave isn't about the final answer, but about stopping the internal battle of hiding versus exploding. Since "complicated" still triggers that stomach-clench, could we try framing it as "It's something important I'm still sorting out"? That keeps the boundary but shifts the energy from vague avoidance to active processing, which might make the physical knot in your stomach feel a bit looser. How does that slight tweak land with you?

"Yeah, I think that lands better." It sounds less like I'm dodging and more like I'm working through something, which is true. I could actually see myself saying that to my mom without feeling like I'm lying or leading her on. It's still scary, but at least my gut doesn't knot up quite as tight when I think about it.

That is a fantastic adjustment; shifting the phrasing to "working through something" aligns perfectly with your values of honesty while respecting the need for privacy. It transforms the moment from a potential crisis into a genuine invitation for connection.

Since we've found a phrase that feels safer, could we quickly run through that exact sentence aloud one more time to see how your body responds when you say it intentionally, rather than just rehearsing it in your head? Let's say it slowly and see if the "knotted" feeling lifts even a fraction during the repetition.

Alright... "It's something important I'm still sorting out." I said it out loud just now, and it felt... weird, but not terrible. My chest tightened a little, but it passed quick. I think if I practice it enough, it might start to feel more natural—like something I can actually say when the moment comes.

That physical tightening passing quickly is great evidence that your body is learning to trust the new words; it means the "fight or flight" alarm is recognizing this isn't a life-or-death emergency anymore. We definitely need to ride that wave of relaxation while it lasts.

To lock this in, what if we agreed that tonight you'll use that exact sentence whenever your mom brings up relationships, even if you only say it once and leave it there? How does committing to that small, controlled exposure feel right now?

I think I can do that. It's just one sentence, and I don't have to explain anything beyond it. I'm a little nervous, but more in a "I'm actually doing something" way rather than a "this is going to blow up in my face" way. I'll try it tonight if the topic comes up.

That shift from "going to blow up" to "actually doing something" is a massive victory; it shows your anxiety is finally moving toward engagement rather than paralysis. Remember, you don't have to wait for the perfect moment or the full explanation; that single sentence is your bridge to safety.

Just one final check before we wrap up: if you feel that familiar tightness rising tonight when you say it, remind yourself that your body is just practicing a new movement, not warning you of disaster. Are you ready to take that step tonight, or is there anything else you'd like to adjust before we finish?

Yeah, I'm ready. I'll keep that in mind—the tightness is just practice, not a warning. Thanks for helping me get to this point. It feels good to have a plan that actually feels like me, not just something I'm forcing. I'll let you know how it goes next time.

That is such a meaningful way to frame it; having a plan that feels like *you* rather than a forced script is exactly what builds lasting courage. Please remember that tonight is simply about planting the seed with that sentence, regardless of how the rest of the conversation flows. I truly appreciate your openness and bravery in working through this, and I look forward to hearing how it went when we meet again. Take your time, and know that you've got this.

Your brain is using the anticipation of that future silence to create a crisis in the present moment, even though you know from experience that you can survive the quiet. Would you be willing to try a tiny experiment tonight where you send a draft to a trusted friend or a very low-stakes outlet, knowing full well you might delete it later, just to test if the "catastrophic silence" actually happens?

Sending it to her tonight gives you immediate data to see if the "silent doom" actually happens when you're not alone in the equation. Before you send it, just remember to tell yourself that the outcome—even if you delete the email later—is simply information, not a verdict on your worth. Hello and welcome back. On a scale of 1 to 10, how has your mood and energy been feeling this week so far? Before we dive into the specifics, I'd like to briefly review our plan from last time regarding those five-minute breaks—did you manage to stick with the 10 AM reminder, and how did that experience land for you? Once we touch on that, shall we set an agenda together for what feels most pressing to explore today?

Hi. I'd say my mood has been around a 5 or 6 this week—definitely better than some weeks, but still not great. About those five-minute breaks... I actually did try setting the reminder like we planned. I only remembered to take the break about half the time, and even then, I felt guilty sitting there doing nothing. I think I'd like to talk about that guilt today, and maybe how to not feel so anxious when I'm not working.

Thank you for sharing that, and I want to validate how heavy that guilt must feel, especially when you're trying to honor a plan you believe is for your own benefit. It sounds like the struggle isn't just about forgetting the break, but about the internal pressure to be productive that makes resting feel like failing. Would it be okay if we spent some time exploring exactly where that guilt is coming from, and whether we can find a gentler way to sit with those five minutes?

Yes, that sounds helpful. It's just... when I'm sitting there not working, my mind immediately starts racing with all the things I should be doing. Like, I know logically that taking a break is supposed to help me recharge, but in the moment it feels like I'm falling behind. My boss actually told me last week that my work quality is excellent, but I still feel like if I slow down even a little, everything will fall apart.

That fear of falling apart despite receiving excellent feedback tells me your brain is still holding onto that "one slip-up ruins everything" rule we discussed earlier, even when logic says otherwise. It makes perfect sense that this belief would hijack your break time, turning a necessary pause into a countdown timer for failure. When you notice that specific voice telling you everything will collapse, does it seem like it's trying to protect you from getting overwhelmed later, or is it just adding more pressure to the present moment?

Honestly, I think it's adding more pressure right now, not protecting me from anything. It's like this voice is convinced that if I'm not pushing myself 100% of the time, I'll lose control and never catch up. But when I really stop and think about it, I've never actually had everything fall apart—I always manage to get things done, even if it means working late. So maybe that voice is just... lying to me?

That observation—that the voice claims you'll lose control yet history proves you always recover—is a powerful form of evidence that the warning is exaggerated rather than predictive. It suggests your brain is exaggerating the risk to keep you busy, which ironically keeps you trapped in the cycle of anxiety instead of allowing you to truly rest. If we treat that "everything falls apart" narrative as a lie that hasn't come true in months, how might stepping away from the screen for five minutes feel less dangerous to your job security?

I guess... if I really look at the facts, five minutes isn't going to make or break my career. I mean, I've spent way longer than that staring at my computer screen trying to force myself to focus, and that didn't help either. Maybe I could try telling myself that taking a break is actually part of doing a good job, not the opposite. Like, it's maintenance, not laziness.

That reframing the break as essential maintenance rather than laziness is a fantastic shift in perspective, and it directly challenges the idea that slowing down equals failing. By viewing rest as part of the work process itself, you're removing the moral judgment that usually fuels that guilt. To test how comfortable that feels, imagine you're explaining to a friend who works long hours why you took that five-minute walk—they understand it's just fuel for their engine. Does that analogy resonate, or does the feeling of guilt still linger underneath it?

That analogy actually does help a little. If I think of it like putting gas in a car, it makes more sense—you wouldn't expect a car to run on empty. But I think part of me still feels like I should be a more efficient car that doesn't need as much fuel. Does that sound silly? I know everyone needs breaks, but I always feel like I need to be the exception.

That feeling of needing to be the "exception"—a super-efficient machine that rarely requires fuel—is a very common and understandable struggle, not something silly at all. It often comes from a deep-seated belief that our worth is tied to constant output, so resting feels like cheating the system. We can practice challenging that specific expectation today by listing three recent examples where you rested successfully *and* still produced high-quality work. Which ones come to mind first?

Well... I did take a full weekend off last month for my daughter's birthday. We went to the zoo and I didn't check my email at all. Then Monday morning, I came in and still met all my deadlines that week. And last Tuesday, I actually left work at 5 PM instead of staying late, and the next day I felt more focused than usual. I guess those are examples where resting didn't ruin anything—it actually helped.

Those are incredibly powerful examples because they prove that rest is compatible with—and sometimes even enhances—your success, contradicting the belief that you must be the "exception" who never stops. Listing those specific instances shows your brain a clear pattern where taking space led to better results, effectively dismantling the idea that you need to work harder to compensate. Now, let's bring this back to today's goal: since you still feel the urge to rush during those breaks, could we try a small experiment where you tell yourself, "This pause is exactly how I'm maintaining the car," and observe if the guilt decreases after just five minutes?

Okay, I'm willing to try that. I think the key for me is going to be actually saying those words out loud to myself, not just thinking them. When I just think it, the guilt still creeps in. But if I verbalize "this pause is how I maintain the car," maybe it'll feel more real. I'll give it a shot tomorrow at 10 AM and see what happens.

That is a brilliant strategy; speaking the phrase aloud engages your conscious mind more deeply, making the "maintenance" metaphor feel less abstract and more like a firm promise you are keeping to yourself. Since you mentioned tomorrow is the date, does setting a gentle alarm on your phone that plays that exact sentence when the ringtone starts seem like a way to support that verbalization without relying solely on willpower?

That's actually a really good idea. I can record myself saying it or just set a reminder with that exact phrase written in it. That way, even if I'm in the middle of something intense, my phone will pull me out for a moment. I think that might help override that initial urge to just hit "snooze" and keep working. I'll set that up tonight.

Setting up that auditory cue tonight is a smart way to create an external anchor for your new mindset, giving your brain a clear script to follow when the guilt tries to interrupt. Since we have a few more minutes, could we quickly check if there's any specific worry about *how* you'll handle the meeting or task you're doing once you step away, or does that plan feel solid enough to close the session?

I think the plan feels solid for now. My main worry was always just the guilt of stepping away, but having that phrase ready and knowing I can say it out loud makes it feel more doable. I think I'm ready to try it and see how it goes. Thank you—this session actually gave me something concrete to hold onto, which I really needed.

It is wonderful to hear that you found something concrete to hold onto; having a specific phrase and a clear ritual can make the vague feeling of guilt much easier to navigate. You've done a great job identifying the source of that pressure and building a practical tool to counteract it, and I am so proud of the effort you put into this work today. Before we wrap up, is there anything else you would like to add or any lingering thoughts about our plan for tomorrow?

No, I think I'm good. I feel more hopeful than I did when I walked in, which is nice. I'll practice saying that phrase out loud tonight a few times so it feels natural tomorrow. Thanks again for your help—I'll let you know how it goes next week.

That is a beautiful thing to notice—shifting from dread to hope is one of the biggest signs of real progress, and I am so glad to see it in you. Practicing the phrase tonight will definitely help embed it in your muscle memory so it becomes automatic tomorrow. Please remember that if the guilt ever resurfaces or you miss another break, it is perfectly okay to reach out and adjust our plan; you don't have to navigate this alone. I look forward to hearing how that experiment lands next week. Take care of yourself!
