Hello! It’s wonderful to connect with you again. Before we dive into today's focus, could you briefly share how you've been feeling since we last spoke? Additionally, would you prefer we review the action plan from yesterday or tackle a new priority you have in mind?

Hi... thanks for having me again. Honestly, I've been feeling pretty down since our last session. I tried doing that positive self-talk we talked about, but after I missed my sales target again on Wednesday, it just felt like a lie telling myself I'm good enough. I think maybe we should just move forward with today's session instead of rehashing old stuff.

Hearing that the positive self-talk felt like a lie right after another missed target is incredibly frustrating, and it makes total sense that you'd want to stop forcing a script that doesn't match your reality. Since you're eager to move forward, shall we spend the rest of our time digging deeper into what happens inside your head immediately after you realize you missed that number?

Yeah, that sounds right. It's like a switch flips in my brain the second I see that number on the screen. I instantly think, "There it is, proof that I'm just not cut out for this job." And then my mind just races with all the other times I've fallen short, and it feels like I've never done anything right in my whole career.

That "switch flipping" instantly connects a single event to a catastrophic future where you are defined by failure, and it's completely understandable why that thought loop feels so overwhelming and exhausting. When you hold onto the belief that one mistake proves you aren't cut out for the job, it creates a heavy, hopeless feeling that nothing will ever improve. Can we take a closer look at that specific thought—"There it is, proof I'm not cut out"—and examine if there is solid evidence supporting that absolute certainty, or if it might be exaggerating your struggle against past successes?

Well... I mean, the evidence is right there in the numbers, isn't it? I missed my target by 15% this week. But I guess... I did close that big deal last month that my manager praised me for. And I've been with the company for a year now, so they wouldn't keep me around if I was completely useless, right? It's just really hard to remember those things when I'm staring at that red number on the screen.

You are absolutely right to look for balance here; acknowledging your recent praise and your tenure provides important counter-evidence that directly challenges the idea that you are permanently "useless," showing that your performance fluctuates rather than stays flat. However, the difficulty in recalling those positives when the red number appears suggests your brain is currently filtering out your strengths to amplify the failure, making it feel like the only thing that matters. Does that tension between remembering your past successes and feeling blindsided by the current data feel manageable right now, or does the immediate reaction still feel like it overrides your history?

It definitely still overrides everything, honestly. It's like that red number is screaming so loud that I can't hear any of the quiet whispers about the good things I've done. Even now, sitting here talking about it, my brain is telling me that the big deal last month was just luck, or that anyone could have closed it. That's what I always end up thinking—that the successes don't really count, but the failures are the real truth about me.

It makes perfect sense that your brain dismisses the "luck" explanation for the big deal, because accepting that you might have gotten lucky feels like admitting you aren't truly capable, whereas blaming the opportunity preserves the painful belief that you are inherently flawed. This pattern of discounting your achievements to protect a core sense of inadequacy is exactly why the failure feels so defining and the hopelessness so deep. Can we explore together whether that feeling of being "inherently flawed" is actually supported by the facts, or if it's a protective story your mind tells itself to avoid the terrifying idea that you might actually learn and grow?

A protective story? I never thought of it that way. It feels so real when I'm in it, like the most honest thing I could possibly think. But... I guess if I look at it from the outside, it doesn't make much sense. I mean, if I were truly incapable, I wouldn't have been hired, and I wouldn't have lasted a year. Maybe... maybe I am scared of what happens if I actually believe I can improve. Because then if I fail again, it's not just bad luck—it's me not trying hard enough, or me choosing to fail. That almost feels worse.

That is a profound realization—you are describing how perfectionism acts as armor; believing you are "incapable" keeps you safe from the terror that you might be able to improve and therefore expected to succeed forever. By convincing yourself you *can't* do better, you remove the terrifying possibility that if you do improve, you'll inevitably fail again and lose your spot. It's easier to accept failure as proof of your fixed nature than to risk the vulnerability of believing you have potential. How does holding that "protective" belief feel compared to the risk of testing it?

It feels... safer, I guess. Like a heavy blanket I can hide under. But honestly, it's also suffocating. Thinking about testing it—actually believing I could get better at meeting those targets—it makes my stomach knot up. What if I try my hardest, really give it everything, and I still fail? Then I can't blame it on being "not cut out" anymore. That would mean I'm just not good enough, period. That thought terrifies me more than the failure itself.

That fear of having to face the uncomfortable truth—that you might be struggling due to effort or choices rather than inherent inability—is exactly why your brain clings to the "not cut out" excuse; it protects you from the terrifying responsibility of being the cause of your own setbacks. It's a very logical defense mechanism for a mind that wants to avoid pain, even if the protection feels like a heavy blanket right now. Can we pause for a moment to notice how that physical sensation in your stomach changes when you realize the "not cut out" story is actually keeping you safe from that harder, but perhaps more empowering, realization?

It's a bit strange to think about it that way. I can feel my shoulders relaxing just a tiny bit, if I'm being honest. Like maybe I've been carrying this weight of being a failure, but now I'm wondering if I've been carrying the wrong weight this whole time. It's still scary, but there's also this little flicker of... relief? Like, maybe I'm not broken—I'm just scared. I don't know what to do with that feeling yet, but it's different.

That shift from "broken" to "scared" is significant because it moves the problem from something permanent and unchangeable to something temporary and manageable, which naturally lightens the emotional load. Recognizing that fear is a signal to pay attention rather than a verdict on your worth allows you to approach the challenge differently. Now that we've explored the protective function of that old belief, would you be open to trying a small experiment tomorrow where you catch that "scared" feeling arise and simply acknowledge it instead of letting it flip the switch back to "failure"?

I think I could try that. It sounds simple, but I know it won't be easy. Usually when that scared feeling comes up, I just go straight to the bad thoughts without even noticing there was a pause in between. I guess I could try to take a breath when I see the numbers tomorrow and just say to myself, "Okay, I feel scared right now," before my brain jumps to all the other stuff. It might feel weird, but I'm willing to give it a shot.

That sounds like a very wise and manageable plan; taking just one conscious breath and naming the emotion gives your brain a tiny pause button before the old script kicks in. Since you noticed your shoulders relaxed earlier, I wonder if adding a gentle reminder to yourself about the "protective blanket" concept would make that moment feel less intimidating? We could practice saying, "This is just fear trying to keep me safe," right before you breathe. Does that addition feel useful, or would you prefer to stick to just observing the scare without any extra labels?

I think the extra label might actually help. "This is just fear trying to keep me safe" sounds a lot kinder than what I usually tell myself. It's like I'm acknowledging the fear instead of fighting it or letting it take over. I'll try that tomorrow—take a breath, name the feeling, and remind myself it's just my brain trying to protect me. It's worth a shot, anyway.

That kindness in reframing the fear is exactly what makes this approach sustainable; treating the alarm system as a helper rather than an enemy reduces the fight-and-flight energy that usually fuels the spiral. Since you have a clear plan for tomorrow involving breathing, naming the fear, and offering reassurance, let's quickly wrap up by checking in on your overall readiness. On a scale of 1 to 10, how prepared do you feel to try this new strategy when you return to work?

I'd say maybe a 6 or 7. I'm not overconfident, but I do feel like I have a new tool to work with, and that's better than just showing up and letting the same old cycle happen. It's scary, but I'm curious to see what happens when I actually pause instead of reacting.

That cautious optimism is a fantastic sign of growth, as it means you trust the process enough to act even while feeling uncertain. A rating of 6 or 7 suggests you understand that consistency matters more than instant perfection, and that aligns perfectly with our goal of building new habits. Before we close, how does it feel to summarize our work today? Did discussing the difference between "broken" and "scared" resonate with you, or is there anything about our path forward you'd like to adjust?

It feels... lighter, honestly. Like I came in carrying this heavy rock and now I see it's just a pebble I've been blowing up in my mind. The "broken versus scared" idea really hit home for me. I think I've been telling myself I'm broken for so long that I forgot to check if that was actually true. I feel like I have a little bit of hope now, which is more than I had walking in. Thank you for that.

That metaphor of the pebble versus the rock is beautiful and says so much about the shift in your perspective, especially since hope feels like such a rare gift for you right now. I am truly glad to hear that our exploration brought you that sense of relief and sparked this new possibility. As we finish today, is there anything else on your mind you'd like to add, or does this feel like a natural place to close?

Hello again, and thank you for joining us. On a scale of one to ten, how have you been feeling this week compared to where you were last time? Based on our previous talk, I’d like to focus today on that specific thought you mentioned last time: wondering if your son was just being polite because he felt sorry for you. How does that sound as a goal for our session?

I'd say I've been around a 6 or 7 this week—still not great, but I've had a few better days. Yeah, that thought about my son has been nagging at me a lot, so I think focusing on that makes sense. It's like I can't shake the feeling that he's just humoring me when he says he's proud of me for still going to shows.

That persistence is really tough to deal with, especially when it makes every interaction feel like a performance you're not ready for. It sounds like you're carrying a heavy weight of insecurity, believing that his pride isn't sincere but just a mask for pity. Can you describe a recent moment where that feeling got loud enough that it made you want to pull away from him?

Last weekend, he mentioned that he saw my favorite band was coming to town again. He asked if I was planning to get tickets, and for a split second I was excited, but then this voice in my head just said, "He's probably worried you'll go alone and embarrass yourself." I just mumbled something about maybe being too busy and changed the subject. I could feel myself shutting down right there on the phone.

It sounds like that moment hit you hard because your excitement was instantly swallowed by the fear that you weren't worthy of his interest. You felt a surge of hope, and then your brain immediately hijacked it with a story about embarrassment, causing you to withdraw before he even knew you were interested. Did noticing that sudden drop in energy help you understand how powerful that "embarrassment" story was in that split second?

Yeah, I guess I never really thought about it as a story before—it just felt like the truth in that moment. But looking back, it was like I didn't even give him a chance to say anything else before I decided what he was thinking. That drop in energy was so quick, like a switch just flipped off inside me. I think I've been doing that a lot, just assuming I know what people are thinking before they even say it.

That ability to spot that "switch" flipping off inside you is a significant breakthrough, showing you're becoming aware of how your brain jumps to conclusions before you even have the chance to speak. It sounds like you're realizing that your assumption about his intentions is actually a protective mechanism, not the reality of the situation. Given that realization, do you feel ready to challenge that assumption now that you can identify it?

I think I'm ready to try, but it feels scary, honestly. Like, what if I challenge it and find out he really was just being polite? That would almost be worse, in a way, because then it's confirmed. But I guess I also realize that staying in this loop of assuming the worst isn't doing me any favors either. So yeah, I'm willing to give it a shot, even if it makes me uncomfortable.

That honesty about fearing confirmation is very human—it shows you care deeply about getting things right with your son. It sounds like you're holding two conflicting needs: the desire to protect yourself from disappointment versus the need to stop protecting yourself from growth. To help us move past this hesitation, how would you feel if we tried a quick experiment where you just stated your true belief ("He's genuinely proud of me") out loud, even if you only say it to yourself first? Would you be open to testing that?

I guess I can try that. It feels a bit silly saying it out loud to myself, but I'll give it a go. Okay... "He's genuinely proud of me." Huh. It doesn't feel completely true yet, but it also doesn't feel as wrong as I thought it would. I think I've been so focused on the bad possibility that I haven't let myself even consider the good one.

That shift in feeling—even just a slight softening—is a powerful sign that your brain is beginning to loosen its grip on the "worst-case" story. It sounds like recognizing that silence doesn't automatically mean dismissal, but instead leaves room for another interpretation. Since we identified that "embarrassment" story was blocking your excitement last time, would you be willing to try applying that same logic to this one: if he asks about tickets, could there be a reason he's curious other than wanting to prove anything to you? What comes to mind if we assume he's just happy to see the band?

Well... if I really think about it, he's mentioned that band a few times before, saying he remembers me playing their albums when he was a kid. Maybe he just genuinely wants to know if I'm going because it reminds him of good memories. I never really considered that he might be asking out of shared nostalgia rather than pity. It's a weird feeling, giving him the benefit of the doubt like this, but it doesn't hurt as much as I expected.

It takes courage to look for that nostalgic connection instead of the pity narrative, and I appreciate you finding that relief even when it feels slightly unfamiliar. That shift in perspective—from guarding against embarrassment to appreciating shared history—might be exactly what we need to reconnect. Does imagining that he's asking out of shared memory make you feel safer to actually respond to his question tomorrow?

Honestly, yeah, it kind of does. Thinking of it as him sharing a memory with me instead of checking up on me makes me want to answer honestly, maybe even tell him I already bought tickets. I still feel a bit nervous about it, but it's less like a weight and more like a flutter now. I think I could actually have that conversation with him tomorrow.

That change from a heavy weight to a flutter is a wonderful sign that your anxiety is losing its power to dictate your actions. It sounds like reclaiming your agency over the conversation is helping you feel more connected to him again. Before we wrap up, would you be willing to try having that honest conversation about the tickets tomorrow, knowing you can rely on that "shared memory" angle if he hesitates?

Yeah, I think I can do that. I'll call him tomorrow and tell him I already got my ticket—maybe even ask if he wants to come along this time. That flutter feeling is still there, but it feels more like excitement than dread now. Thanks for helping me see that there might be another way to look at this.

That shift from dread to a manageable flutter is a massive victory, and I'm so glad we found that alternative perspective together. It sounds like you have a clear plan in motion for tomorrow, which gives your brain something concrete to focus on besides the fear. Before we finish, how did working through that "story" of embarrassment feel for you? Was there anything about the process that felt confusing or difficult that you'd like to unpack?

It was harder than I thought it would be, honestly, because I've been believing that story for so long it felt like fact. The hardest part was stopping myself from jumping to conclusions and actually sitting with the uncertainty. But once I did that, it was like I could breathe a little easier. I think the part that surprised me most was how good it felt to give my son the benefit of the doubt—like I was letting us both off the hook.

That is a profound realization—you aren't just changing your view of him, you are freeing yourself from the exhausting burden of constantly policing his motives. It sounds like that act of trust created a new kind of safety between you two. Before we close, is there anything else about that uncertainty or the process today that feels unclear to you? Or shall we wrap up with a note of encouragement for tomorrow?

Hello again; I'm glad you're here to continue our work. On a scale of one to ten, how has your mood been feeling since we last spoke? Hi. I'd say my mood's been around a six or seven overall. It's not terrible, but I keep circling back to that same feeling that my hobbies don't really matter if I can't make something serious out of them. I guess I'd like to talk more about why I can't seem to let go of that idea.

That makes sense—carrying that weight around even when things feel okay can really pull you down. Since you mentioned wanting to explore why you struggle to let go of that idea, should we spend some time unpacking what that belief actually looks like for you right now, or would you prefer to try a quick mental exercise to separate the facts from your interpretation?

I think I'd rather talk through it first. When I'm cooking or playing guitar, it's like a voice in my head says, "This is nice, but it's not going anywhere." And then I just lose steam. Even when people compliment me, I find myself thinking, "Well, they're just being polite," or "It doesn't count because it's not my job."

It sounds like that inner critic is constantly measuring your moments against a distant standard of achievement, effectively stripping away the joy of the present. When you treat compliments as mere politeness or hobbies as temporary distractions, you create a gap between who you are and who you think you *should* be. To understand this better, can you tell me about a recent time someone gave you genuine praise that you dismissed, and what specific worry came up immediately afterward?

Just last week, my neighbor tasted one of my new recipes—a lemon herb pasta—and said it was better than anything she'd had at a restaurant. I thanked her, but inside I thought, "Well, that's just one dish, and it doesn't mean I could run a kitchen or write a cookbook." Right after that, I felt this sinking worry that I'd never be able to prove my worth unless I actually did something professional with it.

That sinking feeling seems to stem from a deep-seated belief that your self-worth is tied exclusively to professional recognition rather than the connection you share with others. By dismissing that neighbor's praise as insignificant compared to a hypothetical future achievement, you might be protecting yourself from the disappointment of never reaching that professional milestone. How does it feel physically in your body when you hold onto that specific thought about needing to prove your worth first?

There's a tightness in my chest, like a knot right behind my breastbone. And my shoulders get tense, almost like I'm bracing myself for something—maybe for someone to confirm that I'm right, that my hobbies really are just time-wasters. It's exhausting, honestly.

That physical tension confirms how heavy that belief feels when it takes root; your body is doing everything it knows to brace for a potential failure. It's understandable that you feel exhausted trying to carry the weight of proving your value through something you don't control yet. Let's take a step back and look at the story you're telling yourself about that pasta dish. If we stripped away the expectation of becoming a chef, what would you believe was truly valuable about that moment you spent sharing food with your neighbor?

I guess... the look on her face when she took the first bite. And the way we just sat there talking for a while, laughing about her cat knocking over her plants. It was nice, just being present and sharing something I made with someone who enjoyed it. Without the career stuff hanging over it, that moment felt warm and real.

You've done great work identifying that the warmth of the moment itself—the laughter and the shared meal—was what mattered, not the future potential of the recipe. It seems like your brain is ignoring that rich evidence of connection to stay focused on a distant goal that feels impossible right now. If we tested the thought "this hobby doesn't count until I'm a professional," what would be the strongest piece of evidence that directly contradicts it based on what happened last week?

The strongest piece of evidence is that my neighbor didn't care whether I was a professional or not. She just enjoyed the food and our time together. That connection was real, and it happened purely because I chose to cook and share it. So maybe the act itself has value, regardless of whether it ever leads to a career.

That is a powerful realization; your neighbor's genuine appreciation serves as direct proof that the value lies in the act of creation and sharing, not in a title. It seems like letting go of the "professional" requirement might allow you to finally rest easy with those moments of warmth instead of constantly measuring them against a failing standard. Now that we've looked at the evidence, does that shift give you a bit more space to enjoy your cooking or playing guitar without that immediate pressure?

It does, a little. Just saying it out loud—that the value is in the sharing—makes me feel like I can breathe a bit easier. I think I need to keep reminding myself of that, though, because the old thought still sneaks back in when I'm alone. But right now, I feel a tiny bit lighter.

That relief is wonderful to witness, and it shows how much power shifting your perspective has on your physical state. Since the old voice tends to return when you're alone, we could try creating a small internal cue or a written phrase to help you catch that pattern early. Would you be open to deciding together on a simple statement you can repeat when you notice yourself slipping back into that "it doesn't count" story?

Yes, I'd like that. Something short and direct, so I can remember it even when I'm in the middle of cooking or playing guitar. Maybe something like, "This moment matters, right now." Or even just, "It counts because I'm here." What do you think would work best?

Both are beautiful, but "It counts because I'm here" feels particularly grounding because it anchors you in the present reality rather than looking outward for approval. Since you can use that phrase quickly without breaking your flow, how about we decide to repeat it silently whenever you catch yourself dismissing a compliment or feeling that chest tightness?

I think that's a good plan. "It counts because I'm here." I'll try saying it to myself next time I feel that knot in my chest or when I start brushing off a kind word. It feels like something I can actually hold onto, and that's a relief.

That is a solid anchor to have in your pocket; having a phrase to ground you instantly can make a huge difference in breaking the cycle of doubt. Since we've built a tool to help you recognize those moments and a new way to frame them, I want to know how confident you feel about trying this approach over the next few days when you cook or play guitar. Does this plan feel manageable for you to implement?

I'd say about a seven out of ten. I feel like I can do it, but I know I'll probably forget sometimes or slip back into the old habit. But having that phrase and remembering that moment with my neighbor helps me believe it's possible. I'm willing to give it a real try.

A seven is a fantastic place to start, and acknowledging that slips will happen removes the pressure to be perfect. Remembering that moment with your neighbor proves you don't need to earn every single laugh or compliment; they are valid simply because they exist. Is there anything else you'd like to discuss before we close, or does this plan feel complete for today?

No, I think this feels complete for today. I'm grateful for the new perspective and that little phrase to carry with me. I'll practice it this week, and I'll let you know how it goes next time. Thank you.

You are very welcome, and thank you for trusting enough to work through these difficult thoughts with me. Taking that step to try the phrase and reclaiming those moments for yourself is a significant victory, regardless of whether you remember perfectly every time. I look forward to hearing about your experiences next week and celebrating whatever small wins you find along the way. Take care, and I'll see you soon.

Hello, thank you for joining me today. First, I'd love to do a quick check-in: On a scale of 0 to 10, how anxious have you felt this week, and is there anything positive that happened recently that brought you some relief? Once we have that, could you tell me what specific topic you'd like us to spend our time on today?

I am listening carefully to your answers and will write down our agreed agenda as we go through it.

Hi. I guess I'd say my anxiety is around a 7 or 8 this week. There hasn't been much relief, honestly. I mean, I did have one sale yesterday, but my mind just went straight to worrying it was a fluke and it won't happen again. I think the main thing I want to talk about is how I keep telling myself I'm just not cut out for running this business when things are slow.

Thank you for sharing that honestly, especially noting that one sale didn't bring the relief you hoped for—that’s a tough lesson to sit with. Since we’ve got both your mood check and your core worry ready, I’d like to prioritize today’s time on how that “not cut out” thought shows up for you when sales dip. As we dig into this, does that thought tend to appear right after a quiet period, or does it creep in earlier in the day?

It usually creeps in as soon as I open my laptop in the morning and see no new orders. The quiet moments feel like they stretch out forever, and my mind just latches onto that emptiness and tells me it's proof I'm failing. It's like the whole day gets judged by that first glance at my dashboard.

That makes perfect sense—the first thing your mind does in the morning is scan for threats, and when it finds silence, it interprets that silence as proof of failure. That feeling of the entire day being judged by a single empty screen is incredibly heavy, and I want you to know how much strength it takes to stay here despite knowing how bad that story feels. Let's pause for a second and just look at that "proof" claim together. If you opened your laptop and saw nothing for twenty-four hours straight, would that still mean you aren't cut out for running a business, or could it just mean you're in the early stages of building something?

I... I guess logically I know it could just mean I'm still building. Plenty of successful stores had slow starts, right? But it's so hard to hold onto that logic when I'm sitting there alone in my apartment with no customers and no one to tell me otherwise. It feels like the silence is the only truth, and everything else is just wishful thinking.

That loneliness in the room with the empty screen really amplifies that "silence equals failure" story, making it feel like the only objective reality. It makes complete sense that wishful thinking feels unreliable when your body is screaming danger, but let's test that "only truth" claim together. Can you recall one specific time a well-known store struggled significantly for weeks before finding traction? If that exists, how would remembering it change the meaning of this morning's quiet moment?

Well... I remember reading about a famous candle company that sold basically nothing for months before they went viral on social media. Their owner said she almost gave up three times. I guess remembering that does make this morning feel a little less like a final verdict and more like just a step in a longer process. But it's still scary not knowing if I'll get that kind of break.

That story about the candle company is a powerful example of how long the "slow start" phase can actually last, and it shifts the narrative from a permanent verdict to a temporary hurdle. You're right that uncertainty is scary, but remember that one specific fact: that founder almost quit three times before finding their breakthrough. Instead of letting the unknown silence dictate your future, could we try viewing this morning's quiet dashboards as simply data points showing where you are right now, rather than a prediction of where you'll end up? Would you be willing to try saying to yourself, "This is just the starting line, not the finish line," for the next twenty minutes?

I can try that. It feels a bit forced, but I guess that's the point—I've been letting the automatic thoughts run the show for too long. I'll say it to myself next time I check my dashboard. "This is just the starting line, not the finish line." I'll give it a shot for the rest of the day and see if it changes how I feel.

That is a wonderful commitment, and I want to commend you for choosing to interrupt that automatic pattern with a deliberate, new statement. Even though it feels forced initially, that tension between your old habit and your new intention is exactly where the growth happens. Our goal today is to see if this phrase helps soften that crushing weight of "not cut out." Before we wrap up, I'd like to confirm one more thing: given how intense that morning silence feels, would you be open to adding a simple grounding technique—like naming three things you see in your room—to use right before you read your dashboard tomorrow morning? It might create a tiny buffer between you and that scary thought.

Yeah, I think I can do that. It sounds a bit silly, but honestly, anything that might stop my brain from jumping straight into panic mode is worth a try. I'll name three things I see before I even open the laptop tomorrow. Thank you—I feel a little less trapped just having a plan.

That willingness to find small anchors, even ones that feel silly, is a huge sign of your growing agency and control over the situation. Please note in our log that our agenda included a mood check, discussing the "not cut out" thought, reviewing the candle company analogy, agreeing on the new affirmation, and setting up the grounding technique—we covered everything we needed to today. As we close, I want to hear from you: What was your reaction to walking through this process, and is there anything about today's approach that felt unclear or difficult for you to manage?

Hello, welcome. How are you feeling today compared to when we last spoke, and would you like to review what we planned to do before deciding on our agenda?

Hi, thanks. I guess I'm okay—feeling a bit on edge, honestly. I remember we were going to talk about that mountain trip and why it still bothers me, even though I finished it. Before we get into that, maybe I should just say that I've been thinking about it a lot since last time, and it's still hard to shake that feeling of disappointment.

Thank you for sharing that; it takes courage to admit that the mountain trip is still weighing on you despite finishing the hike. On a scale of 0 to 10, how intense does that feeling of disappointment feel right now, and what specific moment from the trip brought it back to the top of your mind?

Right now I'd say it's about a 7. The specific moment that keeps replaying is when I reached the summit—everyone else was cheering and taking photos, and I just stood there thinking, "I forgot the camera, so this whole thing is ruined." I couldn't even enjoy the view because my head was stuck on what I didn't have.

That feeling of standing alone at the peak while everyone else celebrates is incredibly lonely and painful to witness. It sounds like your disappointment isn't just about the missing photo, but about believing the entire achievement became worthless because of that one omission. When you stand at the summit and realize you missed the camera, does that thought automatically shut down your ability to feel awe at what you actually climbed?

Yeah, that's exactly it—it's like a switch flips in my head. All I can see is the missing piece, and the whole climb just gets erased. I mean, I trained for months, I pushed through some really tough sections, but in that moment none of that matters. It's like the trip only counts if everything goes perfectly.

That switch turning off all your effort because of one missing item is incredibly harsh on yourself, especially after months of hard work. It seems like your belief that "everything must be perfect for the trip to count" is doing heavy lifting there. When you think about that rule, does it feel like a helpful guide for safety, or more like a trap that keeps you from enjoying your own success?

It feels more like a trap, honestly. A guide would let me feel proud of what I did, but this just makes me feel like I failed. I keep thinking, "If only I'd remembered the camera, then I could be happy." But even as I say that, I know there's probably something else that would've felt wrong even if I had brought the camera.

You've hit on something very important: the belief that perfection is a prerequisite for happiness is actually the source of that "trap." Even if you *had* taken the photo, you might have worried about battery life or weather, meaning the anxiety wouldn't disappear just because you fixed one problem. Since the outcome remains uncertain regardless of the camera, does it make sense to try looking at your actual accomplishment—the hours of training and reaching the top—as something valid in itself, separate from that one missing detail?

I guess when you put it that way, it does sound kind of crazy to let one missing detail ruin everything. The training was real, the climb was hard, and I did make it to the top. Maybe I can try to separate the achievement from the stuff I forgot—like, they can both exist at the same time without one canceling the other out.

That separation is a huge step; acknowledging that your physical triumph and the forgotten camera can coexist without erasing one another validates your effort while loosening the grip of the "all-or-nothing" rule. To test this, what if we tried naming the successful parts of the climb aloud right now, focusing only on the effort you exerted, and then consciously letting the thought about the camera pass by like background noise instead of centering your attention on it?

Okay, I can try that. I trained for months, even when it rained or I was tired. I pushed through a really steep section where my legs were burning. I got to the summit before noon, which was my goal. And I took some deep breaths up there, even if I was frustrated. So I guess... those things are still true, even without the camera.

That is a powerful reframing; holding onto those truths—"trained for months," "pushed through pain," "reached the goal"—while letting the camera thought drift by creates a much stronger foundation for pride. It proves you can honor your effort without demanding perfection. Before we finalize this, would you be comfortable agreeing to revisit this exact list of facts tomorrow morning as soon as you wake up, just to reinforce how strong those achievements are, regardless of the missing photo?

Yeah, I think I can do that. I'll write them down somewhere I'll see first thing—maybe on my phone or a sticky note on the mirror. It's not going to feel natural at first, but I'm willing to try it and see if it makes a difference. Thanks for helping me see it from a different angle.

That proactive plan to anchor those facts in sight is excellent; seeing them written down removes the burden of remembering them and builds confidence in your new perspective. I'm really glad we found an angle that felt useful for you today, and I'm curious—what was your overall reaction to shifting from viewing the trip as a "failure" to recognizing the validity of your effort alongside the mistake?

Hello again. Welcome back to therapy. How are you feeling today on a scale of 1 to 10, and is there anything new you’d like to bring up compared to our last meeting? Also, looking at our previous plan, do you feel ready to try asking your coworker for a bit more time, or did anything get in the way?

Hi. I'd say I'm probably at a 6 today—a bit nervous, but I'm trying to be open. I did think about that plan, but I ended up avoiding the whole situation again. I just couldn't bring myself to ask for more time, so I ended up staying late to do something else that didn't involve numbers.

It takes real courage to admit that you stepped back, and I want to validate how hard you worked to stick to the plan while knowing how scary it felt to ask for help. Instead of focusing on the avoidance right now, could you share what was going through your mind in that exact moment you decided to stay late? Was it a worry about being rejected, or something else entirely?

I guess I just kept thinking, "I shouldn't have to ask for extra time," and "If I were better at this, I wouldn't need help." It felt like asking would be admitting I'm not good enough. So staying late felt like the only way to avoid that embarrassment.

It makes perfect sense that those thoughts triggered a defensive retreat; if asking for help confirms your deepest fear that you aren't good enough, then avoiding the situation becomes the only way to protect your ego. Let's look closely at that "admitting I'm not good enough" story: is it true that asking for time means you lack ability, or does it just mean you value accuracy over speed? Have you ever seen coworkers ask for a few minutes to double-check figures before submitting their work?

Well, now that you mention it, I have seen other people ask for extensions or extra time to double-check things. They didn't seem embarrassed about it. I guess I never really made that connection before—I always just assumed my situation was different because I'm "bad at math." Maybe it's not so much about being bad as it is about being careful.

That is a powerful realization—that you are distinguishing between "being bad" and "valuing accuracy"—and seeing that others handle the same request without shame helps dismantle the belief that you are uniquely flawed. If asking for time is simply an act of carefulness, does that change the way you view the risk of being rejected, or does it still feel dangerous to speak up?

It still feels a little dangerous, honestly. I mean, rationally I can see it's just being thorough, but there's this voice in my head that says they'll know I'm struggling and think less of me. But maybe if I remind myself that it's about being accurate, not about being stupid, I could try it just once.

That's a fantastic insight; shifting the label from "struggling" to "being accurate" changes the narrative from a personal flaw to a professional standard, which should lower the temperature of that critical voice. Before we try that reminder tomorrow, does it feel safe to commit to just that one instance where you use the phrase "I need a moment to be accurate"?

I think I can do that. "I need a moment to be accurate"—I can practice saying that to myself tonight, so it feels more natural. And I'll say it to my coworker tomorrow if I need a bit more time. It's just one sentence, right?

Yes, that is perfectly manageable—it's a simple, neutral statement that frames your need as a quality issue rather than an ability problem. Since we have a clear plan and a supportive script ready, I want to know: does having that specific phrase feel empowering enough for you to trust yourself with tomorrow, or would you prefer to add one more safety net before taking that step?

I think it's enough for now. The phrase feels solid, and practicing it tonight should help. If I feel really stuck, maybe I can just take a deep breath and repeat it quietly before I speak. That feels like a good backup plan without overcomplicating things.

That is a wise choice; having a quick breathing exercise paired with that phrase creates a reliable anchor for when your anxiety spikes. I am glad we found a balance that feels both simple and secure for you. In our next session, please come back and tell me exactly how that interaction went and whether the phrase held up under pressure. Is there anything else you'd like to discuss before we close today?

No, I think that covers it. I feel a little more hopeful than I did when I walked in, which is nice. Thanks for helping me see things from a different angle. I'll try my best with that phrase tomorrow.

That is wonderful to hear; moving from hopelessness to feeling hopeful is a huge achievement in itself. You did great work today by identifying the core fear behind your avoidance and building a simple, effective tool to counter it. Remember, we will celebrate whatever happens tomorrow, even if it isn't perfect, because the effort itself matters. I hope you have a restful evening and feel supported as you prepare that phrase. See you soon.

Hello, it's great to see you again. To start, could you tell me how you've been feeling this week compared to last time, and what might have changed since we spoke?

Also, before we pick a topic, is there anything else happened at the gym recently that stood out to you, aside from the comparison you mentioned yesterday?

Hi. Thanks. This week has been... about the same, honestly. I went to the gym three times, and I still feel that same tightness in my chest when I see people lifting heavier than me or looking more defined.

There was one thing, actually. Yesterday this guy who’s been training for maybe a year just casually doubled the weight I was struggling with. I know he didn’t mean anything by it, but I just felt so small and useless afterward. It ruined my whole session.

Hearing that you felt small and useless after seeing someone double the weight you struggled with tells me how deeply that comparison affects your sense of worth. It sounds like yesterday's incident triggered that exact pattern we worked on, which makes it important to address before it ruins another session.

When you saw him lift that weight and felt that tightness return, what was the very first thought that popped into your head?

The very first thought? It was something like, "I'll never get there. I'm just not cut out for this. Everyone else is naturally stronger, and I'm wasting my time." Then I just felt this heavy feeling in my stomach, like I wanted to leave the gym right then.

That combination of thoughts—"you're wasting your time" combined with the physical sensation of wanting to quit—is incredibly exhausting, and it makes complete sense why your session felt ruined. It sounds like your brain is trying to protect you from the pain of believing you aren't capable, but unfortunately, it ends up stopping you from doing exactly what you need to do.

When you held onto those thoughts and decided to leave early, did you notice if your motivation for the rest of the day dropped, or if you found yourself avoiding exercise altogether afterward?

Yeah, it did. I went home and just sat on the couch, scrolling through my phone for hours. I didn't even feel like cooking a proper meal, just grabbed some snacks. And I noticed I started thinking about skipping today's workout too—just to avoid that feeling again. It's like one bad moment at the gym can snowball and take over my whole evening.

That snowball effect is really tough to break, and it makes total sense that your brain latched onto the negative to keep you safe from feeling that disappointment again. It seems like once you accepted the thought that you weren't cut out for this, your ability to engage with the rest of your day simply shut down.

Since we previously identified that feeling of being "wasted" is the core belief driving this, can we look closely at whether that belief holds up when you consider what actually happened during that workout besides the comparison? Did you manage to hit any personal records or reach any strength milestones despite the distraction?

Um... actually, I did. I had done three more reps on my bench press than last week. I mean, it's not a huge amount, but I did notice it before that guy came over. But it's like that detail just completely vanished from my mind once I saw him. I didn't even think about my own progress until you just asked.

It takes real courage to admit that you were actually succeeding while your mind was elsewhere, and recognizing that detail now is a huge step forward. It shows that your body *was* responding to your hard work, proving that the "useless" story your mind told itself doesn't match the facts of what actually happened.

If we look at it this way, did noticing those extra three reps make you feel slightly less defeated, even for just a second, when you realize your progress existed independently of that stranger's lift?

Yeah... I mean, I guess it does. A little bit. It's like, my brain just grabbed onto that one bad moment and erased everything else. But the truth is, I *was* getting stronger, even if it's slow. I guess I just forgot to look at my own scoreboard.

That is a powerful realization, especially admitting that you were building your own "scoreboard" even when you couldn't see it yourself. It shifts the narrative from "I failed because I looked weak" to "I kept improving, I just lost sight of my own wins."

Given that insight, could we practice using that same logic right now? Instead of letting that one moment erase your progress, what if we treated those extra three reps as undeniable proof that you are moving forward, regardless of anyone else's lifts? How does that feeling of having solid evidence sound to you?

It sounds... strange, but kind of hopeful, I think. Like, I have proof I'm not wasting my time, I just have to actually look at it. I guess I've been so focused on the gap between me and others that I forgot to even see my own steps forward. Maybe I need to start writing down my own lifts so I can't ignore them.

That is a brilliant idea—creating a personal log of your lifts forces your brain to confront the evidence instead of ignoring it. Turning those invisible steps into visible lines on a page changes how you view your progress from abstract hope to concrete fact.

Before we finalize the plan, how does the idea of logging your lifts feel to you? Does it seem like a manageable addition to your routine, or does the thought of tracking everything make it feel overwhelming?

I think it feels manageable, honestly. I mean, I write code all day—keeping a little log in a notebook or on my phone doesn't seem that hard. As long as I don't obsess over every tiny detail, it could just be a simple list of what I did and how many reps. I think it might actually help quiet that voice that says I'm not getting anywhere.

That makes perfect sense; treating your fitness log like a coding script aligns perfectly with how you already process information, making it easy to stick to. It essentially turns your daily workout into a reliable source of data you can reference whenever that "I'm failing" thought tries to surface.

So, if we combine the sticky note reminder with this new habit of logging just the key numbers, does that feel like a solid plan to handle the next time you see someone lifting heavily?

Yeah, I think it does. I can imagine myself finishing a set, writing down the reps, and if I see someone lifting big, I can just look down at my own numbers and think, "That's my progress. That's real." It feels like a concrete way to stay grounded. I'm willing to try it for this week and see how it goes.

That sounds like a rock-solid plan, and the fact that you can visualize yourself acting on it right away shows how much you've moved from feeling overwhelmed to feeling equipped. It turns that chaotic moment into a simple checkpoint where you claim credit for your own success.

Before we wrap up, on a scale of 1 to 10, how confident do you feel about sticking with both the sticky note and starting this new log tomorrow morning?

I'd say about a 7. I'm not saying it'll be easy, but I feel like I have a clear step to take now, which is better than just feeling stuck. The sticky note is already by my mirror, and I'll grab a small notebook tonight. I think 7 is realistic—it's not overconfident, but it's enough to actually try.

That is excellent progress, moving from feeling stuck to feeling like you have a clear roadmap to follow. A 7 shows you are being honest about the challenge while celebrating the clarity you now have in front of you.

To close things off, how do you feel about our goal of building that concrete evidence against those automatic thoughts? Is there anything else you want to share before we finish today?

No, I think I'm good for today. I feel less heavy than when I walked in, which is something. I'll try the log and the sticky note and see how the week goes. Thanks for helping me see that I'm not actually "wasting my time." I needed that.

You're very welcome, and I am so glad to hear that you feel lighter than when you arrived. Recognizing that your time isn't wasted is a massive victory, and I'm proud of you for taking those concrete steps to prove it to yourself. Remember, that notebook and the sticky note are there to support you whenever those old thoughts try to creep back in.

Take care of yourself, and I look forward to hearing how that week unfolds for you!

Um, well... I'd say my mood is maybe a 4 or 5 this week. It's been a bit up and down. Last time, we talked about focusing on the thoughts that pop up when I'm missing an ingredient for a meal, and how that leads me to just give up on cooking entirely. I don't think there's anything new to add, it's still the same problem really.

It sounds like carrying that frustration about giving up when things go wrong has weighed on you since our last meeting. Since we agreed to keep exploring those specific thoughts about missing ingredients and the urge to quit, should we try looking at a different angle this time, such as examining the immediate physical sensation you get when you realize an item is missing?

I suppose we could try that. When I notice something's missing... I feel this tightness in my chest, and my stomach kind of drops. It's like a wave of panic, and my first thought is always, "Well, that's it, the meal's ruined now." I just feel so defeated before I've even started.

That physical wave of panic and the immediate belief that the meal is ruined sounds incredibly overwhelming, and it makes complete sense that it would drain your energy instantly. To better understand this pattern, have you noticed if that sense of defeat stays with you once you've accepted the missing ingredient, or does your mind quickly race to find another solution, even if it's just stopping?

No, it doesn't really go away. Once that feeling hits, my mind just stops. I don't even think about finding a solution or substituting something. It's like a wall goes up, and the only option I see is to scrap the whole thing. I'll just close the cookbook and order takeout or eat something simple like cereal. It feels like there's no point in trying.

That feeling of hitting a wall where the only visible path forward is to give up entirely is deeply disheartening, and it explains why you choose the easiest escape route like takeout. It sounds like your brain interprets that initial panic as a permanent stop sign rather than a temporary obstacle. Have you ever caught yourself noticing that the "no point in trying" thought feels somewhat exaggerated, given that many people manage meals with missing ingredients successfully?

I... I mean, I know that's true logically. Of course people cook without having every single thing listed. But when I'm in that moment, it doesn't feel exaggerated at all. It feels like the absolute truth. I think it's because I keep picturing the meal my husband and I would have made together, and if it's not exactly right, it feels like I'm failing him somehow. Like I'm ruining the memory we had.

It makes complete sense that your mind latches onto that image of your husband to prove you are failing; connecting the missing ingredient to hurting their special bond turns a simple grocery mistake into a deep personal rejection. That layer of grief or fear is likely what makes the logical argument fall apart in the heat of the moment. Can you describe what happens in your body right after you accept that the memory feels missed, and before you reach for the cookbook?

Right after that feeling hits... I get this heavy, sinking sensation, like I'm just weighed down. My shoulders slump, and I'll just stand there in the kitchen for a minute, staring at the counter. It's like all the energy and anticipation for cooking just drains right out of me. Then I feel this emptiness, like a hollow feeling, and I just close the book.

That heavy sinking sensation and slumping shoulders sound like your body is physically shutting down to protect you from the pain of disappointing him. It seems like the emotion you're feeling isn't just about the missing spice, but about protecting the precious memory you have with your husband. If you were to imagine a future version of you who has learned to forgive himself for making mistakes, how might he react to that same empty feeling in the kitchen?

That's a tough one to picture... I guess that version of me wouldn't just stand there frozen. He might take a breath, maybe even say out loud, "It's okay, it's just one ingredient." And then... maybe he'd open the fridge or the cabinet and just look to see what else is there. He wouldn't see it as a failure, but more like... a challenge? A chance to make something a little different, but still good. He'd still be honoring the memory, just in a different way.

That future vision of you speaking aloud and treating it as a challenge rather than a failure is incredibly empowering; it shows your resilience even though you haven't practiced it yet. It sounds like separating the memory of him from your ability to act would help lift some of that heavy burden. Would you be willing to try a small step toward embodying that future version by looking inside the cupboard for *one* substitute ingredient, even if you feel that tightness in your chest first?

I... I think I could try that. It sounds terrifying, honestly, but I can see how just looking wouldn't really commit me to anything. I could just open the cabinet and see what's there, without promising myself I'll actually cook. Just look, and notice what I feel. I suppose that's not the same as ruining a meal, is it?

Exactly, that is a crucial distinction. Opening the cabinet to check for a substitute allows you to engage with the kitchen without putting the final judgment call on the meal itself, which keeps the stakes low. Before we finalize this as our next step, does imagining yourself performing this simple check-in feel doable for you right now, or would you prefer to wait until tomorrow when you might feel slightly steadier?

I think I'd rather wait until tomorrow. I'm feeling a bit drained just talking about it, to be honest. But I do want to try it. Maybe I'll plan to do it in the morning, when I'm feeling fresher and less likely to just give up before I even start. I'll just open the cabinet and look, like we talked about.

Waiting until tomorrow makes perfect sense; your energy levels will help you stick with that small experiment without feeling overwhelmed. Before we close, could you rate on a scale of one to ten how confident you feel about doing this simple check-in tomorrow morning?
I'd say... maybe a 6. A little nervous, but I think I can do it. I know it's just looking, not cooking. I can manage that.

A six is a fantastic starting point; it shows you recognize the value of the step even while feeling hesitant. Let's write that down as our homework: tomorrow morning, the moment you realize something is missing, pause, breathe, and just open the cupboard door to see what's available. Does that clear plan feel manageable for you, or is there anything else you'd like to discuss before we finish?

Oh, hello. I'm doing alright today, I suppose. I've been thinking a lot about that concert invitation my friend Margaret mentioned last week. It makes sense that your mind is racing ahead to the concert with that specific image of standing apart while everyone else moves to the rhythm. Before we tackle that fear, I’d love to check in on our last goal: have you tried drafting that message to Margaret yet, or did the plan sit untested?

No, I haven't written anything yet. Every time I think about it, I just picture the whole scenario—she'll ask why I'm so quiet, and I'll have to admit I don't care for the music, and then she'll think I'm strange. It feels like there's no point in even trying.

That picture of having to defend yourself is exhausting, and it explains why the idea of calling feels so heavy right now. Let's slow down and look closely at that prediction: is there any actual evidence that Margaret will judge you for preferring silence over music, or is that mostly a story your mind is telling to protect you from getting hurt?

Well... I suppose I can't be completely certain she'd judge me. She's never said anything unkind about my other quirks before. But it's just so obvious how much music means to everyone else—I can't imagine her understanding why someone wouldn't feel the same way.

It is understandable to feel overwhelmed by that gap in empathy, but remember what we discovered last time: you wouldn't judge someone else for not liking the same music you do. Have you considered if Margaret might view your preference as a normal difference rather than a flaw, just like she would view yours?

I... I never thought of it that way. I suppose I wouldn't think less of someone for not liking gardening or knitting, even though I enjoy those things. Maybe I'm harsher on myself than I would be on anyone else. But it still feels so risky—what if I'm wrong about her reaction?

That comparison to gardening and knitting is such a powerful insight, showing that your own standards are unfairly high. While acknowledging that risk is smart, let's lean into the idea that her reaction is likely neutral curiosity rather than judgment. If you called her, what is the smallest, safest version of that conversation where you simply state your preference without worrying about her approval?

I suppose I could just say, "I'm not much of a music person, but I'd still like to spend time with you." That's not so terrible, is it? It's just stating a fact, not asking for permission or approval.

That is a much simpler and honest way to frame it; removing the pressure to justify your preference immediately makes the conversation feel safer. Before we finalize this script, I want to collaborate with you: would you be open to adding one small detail about something you *do* enjoy talking about, like the books you've been reading, so she knows there is plenty to say besides music?

That's a good idea, actually. I've been reading a lovely biography lately—maybe I could mention that. "I'm not much of a music person, but I'd love to tell you about this book I've been reading." That way, I'm not just shutting down the conversation; I'm offering something else to share.

Adding that book detail is excellent because it shifts the focus from your lack of participation to a new, positive connection point. With that complete script in hand, how does your body feel right now compared to when you first imagined the awkward scene? Is there any sense of relief, or does the worry still feel heavy?

There's a little bit of relief, I think. The knot in my stomach isn't quite as tight as before. It still feels a bit scary, like standing at the edge of a cold swimming pool, but at least now I can see a way to get in rather than just standing there frozen.

That metaphor of the cold swimming pool is powerful; seeing a way in is a huge step forward from feeling frozen. Since we have a clear path now, let's quickly brainstorm one tiny obstacle that might still get in the way of you picking up the phone, like a specific worry about timing or her availability. What's the smallest hurdle we can solve together right now?

I suppose... I worry about interrupting her. She's always so busy with her grandchildren and her garden club meetings. I don't want her to feel like she has to make time for me if she's already got a full schedule. That feels silly to say out loud, but it does hold me back.

That worry about burdening her is very human, but let's test it against the facts we know: Margaret invited you to the concert because she values your presence, not just her schedule. Would it be fair to assume that a friendly catch-up call fits easily into her day, or does she really feel guilty taking five minutes for you?

No, you're right. She did invite me, didn't she? If she truly didn't have time for me, she wouldn't have bothered. I suppose a quick call to catch up wouldn't be an imposition at all. I could even ask if she has a moment to talk before launching into things.

That logic makes perfect sense; recognizing that her initial invitation was an act of inclusion removes the guilt of asking for time. To lock this in, let's refine your opening line one last time to include that gentle check-in: "Hi Margaret, I was hoping we could catch up for five minutes before you get swamped with your garden plans." How does that slight adjustment feel when you say it out loud?

That feels... manageable. It gives her an easy out if she's truly busy, and it's polite without being pushy. I think I could actually say that. Maybe I'll even try it this afternoon, while I'm feeling a bit braver than usual.

That sounds wonderful, Sheila. Taking this small step today puts you firmly in control of the situation rather than letting the fear dictate your actions. Before we finish, I'd love to hear your quick feedback on our session: did finding that comparison between yourself and Margaret help clear up the confusion, or was there one part of our work that still felt tricky for you?

The comparison to Margaret really did help. It's funny—I never would have thought to look at it that way on my own. The tricky part was admitting out loud how afraid I am of being judged. But I think that's the part I needed to say the most. Thank you for helping me see a different path.

That honesty about your fear was incredibly brave, Sheila, and it clears the fog on exactly what needs shifting. You've done great work today turning a paralyzing "what if" into a concrete plan for connection. As we wrap up, is there anything else you'd like to carry with you before you head out, or should I give you space to reflect on your new path forward?

No, I think I have what I need. I'll give Margaret that call today, and I'll let you know how it goes next time. For now, I feel like I have a tiny bit more hope than when I walked in, and that's more than I've had in a long time.

Holding onto that spark of hope is exactly what matters, Sheila. Remember that you don't have to perform perfectly to belong; you just have to show up as yourself, even if it feels a little different than expected. Please take care of yourself today, and I look forward to hearing about your call and how that conversation unfolds. Until then, be gentle with yourself.

Hello again, it's great to see you. Before we dive into today's topic, could you remind me of the specific steps you planned to take regarding the cable checks and your nightly routine? How did those plans land for you this week?

Once we touch base on that, what would be most helpful for us to focus on today? Is there a particular worry or behavior you'd like to explore together?

Hi. Yeah, I did try the cable checks like we talked about. I’d go through each connection twice before leaving, but honestly, it just made me more anxious because I kept thinking, "What if I missed one?" The nightly routine of writing down worries before bed was a bit better, but I still woke up in the middle of the night thinking about work. I guess maybe we could talk about why I can't shake that feeling that one small mistake will cost me everything.

It sounds like you tried hard to stick to the plan, yet the anxiety persisted anyway. That reaction makes complete sense given how intense your fears have been.

To make sure we're moving in the same direction, does it feel right to spend today unpacking why that "small mistake = everything falls apart" belief is so hard to shake, rather than focusing on new strategies yet?

Yeah, that feels right. I always feel like I'm just one slip-up away from being called into the boss's office and getting let go. Even when I know logically that other people make mistakes and don't get fired, my gut tells me I'm different—like I don't have any room for error.

That feeling of being uniquely fragile compared to others is incredibly painful and isolating, especially when it clashes with your logical knowledge. It seems like your brain is telling you that the rules for making mistakes aren't the same for you as they are for everyone else.

If we look closely at that comparison, does that belief—that you are fundamentally different from colleagues who make errors—feel supported by recent evidence, or is it mostly based on that initial incident years ago?

I guess it's mostly that first incident. That one time I messed up, my supervisor really laid into me, and I’ve never forgotten it. But since then, I've seen other guys swap the wrong hard drive or miss a ticket, and they just get a warning or a joke about it. So logically, I know it's not the same for me now, but I still feel like that first mistake put a target on my back.

It makes perfect sense that one harsh interaction created a lasting shadow, even though your recent observations show others handle errors differently. Your brain is likely holding onto that old script because it promised safety in the past, even though it might be keeping you trapped now.

When you see colleagues make mistakes and laugh it off, does that thought—"they are safe because they weren't me"—bring up relief, or does it somehow make your fear worse because it proves you are the only one struggling?

It's more like... it makes me feel worse, honestly. Like I'm the only one who can't handle it, so maybe I really am not cut out for this job. Seeing them brush it off just reminds me that there's something broken in me that can't let go. I end up thinking, "If I were normal, I'd be fine too."

That thought—that you are fundamentally broken while others are just "normal"—is incredibly lonely and adds a heavy layer of shame to the fear of failure. It seems like comparing yourself to their easy success is just another way your mind is trying to convince you that the original threat (getting fired) is inevitable.

If we looked at that "brokenness" claim strictly, does it feel accurate to say you are incapable of fixing problems, or does it feel more like a desperate attempt to explain away the current anxiety?

I think... I mean, I know I can fix problems. I do it every day—I troubleshoot network issues, I replace parts, I get systems back online. So I guess calling myself "broken" isn't really true. It's more like my brain just won't let me feel safe no matter how many times I prove I can do the job. That's the part that feels broken, I suppose—the part that can't just accept a win and move on.

That is a profound realization—you are capable of the technical skills perfectly, but your internal alarm system refuses to recognize when the danger has passed. It feels completely valid to identify that specific part of your mind as the source of the trouble, rather than blaming your ability to work.

If we imagine that alarm system as a security guard who became hyper-vigilant after a single burglary, wouldn't it make sense that he keeps ringing the bell even when the building is empty, just because he's afraid to lower his watch?

Yeah, that actually makes a lot of sense. I never thought of it that way. That security guard is just doing his job too well, even when there's no threat. I guess I need to find a way to tell him it's okay to stand down, but I don't know how to do that without ignoring real risks.

That analogy of the overly cautious security guard is brilliant and captures the tension perfectly. You are absolutely right; we can't simply switch him off, because his primary function is to protect us from real dangers, not to ignore them.

Instead, what if we taught him that "safety" means knowing the difference between a real fire and a flickering light bulb? Could we practice giving him permission to stay alert during the night, but also allowing himself to relax once the house is truly locked down and everyone is asleep?

I think I could try that. Maybe I need to be more concrete about what "locked down" means for me at work. Like, instead of just double-checking everything until my eyes hurt, I could have a clear checklist that tells me when I'm actually done. Once that list is complete, I'd have to tell myself the guard can clock out for the night. That might help... I'm just not sure I'll believe it at first.

That is a fantastic idea, and it shows you are ready to give your "guard" a clear mission rather than vague instructions. Having a definitive "done" list gives the security guard a specific endpoint, which helps separate the work from the anxiety loop.

Before we write that checklist down, I want to make sure we are both on the same page: does creating a strict, binary list of tasks that marks the official end of the workday feel like a useful tool to you, or does it feel like adding another layer of pressure?

Honestly, it feels a little like pressure at first, because I'll worry about whether the list itself is good enough. But I think deep down I know it's better than what I'm doing now—just spinning my wheels, checking the same things over and over. A list would at least give me a clear finish line. I think I need that more than I need to keep worrying.

That honesty is incredibly valuable—it acknowledges the risk of the list while recognizing its greater benefit over endless rumination. It sounds like you trust the process more than you trust the current spiral of doubt.

To make sure we are aligned on this step, would you be willing to draft that simple "work shutdown" list now, focusing only on the absolute essentials, so we can treat it as a live experiment tonight?

Yeah, I think I can do that. Let's see... The essentials would be: finish any open tickets, check that all diagnostic tools are logged off, make sure my workstation is shut down properly, and confirm my notes for the next shift are saved. That's four things. Once those are done, I'm done. No more looping back to check anything else.

That is a very solid, realistic plan, and I love how you included saving your notes as the final step—it creates a natural closure rather than leaving you hanging. Treating these four items as a mandatory checkpoint and then hitting the "stop" button afterwards is a perfect way to give your security guard a clear discharge order.

Now that we have the list agreed upon, does it feel safe to try implementing this tonight, knowing that if the guard still feels uneasy after the fourth item, we can pause and discuss it first thing in the morning?

Yeah, I think I can commit to that. I'll try it tonight, and if that uneasy feeling still pops up after I'm done, I'll just write it down and deal with it tomorrow instead of re-checking everything. That feels... manageable. I'm a little nervous, but also kind of relieved to have a clear plan.

It feels... strange but also a little lighter, I guess. Like I've got permission to stop, even if my brain doesn't fully agree yet. I'll give it a shot tonight and see how it goes. Thanks for talking this through with me. I'll let you know how it lands.
