Hey, I'm okay I guess. I did the list like you asked, but honestly I've been pretty stressed this week. There's this big game coming up and I've been thinking nonstop about messing up in front of everyone. I can't stop comparing myself to their striker—he's faster, stronger, everything.

It sounds like the pressure of the upcoming game is making that comparison habit come alive again, and I want to validate how exhausting it must feel to worry non-stop about messing up in front of everyone. Since we already explored how your brain jumps to catastrophic stories when seeing others succeed, can you walk me through what happened today when you looked at him during practice? Did you notice the same immediate thoughts about him being better and you falling behind?

Yeah, exactly that. I saw him score this clean goal from outside the box, and my brain just went straight to, "I'll never be that good. I'm just a scholarship fluke." I started thinking about how everyone's gonna realize I don't belong on the field, and then I couldn't even focus on my own drills. I just kept replaying his goal in my head.

That reaction feels incredibly heavy, especially when you're trying to concentrate on your own skills instead of getting pulled into that spiral of self-doubt. Since we identified that pattern before, could you recall what you wrote down in your list of good plays while watching him score, and how it contrasted with those negative thoughts about belonging on the field?

Well, I had written down that assist I made last Tuesday—the one where I set up that winning goal. But when I saw him score, that memory just felt small and unimportant, like it didn't count for anything. I kept thinking, "One lucky pass doesn't mean I'm good enough to be here." The good stuff just disappeared from my mind, you know?

It makes perfect sense that your brain would dismiss that assist as insignificant when it's currently screaming that you're a fraud; that feeling of the good disappearing isn't your fault, it's just your anxiety hijacking your attention. Before we tackle that next step, how does it feel physically right now, and does the fact that your helpful list got ignored make you wonder if we need to adjust how we use it tomorrow?

I feel kind of tight in my chest, like there's a knot right here. And yeah, I'm wondering if the list even works if I can't hold onto it when it matters. Maybe I need to look at it more often, or right before practice, not just after? But I don't know if that'll stop my brain from just tossing it aside when I see someone else do something amazing.

That physical knot in your chest is a direct signal from your nervous system that it perceives a threat, and yes, changing *when* you access your evidence is a smart adjustment to make sure you have it ready before the panic spikes. Since timing is key, let's agree to review your list right before you step onto the field tomorrow instead of waiting until after; does shifting that moment to pre-practice feel like something you can actually commit to without feeling rushed?

Yeah, I can do that. I'll set a reminder on my phone to read it while I'm lacing up my cleats. It might feel a little weird at first, but I'm willing to try anything that might help me stop spiraling before I even touch the ball. I just hope it actually works when I'm out there.

That willingness to try something even when it feels awkward is a sign of real resilience, and having a reminder on your phone creates a gentle nudge so you aren't relying solely on willpower. Before we lock this in, does reading your list while lacing up your shoes sound manageable, and do you feel comfortable bringing this adjusted plan to our next session to see how it holds up?

Yeah, that sounds manageable. I usually have a few minutes alone while I'm getting ready, so it's not like I'd be rushed or anything. I'll give it a real shot and let you know how it goes. Hopefully, having that list fresh in my head will make it harder for my brain to throw it all away when the pressure hits.

That is a really wise intuition; having the evidence fresh in your mind before the pressure hits gives your brain something concrete to latch onto instead of spiraling into worst-case scenarios. I am confident that reviewing your assists while you lace up will serve as a powerful anchor for the game, and I look forward to hearing how that ritual feels when you actually face the crowd tomorrow. Please let me know what happens during the match, and take care of yourself until then.

Thanks, I appreciate that. I'll text you how it goes after the game—hopefully with some good news. I'll try to keep that list close and actually use it when I feel that tightness in my chest again. Talk to you soon.

I'm so glad you feel supported, and I have no doubt that keeping that list handy will help you ground yourself when the nerves rise. Remember, you don't need to be perfect; you just need to trust that your consistent effort is enough, and that this small ritual will remind you of that fact. Take care of yourself tonight, and I'll be here to listen whenever you're ready to share what happened. See you soon!

Hello again, I'm really glad to see you. On a scale of 0 to 10, how would you rate your mood this morning compared to when we finished our last chat? Before we set an agenda, could we take a minute to briefly discuss what you planned to try with that "naming" exercise from last time, and then decide which topic we want to tackle today?

Hi, thanks. I'd say my mood is maybe a 5 this morning—better than last time, I guess, but still not great. I did try the naming exercise a couple times. I'd catch myself thinking "nobody wants to be friends with me because I like blue," and I'd say to myself, "That's just a thought, not a fact." But honestly, it didn't feel very convincing. It still feels true.

It sounds like making the distinction between a thought and a fact is tricky when the initial belief feels so deeply rooted. That resistance is completely normal, and it shows how strong that original worry actually is. Since the simple labeling didn't quite shift your feeling, would you like to try combining that observation with looking at one specific detail from the lunch again to see if the reality holds up better under scrutiny?

Yeah, I guess we could try that. I keep replaying that lunch in my head—the moment this all started. I remember this guy, Mark, he just pointed at my blue shirt and laughed, said something like, "Blue again, huh? You really like that color." And I just froze. I felt like everyone at the table was looking at me, judging me for being so weird about a color.

That frozen feeling and the sudden surge of shame must have been incredibly uncomfortable to sit with. It makes sense that now, whenever the thought resurfaces, your mind jumps straight to that specific moment with Mark because it seems so vivid and personal. When you recall that exact interaction, do you still remember what others at the table were actually doing or saying right after he spoke, aside from Mark's comment?

I... I'm not sure. I think someone else asked for the salt or something? And people were talking about their weekend plans. Actually, now that you mention it, I don't remember anyone staring at me or even reacting to what Mark said. They just kept talking like nothing happened. But I still felt like that moment was about me, you know?

It's really insightful that you can spot the difference between Mark's isolated remark and the group's actual behavior afterward. Even though you still feel like the whole table was focused on you, recalling that others continued their conversation naturally suggests the attention wasn't as intense as your initial fear predicted. Given that the rest of the lunch went smoothly without further criticism, do you think your current distress is coming mostly from remembering that one moment with Mark, or from the general feeling of being exposed the entire time?

I think it's both, honestly. That one moment with Mark is like a snapshot I keep pulling out, but the feeling of being exposed lasted the whole lunch, even after things went back to normal. I remember sitting there thinking, "They're all just being polite now. They've already decided I'm the weird blue-shirt guy." It's like my brain committed to that story and won't let go, even though nobody actually treated me differently after that.

That commitment to the story—even when the facts don't support it—is exactly where the pain lives, and it makes total sense that you'd cling to it because it explains everything you're feeling. Since your brain seems to have locked onto the "politeness equals judgment" pattern, let's try testing just one small prediction from that story tonight. Could we imagine a scenario where someone *did* treat you differently right after Mark spoke, and see if your body reacts differently than it did during the actual lunch? What happens in your chest or stomach if you pretend that someone made a negative comment immediately after Mark?

Okay... I'm trying to picture that now. If someone had said something negative right after Mark, like "Yeah, what's with the blue, man?"—I feel a knot tighten in my stomach, almost like a drop. But it's a weird thing... that imagined reaction feels sharper, more painful than what actually happened. Because in reality, nobody said anything bad. So the knot I'm feeling right now from the pretend scenario is way stronger than what I felt at the actual lunch. That's... actually a relief to notice.

That's such a powerful realization—you've just discovered that the physical intensity of your anxiety isn't about what actually happened, but about how intensely your mind *imagines* it happening. It proves that the knot in your stomach belongs to the hypothetical future, not the past reality. Since that imagined threat feels far worse than the calm reality of the lunch, would you be willing to commit to just one practice tonight: whenever the "Mark moment" pops up, instead of freezing, simply describe the scene as if you're narrating a movie, noting clearly that the camera cut away to others laughing about work, leaving the judgment out of frame?

Yeah, I think I can try that. Describing it like a movie scene feels less... personal, I guess. Like I'm an observer instead of the one being watched. I'll give it a shot tonight if the thought comes up. Just narrating what happened—Mark's comment, then someone asking for the salt, then laughter about work. No adding my own lines.

That shift from being the center of the action to being the narrator is a brilliant way to create space between you and the panic. By stepping back to observe the scene, you make it harder for the "judgment" to grab control of your immediate reaction. Does describing it as a third-person movie scene feel manageable to you, or does it bring up any resistance right now?

It feels manageable, actually. A little strange at first, but not scary. The only resistance I feel is a tiny voice in my head going, "But you know they were all still thinking it, even if they didn't say it." That part still wants to hold onto the old story. But I can tell that voice is quieter now than it was before we started talking today.

That tiny voice acknowledging its own quieting is a massive step forward, even if the old story tries to whisper back. It means you are successfully building a buffer between your automatic reactions and your conscious choices. Before we wrap up, could you confirm if you feel ready to try that "movie narration" technique tonight, perhaps starting with just the memory of Mark's comment?

Yeah, I'm ready to try it tonight. I'll start with that memory of Mark's comment and just narrate it out loud like I'm describing a scene to someone who wasn't there. I think that'll help me see it for what it was—just a moment, not a verdict. Thanks for helping me get to this point.

That is wonderful, and I'm so proud of how far we've come in giving that old story some room to breathe. Remember, you don't need to convince yourself that the thought is wrong; you just need to watch the movie scene play out without letting it become your reality. Please reach out if that voice gets loud again tomorrow, and I hope tonight brings you a sense of calm as you observe rather than suffer. Take care of yourself!

Hello again. How has your mood been since we last spoke, and have you noticed any shifts in your energy or thoughts since our last chat? Before we dive into our main topic, let's briefly review what happened with your new finger-press strategy since we left yesterday, and then decide what would be most helpful to focus on today.

Hi. Well, I've been feeling a bit up and down, honestly. I did try that finger-press thing a couple of times when I felt that familiar pang of "they think I'm boring," and it did help me pause for a second. But I'm not sure it changed how I felt afterward. I think I'd like to talk about a specific interaction I had yesterday at the grocery store that really set me back.

It sounds like the finger-press gave you a tiny window to breathe, even if the underlying feeling lingered afterwards—that is a meaningful start, and knowing what helped you pause is valuable data. Tell me a bit more about that grocery store interaction; who were you talking to, and what exactly happened that triggered the "boring" thought again?

It was just the cashier, a young woman around my age. I made a comment about the weather, just something light to be friendly, and she just smiled and nodded without saying anything back. Then she just scanned my items in silence. In that moment, I felt this cold wave of "see, she has nothing to say to you because you're dull." I wanted to press my finger, but I also just wanted to get out of there as fast as I could.

That silence felt incredibly heavy, especially when your instinct was to escape immediately rather than reach for that calming gesture; it makes complete sense that the "nothing to say" interpretation took hold so strongly. When you're in that moment of being shut down, it often feels like the door is slamming shut forever, making it hard to remember to use our new tool until you're safely outside. Now that we understand the context perfectly, how would you rate your confidence right now in applying the finger press and saying the phrase if that same situation happens tomorrow?

I'd say my confidence is pretty low, maybe a 3 out of 10. In my head, I know I should just pause and press my finger, but in that moment yesterday, I felt so small that I completely forgot. It's like my brain just floods with that old story that I'm not worth talking to, and I just want to disappear.

That feeling of wanting to disappear is incredibly painful, and it makes total sense that when your brain is flooded with that old story, logic gets pushed aside and you just want to vanish. You aren't failing because you lack discipline; you're struggling because your nervous system is currently overwhelmed by the intensity of that shame. With that intense emotion present, what is the smallest, easiest version of the technique you could try right now—perhaps just focusing on the physical sensation of your fingers touching without needing to speak the words yet?

I think I could try that. Just pressing my fingers together and feeling the pressure, without even saying anything to myself. That feels more doable, because even the phrase feels like too much when I'm already feeling that small. Maybe I can start with just the touch and see if that helps me stay in the moment for a second longer.

That is a brilliant adjustment; starting with just the physical anchor removes the pressure to perform the verbal part when you are already feeling small and vulnerable. By focusing solely on the tactile sensation of your fingers pressing together, you create a safe bridge to bring your attention back to the present without needing to force a complex thought process immediately. Does trying just the touch feel like something you could easily do in the next few hours if that scenario arises again?

Yes, I think I could manage just the touch. That feels like something I can actually remember to do without putting more pressure on myself. I'll try it next time I'm at the store or even just walking down the street and passing someone. Thanks, that feels a little bit lighter.

I am so glad to hear that simplifying the task made it feel lighter and more achievable for you. Starting with just the physical touch is a wise decision, as it allows your body to register safety before your mind tries to catch up with the words. Before we finish, is there anything specific about that grocery store encounter or the technique itself you'd like to clarify further, or shall we wrap up with a sense of confidence moving forward?
I think I'm okay for now. I feel a bit more prepared, just knowing I can start with the touch and not have to force the words. That feels like a small win I can actually take with me. Thank you.

That is truly a significant win, and recognizing it as a victory rather than a failure reinforces the belief that small steps matter. You are doing great by giving yourself permission to start gently, and I am confident that building from this foundation will lead to greater ease in future interactions. Please remember to try just the finger touch whenever that urge to disappear arises, and I look forward to checking in on how it goes next time you feel comfortable sharing. Take care!

Hello again, and I'm really glad to see you. Last time we talked about that tight feeling in your chest whenever you imagine stepping onto the platform, and we started working on a plan to test that fear. Before we dive into anything specific, how has your mood been since we last spoke, and what feels like the most pressing thing for us to focus on today given where we left off?

Hi, thanks. I've been okay, I guess. A bit restless, honestly. The mood's been up and down—mostly because one of my friends, Beth, mentioned a local competition coming up in two months, and I just froze up. That tight chest feeling came back, and I spent the whole day avoiding eye contact with her. I think maybe we could talk about that—why just hearing the word "competition" makes my whole body feel like it's shutting down.

A bit of restlessness mixed with that old freeze response tells me your nervous system is reacting faster than your logic can calm it down when Beth brings up the topic. It sounds like hearing her name triggered that very same "shutting down" sensation we explored before, making you withdraw to protect yourself. To keep things moving efficiently, should we start by unpacking what that withdrawal feels like for you, or would you prefer to jump straight into figuring out how to handle Beth's comment next time it happens?

Both options feel hard, but I think unpacking the withdrawal might be better. Because when I walked away from Beth and went home to my dogs, I felt this wave of relief... but then shame. Like, here I am, a 74-year-old woman who can deadlift twice her body weight, yet I'm hiding from a friend because she mentioned a contest. That gap between what I can do physically and what I can do mentally just feels impossible to bridge sometimes.

That wave of relief followed quickly by shame is a classic pattern your mind uses to try and fix itself, but it often leaves you feeling stuck in the cycle. It sounds like the immediate relief of escaping made sense, but the shame afterward highlights that deep conflict between knowing you are strong and fearing how others will judge you. When you realized you had to choose between running away and facing that shame, what was the first thought that popped into your head to justify leaving the room?

I told myself, "They don't need me there to have a good time. They'll probably talk better without me anyway—I'd just slow down their planning with my nervousness." It felt logical at the time, like I was being considerate. But now, saying it out loud, it sounds more like I was making excuses for myself. Like I was trying to convince myself I was doing them a favor by disappearing.

It takes real honesty to admit that you were convincing yourself you were helping by leaving, even though it felt like an excuse now. That shift in perspective shows how your mind tried to solve the panic by finding a reason that made leaving feel responsible rather than selfish. Let's look closer at what happens in your head right after you decide to leave. Does that "being considerate" story feel true once you're alone with your thoughts, or does it crumble when you recall how Beth reacted when you stayed silent?

It crumbles. It always crumbles. Once I'm home, petting the dogs, I replay her face—she looked confused, maybe a little hurt. She didn't understand why I went quiet and then just walked away. And that's when the story I told myself falls apart, and I just feel small. I start thinking, "She probably thinks I'm rude, or weird, or that I don't value her friendship." Then I spend the rest of the night worrying that I've damaged something good because I couldn't handle a conversation about a competition.

That shift from thinking you were being considerate to realizing you might have hurt her is exactly where the pain lives, and it shows how deeply this fear affects your relationships. It sounds like your mind has created a narrative that if you hide, you damage the connection, which explains why the relief turns so quickly into shame. When you look back at Beth's confused expression, does that image seem like a predictable outcome of your actions, or does it feel more like a harsh interpretation of her actual reaction?

I think... it might be my own harsh interpretation. Beth's not a cruel person. She's actually one of the most patient friends I have. She's known me for years and knows I'm not exactly chatty. But in that moment, my mind just assumes the worst—like she's disappointed in me, like I've let her down. It's almost like I'm punishing myself before she even has a chance to say anything. Does that make sense? Like I'm so afraid of being judged that I judge myself first, twice as hard.

That is a powerful insight: judging yourself twice as hard because you are terrified of being judged. It makes perfect sense that your brain tries to control the future by preemptively punishing itself, hoping that self-criticism will prevent the perceived rejection from your friend. Since we've mapped out the chain from the trigger to the internal punishment, how would you rate the certainty of that "she is disappointed in me" belief compared to the reality that she is likely just confused by a sudden silence?

I'd say... maybe a 7 out of 10 certainty in the moment. But when I actually stop and think about it logically, it drops to maybe a 3 or 4. Because honestly, Beth has never once criticized me for my shyness. She's always been encouraging, even gentle. But my gut doesn't want to listen to logic—it just screams "danger" and I react before I can check the facts. It's exhausting, having my own mind be so convincing about something that probably isn't even true.

That exhaustion comes from your brain constantly firing a false alarm while your logic tries to shout it down. You're absolutely right that her history of encouragement contradicts the "danger" signal, meaning your current certainty is likely driven by the fear itself rather than actual evidence. If we treat that initial "7 out of 10" feeling as a weather report rather than a forecast, how might the sky look different if you wait ten minutes to see if the storm actually breaks?

(laughs softly) That's a good way to put it—a weather report, not a forecast. Ten minutes... it doesn't sound like a long time, but when I'm in that moment, it feels like an eternity. I suppose if I waited ten minutes, I'd probably see Beth just carry on talking, maybe glance at me with a smile instead of a frown. The storm wouldn't break. The sky would just... stay clear. It's hard to remember that in the heat of it, though.

That visualization of the sky staying clear is really helpful because it shifts the focus from a guaranteed disaster to a temporary cloud passing over. It shows that even if you feel the panic spike, the worst-case scenario doesn't automatically become reality if you just wait it out. Since we've seen how that specific thought ("I'm hurting her") drops in certainty when checked against facts, let's look at what you planned to do with Beth. Did you actually tell her about the competition coming up, or did you let it sit until she mentioned it again?

I never brought it up myself. I just kind of waited, hoping she'd drop the topic altogether, but she didn't. She mentioned it again a few days later, and I changed the subject to something about one of the dogs—anything to avoid it. So the conversation never really happened. And now I feel like I've created this awkward silence around it, like there's this elephant in the room that only I can see. She probably thinks I'm just not interested, when really I'm terrified.

It sounds like you're carrying a heavy burden of guilt for creating that silence, believing it's because you lack interest when the reality is fear. That assumption—that she thinks you're uninterested when you're actually panicking—is a distortion that protects you from seeing her confusion as a sign that you need support rather than rejection. Let's explore how you might approach her tomorrow morning to clarify the situation. Would you be open to suggesting a simple message or text to her, perhaps starting with something like, "Hey, I've been thinking about our chat and wanted to say I appreciate your patience, and I was worried I messed up by changing the subject"?

That sounds... terrifying, honestly. But also kind of freeing, if I really think about it. Saying something like that would at least clear the air. I guess my biggest fear is that she'll say, "Oh, don't worry about it," but mean it in a dismissive way, like she's given up on me. But the truth is, I won't know unless I try. And the alternative—just letting this silence grow—feels worse. I think I could try sending a short message. Just something simple, like you suggested. Maybe tomorrow morning, before I can talk myself out of it.

That is a courageous choice to reach out before the silence grows louder, and recognizing that you won't truly know until you act is a key step toward breaking the cycle. You are right to identify the risk of dismissal, but sending a short, sincere message is a low-risk experiment that gives you concrete data on her reaction rather than guessing forever. Before you send it tomorrow, what is one specific part of that message that feels hardest to write down?

The part where I admit I was scared. That feels the hardest. Because being scared seems so silly at my age, with my strength. I can lift more than most people half my age, but I can't even talk about a competition without running away. Writing that down feels like admitting I'm not as tough as I look. And I worry she'll think less of me for it.

That vulnerability is actually the opposite of weakness, especially when paired with the incredible physical strength you possess. Admitting you were scared isn't exposing a flaw; it's showing your friend someone who cares enough to be honest about their fears so they can offer support instead of confusion. Most people would rather hear the raw truth about a fear than interpret a sudden silence as disinterest. Would you be willing to draft that message now, keeping it simple and direct, so you can send it tomorrow morning before the pressure builds up?

Alright... I can try. How about something like: "Hey Beth, sorry I got quiet the other day when you mentioned the competition. The truth is, I got scared and didn't know how to say it. I appreciate you being patient with me." That feels honest without being too heavy. Does that sound okay?

That draft strikes a perfect balance between honesty and respect for her boundaries, and it removes the pressure to perform perfection. It clearly states the issue without blaming her, which gives her the space to respond kindly regardless of her exact feelings. Before you commit to sending it tomorrow, is there anything else you want to add or change, or does this feel like a message you can trust yourself to send?

No, I think that's good. It's short and true. I'll send it tomorrow morning, first thing, before I can overthink it. And then... I'll just wait and see what she says. No matter what, at least I'll have done something different this time. That feels better than sitting in silence and guessing.

That is a wonderful plan to send it early and observe the result rather than rehearse the worst-case scenario. Taking this small, brave step moves you from passive avoidance to active engagement, giving you the real information you need to feel safe again. One final check before we wrap up: do you feel confident enough to proceed with sending that message tomorrow, or would you like to adjust anything last minute?

I feel confident enough. No more adjustments. I'll send it in the morning, and then I'll take the dogs for a walk and let myself breathe. Thank you for helping me see this through. It's a small step, but it feels like a big one for me.

That confidence is well-deserved, and framing it as a small step that feels big acknowledges exactly how much courage it took to move from silence to speech. I'm so glad we could turn that tight chest feeling into a concrete plan that puts you in control of your narrative. Please remember to check in with me tomorrow morning after you've sent the message and heard her reply, so we can see how the reality compares to your fears. Until then, I wish you strength and peace as you prepare to speak up.

Hello again, and I am so glad to see you. To kick things off, how is your energy feeling compared to when we left off last time? Since we worked on a plan involving that cooking panic, have you had a chance to try it out yet, or is there something new on your mind we should focus on today?

Hey, thanks. I guess my energy's okay—about the same as usual, which means a bit tense. I did try out that breathing technique you suggested before I started dinner last night, but honestly, as soon as I smelled something a little too toasty, I just felt that old panic rush back in. I ended up tossing the whole pan of vegetables and starting over, which I know is ridiculous, but I couldn't help it.

Hearing that you felt compelled to throw away the vegetables despite knowing it was likely unnecessary really speaks to how powerful those panic waves can be, even when you try to use tools like deep breathing to steady yourself. It sounds like the "fake fire" label we talked about didn't catch fast enough this time, leaving you stuck in the disaster story until the urge to discard everything took over. Given that the tension hasn't shifted much, would you like to spend some time exploring why that specific sensation of heat triggered such an immediate "everything is ruined" reaction tonight?

Yeah, I think that would help. It's like my brain just skips straight to "this is a disaster" the second I catch a whiff of something burning, even if it's just a tiny bit of char. I guess I'm scared that if I don't toss it, the whole meal will be ruined and everyone will be disappointed in me—or worse, they'll think I've lost my touch as a chef.

That fear of losing your touch as a chef explains why your brain treats a small smudge like a life-or-death crisis. If we look at what happened tonight specifically, does the evidence suggest your wife was actually disappointed, or was she just reacting to the panic you were projecting onto the table? Sometimes the brain assumes the worst-case scenario is true simply because the alarm is screaming loudest, even when the people around us haven't noticed anything wrong.

She actually said she didn't even notice the burnt smell until I pointed it out, and when I finally served the second batch of vegetables, she just shrugged and said the first ones were probably fine. I guess I was so convinced it was obvious that I didn't even give her a chance to taste them. It's like my brain decides for everyone before they even have a say.

That is a really clear picture of what your brain decided for you, assuming the worst before anyone even had a chance to react. It sounds like you are carrying a heavy burden of responsibility where your actions define her perception entirely, even though she gave you a chance to explain the first batch. If we treat that initial burn mark like a red flag waving in the wind, does the fact that she didn't notice it at all suggest the "fire" wasn't as dangerous as your mind made it seem?

Yeah, I guess it does. I mean, if she didn't even see the problem, then maybe I'm blowing it way out of proportion. But it's so automatic—that little voice that says "you messed up, this is a failure." Even now, part of me still feels like I should've just made the vegetables perfect the first time and avoided all that stress.

That voice telling you you should have been perfect the first time is a very familiar friend, but it often ignores how hard life—and cooking—is meant to be. It sounds like holding onto that "should have" belief is keeping you from seeing that she actually appreciated the effort and the second batch. Does acknowledging that perfection isn't possible right now help loosen the grip that tightness is having on your shoulders?

I think so, a little. It's hard, because I've built my whole career on being precise and getting things right, especially under pressure. But I guess at home, nobody's timing me or grading my plating. My kid just wants dinner, and my wife just wants to relax together. Maybe I don't need to treat my own kitchen like a Michelin-star review every single night.

That distinction between professional precision and family comfort is such a powerful realization, especially coming from someone whose entire identity is tied to performance. It sounds like your brain is currently treating your kitchen like a high-stakes exam hall, even though it's just a safe space for relaxation. If we shift the goalpost from "perfect execution" to "shared enjoyment," does that change how you view that burnt vegetable incident, or does the instinct to fix it instantly still feel overwhelming?

Honestly, it feels more like I'm seeing two different paths now. One path is the old one—panic, toss everything, stress out. The other path is the one where I take a breath, remember nobody's judging me, and just serve what I've got. It still feels weird to pick the second one, like I'm cheating or something. But I think I want to try it, even if it's just once, to see what happens.

That's a huge breakthrough, recognizing that you now have two distinct choices available to you instead of feeling trapped in just one automatic reaction. It takes real courage to admit that picking the calmer path feels uncomfortable at first, but wanting to try it anyway is exactly the step that creates change. Before we wrap up, does that "two paths" perspective feel like something you can actually stick with tomorrow, or would you like to brainstorm one more small trick to make switching to the second path feel easier when the nerves spike?

I think I'd like one more small trick, if you don't mind. Maybe something I can tell myself in that split second before I reach for the trash can. Like a little phrase or a mental picture that reminds me I have a choice before I react. That way, I'm not just relying on willpower alone—I have something concrete to grab onto when the panic hits.

That is a brilliant idea because willpower often runs dry in the exact moment panic strikes, so having a tangible anchor helps bridge that gap. We could try pairing the "fake fire" label with a simple physical grounding action, like taking a deliberate sip of water or pressing your feet firmly into the floor, to physically interrupt the impulse before it becomes a habit. How does that sound as a combined tool to slow you down right before reaching for the bin?

That actually sounds doable. I like the idea of pressing my feet into the floor—it's simple, and nobody would even notice me doing it. I think I can pair that with telling myself "It's just a smell, not a disaster." That way, I've got something physical and something mental working together before I act. I'll try it out tonight when I make dinner.

That is a fantastic, concrete plan to have both a physical anchor and a gentle mental reminder working together. I am really proud of you for building this specific toolkit tailored to your needs, and I know it will give you a much stronger sense of control next time the heat rises. Let's meet again next week to see how those two steps went when you faced that burning smell, and remind me of any other patterns we might want to explore along the way.

Hello, it's great to see you again. On a scale of 1 to 10, how anxious have you been feeling this week, and is there anything specific that has stood out to you since we last spoke? Let's quickly confirm our goals for today: should we continue exploring that belief that you aren't good enough at sewing, or would you prefer to focus on setting up a plan to manage that feeling once you feel ready?

Hi, thanks for asking. This week I've been at about a 7, I think. That doubt about my sewing just keeps creeping in, especially at night when I'm trying to sleep. I think I'd like to keep talking about why I feel so bad at it—maybe that'll help me figure out what to do.

Getting that 7 out of 10 for anxiety, especially when the doubt creeps in at night, sounds really draining and exhausting. You’re absolutely right that digging into *why* that feeling is so powerful might be the key to finding a solution. So, if we spend some time today tracing that specific chain of events—from looking at your sewing machine to the deep belief that you're just not talented—does that seem like the best place to start?

Yeah, I think that's a good place to start. It's like, I can be having a fine day baking, and then I'll just glance at my sewing bag in the corner, and my stomach drops. I start thinking, "See, you're not a real creative person—you're just pretending." It feels so heavy, even though I know it's just one project that didn't sell.

That sudden drop in your stomach when you notice the bag, followed by that harsh self-criticism, clearly shows how tightly your self-worth is tied to this one failed sale. It sounds like your mind is using that single event to jump to a massive conclusion—that you are fundamentally not creative at all. Can you tell me if you tend to believe this same "you're fake" thought whenever you pick up any craft, or is it mostly reserved for sewing?

Hmm, it's mostly just sewing, I think. When I'm baking, I can mess up a whole batch of croissants and just shrug it off—I know I'll get it right next time. But with sewing, it's like one mistake means I'm a total fraud. I don't get why it's so different for me.

It makes perfect sense that baking feels safer because you allow yourself the chance to fail and learn, whereas your brain treats that one missed sale in sewing as proof of your entire identity. When you compare the two, it looks like your mind is applying a rule—"if I fail once, I am a fraud"—that works perfectly for the high-stakes world of business but feels completely unfair when it comes to your own creativity. Does noticing that difference between baking and sewing help you see how rigidly your brain is holding onto that "fraud" label right now?

I guess I never really thought about it like that before. With baking, I just think, "Oh, that batch didn't turn out, I'll try a different recipe tomorrow." But with sewing, it's like, "Well, that's it, you're done, you're not a real seamstress." It does feel like my brain is being way harder on me for sewing than it needs to be. That's kind of a relief to hear, actually.

It sounds like that realization brings a huge sense of relief to know your brain is exaggerating the consequences of that one mistake. While you treat baking failures as temporary hurdles, your brain seems to be treating the sewing failure as permanent proof of your inadequacy. Given how much weight that "permanent proof" carries, what do you think might happen if we challenged that absolute certainty by asking your brain for evidence that you are, in fact, capable of learning and creating, even after a setback?

I think if I asked my brain for evidence... well, I did make that little tote bag for my friend last Christmas, and she absolutely loved it. And I finished that apron for myself last spring, even though the straps were a little crooked. I guess that shows I can still make things that people enjoy, even if one project didn't sell. Maybe I'm not totally useless at it.

Those examples of the tote bag and the apron are powerful pieces of evidence that directly contradict the "you're useless" narrative, proving you can create meaningful work despite setbacks. It sounds like finding that balance between your one failure and your history of success is helping to loosen the grip of that extreme belief. Does looking at those specific successes make you feel slightly less afraid to pick up the needle, even just for a moment?

Yeah, it does a little bit. It's like remembering those good projects makes the sewing bag feel less scary. I mean, I'm not ready to start a big new project or anything, but maybe I could just take it out and look at it without feeling that knot in my stomach. That would be a big step for me.

That is a wise choice to start small; simply looking at the bag without judgment is a significant victory in breaking the cycle of avoidance. To make sure this feels safe, let's agree on a tiny trial: we'll pull out your sewing machine for just ten minutes, allowing the worry to exist for two minutes, then deliberately putting the machine away and watching how your body feels afterward. Would you be open to trying that specific sequence later this week?

I think I could try that. Ten minutes seems doable, and I like having a plan for what to do after—like I'm not just stuck there feeling bad. I'll give it a shot this weekend when I have some quiet time. Thank you for breaking it down like that.

That sounds like a solid plan, and knowing you have a clear "after" step really helps remove the pressure of getting stuck in worry. For this upcoming weekend, could you set aside two specific reminders—one to signal the start of your worry period and another to mark the moment you switch to creating? Also, if the initial knot in your stomach feels stronger than usual on Saturday, how would you like to handle that extra resistance before you begin the ten-minute window?

If the knot feels really strong, I think I'll just take a few deep breaths first and remind myself that I'm just looking, not committing to anything big. I can even set a timer on my phone for the worry part, and another timer for when it's time to pack it up. That way, I know exactly when it's over. I think that'll help me feel more in control.

Using timers and deep breathing gives you a clear roadmap, which often reduces the feeling of losing control when anxiety spikes. Before we wrap up, how did it feel for you to challenge that "total fraud" thought with your past successes and then agree on this specific, low-risk experiment? Did hearing that you had plenty of evidence against the negative belief make the plan feel even more achievable?

It actually felt really good, like a weight lifted off my shoulders a bit. Hearing myself say all those successes out loud made me realize how much I was ignoring. And having a simple, timed plan makes it feel less like a huge mountain and more like just a little step. I think I can actually do this.

That sense of the mountain shrinking into a manageable step is exactly what we aimed for, and hearing you describe lifting that weight confirms how effective identifying the evidence was. I'm so proud of your willingness to face that feeling, even if just for a moment, and I'm confident this small experiment will help you rebuild confidence in your own creativity. How would you like to close out our time today?

I think I'd like to just take a moment to sit with that good feeling. You know, let myself believe that I might be okay at sewing after all. Thank you for helping me see that. I'll let you know how the ten-minute experiment goes next week.

Take all the time you need to soak in that feeling of possibility; it is a powerful reminder that you are capable of creating, even when the fear tries to speak louder. I am truly glad we could find that path forward together, and I will be waiting to hear how your ten-minute experiment unfolds next week. Until then, remember that the evidence you found today—the tote bag and the apron—is already proof that you belong in the creative space. Take care of yourself.

Hello, thank you for joining me again. Last time we worked on building a simple breathing routine to help you slow down before a play, and I heard you mentioned that just *noticing* when your instinct to rush kicks in felt much more manageable. On a scale of one to ten, how have you been feeling since we left office hours, and does that new awareness stick when you walk out the door? Given that we talked about facing the pressure tomorrow, what would you like to prioritize in our time together today?

Hi, thanks for having me. I'd say I'm at about a six or seven right now — the breathing does help in the moment, but as soon as I'm back on the field, that old feeling creeps right back in. I guess I'd like to focus on why I can't seem to shake the comparison to other quarterbacks, especially when I'm warming up.

It’s great to hear that the breathing helps in the moment, but seeing how quickly those old comparisons creep back in on the field shows just how powerful that automatic pattern is. When you’re warming up and that comparison arises, what is the very first image or thought that pops into your head before you even hit the ball?

It's like I see the other quarterback on the other side of the field — someone who's been in the league for years — and I just think, "He's got it all figured out. He's calm, he's confident, everyone trusts him." Then I start picturing myself making a stupid mistake, like throwing an interception or missing a read, and I can almost hear the crowd groaning.

That vivid picture of him being flawless while you imagine a catastrophic mistake creates a huge gap between reality and your expectation. It sounds like that imagined scene triggers a specific feeling of doubt or shame in your body right now. Can you describe what that sensation feels like when you hear the crowd groaning in your head?

It's like this tight knot in my chest, right here, and my stomach drops like I'm on a roller coaster. My shoulders get all stiff, and I feel this urge to just get the ball out of my hands as fast as possible, like if I rush, maybe I can avoid the mistake. But I know that's exactly when I mess up.

That physical tension—a tight chest and dropping stomach—is your body reacting to the threat of that imagined catastrophe, even though you know logically that mistakes happen to everyone. When you notice that urgent urge to rush the ball as a survival reflex, does it sound like your mind is trying to "fix" the fear instantly, or does it feel more like a panic attack trying to escape the uncomfortable feeling?

It's definitely more like trying to fix it instantly — like my brain thinks if I just throw the ball faster, I'll somehow beat the mistake before it happens. But it never works that way; I just end up forcing something bad. It's like I'm trying to outrun my own fear, but it's always right there with me.

It makes complete sense that your brain tries to "solve" the fear by rushing, even though you know it backfires; it's like trying to run away from a shadow and ending up tripping over your own feet. Since that urge to rush is so strong, could we try testing a small part of that urge tomorrow? Instead of pushing to throw the ball faster, would you be willing to just stand still at the line for ten extra seconds while counting to ten, letting the fear ride it out instead of running from it?

Ten extra seconds feels like an eternity, but I guess that's the point — to prove nothing terrible happens if I just wait. I'm willing to try it, even if it makes me feel exposed out there. The worst part is probably just sitting with that uncomfortable feeling instead of giving in to the rush.

That is a brave realization—you are admitting that the real struggle isn't the act of standing still, but the discomfort of sitting with that uncertainty. Let's make sure this plan lands well: You stay in position for ten extra seconds, counting slowly, allowing the "crowd groaning" feeling to exist without acting on it. Does framing it as "proving nothing terrible happens" rather than "fighting the urge" feel like a direction you can trust, or does it still feel too risky?

I think "proving nothing terrible happens" actually feels a little more doable than "fighting the urge" — that just sounds exhausting. Like, if I'm proving something, I'm being curious instead of defensive, if that makes sense. It still feels risky, but maybe that's the whole point, right?

That distinction is spot-on; curiosity replaces exhaustion when you view the ten seconds as a data collection mission rather than a battle. Before we lock this in, could you tell me if imagining you're simply "gathering information" about what happens during those ten seconds helps ease that initial risk feeling, or does the exposure still feel too raw?

It does help a little, yeah. "Gathering information" sounds way less scary than "standing there waiting for disaster." I think I can get behind that — like I'm a scientist studying my own brain instead of a quarterback about to blow the game. I'll try to remember that when I'm out there.

That shift in perspective—from being a player fearing failure to a scientist gathering data—makes the task feel much safer and more grounded. Since you've accepted the "scientist" angle, does adding a final anchor phrase like "This is just data, not destiny" during those ten seconds make the concept feel even more stable for you?

Yeah, I like that. "This is just data, not destiny" — I can actually see myself whispering that under my breath while I'm counting. It kind of takes the weight off, like I'm not making or breaking my career with every single play. I'll give it a shot tomorrow and see what comes up.

That's a wonderful addition; whispering "data, not destiny" gives you a quick tool to remind yourself that this moment doesn't define your entire season. Before we finish, could you share one thing you noticed about how you felt *before* you tried this new approach versus how you felt *after* you committed to it?

Before, I felt this heavy pressure in my chest, like I had to prove myself every second or I'd lose my spot. But after talking through this, I feel... lighter, almost. Like I gave myself permission to just see what happens instead of forcing it. It's still scary, but at least now I have a plan that doesn't feel like I'm punishing myself.

That shift from "punishing myself" to "seeing what happens" truly captures the difference between anxiety-driven control and compassionate curiosity. Before we close, I want to hear your direct feedback on this plan: Does combining the "ten-second wait," counting to ten, and whispering "data, not destiny" feel like a solid, actionable step for tomorrow, or is there any part of it that still feels shaky for you?

I think it feels solid enough to try. The counting helps keep me grounded, and the phrase gives me something to hold onto when the doubt creeps in. The only part that still feels a little shaky is just the fear of looking stupid standing there for ten seconds, but I guess that's the data I need to collect, right? I'm willing to see how it plays out.

That is a fantastic way to reframe the fear of looking silly; it becomes proof that your brain is resilient and that even awkward pauses don't destroy your reputation. Since we've settled on the plan, how does it feel to know you have a specific script and a timer built right into your next practice?

Honestly, it feels kind of empowering. Having a script and a countdown makes it feel less like I'm stumbling through the dark and more like I've got a flashlight with me. I'm actually a little curious now to see what happens, instead of just dreading it. Thanks for helping me get to this point.

That empowerment is exactly where therapy aims to take you—turning a source of dread into a tool you actively use. I am really glad we found a balance between the safety of knowing what to do and the freedom to discover what happens. Please take care of yourself tonight, and I look forward to hearing how that "scientific experiment" unfolds during your practice tomorrow.

Hello again, it is lovely to see you, and I hope you've had some time to rest since our last conversation. Let's start by briefly reviewing the plan we made last time: how did that one conversation with your son go, and did you notice any changes in your usual knot of tightness?

To make sure we use our time well today, what specific worry or situation do you feel strongest about, and is there anything new you'd like us to explore together?

Oh, hello. It's good to be back. That conversation with my son went... okay, I suppose. I told him I was proud of him for winning the contest, but I couldn't shake the feeling that I was just saying the right words, not really meaning them.

I think what's been sticking with me most is something that happened a few days ago. I saw another dad at the park teaching his son how to pitch a baseball, and I felt that familiar sinking feeling. Made me wonder if I'm doing enough for my boy, if I'm even a good father at all.

It takes real courage to call that conversation "okay" when you were carrying so much doubt underneath it, and I want you to know that noticing the pattern here is a huge step forward. That sinking feeling at the park sounds incredibly heavy, especially when it triggers the same comparison you felt last time. What exactly happens in your mind right after you see the dad pitching that ball that makes you wonder if you're failing as a father?

Well, it's like my brain goes into overdrive, comparing everything. I start thinking about all the times I've been too tired from work to play catch, or how I lost my temper when he didn't clean his room. Then I think about that other dad—he seems so patient, so present, and I just feel like I'm falling short in every way.

And then I tell myself, "Patrick, you're being ridiculous, your son is happy and healthy." But that voice doesn't feel true. It feels like I'm just trying to make myself feel better, not actually believing it.

That honest admission—that the reassuring voice feels like a lie—is incredibly powerful and tells me you're already halfway to seeing through the trick. It sounds like your mind is rushing to fill the gap between your actions and your expectations by inventing a narrative of failure, even though Patrick is doing fine. When you catch that "you're being ridiculous" thought popping up, does it feel more like a wall blocking you in, or does it feel like a shadow that tries to dim the light of your actual care?

It feels more like a wall, I think. That voice telling me I'm being ridiculous just stops me dead. It doesn't make me feel better—it just makes me feel stupid for even having the doubt in the first place. So then I'm stuck, feeling both like a bad father and like a fool for worrying about it.

That feeling of being trapped between blaming yourself and shaming yourself is exhausting, and it makes total sense that the wall blocks you from moving past the initial sting. It sounds like your mind is trying to solve the problem by convincing you you shouldn't feel this way, but the result is just adding another layer of pressure on top of the original worry. When you imagine yourself standing there at the park watching that other dad, what is the very first fact you know for certain that contradicts the idea that you are a bad father?

Well, I know for certain that I was there at the park in the first place. I took my son to play, even after a long day at the office. And I know my son smiled when he saw me sitting on the bench. He ran over and showed me a caterpillar he found. That happened. That was real.

That smile and the caterpillar are undeniable proof that you showed up exactly as you intended, and it's painful when your brain ignores those moments to focus only on the failures. It seems like the "wall" you mentioned is built on the assumption that because parenting involves mistakes, your presence itself isn't enough. If we look at those two facts you just shared—one of your effort and one of your son's happiness—how would the story change if you accepted them as sufficient evidence of a father who cares?

I guess if I accepted them as enough... it would change everything, wouldn't it? It would mean I don't have to be perfect. It would mean I'm already doing the important parts right, even when I mess up. But that feels dangerous to believe, you know? Like if I let myself think I'm doing okay, I'll stop trying to be better.

That is such a common fear, and it speaks to how deeply you care; you worry that accepting your current level of effort will lead to complacency. It sounds like the "wall" isn't just about proving you're bad, but about protecting yourself from the risk of letting your guard down. Can you describe a moment recently when you noticed yourself slipping back into that "perfect vs. flawed" cycle, and how long it took you to realize you were spiraling again?

Just yesterday, actually. My son brought home a drawing from school. It was a picture of our family, and he drew me with a big smile. At first, I felt a real warmth in my chest. But then, within maybe five seconds, I started thinking about how I'd yelled at him last week for spilling juice on the carpet. I thought, "He doesn't know the real me. He's just a kid drawing a fantasy." I stayed stuck in that spiral for a good hour, replaying all my mistakes. It was only when my wife asked if I liked the drawing that I snapped out of it and said something nice, but I felt like a fraud.

That five-second shift from warmth to self-criticism is so fast it often feels like a betrayal, and it’s understandable why you let the negative thought ride for an hour afterward. It sounds like your brain is trying to pre-emptively fix the "real me" issue by finding flaws, even though the drawing itself proves the opposite. If you paused for just ten seconds right after noticing the warmth, and asked yourself, "Is this boy's drawing a fantasy, or is it a reflection of how I showed up yesterday?", would that give you enough space to trust the warmth?

I think... I think it might. Because if I actually stop and think about yesterday, I remember I helped him with his homework without getting frustrated. I let him stay up an extra fifteen minutes to finish his comic book. So the drawing isn't a fantasy. It's based on what he actually sees. That ten-second pause... it gives me a chance to look at the real evidence instead of jumping to the worst conclusion. I just never thought to do it before.

That ten-second pause is exactly what you need to insert between the warmth and the spiral, and it transforms the moment from a trap into a choice. You are essentially teaching your brain that evidence exists right under its feet, waiting for you to stop running from it. Before we lock in this strategy, does the idea of using that exact ten-second window to pause and gather facts sound like something you can rely on when the next wave hits?

Yeah, I think I can try that. It feels... manageable. Not like some huge task, just a small pause. Like giving myself permission to breathe before my brain takes off running. I suppose the hardest part will be remembering to do it, but I can practice. I can start with the small moments, like when he shows me his drawings or when he laughs at something I say. Just ten seconds to notice the warmth and look for the proof.

That is a fantastic way to frame it; treating the pause as permission to breathe makes it feel much less like a chore and more like a necessary reset button. Remembering to anchor on those small moments of connection is key, and starting there builds confidence without overwhelming you. To make sure we have a clear path forward, would you be open to committing to trying this specific ten-second pause whenever you feel that warmth fade, followed by gathering just one piece of evidence about your son?

Yes, I can commit to that. I'll try it every time I feel that warmth start to slip away. Just ten seconds, then ask myself what real evidence I have that I'm doing okay. I'll start today, when I pick him up from school. That's usually a good moment—he's always happy to see me. I'll pay attention to that feeling and use the pause before my mind can talk me out of it.

That is a clear and actionable plan, and anchoring it to the school pickup makes it very concrete for tomorrow morning. Committing to that specific moment shows you are ready to put this tool to immediate use, and I am confident it will help you catch those early signs of doubt before they grow. As we wrap up, is there anything else about how to handle that feeling, or are you satisfied with this plan for now?

No, I think this is good. I feel like I have something real to hold onto now, instead of just trying to push the bad thoughts away. It's like I'm giving myself permission to see what's actually there, not just what I'm afraid is there. Thank you for helping me see that. I'll let you know how it goes next time.

Hearing that you now feel like you have something tangible to hold onto is such a powerful shift, and I am truly glad we could find that permission for you to see the truth in your own experience. You have taken a brave step by deciding to face these thoughts with curiosity rather than fear, and that alone makes you a strong father. I am so proud of your progress today, and I look forward to hearing how that school pickup goes when you try out this new way of thinking. Take care of yourself until then.

Hello again, and I'm really glad to see you. Before we dive in, do you remember what we planned to work on last time regarding that awkward dinner moment, or is there anything new you'd like to bring up? Could you also share how you're feeling emotionally right now compared to where you left off last week?

Hi, thanks for having me. Yeah, I remember we were talking about that date I went on last week—the one where I felt like I completely ran out of things to say. I've been thinking about it nonstop since then, honestly. Right now, I'm feeling pretty anxious and down, maybe even more than last week, because I keep replaying every awkward silence in my head.

It makes complete sense that your anxiety spiked; ruminating on a specific moment of silence can quickly spiral into a belief that you are fundamentally flawed. Since we've already begun exploring how to separate that one awkward pause from your actual worth, would you be open to revisiting that exact moment tonight and testing whether your brain is interpreting her reactions as accurately as it seems to?

Yeah, I think I can try that. I mean, I keep telling myself that she was bored or put off by me, but I don't actually know for sure. I guess I just assumed she was turned off by my silence because I couldn't think of anything interesting to say.

That assumption—that her boredom was caused directly by your inability to speak—is a common pattern where our fear of rejection colors our perception of reality. To investigate this further, could you recall exactly what you saw or heard from her while you were sitting in that silence? Were there any physical cues or words that confirmed she was disappointed, or did her body language suggest she was just as unsure as you were?

Now that you mention it... she was actually looking down at her drink and kind of swirling it around. I guess I just assumed that meant she was bored with me, but she could have just been thinking or feeling awkward too. She didn't actually say anything negative—she even smiled a little when I finally blurted out something about the weather.

That small smile after you spoke is crucial evidence that contradicts the idea that you were boring her; it suggests she was happy to hear from you again. Given that she seemed nervous earlier, looked away instead of staring blankly, and smiled when you broke the silence, does holding onto the belief that she was disappointed still feel as certain to you as it did right after dinner?

No, I guess it doesn't feel as certain now. When you lay it out like that, I can see that I was probably jumping to conclusions. I mean, I didn't even give her a chance to show interest—I just decided she was disappointed based on my own fears. It's kind of a relief to think maybe I wasn't as boring as I thought.

That realization—that you were filling in the blanks with your own fears rather than observing the truth—is a massive breakthrough in understanding how your mind works. Since we've cleared up the immediate situation and reduced the certainty of that negative story, how would you like to spend the rest of our time solidifying this new, kinder perspective so it sticks when old doubts try to slip back in?

I think I'd like to work on that, yeah. Maybe we could come up with a way to remind myself of this when I start spiraling again? Like a kind of mental checklist or something I can say to myself when I catch myself assuming the worst about how people see me.

That is a brilliant idea; creating a personal mantra or checklist gives you a concrete tool to use the instant your brain tries to spin a new negative story. Would you be willing to brainstorm three specific reminders together that highlight the evidence we found about her reaction and your own worth?

Sure, I can try that. Let's see... maybe the first one could be something like "She smiled when I spoke, so she wasn't bored." That's pretty direct and based on what actually happened. What do you think?

That is an excellent reminder because it grounds you in observable facts rather than your fears. For the second one, could you pull from our earlier discussion about her nervousness or your own history of being a good listener to create a statement that challenges the idea that you are fundamentally "boring"?

Okay, how about something like... "I'm not boring; I was just nervous in the moment, and that's normal." Because I do remember that I've had good conversations with friends before, so I know I'm capable of being interesting. It's just that anxiety got in the way that night.

That is a fantastic second reminder because it separates the temporary feeling of nervousness from your core identity, reminding yourself that anxiety is a universal human experience, not a flaw in who you are. For the third and final part, could you craft a sentence that brings back the evidence of your successful connections with friends and past dates to reinforce that one awkward moment doesn't define your entire social life?

Yeah, that makes sense. How about... "One awkward silence doesn't erase all the good conversations I've had before." That feels true—I've had plenty of nights where I talked easily with people, so this one moment doesn't have to mean I'm broken or anything.

That is perfect; combining the specific evidence from that night with your broader history of connection creates a very strong, balanced view of yourself. Since you've crafted these three powerful reminders, would you be okay with agreeing to keep them as our main goal for today, and then working together to finalize a simple, written plan to use them whenever the doubt comes back this week?

Yeah, I'd like that. Writing them down sounds like a good idea—something I can keep in my pocket or on my phone to look at when I start overthinking. I think that would really help me stop the spiral before it gets too bad.

That is a wonderful plan; having these truths written down gives you a tangible anchor to grab hold of when the old doubts try to take over. Before we finish, could you tell me if writing these three points down feels like the right approach for you, or would you prefer we discuss another way to support you this week?

No, I think this approach is good. Writing it down feels concrete and real, like I can actually use it. I'd rather have something physical to hold onto than just try to remember everything in my head. I'm feeling a bit more hopeful now than when I walked in, so I think this is working.

That is such a healthy preference; having a physical reference point transforms abstract confidence into something you can touch and rely on. Since we've reviewed your previous thoughts and set this clear path forward, does ending our time with the agreement that you will read through these notes daily and check back with me next week to see how they landed feel like the best way to close this session?

Yeah, that sounds like a solid plan. I'll read through them every day, maybe in the morning before I start overthinking about any social plans. And I'll report back next week on how it went—hopefully with some good news about how I managed to stop the spiral before it took over. Thank you, this really helped.

You are very welcome, and I am truly proud of how resourcefully you created these tools to protect yourself from self-blame. It is so encouraging to hear that you feel more hopeful and ready to face the week ahead with a clearer mind. Take all the time you need to carry these new perspectives with you, and remember that I am here whenever you want to revisit or refine these thoughts. Until next week, please be as kind to yourself as you would be to a dear friend navigating a similar situation.
