Hello, and thank you for meeting with me today. On a scale of one to ten, how have you been feeling since we last spoke, and is there anything new that has come up? To make sure we get the most value out of our time, could you quickly confirm what we agreed upon yesterday regarding the three photos, and then tell me what topic we should prioritize for today?

Hi, thanks. I'd say I'm at about a 4 today... maybe a 5. And yes, I remember — we agreed I'd take three photos this week, ones that felt meaningful in some way. I did take them, but honestly, I'm not happy with any of them. I think I'd like to talk about that feeling today — why I can never seem to see my work as good enough.

It is completely understandable that your mood dipped today, especially given how difficult it is to disconnect from that critical inner voice when you haven't quite found your footing yet. You mentioned that even though you followed through with the plan, none of the photos felt satisfying, which suggests we still need to explore the gap between taking the shot and accepting what it represents. Before we dive deeper, I want to check in on how the idea of "taking three photos without judging" landed for you yesterday; did the absence of immediate deletion help lower the pressure, or did the doubt sneak in anyway?

The doubt sneaked in anyway, if I'm being honest. I kept the photos on my camera, but I found myself mentally criticizing each one as soon as I pressed the shutter. It's like I can't stop myself from judging before I've even given them a chance. I wanted to just enjoy the process, but my brain kept telling me they weren't good enough.

That is a very honest observation, and it tells me the "no judging" rule alone wasn't strong enough to override your automatic habit of finding faults. Even though you physically stopped deleting them, your mind was still running the script of perfectionism, which explains why you didn't feel lighter afterward. Since we know that comparing yourself to an idealized version of a professional often fuels this criticism, could you identify the specific thought that popped up right after you clicked that first photo? Was it something like, "This is messy," or perhaps, "I missed the mark"?

It was more like, "This isn't what I imagined," and then right after that, "What's the point of even trying?" That second thought really stung. It felt like I was giving up before I even had a chance to fix anything in editing or try a different angle.

It makes perfect sense that "This isn't what I imagined" triggered the feeling of failure, leading directly to the thought that there was "no point" in continuing. That spiral from disappointment to hopelessness is a common pattern when our expectations are tied to a specific outcome rather than the experience itself. Let's gently test that belief: if you were watching someone else shoot three random pictures and they looked imperfect, would you think *they* shouldn't try anymore, or would you encourage them to keep going because they were present in the moment?

I'd never say that to someone else. I'd probably tell them that every photo is a step forward, or that even the imperfect ones have value somehow. But somehow, I can't give myself that same kindness. It's like I hold myself to a completely different standard, and I don't know how to stop.

That contrast between how you speak to others versus how you speak to yourself reveals a core issue: you've unconsciously adopted an impossibly high bar for your own worthiness that doesn't exist for anyone else. It sounds like you're treating the camera lens like a courtroom verdict, where every single image must pass inspection to be considered valid, whereas life—and art—is often messy and incomplete. Since you noticed that holding yourself to a higher standard than others creates this paralysis, could you recall a time you successfully took a step back and accepted an imperfect result, even when it didn't meet your original vision? What happened to your feelings in that moment?

I actually do remember one time, a few months ago. I was out shooting at sunrise, and the lighting was all wrong — harsh shadows everywhere. I was frustrated at first, but I decided to just keep shooting anyway. When I looked at the photos later, I actually liked one of them a lot. It had this dramatic contrast that I hadn't planned for. I felt... relieved, I think. And a little proud. But that feeling faded pretty quickly, and I haven't been able to recreate it since.

It takes great courage to recognize that moment of relief and pride, especially knowing how easily that feeling evaporated when the reality of your self-criticism returned. That sunrise example proves that unexpected outcomes can indeed lead to satisfaction, yet your mind seems unable to sustain that joy long enough to cement it as a valid success. Since you mentioned that feeling faded quickly, could you walk me through what happened internally right after you realized you liked that unplanned photo? Did your critic whisper that you "should have known better" or "missed the mark," and how did that interrupt your sense of accomplishment?

I remember thinking, "Well, that was just luck, not skill." The voice inside said I didn't really earn that good shot — it just happened by accident. And then I started thinking about all the photos I'd taken that day that I had deleted or didn't like, and that one lucky shot didn't seem so special anymore. It's like I can't let myself have a win without immediately tearing it down.

That is a classic distortion known as the "luck fallacy"—your mind dismissed your success as accidental while ignoring the fact that you had the patience to keep shooting until you found something worth keeping. By immediately comparing that one successful shot to all the failures, you diluted its value and stole the credit from your persistence. If we were to challenge that thought, could you list the specific skills you brought to that sunrise that made you eventually spot that contrast, rather than assuming it was purely random chance?

Well... I did wake up early to catch the sunrise. And I chose to keep shooting even when the light felt wrong. I also knew how to adjust my settings to work with the harsh shadows instead of against them. I guess that's not just luck — I made decisions that led to that photo. But it still feels like I'm making excuses when I say that out loud.

It is natural to feel defensive when pointing out your own competence, but please note that identifying those deliberate choices—the early rise, the decision to persist, the technical adjustments—is actually the opposite of making excuses; it is building evidence for your own capability. Your mind might be dismissing this logic to protect you from the pain of realizing you are capable, yet acknowledging these facts directly contradicts the idea that you are simply unlucky. Since you recognized those intentional actions, how would you feel if we treated that sunrise photo not as a "lucky break," but as a direct result of your preparation and resilience?

I think... that would feel uncomfortable at first, like I'm bragging or getting ahead of myself. But if I really sit with it, it also feels a little bit freeing. Like maybe I don't have to be perfect every time — I just need to keep showing up and making those small decisions. I guess I never really thought of it that way before.

That shift—from needing to be perfect to valuing the small, daily decisions to show up—is exactly the kind of reframing we need to build a sustainable relationship with your craft. It removes the pressure of a single "masterpiece" and replaces it with a continuous story of effort and adaptation. Before we finalize our plan for this week, does viewing your recent struggle through the lens of "trying again rather than failing" feel like a useful way to approach your upcoming shoots, or does it still feel a bit abstract for you right now?

It feels a bit abstract, to be honest. I can see the logic in it, but I'm not sure I can hold onto that thought when I'm actually out there with my camera. I think I need a more concrete way to remind myself of this, maybe something I can do or say while I'm shooting. Otherwise, I'll just fall back into the same old pattern of judging every shot.

That is a very smart instinct; relying solely on abstract concepts often fails when the brain is under stress or tired, so creating a tangible tool is essential for consistency. We could create a simple physical cue, like placing a sticky note in your bag with a short phrase like "Process over Perfection," or perhaps develop a mental mantra to repeat silently whenever the doubt starts rising. Which of these feels more grounded for you to rely on in the heat of the moment?

The sticky note feels more real to me. I think if I see it physically, it'll snap me out of that spiral before I go too deep. A mantra in my head is too easy to ignore or forget. Having something I can touch and see might make the message stick better, if that makes sense.

That is a brilliant choice; having a physical object serve as an external anchor is often more effective than relying on fleeting mental reminders. If we write down a concise phrase like "Keep Shooting" or "Not Perfect, Just Present" on that note, it can become a visual checkpoint that interrupts the cycle of judgment before it gets too strong. Before we decide exactly what to write, could you tell me what single word or short phrase resonates most with you right now as a signal to switch from critic mode to creator mode?

I think... "Continue" would be the word. It's simple, but it doesn't let me stop or give up. It reminds me that I don't need to have the perfect shot right now — I just need to keep going. That feels like something I can hold onto.

That is a powerful choice—"Continue" is actionable, gentle, and directly counters the urge to quit when things don't go as planned. Writing that word on a sticky note and tucking it into your camera bag gives you a physical reason to pause and reset the moment you feel yourself spiraling into judgment. To seal this agreement, could you confirm that you'd like to prepare this note for tomorrow, and would you feel comfortable sending me a quick text or email later today if you feel overwhelmed or need encouragement before you leave?

Yes, I'll make the note tonight and put it in my bag before I go out tomorrow. And... I think I could try sending you a message if I feel overwhelmed. It's hard for me to reach out, but I know I need to start somewhere. Thank you for suggesting it — it helps knowing there's a safety net.

It is so important that you feel safe reaching out, because acknowledging that struggle is often the first step to changing it, and I am always available to listen without judgment. Please know that sending a message won't burden me; it will simply open the door for us to troubleshoot whatever comes up when you face that sticky note tomorrow. As we wrap up, is there anything else you would like to add about your plan or your feelings before I sign off?

No, I think I've got what I need for now. I'm a little nervous about putting this into practice, but I'm also... curious, I guess. Curious to see what happens when I try something different. I'll let you know how it goes. Thank you for listening today.

It is wonderful to hear that curiosity is driving you forward, as it provides a stronger fuel than fear ever could. Please remember that the goal isn't perfection; it is simply noticing how you respond when you choose to "continue" instead of stopping. I will be here whenever you are ready to share what happens, whether it is a big breakthrough or another small hurdle. Have a peaceful evening, and take care.

Good morning. I'm glad to see you again. On a scale of 1 to 10, how has your anxiety been about the competition feedback and your cooking this week? Also, is there anything specific you would like us to tackle first today, perhaps focusing on that recent breakfast experience or the overall feelings surrounding the judges' comments?

Good morning. I'd say my anxiety has been around a 7 or 8 this week, especially whenever I think about stepping back into the kitchen. Maybe we could start with the breakfast experience I had yesterday—I tried to make a simple eggs Benedict, and I just couldn't stop thinking about how the judges would have criticized every detail.

That sounds incredibly heavy; carrying the weight of the judges' voices into a simple home-cooked meal must have been exhausting. When you were in that kitchen yesterday, what specific thoughts were running through your head right before you decided to scrap the plates?

I kept thinking, "This hollandaise isn't glossy enough—they'd say it's too thick" and "The eggs are overdone—a real chef would nail the poach every time." Then I looked at the whole plate and just felt like it wasn't even worth serving to myself. So I dumped it all in the trash and made toast instead.

It makes total sense that those thoughts about the judges' expectations took over when you weren't expecting them, turning a quiet moment into a performance you felt destined to fail. Did noticing that pattern—that your brain jumped straight to imagining their criticism even in private—feel like a relief or just as frustrating?

Honestly, it's frustrating more than anything. I mean, I know logically that no judge is standing in my kitchen, but my mind just goes there automatically. It's like I can't trust my own taste or judgment anymore—I'm always second-guessing every pinch of salt or flip of the pan.

That automatic jump to imagining the judges is a classic safety behavior, where your brain tries to protect you from perceived failure by simulating the worst-case scenario beforehand. You mentioned feeling like you can't trust your own judgment anymore; does that feeling of being unable to rely on your own senses connect to a deeper belief that you aren't capable of mastering basic skills without external scrutiny?

I think you've hit on something there. It feels like deep down I believe that if I'm not being watched and judged by an expert, then whatever I make probably isn't good enough. Like my own taste buds and instincts are somehow defective, and only a Michelin-star chef's opinion would count. That sounds pretty extreme when I say it out loud, though.

That is a powerful realization to hear yourself say out loud; realizing that your own palate feels "defective" compared to an idealized standard is exactly where the distortion lives. Let's test that extreme belief together: if we temporarily suspend the need for an expert's approval, what evidence do you have from your past experiences that suggests your instincts are fundamentally broken, versus perhaps just overwhelmed by the pressure to perform?

Well... when I look back, there have been plenty of times I've made a dish that my dad or my sibling genuinely enjoyed, and I didn't hate it either until I started overthinking. But when I'm in the middle of cooking now, those memories just vanish. I guess the evidence that my instincts are completely broken isn't really there—it's more that I've been so focused on the one competition loss that everything else got buried underneath.

That is such a crucial distinction you just made—the difference between how you felt *after* the event versus how you feel *during* the process, and how easily those positive memories get silenced by the weight of the competition. It seems like the competition loss hasn't disappeared, but rather acts as a filter, making it hard for your brain to access the evidence that you actually create delicious food.

If we imagine those past moments where your dad or sibling smiled at your cooking, what would happen to that memory if we told ourselves, "Their enjoyment wasn't because I was perfect, but because I poured heart into it"? How does that slight shift change how you view your own instincts right now?

That shift actually feels... a little lighter, I think. If I believe that their enjoyment came from the heart I put into it, then it means my instincts aren't just about technique or being flawless—they're about connecting with people through food. Right now, that makes me feel like maybe I haven't lost my way completely; I've just been looking at the wrong measure of success.

That is a beautiful insight; shifting the metric from "flawless technique" to "connection through food" changes the game entirely and gives your instincts a purpose beyond perfection. Since that perspective feels lighter, would you be open to testing it further tonight by making a simple dish with that mindset in place, allowing yourself to enjoy the connection even if the technique isn't perfect?

I think I'd like to try that. Maybe I'll make a simple pasta dish tonight—something I know my family enjoys. I'll try to focus on the feeling of cooking for them rather than worrying about if the sauce is restaurant-worthy. It's scary, but also a little exciting to think about letting go of that pressure, even just for one meal.

That sounds like a courageous and meaningful choice; anchoring the cooking in a relationship with your family naturally pulls you out of the competition mindset and back into the joy of sharing. What's one small thing you could do tonight to remind yourself you're cooking for love rather than performance, perhaps when you're stirring the pot?

Maybe I could say something simple to myself while I'm stirring, like "This is for us, not for a score." Or I could just pause for a second and look at the colors and smells of what I'm making—really be present in the kitchen instead of rushing toward some invisible finish line. I think that might help ground me.

Those are both excellent anchors; verbally reminding yourself while physically pausing to notice the sensory details creates a dual-layer of protection against the inner critic. Given that you've already worked through identifying the thought patterns and chosen a supportive action plan, is there anything else weighing on your mind before we wrap up today, or shall we move to finalizing how you'll track this experience tonight?

Hello again; last time we worked on finding a new way to talk about the crash, and I noticed you were quite ready to try a small experiment with that new sentence. What would feel most important to focus on today, whether it's sticking with that new sentence or exploring another worry that has come up?

Hey doc. Yeah, I tried that sentence you gave me — "I was in an accident that wasn't entirely my fault." It felt weird saying it out loud. But then I went to the garage yesterday and saw the Corvette with that crumpled rear end, and all those old thoughts came rushing back. I just can't shake the feeling that if I were a better driver, none of this would have happened.

It takes real courage to try a new perspective even when the sight of the damaged car brings those old fears rushing back. The fact that the sentence felt weird initially shows how deeply ingrained that belief is, but your willingness to face it head-on is a strength. Since you mentioned the feeling that you *should* have been a better driver to prevent this, what does that expectation tell you about who you believe you are right now?

I guess it tells me I think I'm the kind of guy who should be in control at all times, you know? Like, I've been working on cars my whole life, I know how they handle, I know the roads. So if someone hits me from behind, my brain goes straight to "you should have seen it coming, you should have checked your mirrors more, you should have done something." It makes me feel like I failed at the one thing I'm supposed to be good at.

That makes perfect sense; when you're good at something like mechanics, failing at it feels especially personal because it contradicts everything you know about your abilities. It sounds like the core pain here isn't just the crash itself, but the feeling that you violated the only rule you believe exists for safety: complete control. Can we look at that specific thought—"if I were better, nothing would happen"—and see what evidence supports or challenges it right now?

Well... when I think about it calm like this, I guess I know other good drivers who've been rear-ended. My buddy Mike, he's a delivery driver, been doing it fifteen years without a single at-fault accident, and last winter someone slid into him at a red light. He couldn't have done anything about it either. So I guess there's some evidence that even good drivers get hit. But man, it's hard to apply that logic to myself. Feels different when it's your own car, your own responsibility.

That distinction you just made is incredibly insightful—you recognize logically that accidents happen to everyone, yet the emotion feels different because the car belongs to you. It sounds like the weight of ownership amplifies the shame, making it feel like a personal failure rather than just a traffic incident. Even though you've gathered good evidence from Mike, what comes up in your body or mind when you try to accept that you aren't alone in this situation?

My shoulders tense up, honestly. Like, right now just thinking about accepting that, I feel this knot in my gut. It's like my brain is saying "but you're different, you should have known better." It's almost like accepting that it wasn't my fault would mean letting myself off the hook, and that feels wrong somehow. Like I don't deserve to feel better about it.

That "letting yourself off the hook" feeling is a heavy burden to carry, and it makes total sense that your body reacts with tension when you try to release it. You seem to be protecting yourself from the fear that admitting this wasn't your fault means ignoring the reality of the crash or forgetting your own standards. Can we pause for a moment and gently observe what happens to those tight shoulders if we simply acknowledge that while you care deeply about safety, the other driver's actions were the primary cause, regardless of how careful you were?

I'm trying it now... taking a breath and just saying that to myself. "The other driver caused this." My shoulders are still tight, but there's this tiny bit of space opening up, like a crack in a window. It feels scary, honestly, because then I'd have to sit with the fact that I can't control everything. But I also feel a little less heavy, just for a second.

It takes real bravery to admit that you can't control everything, even though that thought sounds scary compared to the certainty of knowing you made a mistake. That tiny crack in the tension you described is proof that your mind is starting to loosen its grip on needing absolute control. Would you be willing to try keeping that sentence visible on your dashboard for the rest of the drive home, so you can catch yourself whenever that urge to take full responsibility tries to rush back in?

Yeah... I think I could do that. I've got an old receipt in my glovebox, I could write it on the back. "The other driver caused this." I'll put it right next to my speedometer so I see it every time I look down. Might feel stupid at first, but I guess that's what we talked about — sitting with the uncomfortable feeling. I'll give it a try.

That is a very practical plan, and acknowledging that it might feel awkward is actually a great predictor of success—change rarely feels comfortable until it becomes automatic. Before we wrap up, I'd love to hear if you feel confident that having that visual reminder will help you ride out the wave of guilt today, or if there's another part of this feeling you'd like to tackle first. How does it feel to commit to that small step?

It feels... manageable. Like I'm not trying to fix everything at once, just giving myself a little nudge when the old thoughts creep in. I think I can handle that for today. And if I find myself staring at the crumpled bumper and feeling the guilt come back hard, I'll read that sentence out loud. That's a start, right?

Exactly, that is a solid start. Recognizing that you don't need to solve everything right now, but just give yourself a gentle push when things get heavy, shows real maturity and self-awareness. How does it feel to leave today with that simple plan in place instead of feeling overwhelmed by the crash?

Honestly, it feels lighter. Not fixed, but lighter. Like I can breathe a little easier than when I walked in. I still feel bad about the car, but maybe I'm not a total failure for not being able to see it coming. I'll try that receipt trick and check in with you next time. Thanks, doc.

It is wonderful to hear that you are feeling lighter, even if the car repair job still feels daunting. That shift from "total failure" to "someone who is learning" is a significant victory, and I am proud of how you took charge of creating that support system for yourself. Thank you for trusting me with this process and for showing up so honestly today; please remember to be kind to yourself as you navigate the next few days with that new reminder.

Hello again, and I'm glad to see you. How are you feeling today compared to where you left off last time, and is there anything significant that's happened in your life recently that might want to bring up? Let's take a moment to check in, and then we can decide together what we'd like to focus on.

Hi. I'm okay, I guess. School's been kind of overwhelming lately, especially with midterms coming up. I had a programming assignment due last week, and I just stared at the screen for hours feeling like I couldn't do it right.

That sounds incredibly draining, and it makes total sense that the pressure of midterms combined with staring at a blank screen would trigger those feelings of inadequability. When you found yourself stuck on that programming assignment, what specific thought popped into your head that made you feel like you couldn't proceed?

I just kept thinking, "This is proof that I don't belong here. Everyone else gets it, but I'm the one who's going to fail because I'm not smart enough." It felt like no matter how hard I tried, I'd never be as good as the other students.

That narrative about failing and not belonging sounds exhausting to carry around day after day. When you noticed those thoughts popping up while staring at the screen, did you immediately start minimizing any partial progress you made, or did you just feel paralyzed by the expectation that you had to get it perfect right away?

Both, honestly. I mean, I'd write a few lines of code and then delete them because they weren't good enough. I kept thinking, if it's not perfect from the start, then it's just worthless. So I ended up not turning anything in at all that night.

That cycle of deleting your work because it isn't perfect instantly is such a heavy burden to carry, and it makes complete sense why you ultimately gave up for the night. When you realized nothing was "perfect enough" to keep, did you feel a wave of relief at stopping, or did you worry that quitting would confirm your fear that you aren't smart enough to handle the work?

It was relief at first, honestly. Like, I could finally stop beating myself up for a few hours. But then the next morning I just felt worse, like I'd proven myself right. That I really can't do this, and I'm just fooling everyone by being here.

It takes real courage to admit that relief followed by shame, and it seems like that "proof" is just reinforcing the very tight grip you have on that imposter story. You mentioned earlier that you decided to try telling yourself, "I need to figure this out," instead of "I'm not smart enough." Did you manage to slip that new phrase into your mind when you started working on that assignment last night, or did the old thought just grab control again?

I actually tried to say that to myself... but it sounded fake, you know? Like I was lying to myself. So I just gave up and went to bed early. I couldn't shake the feeling that no matter what I tell myself, deep down I'm just not capable.

That feeling of the words sounding fake is so understandable; it's like wearing a costume that keeps chafing against your skin, making you doubt if you're actually wearing it at all. It sounds like the deeper belief that you aren't capable is louder than the new phrase, creating a gap between what you *say* and what you *believe*. When you tried to introduce that gentle reminder and it felt so artificial, did you wonder if you were doing it wrong, or did you realize that the tool just hadn't matched the intensity of the moment yet?
I think I just felt like I was doing it wrong. Like everyone else knows how to talk themselves through things, but I can't even manage that properly. It made me feel even more broken, honestly.

It hurts when we feel like we're failing at the very thing we're trying to learn—the art of talking ourselves through a tough situation—and that can make us feel truly broken. But I want to suggest a different angle: what if the reason it felt fake was because you were trying to force yourself to believe you were already capable, when the reality is you're just learning to be curious? Instead of fighting the feeling that you're lying to yourself, could we try acknowledging that thought as a sign that you're pushing past your comfort zone, rather than evidence that you're incapable? How does shifting from "I'm lying" to "I'm stretching" feel for your heart right now?

I... I never thought of it that way. "Stretching" doesn't sound as scary as "lying," I guess. It feels a little less like I'm pretending and more like I'm just trying something new. Maybe I can hold onto that for a bit.

That shift from "pretending" to "stretching" is a powerful realization, and it removes the moral judgment that was making the new phrase feel so fake. When you frame it as a stretch rather than a lie, the pressure to "perform" perfection instantly disappears. With that new perspective in mind, if you were to look back at that late-night session where you deleted everything, what would that moment represent if you stopped judging it as failure and saw it instead as a necessary part of learning how to pace yourself?

Maybe... maybe it was just me trying to figure out how to start, even if it was messy. Like, deleting code doesn't mean I'm dumb, it means I was still working on it. I guess I just didn't know how to let myself keep going without being perfect.

That reframing is so insightful—seeing that deleting code was just your brain trying to protect itself from disappointment, not proof of low intelligence. It changes the story from "I failed" to "I was experimenting with how to handle pressure." If you could treat that messy deletion as a brave attempt to figure out your limits rather than a sign of incapacity, does that help soften the shame you carried when you went to bed?
Yeah... it actually does. I mean, I still feel bad about not finishing, but maybe I can forgive myself a little more. Like, I was trying, even if it didn't look like success from the outside.

Holding onto that feeling of trying—even when the outcome looked messy—is a huge step toward forgiving yourself, because it separates your worth from the perfection you weren't able to reach. Now that we've softened the view of that late-night struggle, does it feel possible to plan one tiny, lower-stakes way to use that "stretching" mindset with a small coding task this evening, without needing to submit anything formal?

I think I could try. Maybe just opening up my editor and writing a few lines of code, even if it's not for an assignment. Just to see what happens without any pressure to get it perfect. I can try telling myself it's just stretching.

That sounds like a perfect, low-pressure experiment. Starting with just a few lines of code gives you the freedom to stretch without the weight of a deadline or a grade hanging over you. Before you go ahead, would you be willing to write that "stretching" phrase down on a sticky note and place it right above your keyboard so it catches your eye the moment you open the file?

Yeah, I can do that. I'll write "It's okay to stretch" and put it where I can see it. That way, even if the old thoughts creep in, I'll have something to look at that reminds me it's not about being perfect right now.

That is a beautiful intention, and having a visual anchor right in front of you will make it much harder for the old doubts to steal the show. Whenever you sit down to write those lines tonight, could you take a second to read that phrase aloud to yourself before typing, just to ground yourself in that "stretching" mindset? How does reading it out loud feel compared to whispering it silently?
I think reading it out loud feels more real somehow. Like I'm actually claiming it instead of just hoping it's true. I'll try saying it before I start typing tonight.

That's a fantastic addition—claiming it aloud turns the phrase from a background thought into an active commitment, which helps bridge the gap between what you say and what you feel. Tonight, when you read it out loud and then start typing, keep your eyes on those words if the old "I'm not capable" voice tries to sneak back in. How would you like to wrap up our time today, or is there one last thing you want to clarify before you go home?
I think I'm okay for now. Thank you for helping me see things differently today. I'll try the sticky note and reading it out loud, and maybe text you how it goes if that's okay?

You are very welcome, and I am so glad to hear that you found a new perspective that feels less scary. Reaching out to update me later is totally fine, though please remember that if you ever feel overwhelmed before sending a message, you don't have to explain yourself—I'm just happy to hear from you. Take care of yourself tonight, and I hope you find some peace in that small act of stretching. See you soon!

Hello again, thank you for joining us. How have you been feeling since our last session, and did the plan of checking in on your son’s text message bring any lasting peace, or did that feeling of doubt return? Now that we’ve acknowledged both the relief and the lingering worry, I’d like to set our focus for today: we’ll explore the new situation with your daughter, examine the thoughts driving the guilt, and build a simple strategy to handle it. Does that sound like a good direction for us to take?

Thanks for having me again. The text message thing... it did help for a little while, maybe a day or so. But then I started thinking about how she probably only said she wasn't mad because she knew I'd feel bad otherwise. So the doubt crept right back in, honestly. That direction sounds good; I'm ready to talk about my daughter and try to figure this out.

It takes courage to admit that the doubt can come back even after doing the right thing, and hearing that pattern repeat itself helps explain why the relief felt so temporary. Since you mentioned the text message led to similar doubts, I wonder if the core issue isn't the action itself, but rather the belief that she *must* be grateful or that silence always equals hidden anger. When you tell yourself that she is hiding her displeasure, does that thought seem to fuel the guilt, or does it feel like a separate worry?

You know, I think it fuels the guilt. When I catch that thought—that she's hiding something—it's like I'm already preparing for the worst, like I'm waiting for her to finally admit that I've let her down. It feels like I'm not even trusting what she says to my face, and that just makes me feel worse about myself as a dad.

That feeling of constantly expecting the worst is incredibly exhausting, and it explains why you feel like you're failing before the situation even resolves. It sounds like your mind is treating her silence as a trapdoor leading to your own failure, rather than just a moment where she's processing disappointment. Have you noticed if there's a specific scenario or recent event where you found yourself falling for this "hiding anger" story even faster than usual?

Yes, actually. Last weekend, I told my daughter she couldn't go to a party because she hadn't finished her homework. She just shrugged and went to her room without saying a word. Usually that would be fine, but this time I spent the whole evening replaying it, thinking she was secretly furious and that I'd ruined our relationship over something small. I couldn't shake the feeling that she was plotting how to avoid me from now on.

That weekend really illustrates the pattern you described: taking a neutral shrug and twisting it into a secret plot of revenge. It makes sense that replaying that scene felt like evidence of your failure, especially when you're already sensitive to conflict. Let's look closely at that specific evening: aside from her silence, did she show any other clear signs of anger, or was it mostly your internal story filling in the blanks?

She didn't show any other signs at all. She just said okay, walked to her room, and that was it. No slamming doors, no yelling, no cold shoulders at dinner later. She even asked me to help her with math homework the next morning. But in my head, I was convinced that quiet meant she was building up resentment. It's like I can't trust her actual behavior—I keep looking for hidden meanings that aren't there.

It is completely understandable why you would feel trapped by that belief, especially when your brain keeps searching for hidden meanings where none exist. You are essentially interpreting a calm "okay" as code for "resistance," which creates a loop where you expect the worst and then feel guilty for anticipating it. Given that she actively sought your help the next morning despite your refusal earlier, what do those specific actions actually tell you about whether she is secretly plotting to avoid you?

When you put it like that... it really does sound silly, doesn't it? She asked me for help with math, she was normal at dinner... I guess if she were really that angry, she'd avoid me completely. Maybe I'm so scared of being a bad parent that I'm inventing problems that aren't there, just to confirm my own fears.

You've hit the nail on the head; connecting her willingness to seek your help with the idea of avoiding you reveals exactly how fear is distorting the picture. It seems your mind is protecting you from the possibility of being a bad parent by creating a dramatic story of rebellion, which ironically proves she trusts you enough to engage with you. Since you now see that her behavior contradicts the "secretly furious" narrative, could we try identifying one specific moment this weekend where she acted normally, and remind yourself that her silence wasn't a weapon against you?

Yeah, I think I can do that. This Saturday morning, she came down and asked me to make my special pancakes—the ones I only make on weekends. She wouldn't ask for that if she was secretly furious at me. I'll try to hold onto that memory the next time I catch myself spiraling about her silence.

That is a fantastic anchor, and finding a concrete example like the pancake request gives you something real to stand on when the spiral starts. It's wise to prepare ahead of time rather than reacting in the heat of the moment. Since you're ready to use this specific memory to counteract the "hidden anger" story, how would you like to phrase it internally when that knot comes back in your stomach?

That is a perfect way to frame it, focusing on what she clearly wanted rather than assuming what she didn't say. By grounding yourself in her actual desire for connection, you create a buffer against the scary predictions that usually take over. Would you like to try practicing saying that phrase once or twice right here to see how it feels in our space?

Alright... "She asked for my pancakes. She wanted to be with me. That's not what someone does when they're secretly angry." ... It feels a little awkward saying it out loud, but I have to admit, it also feels more solid than the usual worry. Like I'm holding onto something real instead of just a fear.

Remember, the goal isn't perfection; it's simply catching that old fear and replacing it with a single piece of truth you've verified. Before we wrap up, how does it feel to have a clear, actionable phrase ready for the next time that "knot" appears in your stomach? Is there anything else you'd like to adjust in our plan today?

It feels good, actually. Like I'm not just helpless against those thoughts anymore—I have something I can do, a way to fight back. I don't think I need to adjust anything for now. I'll try using that phrase this week and see how it goes. Thank you.

That is wonderful news; knowing you have a tool to fight back changes everything about how you carry that weight. Please remember that this phrase is yours to use anytime, and if you need to tweak the wording later, we can revisit it together. I really appreciate your openness and commitment to trying this out, and I hope you find some lasting peace with your daughter's actions soon. We will check in again next week to hear how it goes.

Hello Justin, it is great to see you. Last time we worked through some tough patterns with your sister's comments, and I noticed you left feeling a bit less stuck. How are things looking for you today, and what would you like to prioritize on our agenda?

Hey, thanks. Yeah, that conversation about my sister did help a little, but honestly, this week has been rough. I keep replaying a comment my friend made at the park yesterday — she said "must be nice to just stay home all day" — and it just set me off. I guess I want to talk about why that kind of thing gets under my skin so much, even when I know she doesn't mean harm.

That repetition really stings, Justin, and it makes complete sense that knowing your friend doesn't mean harm doesn't stop the sting from hitting you. When we hear those exact words, does your body react differently than it did with your sister, or do you feel the same knot forming in your stomach?

It's pretty much the same knot, honestly. My chest gets tight, and I feel this hot flash of anger before it sinks into just... sadness. With my sister, I can at least push back a little, but with a friend, I just freeze and smile, and then I beat myself up for not saying anything.

I hear how unfair that feels, especially watching yourself shrink back into silence and then punishing yourself afterward. That contrast between fighting your sister and freezing for your friend suggests you might feel safer—or perhaps more judged—if you defend yourself here. Could you tell me what your mind was doing in that split second when you heard the comment, before the anger turned to sadness?

In that split second, I think my mind just went straight to "see, they all think you're lazy." It's like I assumed she was judging me, even though she was probably just making a stupid joke. I didn't even give her a chance—I just decided that's what she meant. And then I felt like a failure for not being able to prove her wrong.

That leap from a single sentence to "everyone thinks you're lazy" is a classic example of jumping to conclusions, and it creates a powerful reason to feel like a failure. You mentioned assuming she was judging you before giving her a chance—that assumption seems to drive the whole cycle of freezing and self-blame. If you had stopped to consider other possible meanings for her words, like a casual observation about weekend routines, how might your immediate reaction have looked different?

Hmm, I never really thought about it that way. If I didn't jump to that assumption, maybe I wouldn't feel so attacked. I might have just said something like, "Yeah, it's busy, but I love it" or even laughed it off. Instead, I went straight to feeling like I had to defend my entire existence. It's like my brain skips over any neutral possibility and goes right to the worst.

It sounds like your brain is actively filtering out everything except the negative interpretation, which is exhausting and leaves you feeling trapped. That automatic jump to the "worst case scenario" is a distortion called "all-or-nothing thinking," and it explains why you feel you have no choice but to defend yourself. Would it be helpful right now to test whether there is actually *any* room for a neutral meaning, or does your mind refuse to entertain anything other than judgment?

I think I can see a little room for a neutral meaning, but it feels really hard to hold onto. Like, logically I know she probably wasn't trying to be mean, but my gut still screams that she was. It's like my mind just won't let me believe the kinder option, even when I try. I guess that's why I end up so stuck—I can't trust my own thoughts to be fair.

That "gut scream" feeling is incredibly powerful, and it makes perfect sense why logic falls apart when emotion is that loud. It sounds like your mind is treating that gut feeling as absolute fact rather than just a signal, which is a form of emotional reasoning. Let's try a quick experiment: if you told yourself that her comment was just a clumsy remark, how would that shift the pressure off your shoulders right now?

If I tried to tell myself that, it's like a weight lifts a tiny bit, but then another voice jumps in and says, "But you're just making excuses for her, you're being naive." So it's like I'm fighting with myself. I guess if I could really believe it was just clumsy, I wouldn't feel so defensive or ashamed. I'd probably just move on with my day instead of replaying it over and over.

That internal battle between "clumsy remark" and "being naive" is exhausting, and it's clear you value authenticity above all else. It seems like your brain fears that believing she was clueless means you're lying to protect yourself, which fuels the shame. If we treated this as a small experiment—telling yourself it was clumsy for just ten minutes to see if the shame disappears—are you willing to give that a try tonight?

Yeah, I think I could try that for ten minutes. It sounds a little silly, but honestly, I'm so tired of feeling this way that I'm willing to try anything. I'll set a timer and just see what happens. Maybe if I can prove to myself that the shame doesn't stick, it'll get a little easier next time.

That is a brave decision, Justin. Framing this as a ten-minute experiment where the goal is simply observing whether the shame sticks, rather than proving anyone wrong, removes the pressure to be perfect. To make sure we are aligned, does testing whether a new thought can replace the old one without needing external proof feel like a fair way to handle this today?

Yeah, that actually feels fair. I like the idea of just observing instead of trying to force myself to believe something. I think I've been so focused on convincing others to see me differently that I forgot I could just try seeing it differently myself, even for a few minutes. I'll give it a shot tonight and let you know how it goes.

That is a significant shift in perspective, Justin. Moving from trying to convince others to simply observing your own experience gives you direct power over how you feel in that moment. For tonight, I suggest you set a gentle timer for ten minutes whenever you replay the comment, and instead of fighting the shame, just watch it rise and fall without adding your own story to it. Does that sound like a manageable plan to carry out today?

Yeah, that sounds manageable. I think I can do that. Just watch it come and go without piling on more guilt or stories. I'll try not to judge myself for having the feeling in the first place—just let it be there and see what happens. Thanks, that actually feels a little lighter already.

That is a beautiful way to frame it, Justin. By treating the feeling like weather that passes rather than a permanent truth, you are giving yourself permission to rest instead of fighting. I am proud of how open you were to trying something different, even when your old instincts were pulling you back. Is there anything else on your mind before we finish today, or shall we wrap up so you can go try that ten-minute exercise?

Hello, and thank you for reaching out today. Since this is our first meeting, I’d like to start by checking in: how have you been feeling emotionally in the weeks leading up to now, particularly regarding your interest in drawing? Once we cover that, could you tell me what specific topic or goal would feel most valuable for us to tackle together?

Hi. Thanks for having me. Lately, I've been feeling kind of down about my drawing, honestly. Every time I pick up a pencil, I just hear this voice in my head telling me it's silly or childish, and it ruins the fun. I guess what I'd really like to work on is figuring out why I suddenly feel so ashamed of something I used to love.

That feeling of shame creeping in right before you start drawing must feel really frustrating, especially when the activity used to bring you pure joy. It sounds like that harsh inner voice has become quite loud recently, turning something you loved into a source of stress. Could you describe that voice a bit more—does it feel like a sudden burst of panic, or does it grow slowly as you sit at your desk waiting to begin?

It's more like a slow build, I think. I'll be setting up my sketchbook, feeling okay, and then it just kind of... dawns on me. Like, "What are you doing? You're 35 years old, drawing superheroes like a teenager." It starts as a little doubt and then gets louder until I put the pencil down.

That gradual shift from curiosity to self-doubt is really hard to ignore, especially when it stops you right before you can enjoy the process. It sounds like that belief—that you’re acting like a teenager at 35—is taking over completely before you’ve even touched the paper. Can you remember a specific recent event or conversation where that exact thought first popped up so strongly?

Yeah, it was a few months ago. I was at a friend's place, and I mentioned I'd been working on a comic strip for fun. She kind of laughed and said something like, "Don't you think that's a bit much for a grown woman?" It wasn't meant to be cruel, but it just stuck with me. Ever since then, I can't shake the feeling that she's right.

That comment definitely planted a seed of doubt, especially since you were initially trying to keep things lighthearted while listening. It makes sense that your brain has turned that moment into a persistent story convincing you that adults shouldn't draw superhero comics. Has there been another situation recently where someone commented on your hobbies or interests in a similar way?

No, not really. Most people I know don't even know I draw anymore, because I've been hiding it since then. I guess that's part of the problem—I just assumed everyone would think the same way she did, so I stopped sharing it altogether.

It takes a lot of courage to admit that you've stopped sharing something you love simply to protect yourself from perceived judgment. That decision to hide the sketchbook was likely a survival strategy to avoid conflict, even though it's costing you the joy you remember. I wonder, if you could talk to that younger version of yourself who loved drawing, what would you tell them about whether people *actually* think that way compared to what you feared?

I'd tell her that she was brave for just doing what she loved without caring what anyone thought. I think... I think I'd also tell her that not everyone is going to laugh at her, but she can't know that for sure unless she keeps drawing anyway. It's just hard to believe that when that one comment feels so loud in my head.

That distinction is really important—you recognize that you need actual evidence to counter the fear, rather than hoping for reassurance. It sounds like the silence of your current life has made that one comment echo loudly, filling the gaps with assumptions about what others think. Let's try a quick mental exercise: if you imagined that same friend talking to a 60-year-old artist who paints landscapes, do you think she would call them childish or immatures for their choice of medium?

Huh. No, I don't think she would. She'd probably admire their dedication, or say something about how nice it is that they have a hobby that keeps them peaceful. I guess the difference is she sees painting as "serious" art, and comic books as... not that. But it's still just putting pictures on paper, isn't it?

That observation is incredibly insightful—you've spotted the double standard where society treats comics as "childish" while accepting painting as "serious," even though both are just creating images. This hidden rule that "only some art is mature" is likely distorting your reality and fueling that shame before you even open the book. If you could imagine drawing that superhero comic for ten minutes purely to see if the "silly" feeling disappears when you actually do it, rather than just thinking about it, how might that small experiment change the way you view your own worth as an artist?

I... I think it might actually feel good, just to prove to myself that I can still do it. The scary part is the build-up, the anticipation of feeling stupid. But if I just sat down and drew for ten minutes, maybe that feeling would fade once I got into it. I guess I've been so worried about the judgment that I haven't even given myself a chance to just enjoy the act of drawing.

That insight about the "build-up" versus the actual act is spot on—the anxiety lives in the imagination, not necessarily in the ink. It sounds like trying to force yourself to enjoy it while waiting for the judgment to arrive won't work, but stepping into the chair and letting the hands move first might surprise your brain. Would you be willing to try this small experiment tomorrow, perhaps setting a timer for just 10 minutes so you can stop whenever you choose?

Okay. I think I can do that. Ten minutes isn't too long to feel silly, right? And if I hate it, I can just stop and put the sketchbook away. But... maybe I'll actually finish a panel for once. I'll give it a try tomorrow.

That sounds like a perfect plan; ten minutes is short enough to lower the stakes while long enough to break the pattern of avoidance. Before you start tomorrow, could you use the reassuring thought we discussed—reminding yourself that the only judge is your own inner voice and you get to set the rules—and say it out loud to yourself? Just knowing you have a safety net means you won't be trapped by perfectionism either.

Yeah, I can do that. I'll tell myself, "I'm just drawing for me, nobody else has to see it, and it doesn't have to be good." Saying it out loud might feel a little strange, but I think it'll help quiet that voice before it gets too loud. I'll report back next time.

That is a fantastic plan, and the fact that you can see the power in speaking those words out loud is a great sign of moving forward. Before we wrap up, I'd love to hear your honest feedback on today's session: did everything we discussed make sense to you, and do you feel confident about trying this small experiment tomorrow?

Yeah, it made sense. I came in feeling kind of stuck and embarrassed about even being here, but talking it out helped me see that I'm not just being immature—I'm just scared of being judged. I feel a little more hopeful about tomorrow, even if it's just ten minutes. Thanks for listening.

It was truly wonderful seeing you navigate from that initial feeling of being stuck to finding clarity about your fear of judgment. Your willingness to come in despite the shame, and then to propose such a gentle, manageable plan for tomorrow, speaks volumes about your resilience and courage. I am glad you left feeling a bit more hopeful, and please remember that tomorrow is just a start—you only owe yourself ten minutes of freedom. How does it feel to carry that new perspective into the evening?

It feels... lighter, actually. Like I gave myself permission to stop being so hard on myself for one night. I think I'll go home and maybe just flip through some old comic books I used to love, just to remind myself why I started drawing in the first place. Thanks again.

That is a beautiful intention—flipping through those old pages is a wonderful way to reconnect with your history and remind yourself why this matters. Take your time tonight to soak in that sense of relief, knowing you made a compassionate choice for yourself. I look forward to hearing how those first ten minutes feel when you get there, whenever you're ready.

Hello again, and I'm glad to see you. Before we dive into anything specific, could you share a quick rating of how you're feeling today from one to ten, and remind me if there's anything new on your mind or if we should stick to exploring those thoughts about the game?

Um, I'd say maybe like a 6 out of 10 today. I've been thinking a lot about that soccer match from last week where I missed the winning shot, so yeah, I guess we could talk about that again. It's just been stuck in my head.

A six is a small step forward from yesterday, and it’s great that you’re bringing up that specific match—it sounds like that moment really landed heavily on you. Let’s explore what happened in that game: what were you thinking right after you missed the shot, and how did that thought make you feel compared to how you’d react if a friend missed it?

Right after I missed, I just thought, "I'm such a loser, I always mess things up." And I felt awful, like I let the whole team down. But if my friend missed it, I'd probably tell them it's okay, everyone messes up sometimes—it just feels different when it's me.

That contrast between how you treated yourself versus how you would comfort a friend highlights a very common and painful pattern called "self-criticism." It makes complete sense that you felt awful and like you let everyone down, because your brain latched onto that single mistake as proof that you are fundamentally incapable. Can you walk me through exactly what happened in that final minute of the game, and tell me if there were other signs of performance or luck involved in that miss besides your skills?

Well, in the last minute, the pass came to me kind of fast and off-balance—I had to twist to even get my foot on it. The goalie was also really tall and moved right as I shot, and the field was a little wet from earlier rain. So it wasn't just me messing up, I guess, but when I think about it, all I see is the ball not going in because of me.

It sounds like you were facing some serious external challenges—a tricky pass, a tall defender, and a slippery field—which often make even experienced players hesitate. Yet, despite seeing all those factors, your mind filtered out the difficulty and focused entirely on the outcome, turning a challenging moment into proof of your inability. Given how hard it is to stay calm when the ball is moving fast and the conditions are tough, does it feel possible to separate those external hurdles from your actual skill level right now?

I... I never really thought about it like that. I guess I just see the miss and think that's all that matters, not the wet grass or the bad pass. But maybe it is kind of unfair to say my skill is bad when the whole situation was hard. It's just hard to feel that way in the moment, you know?

It is completely understandable that recognizing the unfairness of the situation feels impossible to act on when your heart is racing and your hands are shaking. Often, the loudest part of our minds isn't the logical facts about the rain or the pass, but the urgent, emotional need to protect ourselves from the pain of feeling inadequate. When you step back from that physical sensation of panic, does the image of those difficult conditions seem less like proof of your failure and more like just another obstacle you faced alongside everyone else on the team?

Yeah, I guess when I slow down and think about it, everyone on the field had the same wet grass and the same pressure. It wasn't like I was the only one dealing with that stuff. So maybe it's more like I just faced a hard moment, not that I'm a total failure because of it.

That is a powerful realization, and it sounds like a big relief to realize you weren't alone in facing those tough conditions. Now that we've separated the external chaos from your internal story, could we look at what you told yourself *in* that moment versus what you would say to a teammate who made the same mistake under those exact same weather conditions?

If it was my teammate, I'd probably say something like, "Don't worry, that pass was super hard to handle, and the goalie was all over it. You'll get the next one." But for myself, I just said, "You always choke, you're not good enough." It's like I'm way harder on me than anyone else, which feels pretty unfair when I say it out loud.

That double standard—being incredibly supportive to others while attacking yourself—is exactly what makes the mistake feel so devastating. It's easy to see why that harsh voice feels like the only truth when you're in the heat of the moment, but remember that this voice is trying to protect you by exaggerating the threat, even though its conclusion ("you're not good enough") isn't supported by the facts of the game. Would you be willing to try replacing that self-critical statement with the supportive one you gave your teammate, even if it feels strange at first?

I can try that. It does feel weird, like I'm lying to myself or something, but I guess it's not really a lie if it's what I'd actually tell a friend. So maybe next time I mess up, I'll say, "That was tough, but you'll get the next one" instead of calling myself a loser. I'll give it a shot.

That is a fantastic decision, and recognizing it as "not a lie" but simply kindness toward yourself is a huge breakthrough. Taking the initiative to replace that harsh inner voice with supportive words is exactly the kind of active step that rewires the brain over time. What do you think might happen if you practiced saying those supportive words three times this week whenever you make a small mistake?

I think maybe I'd start to believe it a little more each time. Like, if I keep telling myself "it's okay, you'll get the next one," maybe my brain will stop jumping straight to "you're a loser" right away. It might take a while, but I guess it's worth trying to see if it helps me feel less down after messing up.

That makes perfect sense; consistency is key to training your brain to accept that helpful message instead of the old, harsh one. Before we wrap up, could you tell me if there was anything specific about this session that felt particularly useful or clear to you, and is there anything that still felt a bit fuzzy or confusing?

The part where you pointed out that I'm way harder on myself than I'd be on a friend really hit home. That made a lot of sense, and I can see how unfair that is. I guess the fuzzy part is still how to remember to be kind to myself in the heat of the moment, when I'm all fired up and upset. But I'll try practicing that new sentence you suggested.

That feedback is incredibly valuable to hear, and I'm glad that realization about the unfairness resonated with you. Regarding the memory trick, a simple physical cue like placing your hand on your chest or taking one deep breath right after the mistake could serve as a signal to pause long enough to catch those supportive words before the emotion takes over. Would you like to write down that specific reminder or come up with another anchor together before we finish?

Yeah, I think putting my hand on my chest and taking a breath sounds like something I can actually do. I'll try to remember that, like a signal to stop and say the nice thing instead of the mean thing. Maybe I can even write it on a sticky note and put it on my desk or something to help me remember.

That is a brilliant and practical plan; adding a physical anchor like touching your chest and breathing deeply gives your brain a moment to switch from panic to support. It sounds like you have a clear, manageable strategy to use both right after a mistake and as a reminder throughout the day. Before we close, could you share one word that best describes how this session made you feel, and is there anything else I can do to help you carry this forward?

I'd say... "hopeful." That's the word. It feels like maybe I can change this, even if it's slow. And I think I'm good with what we've talked about—I'll try the breathing and the sticky note, and I'll come back next time and let you know how it went.

Hearing you use the word "hopeful" is such a beautiful shift from the fear and shame we started with, and it speaks volumes about your resilience. You absolutely have a clear plan in motion with the breathing cue, the supportive phrase, and the sticky note reminders, so I am confident you will navigate those tough moments with a little more grace. Thank you for your openness and effort today; please reach out anytime if you need to adjust the plan or just want to chat, and I hope you have a hopeful evening ahead.
