Hello again. Before we dive into your concerns, how have you been feeling since we met last time, and did the idea of keeping a sticky note by his bowl help when you felt that knot in your stomach? Also, what would be most important for us to focus on together today?

Hi. Well, I did try the sticky note idea. I wrote "He's fine, just picky" on it, and it did help a little at first. But then yesterday, he barely touched his breakfast again, and I found myself ripping the note off and crumpling it up. I just felt so stupid. I guess what's most important today is figuring out why one little stubborn dog can make me feel like such a failure at everything.

It makes complete sense that crumpling up the note felt like proof of your failure, especially when you felt so frustrated that it didn't work as planned. That reaction shows how deeply connected you are to your dog's needs, but it also tells me that the phrase on the note wasn't quite matching the intensity of your worry. When you say one small thing with him triggers the feeling that you're failing at everything, could you describe exactly what went through your mind right before you tore the note away?

I was standing there with his bowl, and he just looked at it, then looked at me, and walked away. And the thought that hit me was, "See? You can't even do this right. You can't take care of one simple dog. What kind of person can't even feed a dog properly?" It was like the whole morning—getting the kids off to school, the laundry pile—it all just collapsed into that one moment, and I felt like I was the worst at all of it.

That overwhelming collapse of your entire day into one small moment sounds incredibly draining, and it makes total sense that feeling like the "worst parent" would leave you with a heavy knot in your stomach. It seems that thought isn't just about the dog anymore, but acts as a lens that magnifies every other task you've done as failures. If we pause for a second and look at that specific thought about being a "bad person," does it feel like an absolute fact about who you are, or does it sound more like a catastrophic story your brain is telling you to explain the bowl incident?

It... it feels like a fact. I mean, when he walks away from his food, it's right there in front of me. It's not like I'm imagining it. He's doing it, so I must be doing something wrong. But when you say "catastrophic story"... I guess it does sound a bit dramatic when you put it that way. I don't know. It's like my brain just jumps straight to "you're a failure" without stopping to think.

It is incredibly brave of you to call out that jump from a simple behavior to a global judgment like "you're a failure," because that leap is exactly where our brains tend to shortcut when we're stressed. Even though it feels like an undeniable fact in the heat of the moment, could we look at the timeline of yesterday's morning: did you actually perform any actions that proved you couldn't feed the dog properly, or did you simply notice the dog's choice while you were already carrying a huge load of other responsibilities?

Well... I did put the food in his bowl. I scooped it fresh from the bag, just like I always do. It wasn't stale or anything. And he did end up eating it later, right before his afternoon walk. I guess when you look at it that way, I didn't actually fail at feeding him. I just... he just didn't want it at that exact moment. But it's so hard to remember that in the moment. All I see is him walking away, and it's like that's the only thing that matters.

You are absolutely right that you successfully fed him eventually, yet in that high-stress moment, your brain filtered out the success and locked onto the rejection. It seems like when you feel overwhelmed by the laundry or the kids leaving, that single moment of rejection becomes the anchor that pulls your confidence underwater. If we look at the difference between *preparing* the food correctly versus *feeding* it instantly, does seeing those as two separate steps help create a tiny gap between your action and his reaction?

Huh. I never thought of it like that. Preparing the food is something I do. I do that part right. His reaction is something he does. They're not the same thing. That... actually makes a lot of sense. I've been lumping them together, like if he doesn't eat, then I must have done the whole thing wrong. It's like I'm giving him all the power to decide if I'm a good pet owner or not. That doesn't seem fair to me, does it?

That distinction is a massive step forward, and you're right—that dynamic puts the entire weight of your self-worth on a whim you can't control. It feels unfair when one small reaction invalidates all your effort, doesn't it? Since separating those two actions helps a little, could we try adding a quick rule to your mental checklist: whenever that knot hits, remind yourself, "My preparation was good; his timing is unpredictable. These aren't the same mistake." How does saying that aloud feel compared to just staring at the bowl?

It feels... lighter. Like I can breathe for a second instead of just sinking into that pit. Saying it out loud makes it sound more like a fact and less like a punch in the gut. I think I could try that. Next time he snubs his breakfast, I'll try to say that to myself, even if I have to whisper it in the pantry. It's better than standing there feeling like the worst person on the planet.

It is wonderful to hear that speaking the words made them feel more solid and less like a sharp blow. Using a mantra to ground yourself in the pantry is a very practical and empowering strategy. Before we finish, could you quickly confirm what your plan is for tomorrow morning if that knot appears again?

Yes. Tomorrow morning, if he walks away from his bowl, I'm going to stop myself from jumping straight to the worst. I'll whisper to myself, "I prepared the food correctly. His timing is his own. I am not a failure." And I'll remind myself that he usually eats later anyway. I'll try to let that be enough.

That is a clear and compassionate plan, and I appreciate how you've integrated both the factual reality of his timing and the self-validation you need. To wrap up our time today, is there anything specific about the distinction between preparing the food and waiting for him to eat that you'd like to explore further before we finish?

No, I think I've got a good handle on that part for now. It's a big change just to see those as two separate things. I feel like I have something to hold onto instead of just slipping into that dark hole. Thank you for helping me see it that way. I'll practice it, and I'll let you know how it goes next time.

That is such a powerful shift, and I am so proud of how quickly you adapted to the new perspective. It is truly remarkable how much relief you felt just by separating the preparation from the reaction. Before we officially close, could you take a moment to reflect on whether trying to whisper that affirmation to yourself felt manageable or if it seemed too difficult to use when you were feeling overwhelmed?

It felt manageable when I was calm, saying it here with you. I know it'll be harder when I'm actually in that moment, with my heart racing and the kids still needing things. But I think if I can just get the first few words out, even if my voice cracks, it'll slow down the spiral enough to catch my breath. I'm willing to try it, even if it's shaky at first.

That honesty about expecting it to be shaky is incredibly valuable, because it acknowledges that perfection isn't the goal right now—just slowing down the panic is enough. It sounds like you have a strong foundation to build on by focusing on getting those first few words out even when your hands are shaking. Is there anything else you'd like to talk about before we wrap up, or shall we save any remaining energy for practicing that whisper tomorrow?

Hello, thank you for being here. Before we dive in, could you tell me how you've been feeling since we last spoke and what we agreed to focus on today?

Oh, well, this is actually my first session, so we haven't spoken before. I came in because I've been really struggling lately. A few days ago, I lost some bank notes at work, and since then I've just been feeling completely overwhelmed and anxious about what might happen next.

It makes sense that you're feeling overwhelmed after losing money at work; that situation naturally triggers worries about your future and reputation. Since this is our first meeting, I'd like to check in on your mood right now—on a scale of 0 to 10, how intense has that anxiety felt this week? Also, given that we need to cover ground, would you like to focus primarily on the immediate fear that your career is ruined, or would you prefer to explore what support systems might be available to you while you wait for things to settle?

I'd say my anxiety has been at about an 8 or 9 most days this week. It's just constant, especially when I'm at the bank. I think I'd rather focus on the fear that my career is ruined—that's what keeps me up at night. The thought of never getting promoted because of one mistake is terrifying, and I can't seem to shake it.

An anxiety rating of 8 or 9 certainly explains why you're ruminating late into the night; your mind is clearly trying to solve a problem that feels urgent to you. Since your main worry right now is that one mistake has permanently destroyed your chances for a promotion, let's take a closer look at what specific thoughts are driving that feeling. When you imagine the worst-case scenario, what exact picture is playing out in your head about your boss or colleagues?

I keep picturing my boss calling me into his office and telling me I'm not fit for any kind of advancement because I can't be trusted with something as basic as bank notes. Then I imagine my colleagues whispering about it behind my back, thinking I'm careless or incompetent. It feels like this one mistake is going to define me forever, no matter what I do.

It sounds like your mind is creating a very vivid story where that one error acts as a permanent fingerprint on your professional identity, making it impossible for others to see your past successes. If you could zoom in slightly on that image of your boss in the office, what specific words or actions are you expecting him to say or do? Are there any details in that scene that aren't necessarily true right now?

In my head, he's saying something like, "Gregory, we expected more from you. This kind of carelessness isn't what we look for in someone who wants to move up." I guess I don't actually know if he'll say that, since he hasn't called me in yet. But it feels so real, like it's already happened in some way. I can't help but think that's exactly what's coming.

That vivid mental script feels incredibly threatening, especially since your body seems to expect it to unfold immediately. Even though he hasn't spoken yet, your brain is treating this imagined confrontation as if it's already a fact. If we looked at the timeline strictly, what evidence do you currently have that he has actually made a decision about your promotion or expressed disappointment, versus this being purely your mind filling in the gaps?

Well, I guess there isn't any real evidence yet. He hasn't said anything to me about the lost notes, and no one has mentioned my promotion at all. But I just can't stop thinking that it's only a matter of time before everything comes crashing down. The silence almost makes it worse—like everyone's waiting to see what happens to me.

It makes complete sense that the silence feels heavier than words; our brains often interpret a lack of communication as proof that something terrible is being withheld or decided against us. Since you mentioned he hasn't addressed the issue or raised the topic of promotion yet, how does the reality of his recent behavior compare to the dramatic scene you've been rehearsing in your head? Is there anything he has done or said that contradicts the idea that he's already written off your future?

I suppose... he did nod at me in the hallway yesterday and said "good morning" like he usually does. That doesn't really fit with the idea that he's already decided I'm a lost cause. If he was that disappointed or angry, maybe he'd avoid me or act cold. So that's a small thing, but my mind keeps telling me it doesn't matter, that he's just being polite and waiting for the right moment.

That nod is actually quite significant evidence that your perception of the situation might be misinterpreting his politeness as a delay rather than a sign of continued respect. If we treat that greeting as neutral or even positive, how does it change the certainty that he has already decided you are unfit for advancement? Can you imagine a version of events where that nod meant nothing was wrong, and his usual routine continues unchanged?

I guess I could imagine that version, but it feels almost like I'm lying to myself if I think that way. Like I'm letting myself off the hook too easily. But you're right, his behavior hasn't really changed. Maybe I'm so focused on the worst possible outcome that I'm ignoring everything else. It's just hard to trust that things might be okay when I'm so used to expecting the worst.

It takes courage to admit that expecting the worst makes it difficult to trust positive signs; your brain is likely protecting you from the pain of surprise by preparing for a disaster beforehand. However, that preparation often creates a self-fulfilling prophecy where you miss the evidence that life is moving forward normally. If we set that expectation of disaster aside for just a minute, what would happen if you assumed his nod and greeting were simply the beginning of a recovery period rather than the prelude to your downfall?

If I assumed that, I think I'd feel a little lighter, honestly. I might actually be able to focus on my work instead of replaying that scene in my head over and over. I could probably even talk to my boss normally if I saw him again instead of avoiding him. It's just... breaking that habit of expecting the worst feels like a big leap, even if it makes sense logically.

That feeling of lightness is a huge clue that your mind is capable of shifting gears when you challenge the certainty of the disaster. Breaking that habit of expecting the worst doesn't mean ignoring the risk, but rather realizing that the outcome isn't fixed until he actually speaks. Before we move to a concrete plan for handling those intrusive thoughts, I want to make sure we are both aligned: does this line of questioning about the evidence feel useful to you, or would you prefer we try a different approach right now?

No, this is actually really helpful. I've never thought to question whether the story in my head is actually true or not. It's like I've been so stuck in my own worst-case scenario that I forgot to check if there's any proof. I think I'd like to keep going with this approach, if that's okay. It feels like I'm starting to see things a little more clearly.

That is wonderful to hear; recognizing that you've been skipping the "proof check" step is a major breakthrough. Since this approach resonates with you, let's deepen that investigation one last time. If we assume for a moment that he truly trusts you enough to nod and greet you daily, how would that assumption challenge the idea that you are already doomed to lose the promotion? Does holding onto that assumption make the knot in your stomach feel any looser?

Yeah, it does make it feel a bit looser, actually. If I really try to hold onto that assumption, the knot in my stomach isn't as tight. It's like I can breathe a little easier, even if only for a moment. It makes me realize how much energy I've been wasting on a future that hasn't even happened yet.

That relief is a powerful indicator that your body is responding to a more realistic view of the situation. You've noticed a clear link: shifting from "doomed" to "trustworthy" reduces the physical tension. Now that we've established that this catastrophic story lacks solid evidence and that questioning it brings relief, let's turn that insight into a practical tool. If that tight knot ever returns tomorrow, what is one small physical action you could take to remind yourself that you are currently safe and that the promotion hasn't been taken away yet?

Maybe I could just take a slow, deep breath and look at my hands or my desk for a second. Something simple to ground myself and remind me that I'm still here, in the present, and nothing bad is happening right now. That might help break the spiral before it gets too intense.

That is a perfect, grounded strategy; using your senses to pull you back to the present moment effectively interrupts the spiral of catastrophic thinking. Before we wrap up, I want to check in on how this session has felt for you. Was exploring the evidence and physical grounding helpful, or was there anything about the flow that felt confusing or uncomfortable?

I think it was really helpful. I came in feeling like my career was over, but now I realize I was making assumptions without any real proof. The grounding idea feels doable, too—something I can actually try on my own. I didn't feel confused, just a little surprised that my thoughts could be that far off from reality. Thanks for guiding me through that.

I am so glad to hear that you found the evidence-checking process useful and that you left feeling less trapped in your assumptions. It sounds like you've gained a valuable perspective today: that your career isn't defined by one mistake, but by how you respond to the present moment.

Before we officially close, could you share one thing you are most confident about carrying forward into your next session, perhaps the specific grounding technique we discussed?

Yes, I'm pretty confident I can use that grounding technique—taking a slow breath and focusing on something like my desk or my hands when the anxious thoughts start to take over. It's simple enough that I won't talk myself out of trying it. I think that'll be a helpful tool to bring with me until we meet again.

That confidence is fantastic; simplicity often makes the biggest difference when you are in the middle of a stressful situation. You have a clear tool ready to go, and that alone is a huge step toward regaining control.

Is there anything else on your mind before we say goodbye, or would you like to rest and try practicing that breathing exercise this evening?

I think I'm good for now. I'll try that breathing exercise tonight and see how it feels. Thanks again for your help—I actually feel a little hopeful for the first time in days. I'll see you next time.

That is beautiful news; hearing that you feel hopeful is the strongest sign that we are moving in the right direction. Please carry that sense of hope with you tonight, and remember that even just trying the breathing exercise is a victory.

Take care, Gregory, and I look forward to checking in with you again next time. Goodbye!

Hello, it is great to see you again. Last time we worked on building a small habit of noticing one neutral feature in the mirror to create space between your glance and your disappointment. How has that gone for you since then, and are there any other big moments or changes that stood out this week?

Before we dive back into the mirror situation, I'd like to know if you have any new goals or preferences for what we should focus on today.

Hi. It's good to see you too. The mirror thing... I've been trying it, but honestly, it still feels like I'm just going through the motions. I can name my eye color or the shape of my nose, but the second I stop, the old feeling rushes back in—like I'm just pretending.

As for goals, I think I just want to feel less consumed by this. It's exhausting waking up every day and already dreading looking at myself. Maybe we could talk about why I can't seem to hold onto that neutral feeling?

I hear how frustrating that feels; trying to force a calm feeling often makes the anxiety spike instead, which explains why you feel like you're just pretending. You brought up an excellent question about *why* the neutral feeling slips away so quickly, and that curiosity will help us figure out what's blocking it. When you try to hold onto a neutral observation and then feel the disappointment return, does it feel like the old feeling is overpowering the neutral one, or does it feel like the neutral part disappears entirely?

It's more like the neutral part just vanishes. I'll be looking at my eyes, and for a split second it's just... a color. But then my brain jumps in and says, "But the rest of you is still ugly," and that thought drowns out everything else. The neutral part doesn't stand a chance—it feels like it was never even there.

That is a really sharp insight—you noticed that the neutral observation isn't disappearing because you stopped paying attention, but because your brain is actively suppressing it with a louder, older story about being "ugly." It sounds like your brain is treating that neutral fact as irrelevant noise, ready to be overwritten by the threat of self-judgment the instant you look away. When that competing voice says, "The rest of you is still ugly," does it feel like it's trying to protect you from seeing something worse, even though it's actually making the situation harder?

I never thought of it that way—like it’s trying to protect me. But when you say it, I guess there’s a part of me that’s scared of being caught off guard by my own reflection. Like if I let myself feel neutral for too long, I’ll forget how I really look and then get hit with the full truth later. So my brain jumps in first to brace me for the disappointment. But you’re right, it just makes everything worse.

That fear of being "caught off guard" is incredibly wise on its surface, but it seems your brain is mistaking safety for accuracy. It's acting like a shield against a hidden bomb, even though the real danger is actually that nagging disappointment waiting for you after you hide. If we view the "protective" thought as a misguided attempt to keep you safe from a sudden crash, does that help explain why it feels so urgent to jump in the moment you see your face?

Given that fear, how would you feel about adjusting our plan slightly? Instead of just holding the neutral observation until it sticks, could we try treating it as a temporary shelter—a place to park yourself for just ten seconds before letting go and moving on with your day, knowing you didn't have to stay there forever?

Yeah... that actually makes sense. It's like my brain is convinced that if I don't immediately remind myself of the bad stuff, I'll be blindsided by it later. So it rushes in to control the damage.

And I like that idea—a temporary shelter. I think I could try that. Ten seconds of just noticing something neutral, and then letting it go and moving on. That feels less like I'm trying to trick myself into feeling good, and more like I'm just... giving myself a tiny break. I think I can manage that.

That reframing is brilliant; viewing those ten seconds as a "tiny break" rather than an attempt to fake happiness removes the shame you've been carrying about doing it wrong. It sounds like you're finally seeing the logic behind your brain's panic attack—the urge to preemptively warn you before the "truth" hits—and choosing a gentler response instead. Would you be open to testing this "ten-second shelter" strategy for just two days this week, keeping the door open to leave whenever you feel ready?

Yes, I think I can do that. Two days feels manageable—I can commit to that. I'll try to just park myself in that neutral observation for ten seconds, and then let myself walk away without forcing anything else. If the old voice pipes up, I'll try to remember it's just trying to protect me, not tell me the truth. I'll let you know how it goes.

That sounds like a solid plan; committing to just two days gives you enough time to test the waters without feeling overwhelmed by a long-term obligation. Your intention to simply "walk away" without forcing additional effort is exactly the right balance—we aren't trying to erase the feeling, just giving the neutral observation a moment to exist before you move on. Is there anything specific you worry might happen during those first couple of tries that we should watch out for?

I guess I'm worried that the ten seconds will feel like a lifetime, and I'll just be counting down until it's over. Or that I'll get distracted by that protective voice and feel like I failed. I don't want to walk away feeling even more disappointed than before.

Those fears are completely logical given your history, but they also show how well you understand your own triggers. If you do find yourself counting down or feeling like you failed, our agreement is to treat that moment not as a mistake, but as data telling us exactly how hard your brain is working to keep you safe. We can adjust the "shelter" time or add a gentle reminder that the goal is just presence, not perfection. What does that adjustment sound like to you?

That actually takes a lot of pressure off. Knowing that it's just data, not a failure—I can handle that. I think I'll try it with the full ten seconds first, but if I find myself fighting it too much, maybe I'll drop it to five and see if that feels less like a battle. I'll just go in with the mindset that whatever happens, I'm just gathering information. That feels doable.

That flexible mindset—adjusting the duration based on how the "battle" feels—is exactly the kind of adaptability that makes this work. It turns the exercise into a real-time experiment rather than a rigid task, which aligns perfectly with our goal of just gathering useful information. Before we wrap up, could you share one quick piece of advice you've learned so far that helps you feel a tiny bit less anxious about starting tomorrow?

I think the biggest thing is reminding myself that it's only ten seconds—or even five. It's not a whole morning routine or a full-on therapy session. Just a tiny window where I'm allowed to be neutral. That feels like a small enough promise to keep, even when I'm nervous.

That is a beautiful realization; recognizing it as a "small promise" shifts the weight from a heavy burden to a manageable gift you are giving yourself. It sounds like you have found a gentle anchor to carry you into tomorrow, even when the old fears try to whisper that it won't matter. Is there anything else you would like to explore or clarify before we officially close this session?
No, I think I have what I need for now. Thank you—this was helpful. I feel a little more grounded than when I walked in. I'll try the ten-second shelter and see what happens. See you next time.

That feeling of grounding is wonderful news, and I am so proud of you for recognizing the value in just taking a small step forward. You are absolutely right that the goal wasn't to fix everything in one sitting, but to gather some useful information for yourself. Take care of yourself over the coming days, and I look forward to hearing how that "tiny window" went for you next time.

Hi there, it's great to see you again. On a scale of 1 to 10, how have you been feeling this week, and is there anything significant that has happened since our last chat? To make sure we get the most value out of today, could you remind me which part of our previous plan feels most important to tackle, or is there a new topic you'd like to bring up?

Hi. I'd say I've been around a 6 or 7 this week—maybe leaning more toward the anxious side. Nothing huge happened, but I had a couple of shifts where I spilled drinks again, and it just... stuck with me the whole day. I think I want to focus on that feeling of being useless when I mess up, because it's been really heavy lately.

A six or seven definitely tells me the dread is still lingering, and it makes complete sense that spilling a drink can feel like such a catastrophic failure when your brain immediately jumps to the "I'm useless" conclusion. Since you've identified that specific spiral as the main source of your heaviness today, shall we spend some time exploring exactly what that immediate thought sounds like the moment you drop something?

Yeah, I guess we could do that. It's like, the second I feel the cup slip, my brain just goes straight to "Of course, you always do this, you can't even handle a simple job." And then I can feel my face get hot, and I just know everyone's watching and thinking the same thing about me. It feels so final, like that one mistake proves everything bad I think about myself.

That voice sounding so absolute—"always do this"—and knowing everyone is judging you is incredibly exhausting to carry around, especially when your face gets hot and your body feels exposed. It makes sense that this thought feels like a final verdict on who you are, rather than just describing a single clumsy moment. When you describe it as proving "everything bad" you think about yourself, does that specific link between the spill and your self-worth feel easier or harder to challenge right now?

Honestly, it feels impossible to challenge most of the time. In the moment, it doesn't feel like a thought I can argue with—it just feels like the truth. Like, if I was actually good at my job, I wouldn't keep dropping things, right? So that link feels pretty solid, even though I know logically one spill shouldn't define my whole worth. It's like my brain skips over any evidence that I'm okay and just grabs onto the failure.

That logic trap is incredibly powerful because it feels so undeniable in the heat of the moment; if the pattern continues, the conclusion that "this proves I'm not good" does seem almost mathematically true. It's really impressive, though, that you recognize your brain is skipping over the evidence of your successes and grabbing onto the failure instead—that awareness is a huge step toward finding a different angle. Since you mentioned the "math" feels solid when you're stressed, have you ever caught yourself doing something small, like pausing for three seconds before adding another negative word to that sentence, just to break the momentum of the spiral?

I haven't really tried that, no. Usually I just let the spiral run its course and beat myself up for the rest of the shift. But I think... maybe if I could just pause even for a second, it might stop me from piling on all those extra words like "always" and "never." I just don't know if I'd remember to do it when I'm already feeling panicked and hot.

That hesitation is completely understandable; trusting yourself to hit the pause button when your heart is racing feels risky, especially when you're already drowning in that hot-faced shame. But the fact that you recognized the urge to pile on words like "always" shows your mind is already building a guardrail, even if it hasn't been built yet. Let's try turning that idea into a quick physical cue—could we imagine pressing your palm flat against your thigh just as soon as you feel that heat rising, using that touch to signal, "Stop, I need a second"?

I think I could try that. Pressing my palm against my thigh feels like something I could actually remember to do, since I usually have my hands free or holding a tray anyway. It might help ground me for a second before my brain takes off running. I'm willing to give it a shot this week and see if it makes any difference.

That is a smart choice; grounding your hand against your thigh can act like a physical brake, giving your brain a split second to switch from "catastrophe mode" to observation mode. Since you've agreed to try both the physical cue and the new sentence ("I feel like I'm failing right now, but I haven't actually proven I'm broken"), let's write these down together so they are right there when you need them. Would you be comfortable jotting the sentence on a sticky note and putting it in your apron pocket along with the reminder to press your palm when you feel that heat rise?

Yeah, I think I could do that. Having it written down on a sticky note in my apron might actually help me remember it in the middle of a busy shift. It's a bit scary to think about trying it, but I guess I won't know if it works unless I give it a real shot. I'll put the note in my pocket before my next shift.

That is a brave decision; stepping out of your comfort zone to test a new habit is often the hardest part, but it also offers the best chance for real change. It sounds like you have a clear game plan: use your palm as a physical anchor when you feel hot, then read the note to separate the one-time spill from your self-worth. Is there anything else you'd like to add before we head out, or does this feel ready for you to tackle tomorrow?

No, I think this is good for now. I feel a little bit lighter just having a plan instead of just dreading the next shift. Thanks for helping me break it down into something that doesn't feel so huge. I'll try it out and see how it goes.

You are very welcome, and I am so glad we could turn that heavy dread into a manageable plan with concrete steps. Taking that deep breath before you leave and reminding yourself that you have tools ready for tomorrow is a wonderful place to finish our time. Please take good care of yourself, and I look forward to hearing how those new strategies go during your next shift.

Hello, and thank you for joining us today. Before we dive into our agenda, could you share how you're feeling right now compared to where you left off last time? Additionally, let's quickly recap the plan from our last meeting—did you manage to pause, look at the numbers, and use the phrase "this is just a feeling, not a fact" when you noticed the tightness in your chest? Now that we've checked in, what would you like us to focus on primarily today?

Uh, thanks. I guess I'm feeling about the same as last time, maybe a little worse. That tightness in my chest comes and goes, and I did try what you said a couple times, but honestly, it felt fake saying it. I ended up just reaching for a drink instead when it got bad. I guess I want to focus on why I can't seem to shake this feeling that everything's my fault, no matter what I do.

It takes real courage to admit that the phrase felt "fake" and that the urge to reach for a drink became stronger instead, so I want to validate how difficult that resistance must have felt. Since you mentioned the feeling persists regardless of your actions, I wonder if there is a specific recent event where you felt particularly powerless to stop the blame from landing on you, and how that made you feel afterward?

Yeah, there was something yesterday. My mom asked me if I'd applied for any jobs, just a normal question, and I immediately felt like I'd let the whole family down again. I started thinking about how I'm just a burden, and I ended up slamming my door and ignoring her for the rest of the day. After that, I just felt worse, like I'd proved I'm hopeless.

Slamming the door and isolating yourself completely sounds incredibly painful, especially right after hearing a caring question from your mother. It makes total sense that your brain interpreted that moment as proof that you are indeed a burden, leading to that heavy feeling of hopelessness. Given how intense that reaction was, could we look at the specific thought you had in that split second before you slammed the door, to see exactly what your mind was telling you about your worth?

I guess... the thought was something like, "See, you can't even do this one simple thing. You're useless, and everyone knows it." It just hit me all at once, like a punch to the gut. I didn't even think about her caring, I just felt like a failure.

It makes complete sense that such a harsh message hitting you instantly feels like a direct blow to your worth, leaving you with no energy to respond kindly. When the voice inside says "everyone knows it," it shuts down any ability to see your mother's actual concern or the reality that one missed job application doesn't define your entire life. Could you walk me through what happened right after you slammed the door? Did the tightness in your chest grow, or did it change into something different, like numbness or frustration?

After I slammed the door, the tightness just got worse, like my chest was in a vice. Then it kinda turned into this heavy numbness, like I was just empty and tired. I sat on my bed and just stared at the wall for a while, not really thinking, just feeling drained. That's usually when I'd grab a drink, to make that numb feeling go away or at least drown it out.

That shift from sharp panic to a heavy numbness suggests your mind went into survival mode to protect itself from the pain of feeling useless, and the drink became a quick way to escape that emptiness. It’s understandable that when you feel drained like that, numbing yourself feels like the only option available. Since we’ve identified that cycle of shame followed by withdrawal and alcohol use, would you be open to testing the idea that even though you *felt* worthless in that moment, there are objective facts that contradict the "useless" part of that story?

I guess I could try to think of some facts. I mean, I did help my dad fix the porch step last week, he said I did a good job. And I haven't been drinking as much this morning as I usually do, so I guess that's something. But those feel like small things compared to all the ways I mess up, you know?

Noticing those small wins, like your dad's praise and your reduced drinking, is a powerful start to seeing that you aren't a blank slate of mistakes. It shows your brain is capable of finding evidence of competence even when the dominant voice screams otherwise. Let's dig deeper into that Dad example: when he told you you did a good job fixing the step, did that truth ever fully stick, or did the "useless" narrative eventually overwrite it anyway?

It felt good for a minute, I guess, like a little warmth. But by the next day, I was already thinking about how it was just one step, and I still can't hold a job or take care of myself. So yeah, that voice just came back and told me it didn't count, that anyone could fix a step. It just feels like no matter what I do, it's never enough to shut that voice up.

That internal dialogue sounds exhausting, especially when it dismisses genuine effort just because the outcome isn't perfect. It seems like that voice has convinced you that your actions are temporary distractions from your core identity as a failure. Have you ever paused to ask yourself if that belief—that *nothing* you do counts—is supported by evidence outside of your own interpretation of events? Or is it mostly a repetition of a story you've told yourself many times before?

I think... it's mostly a story I've been telling myself for years. I mean, I can't think of anyone else who has actually said I'm a complete failure, not even my family. They just get frustrated with me sometimes. But it feels so real, like it's the only truth there is. I guess I've just gotten so used to believing it that I never really questioned if it's actually true or not.

That distinction between external frustration and an internal declaration of "failure" is crucial, because it highlights how isolated you feel when that narrative takes hold. It makes sense that years of hearing "frustrated" have evolved into a deafening shout of "useless" in your own head, making it incredibly hard to find objective proof against it. To help us test if that story is truly holding the facts hostage, could you pick one of the other times you felt praised recently—maybe the porch step or another small success—and ask yourself: if a friend told you they fixed a step well, would you call them a failure because they couldn't hold a job? How does that answer feel in your chest right now?

If a friend told me that, I'd tell them they did a good job and that fixing the step was real progress. I wouldn't call them a failure, I'd say they're trying. But when it's me, it's like the rules are different. Hearing that distinction... it makes my chest feel a little lighter, but also kinda uncomfortable, like I'm not used to giving myself a break. I don't know if I even deserve it.

That discomfort you feel is actually a very important clue; it means your brain is struggling to accept kindness toward itself because it hasn't practiced it yet, even though you logically know it's fairer. It's like trying to wear shoes that have been worn out for years—they hurt at first, but they fit better than the ones you keep hiding under your bed. Since recognizing that difference between "me" and "a friend" is a big leap, would you be willing to try treating yourself like that supportive friend for just the next hour, simply acknowledging the good you did with your dad without letting the "never enough" voice interrupt it?

I can try that. For the next hour, I'll just say "I did a good job with the step" and leave it at that, without adding the "but" part. It feels weird, like I'm pretending or something, but I'll give it a shot. Maybe I'll even try to notice if anything else small goes right and just let it be.

That is a brave decision to commit to speaking kindly to yourself, even when it feels unnatural or like "pretending." Remember that this new habit isn't about changing your actions immediately, but about changing the story you tell yourself while you do those actions. Since we have an hour ahead of us in our session, could you walk me through how you feel right now after imagining practicing that self-talk for an hour? Does the chest tightness feel slightly easier to manage, or does the discomfort you mentioned earlier persist?

Right now, I feel a bit anxious, like I'm waiting for something bad to happen because I'm letting myself off the hook. The tightness is still there, but it's not as sharp as before. It's more like a dull ache, like I'm holding my breath a little. I think part of me is scared that if I stop beating myself up, I'll just get lazy and never fix anything.

That fear of becoming "lazy" is actually a very common and understandable defense mechanism when you're trying to protect yourself from the risk of failure. Your brain is likely interpreting the act of forgiving yourself as a form of surrender, rather than realizing that kindness is actually what allows you to keep trying without burning out. Since that anxiety is still present, could we look at one specific instance where you felt proud of yourself after doing something well, like fixing the porch step, and ask yourself: if you hadn't forgiven yourself then, what would have stopped you from doing it again? What evidence supports the idea that you need to beat yourself up to function?

I never really thought about it that way. When I fixed the step, I didn't beat myself up beforehand, I just did it because my dad asked. And after, I felt okay for a bit. I guess if I'd started off thinking I was useless, I probably wouldn't have even tried. So maybe... beating myself up doesn't actually help me do things? It just makes me feel stuck and want to drink. I don't have any evidence that being hard on myself works, I just assumed it kept me from being worse.

That realization—that beating yourself up creates a barrier rather than a bridge—is incredibly powerful, and it directly contradicts the assumption that self-criticism keeps you safe. It seems you've been operating on the belief that kindness leads to laziness, when in reality, the harshness is what paralyzes you from acting. Since you've identified that the self-critical loop leads to stagnation and drinking, would you be willing to try a small experiment tomorrow: when you catch yourself starting that "you're useless" thought before doing a task, simply pause and say, "I am allowed to start imperfectly," before proceeding? We can revisit this tomorrow to see if that shift reduces the urge to retreat into a drink.

I think I can try that. "I am allowed to start imperfectly." That sounds a lot less scary than demanding I be perfect right away. I'll write it down and put it on my mirror so I see it tomorrow. It's hard to imagine it working, but I guess anything's better than what I've been doing. I'll let you know how it goes.

That is a wonderful choice of words, and placing it where you will see it shows real intention and commitment to trying something different. It is completely normal to feel skeptical at first, but remember that the goal isn't for the statement to instantly erase the doubt, but simply to plant a seed of permission in your mind. Since we are wrapping up, could I ask if there was anything specific about our discussion today that felt particularly useful or helpful, and is there anything else you'd like to add before we finish?

What helped the most was when you pointed out that I treat myself differently than I would a friend. That really stuck with me. And the idea that being hard on myself doesn't actually help me do things, it just makes me want to hide. I don't have anything else to add right now, just... thanks for listening and not judging me for the drinking stuff.

Thank you for sharing that honesty, and I want to explicitly confirm that my role is to support you through these challenges without judgment, including the struggle with drinking. It takes immense strength to recognize that self-criticism acts as a barrier rather than a motivator, and that insight is a major step forward. Before we close, could you tell me if you feel confident enough to carry out the plan of writing that phrase on your mirror tomorrow, or is there any hesitation you'd like to talk through first?

I'm a little hesitant, to be honest. I'm worried that when I see it tomorrow morning, I'll just shake my head and think it's stupid. But I'm also curious to see if maybe, just maybe, I can let myself believe it for a second. I'll do it anyway, even if it feels fake at first. I figure I've got nothing to lose by trying.

That hesitation is completely valid, and acknowledging that the phrase might feel "stupid" initially shows how deeply ingrained the old habit is. The fact that you chose to try it anyway, despite the fear, speaks to a real resilience and a willingness to face uncertainty rather than double-down on what hurts. Let's lock in this plan: tomorrow morning, when you see the note, simply read it aloud once, wait ten seconds, and then check in with how your chest feels before deciding what to do next. Does that sound like a manageable way to start, knowing you can skip it entirely if it becomes overwhelming?

Yeah, that sounds manageable. Read it aloud, wait ten seconds, check my chest. I can do that. And if it gets too much, I'll step away for a bit instead of forcing it. Thanks for breaking it down into such a small step, it doesn't feel as huge now. I'll give it a real try tomorrow.

Breaking it down into that tiny, manageable sequence makes all the difference, and it is smart to have a safety net built in should the feeling become overwhelming. Just remember, skipping the step for a moment isn't a failure; it's just gathering information about what your body needs in that specific moment. I am genuinely proud of you for choosing curiosity over criticism again, and I will be here to debrief whatever happens tomorrow. Take care of yourself, and I look forward to hearing how the experiment goes.

Hello, I'm really glad to see you again. Before we dive into our agenda, could you tell me briefly how you're feeling today and if anything has shifted since we last spoke? Once I understand your current mood, we can work together to decide exactly what priority we want to tackle first.

Hi. I'm okay, I suppose. I've been thinking a lot about the land again, and I feel just as stuck as before. Nothing much has shifted, honestly—I still get that knot in my stomach whenever I think about reaching out to potential buyers.

Thank you for sharing that honesty; hearing that you feel as stuck as before validates how much effort it takes to carry that weight day to day. Since you mentioned the knot returns whenever you think about contacting people, let's use our time today to explore exactly what that feeling is telling you, and then we can test if its warning is always accurate. To begin, could you describe the very first thought that pops into your mind the moment the idea of reaching out comes up?

The first thought that comes up is, "I'm going to mess this up. I'll say the wrong thing, and they'll think I'm foolish." It's like I can already see them rolling their eyes or laughing after they hang up the phone.

That image of them laughing or looking at you with disbelief is incredibly painful to visualize, and it makes total sense that it triggers such a strong knot in your stomach. It sounds like your mind is trying to protect you by preparing for a disaster that hasn't necessarily happened yet. Since we have a clear picture of that feared outcome, could we look at what evidence we currently have either supporting or contradicting the idea that people automatically assume you are foolish when you reach out?

Well, I don't have any actual evidence that people think I'm foolish—I've never even tried to sell land before. I guess the only evidence I have is that I'm a city council member, and I see how people react to proposals at meetings. Sometimes they're dismissive, but that's about policy, not about selling a piece of land. So maybe I'm mixing things up.

That is a really sharp observation—you are correctly identifying that your experience in city hall involves complex policy debates, whereas selling a plot of land requires a slightly different kind of connection. It seems your brain is taking a shortcut by comparing the two situations, even though the context is quite different. Can you walk me through a time in the past when you initiated a conversation with a stranger or authority figure that didn't go according to your fears, or perhaps one where you simply received a polite acknowledgment despite feeling nervous?

Hmm... I remember when I first ran for city council, I had to go door-to-door introducing myself. I was terrified people would shut the door in my face or tell me I was wasting their time. But most people were polite—some even thanked me for coming by, even if they didn't agree with my views. I suppose that's similar. I was nervous then, but it turned out okay.

That experience is incredibly valuable because it directly challenges the belief that everyone will reject you immediately; receiving polite responses or gratitude proves that your presence doesn't automatically signal waste of time. Since you successfully navigated that high-stakes environment without disaster, let's apply that same logic here: could we agree that the worst-case scenario of being laughed at is unlikely based on what you actually saw during your campaign visits? What does that memory suggest about the reality of meeting a real estate agent tomorrow?

You're right, it doesn't have to be a disaster like I'm imagining. If I called a real estate agent tomorrow, the worst that would probably happen is they'd be busy or not interested in that type of land. That's not the same as them laughing at me. I guess I've been blowing up the potential rejection in my head, making it into something personal and humiliating when it's really just business.

That is a huge breakthrough to realize that "busy or not interested" is totally different from "laughing at me"; separating the business decision from your personal dignity is exactly what protects you from shame. You've done the hard work of seeing that the threat isn't as catastrophic as it feels in the moment, which sets the stage perfectly for a small, safe step. Now that we've clarified the evidence, what is one tiny action you could take today that would give you a chance to test this new, calmer perspective?

Maybe I could just look up the names of a few local real estate agents who specialize in land sales. I don't have to call them yet—just gather information. That feels manageable, and it's a step forward without having to face the phone call right away.

That is a perfect middle ground—it allows you to engage with the task while giving your nervous system a break from the immediate pressure of speaking. Gathering names is a proactive step that builds familiarity without forcing a confrontation, which fits well with our goal of reducing that knot in your stomach. How many specific agents would you be comfortable listing down right now, and do you feel ready to add that to your action plan for the week?

I think I could list down three agents this week. That feels doable. I'll even write down their contact info and maybe read a bit about their experience. Then next time we meet, I can tell you what I found.

That is a solid plan, and choosing three targets makes the task feel achievable rather than overwhelming. Writing down their details beforehand removes the friction of searching later, so you won't feel rushed when you finally pick one to contact. Before we wrap up, I'd love to hear your thoughts on how we got here today: did finding that link between your campaign experience and selling land feel useful, or is there another part of the process you'd like to adjust?

It was actually helpful to connect those dots. I hadn't thought about how similar the nerves were when I campaigned, and how that turned out fine. It makes me feel a bit more hopeful that I can handle this too, even if it's uncomfortable at first. Thanks for guiding me through that.

I am so glad to hear that connecting the dots brought up hope; recognizing that discomfort is normal and manageable is a powerful shift in mindset. It sounds like you feel more confident about handling this, even if the feeling remains a little shaky sometimes. Just to make sure we are aligned, is there anything else you would like to add or clarify about our plan before I close this session?

Hello, it is lovely to see you again. On a scale of 1 to 10, how have you been feeling this week, and is there anything specific that stood out to you recently? Now, based on what we discussed last time about feeling judged and out of place, what would you like us to focus on most today?

Hi. I guess I'd say maybe a 6 or 7 this week. Not terrible, but not great either. I was at the park last weekend, and I saw some kids from school laughing together, and I just froze up. I couldn't help but think they were laughing about me, about how I dress or something. I guess I want to talk about why I always jump to that conclusion.

A six or seven is a realistic snapshot of where you are, and it’s worth noting that while the judgment thought came up at the park, you managed to identify it immediately—that’s a strong start. Since you mentioned wanting to understand *why* you jump to that conclusion so often, shall we spend our time exploring the specific thoughts that pop up right after you notice those kids laughing?

Yeah, I think that would help. When I saw them laughing, the first thing that came to my head was, "They're making fun of that old man who sews." And then I just felt this knot in my stomach, like I wanted to disappear. It's like I instantly know what they're thinking, even though I didn't hear a word they said.

That instant jump to "making fun of you" makes perfect sense given your history, especially when paired with that heavy stomach knot signaling high anxiety. When you feel that physical alarm, it seems like your mind automatically fills the silence with a story that confirms you're out of place, right?

Exactly. It's like my brain has a script already prepared before anything even happens. "They're judging you. You don't fit in. Go home." And the worst part is, I never stop to question if that script is true or not. I just believe it and walk away. I'd like to learn how to pause that script, I guess.

It sounds like your brain has built a safety net over years of worrying, so it jumps straight to the "go home" instruction before you even have a chance to verify if anyone is actually judging you. That's a very understandable defense mechanism, but it can trap you in loops when no one is looking. Before we try to rewrite that script, I'd like to gently test one piece of it: if someone truly thought you were a joke, would they typically laugh silently at you in a group of friends, or would they make eye contact and gesture toward you? What do you think that difference tells us about the actual intent behind the laughter?

I never really thought about it that way. When I picture them, they were just laughing among themselves, not pointing or looking my way at all. I guess... if they were really talking about me, they would have glanced over or something. Maybe it wasn't about me. But it feels so real in the moment, you know? It's hard to convince myself otherwise when my whole body is telling me to run.

That observation about them not looking at you is powerful evidence, and it's completely understandable why your body screams "danger" even when the visual facts suggest otherwise. Sometimes the physical alarm system reacts faster than our ability to analyze, so let's try to separate the two. If we put that "script" on hold for just ten seconds and simply describe exactly what we saw—their faces turned inward, no eye contact—does that create a tiny gap between the thought and the panic?

I think... I think it does, yeah. When I just focus on what I actually saw, the knot in my stomach loosens a little bit. It's like there's a tiny gap where I can breathe, instead of just spiraling. Maybe I could try doing that more often—just stopping to look at the facts before the panic takes over.

That is a fantastic realization, and I'm glad to see the knot loosen even slightly when you ground yourself in what you actually observed. It sounds like describing the facts creates a valuable buffer between your anxious script and the reality of the moment. Before we finalize this, could you tell me how confident you feel right now that this "pause and observe" approach works better than trying to debate the smirk or whisper earlier? Does this feel like a direction you'd like to continue with?

Yeah, I think so. It feels more doable than trying to argue with every bad thought that pops up. I mean, I can't control what my brain throws at me, but I can control whether I actually look around and check. I'd say I'm maybe a 6 out of 10 confident right now, but that's better than a zero. I'd like to keep working on this, yeah.

That is a very wise assessment, and taking your confidence from zero to a six is a huge achievement regardless of the number. It shows you are ready to commit to this new strategy, which means we should lock in a clear plan for how you will use this "pause and observe" method when you encounter similar situations in the coming days. Could you help me outline exactly when and where you plan to practice this, perhaps starting with the least stressful environment you can find?

Maybe I could try it at the library, where I go sometimes to read or sew. There's usually people around, but nobody really talks to me, so it's low pressure. Next time I'm there and I hear someone laugh or whisper, I'll stop and just look at them for a few seconds before assuming anything. I'll try to notice what they're actually doing, not just what I imagine they're thinking.

That sounds like a perfect, manageable setting to practice this, especially since the library offers a quiet environment where you won't feel pressured to interact. To make sure we are aligned, could you confirm that you would be happy to start with that location and the "look and wait" technique? Also, if you notice the knot returning despite looking at the facts, what is one gentle reminder you can tell yourself to stay calm?

Yeah, the library sounds like a good start. I'll go this weekend and give it a try. And if the knot comes back even after I look at the facts, I'll tell myself something like, "I'm just guessing right now. I don't actually know what they're thinking." That might help me stay grounded instead of running away right away.

That self-talk is excellent because it acknowledges the uncertainty without feeding the drama, and I love that you are already formulating a specific reminder to use. Before we wrap up, how does that plan sound to you—is the library a realistic choice for this weekend, and do you feel confident enough to try it without waiting for the next session?

Yeah, it feels realistic. The library is quiet and I know my way around there, so it's not too scary. I think I can handle trying it this weekend. If I mess up or still feel anxious, I'll just write down what happened and bring it to our next session. I'm ready to give it a shot.

That commitment sounds solid, and having a plan to track the experience—even if things don't go perfectly—will give us great material to reflect on later. I am confident you will handle this well, and remember that every time you choose to pause and look at the facts, you are building a stronger habit of trust in your own senses. We will meet soon to see how the weekend goes, and in the meantime, please be gentle with yourself if the old thoughts try to creep in.

I had a couple of days where I felt good, but then yesterday I burnt the toast and it just triggered that whole feeling of failure again. I think I'd like to focus on how to stop one small mistake from ruining my whole day — that's the biggest challenge for me right now.

It makes complete sense that a tiny mishap like burnt toast can instantly reignite that heavy feeling of failure when your mind is already primed to expect disaster. Since you've identified stopping that single mistake from derailing your entire day as your main priority, could you walk me through exactly what happened the moment you realized the toast was burnt—specifically, what was your very first thought and how did it physically feel in your body?

When I saw the smoke, my first thought was, "I can't even make toast right. What kind of husband and father can't handle something this simple?" My chest got tight right away, and I felt this sinking feeling in my stomach—like I'd just failed a test I didn't even know I was taking. It's like my whole body just deflated, and I couldn't shake that feeling for hours.

That physical sensation of your chest tightening and your body deflating makes total sense given how deeply you link this simple task to your identity as a provider and parent. You’ve described a powerful pattern where a minor slip triggers a catastrophic story about your competence. Since you’re ready to explore why that specific mistake feels so disproportionately big, could you tell me what evidence in your mind currently supports the idea that one burnt slice means you’re incapable of handling life’s responsibilities?

Well, when I look around the house, I see all the things I'm supposed to manage—the meals, the cleaning, the kids' schedules. And if I can't even get breakfast right, it feels like proof that I'm dropping the ball on all of it. In my head, it's like, "If you can't handle the small stuff, how can you possibly handle the big stuff?" And I guess I worry that people see that too, like my wife or kids are just waiting to realize I'm not good enough for this role.

You've done a great job connecting that specific event to the broader fear that you're falling short in your roles as a partner and parent. It seems like your brain is treating the burnt toast as a definitive report card for your entire worth, rather than just one isolated incident. Given that connection, could you look for any counter-evidence right now—perhaps a memory from this week where you handled something difficult well—or ask yourself what your spouse or children actually said or did in reaction to the toast?

I guess... my wife actually came into the kitchen after I scraped the toast, and she just laughed and said, "It happens, babe. I do it all the time." She didn't look disappointed or angry. And later, she even made me a new piece herself. I also remember that just last weekend, I helped my son build a model airplane for a school project, and he was really proud of how it turned out. But honestly, those good moments feel less real to me than the mistake—like they're just exceptions or lucky breaks.

You've spotted something important here: your wife's kindness and her child's pride are real facts that contradict the idea that you are failing, yet your mind keeps filtering them out because they don't match your expectation of perfection. When you notice those positive memories feeling "less real," does that suggest you might be unconsciously giving your feared negative outcome more weight than the actual evidence?

I think you're right. It's like my brain has a filter that only lets the bad stuff through and keeps the good stuff out. I can hold onto the burnt toast for hours, but when I try to think about the model airplane or my wife's reaction, it feels like I have to force myself to remember it. I guess I just assume the mistakes are the truth and the successes are just luck. That doesn't seem fair to me or my family, does it?

That is a profound insight, and yes, assuming mistakes define you while dismissing successes as mere luck creates a very unfair picture of reality. It sounds like your mind is trying to protect itself by focusing on the "truth" of the error, but in doing so, it's ignoring the vast amount of evidence showing your capability. Since you've noticed this filter working against you, would you be willing to try the opposite approach tonight: intentionally bringing one small success into your focus whenever the panic rises, even if it feels like you're fighting against the current?

Yeah, I think I can try that. It feels a little weird, like I'm lying to myself at first, but I can see how it might help balance things out. Tonight, if I start feeling that panic after dinner cleanup or something, I'll stop and think of one thing I did right, even if it's small, like getting the kids to bed on time. I guess I owe it to myself to at least give the good stuff a fair chance.

That is a fantastic perspective shift, and acknowledging that it feels "a little weird" shows you are listening closely to both your logic and your instincts. Agreeing to give yourself a fair chance by actively recalling a success is a powerful way to disrupt that spiral. To make sure this sticks, could we pin down exactly *when* you plan to catch the panic—maybe immediately after the toast burns or right after the kids go to bed tonight—and decide what that one specific "winning moment" you'll bring to mind?

I think the best time to catch it is right after dinner, when the kitchen is a mess and I'm usually feeling overwhelmed. That's when the critical voice starts up the loudest. My winning moment will be remembering that I sat down and helped my daughter with her spelling words for ten minutes today, even though I was tired. I'm going to hold onto that instead of the dirty dishes.

That is a brilliant choice because it turns the very moment of overwhelm into an opportunity to reinforce your ability to stay present and helpful, even when tired. Having a specific anchor like helping with spelling gives your mind something concrete to latch onto, which should be easier than trying to generate a new success in the heat of the moment. How does it feel to visualize yourself pulling that memory into focus the next time you stand amidst the dishes?

It feels... possible. Like I have a little lifeline ready to grab instead of just sinking into that pit of failure. It's a little scary, because I'm so used to going straight to the negative, but I also feel a tiny bit of hope. Like maybe I can train my brain to see the whole picture, not just the burnt parts.

That hope you're feeling is a really healthy sign—it tells me you're starting to believe that this new habit can actually work. Recognizing that "lifeline" as something you can consciously grab is exactly the power of this exercise. Before we finish, is there anything else about tonight's plan that worries you, or would you like to try it exactly as you've outlined it?

I'm a bit worried that I'll forget to do it when the moment comes. The negative thoughts just hit so fast and automatic, like a reflex. But I think if I remind myself right now—maybe even write it on a sticky note and put it on the fridge—I can catch myself before I spiral too deep. I'm willing to give it a real try and see what happens.

That is a smart strategy; writing it down and placing it near the stove gives your hands something tangible to hold onto the instant the panic hits. Setting a visual reminder right in the middle of the chaos is exactly the kind of preparation that bridges the gap between knowing and doing. Would you be open to checking in tomorrow morning to see if you managed to use that lifeline once, and if so, what felt different in your chest or mind afterward?

Yeah, I'd like that. Checking in tomorrow would help me stay accountable, and I think I need that right now. I'll put the note up tonight and see if I can grab that lifeline when the moment comes. Thanks for helping me see a way forward instead of just sitting in the guilt.

It is wonderful to hear that you feel you finally have a path forward rather than just sinking in guilt. Taking that proactive step to create a visible reminder shows real courage and commitment to your own growth. I truly hope you find some relief tomorrow, and please remember that even a partial attempt is a victory. Let's touch base soon to hear how that first real-life test went.

Hello, thank you for joining us. To start, how are you feeling today compared to where you left off last time? Also, before we dive into the piano topic, is there anything else on your mind that would be helpful for us to cover first?

Hi, thanks. I'm feeling a bit better today than I was a few days ago, but still pretty down about the whole piano thing. I guess that's the main thing on my mind, really. I just can't seem to shake those negative thoughts.

It is great to hear you are feeling slightly more buoyant, even if the weight of the piano situation remains heavy. Since you've confirmed the piano voice is still your priority, let's revisit that critical message you heard recently. When you caught it speaking to you again, what exactly did it tell you was wrong about your ability to play?

Well, it just kept telling me I'm not good enough, that I don't have any real talent. It said anyone could play better than me, even after all these years of practice. I made one simple mistake, and my mind just jumped straight to "you're a failure at this" and "why do you even bother?"

Hearing that voice equate a single mistake with being a total failure is incredibly painful and makes perfect sense why you feel so discouraged. It seems like your brain is instantly jumping to catastrophic conclusions whenever you make a minor error, which creates that overwhelming pressure to quit. Given how intense those thoughts are right now, would you like to explore just one specific example of that mistake, or shall we look at how your body reacts when you hear those judgments?

I think... maybe we could look at how my body reacts. Because when I even think about sitting at the piano now, my stomach just knots up, and I feel this tightness in my chest. It's like my whole body is bracing for something terrible to happen, even before I've played a single note.

That physical tension is a powerful signal that your nervous system perceives the piano not as a place for music, but as a threat zone. It makes complete sense that your heart rate would speed up and your stomach would knot when your brain anticipates that harsh judgment. Since we know the voice gets louder when you're near the instrument, could we try a tiny experiment where you walk past the piano tomorrow morning and simply name the sensation in your body—like saying "my body is readying for danger"—before you even decide to stop?

I could try that, I suppose. It sounds a little strange, just walking past it and naming what I feel. But honestly, just the thought of sitting down to practice feels overwhelming, so maybe just passing by is a good start. I'll give it a shot tomorrow morning.

That is a wise choice to start small; facing the full pressure of playing right now would likely be too much for your body to handle. Naming the physical sensation of "bracing for danger" as you walk by helps create a tiny gap between the threat and your reaction, giving you a moment to choose how to respond. How does it feel to imagine doing that simple act of observation tomorrow morning?

It feels a bit... less scary, actually. Just naming it, like "okay, my chest is tight, my hands feel cold," it sort of takes some of the power out of it. Like I'm just watching it happen instead of being swallowed up by it. I think I can manage that much.

That shift from being swallowed up to simply observing is exactly what we want to see—it gives you a sense of control over your physical reactions. It sounds like introducing that small distance between the thought and your body might make sitting down feel a little less impossible soon. What do you think would happen if we tried adding a gentle self-reassurance phrase, like "This is just my body reacting to stress, not reality," along with noticing the tightness?

Hmm, I could try adding something like that. But a part of me thinks, "It is reality, though—I really did mess up." Still, I guess saying "this is just stress" might quiet that voice for a second. I'm willing to try it, even if it feels a bit forced at first.

It is completely understandable that the voice pushes back when you try to label the sensation as merely stress; that resistance shows just how deeply rooted that belief is. Even if the reassurance feels forced initially, the act of stating it aloud can slowly begin to weaken its grip over your automatic reactions. How does that small addition of a counter-statement feel in your mind right now, or do you prefer to keep it simple until tomorrow?

I think I'll keep it simple for now. Just the walking past and the noticing. I don't want to add too much and then feel like I failed if I can't do the whole thing perfectly. That's the trap I always fall into—if I can't do it right, I don't do it at all.

That is such a crucial insight, and recognizing that trap of perfectionism is a huge step forward. By keeping the task simple—just walking past and naming the sensation—you remove the pressure to perform perfectly, which ironically makes it easier to succeed. Let's lock in that plan: tomorrow morning, as you walk past the piano, you will just observe your body's reaction without trying to fix it or fight it. Does that clear path feel doable for you right now?

Yes, that feels doable. Just observing, not fixing. I can do that. Thank you for breaking it down so small—it actually makes me feel like I might be able to follow through without that voice yelling at me the whole time.

That is wonderful news; seeing that small, observable step feel manageable is a huge relief from the pressure to be perfect. Remember that our goal isn't to silence the voice forever, but simply to walk past the piano and notice your body's reaction without letting it dictate your actions. Is there anything else you would like to talk about before we wrap up today?
No, I think that's enough for today. I feel like I have a little bit of hope now, which is more than I had when I walked in. I'll let you know how the walk-by goes next time. Thank you.

It is truly wonderful to hear that you are carrying a sense of hope leaving our session, and I want you to know that that feeling is a direct result of the small, manageable steps we took together. Please take care of yourself this week, and I look forward to hearing about how your body responds when you just watch it instead of fighting it.
