Hello again, I'm so glad to see you. How are you feeling physically and emotionally compared to where we started today? Since we talked about feeling heavy and tired recently, I'd like to check in on that energy level. To make sure we spend our time wisely, could you tell me what specific worries or goals brought you here, and is there anything new you'd like to prioritize for us to explore?

Hi. Thanks for asking. Physically, I'm still pretty drained—like there's a weight that just doesn't lift. Emotionally, I guess I feel the same as always, kind of hollow. I came here because I'm tired of feeling like I don't belong anywhere, like I'm just... passing through people's lives without really mattering. That's what I'd like to work on, I think.

It sounds incredibly exhausting to carry that sense of drifting around and wondering if anyone notices you, especially when your body is already so drained. I hear you saying that you want to explore the deep-seated feeling that you aren't belonging anywhere, and that seems like a heavy theme to unpack today. Before we dive straight into that, does focusing on that specific belief about "passing through" feel like the best place to start right now?

Yeah, I think that's the core of it, honestly. It's like no matter where I go or what I do, I'm always on the outside looking in. People are friendly enough, but there's this invisible wall. I guess starting there makes sense—it's the thing that keeps me up at night.

That image of an invisible wall standing between you and everyone else is really vivid, and it makes complete sense why you wake up worrying about it. It sounds like your brain is constantly scanning for evidence that proves you don't belong, filtering everything through that lens until it seems undeniable. When you bring up that wall, does it ever feel like you're trying to push past it, or does it mostly feel like you're just waiting to see if it will suddenly disappear?

Mostly I'm just waiting, I think. Pushing feels pointless—like, why would the wall move for me? It's been there my whole life, ever since I lost my parents. It's almost like I'm destined to be on the outside, and trying to push through just ends up with me getting tired and disappointed. So I wait, but nothing changes.

Hearing you link that feeling directly to your parents' passing makes so much sense; it sounds like your mind created a permanent narrative based on that early loss, interpreting every new connection as just another attempt to cross a border you can't pass. It's heartbreaking that you feel so powerless against this story, convinced that pushing is futile because the wall is part of who you became. Before we test that idea further, how does it feel in your body right now when you think about walking toward that wall versus staying safely on your side?

When I think about walking toward it, my chest gets tight, and my stomach knots up—like I'm bracing for impact. Staying on my side feels heavier, though, like a dull ache that just sits there. It's familiar, but it's not comfortable. I guess I'm used to the ache, and the tightness scares me more.

That distinction between the acute fear of the tightness and the chronic discomfort of the ache is really important; it shows your nervous system knows the difference between a threat and a habit, yet it treats the habit like a danger zone. You mentioned earlier that pushing felt pointless because it led to disappointment, but that tight chest suggests your body is preparing for a battle it hasn't fought in years. Could we look together at what might happen if you took one tiny step toward that wall—not to break it down, but just to see if the ground beneath you is actually solid?

I suppose... I could try that. One small step doesn't sound as terrifying as trying to tear it down. But what if I take that step and find out the ground isn't solid at all? What if I just fall through? That's the part that stops me cold every time.

That fear of falling through is completely understandable, especially when you've spent so many years believing the floor doesn't exist under you. It makes total sense that your mind would create that worst-case scenario to keep you safe from the possibility of falling. Let's look at the evidence together: when you've taken small steps in the past, like talking to a cashier or knocking on a door, what happened to the ground beneath you instead of falling through?

Well... I guess I didn't fall through. Those small moments, like chatting with a cashier or saying hello to a neighbor, they passed without anything terrible happening. The ground held, I suppose. I just never let myself see that as proof of anything—I always figured they were just being polite, that it didn't really mean anything about belonging.

It is incredibly smart of you to catch that logic trap; you correctly identified that politeness isn't the same as acceptance, yet you dismissed the fact that the ground *didn't* fall away as just noise. This is a crucial breakthrough because it separates the *quality* of the interaction from the *reality* of the outcome—you proved the ground exists, even if it didn't feel like a hug. Does that distinction—that the lack of a dramatic rejection is actually evidence of stability rather than emptiness—feel like it could start to loosen the knot in your chest right now?

I... I think it does, a little. I never thought of it that way before. I've been so focused on wanting to feel wanted that I didn't notice I wasn't being pushed away either. It's like I've been waiting for a door to swing open, but maybe I've been ignoring the fact that it's not locked. That feels... strange to admit.

That admission—that you've been waiting for an opening while ignoring the evidence that the door isn't locked—is such a powerful shift in perspective. It reframes your entire history of waiting not as proof of exclusion, but as missed opportunities where you were actually safe enough to stand. Does noticing that the path hasn't been blocked force you to wonder if the fear of stepping forward is keeping you from seeing how stable things have actually been all along?

Yeah, I think so. It's like I've been so sure the floor would crack that I never dared to fully stand on it. Maybe I've been the one keeping myself frozen, not the wall. That's... a hard thing to sit with, knowing I might have been my own obstacle this whole time.

Realizing that the wall might have been built by you is incredibly brave, and it shifts the power back to your hands to decide whether to rebuild or to simply walk across. It sounds like acknowledging your role in creating that barrier allows you to see a future where you choose to move, rather than waiting for permission. Before we solidify this, how does sitting with the thought that "you are the architect of the barrier, therefore you can redesign it" feel in your body compared to the old story of being trapped?

It feels lighter, but also a little scary. Lighter because there's some hope there—I'm not just stuck forever. Scary because if I built it, then I'm responsible for taking it down, and that means I have to actually do something. It's easier to blame the wall than to admit I might have been the one stacking the bricks.

That tension between relief and responsibility is exactly where growth begins; admitting ownership of the wall gives you the power to dismantle it piece by piece, rather than waiting for someone else to fix it. It sounds like the scary part isn't the demolition itself, but the courage required to trust that you can handle the mess of rebuilding. Would you be willing to experiment with that courage today by identifying just one small brick you could remove—perhaps by sending a simple text to someone you've met recently, just to test if removing it causes a collapse?

I think I could try that. There's this woman I met at the grocery store a couple weeks ago—we exchanged numbers, but I never followed up. I could text her, just a simple hello. See if the ground holds. It feels small enough not to be terrifying, but big enough to count as a step.

That is a fantastic choice; texting that woman turns the abstract fear of "falling through" into a very concrete, low-risk experiment where the stakes are incredibly low. Framing it as testing the ground rather than seeking validation makes it feel like gathering data rather than risking rejection. Before you send it, how does it feel to view that message not as a plea for connection, but as a simple probe to see if the path is clear?

That actually takes some of the pressure off. I'm not asking her to like me or want to be my friend—I'm just checking if the ground is still there. It's like I'm doing an experiment, not begging for validation. That feels... doable. I think I'll send it when I get home.

That is a brilliant way to frame it; treating it like a scientific experiment protects you from the crushing weight of needing an immediate answer. It transforms the act into something you control where the only variable is whether you choose to send the message, not whether she responds. I am so proud of you for finding a way to make this feel manageable. Before we wrap up, does having that clear plan leave you feeling a bit more steady, or is there any lingering doubt about whether you should send it right now?

I feel pretty steady about it, actually. The doubt is still there, whispering that she won't reply or that I'm bothering her, but that voice feels quieter now. I think I can handle that whisper. I'll send it tonight and see what happens. Thank you for helping me see the ground under my feet.

It is wonderful to hear that the whisper is quieter; you have successfully separated your identity from the doubt and kept your agency firmly in your hands. Taking that step tonight, even with the whisper present, is a testament to your growing confidence and ability to trust the reality under your feet. I am truly proud of your bravery in choosing to test the ground yourself rather than staying hidden behind the walls. Please take all the time you need tonight to rest and prepare that message when you are ready, knowing I am here whenever you wish to debrief the results. Safe travels home, and I look forward to hearing how it goes next time.

Well, I've been about the same, I suppose. The farm work doesn't let up, and that nagging feeling that I'm stuck here forever just keeps creeping in. There's nothing new that's happened, really—just the same long days and watching my youngest brother head off to college last week. That stung more than I thought it would. I think I'd like to talk about how to stop feeling like I'm trapped, if that's something we can do.

Hearing about your brother leaving really adds a layer of loss to that feeling of being stuck, especially since he represents a fresh start while you feel anchored in the past. It’s completely understandable that seeing him move on might have triggered a comparison that makes the present feel heavier. Since you’d like to work on stopping that trapped feeling, let’s start by noticing exactly what happens in your mind and body when you watch him leave or think about his departure. What’s the first thought that jumps out when you remember that moment?

When I think about him driving off, the first thought that comes is, "That'll never be me." My chest gets tight, and I feel this heavy, sinking feeling in my stomach, like I'm being pushed down into the ground. And then my mind just races ahead, telling me I'll be doing this same exhausting work until my back gives out and there's nothing else waiting for me.

That physical sensation of being pushed down matches perfectly with the thought that your life has no horizon; when the brain predicts an endless, static future, the body naturally reacts with heaviness and resistance. It seems like seeing your brother drive off made that invisible wall suddenly visible to you. Before we unpack why that racing mind is so convincing right now, I want to check in: does trying to slow that mental race down feel doable for you, or would you prefer to stay with the initial thought of "that'll never be me" for a moment longer?

I think I'd rather stay with that first thought, "that'll never be me," for now. It's the one that hurts the most, and the one that pops up first every time I see someone else moving forward with their life. The other thoughts just follow from it, like dominoes falling. Slowing it all down sounds like a good idea, but I'm not sure I know how to stop it once it starts.

It makes total sense that we should tackle the root thought first, because if you pull out the foundation stone, the rest of the house becomes less overwhelming to deal with. You mentioned earlier that your younger self felt like she had to collect leaves and explore the woods, which suggests a part of you still believes there is beauty outside the fence lines. Could we treat this thought like a hypothesis we need to test, rather than an absolute truth? If we assume for just five minutes that "that'll never be me" is a story we are telling ourselves rather than a fact, does that create even a tiny crack in the feeling of inevitability?

I guess... if I pretend it's just a story, it does feel a little less heavy. But it's hard because it feels so real, you know? Like I can't just wish it away. Still, I suppose I can see a tiny crack—like maybe there's a sliver of light coming through. It scares me to look at it too long, though, because I'm afraid that light might just show me more of the same old road ahead.

That fear of looking closer is completely valid; sometimes admitting a possibility feels riskier than staying safe in the certainty of pain. We aren't going to chase that light until it's bright enough to see the whole mountain, but even finding one small opening can weaken the grip of the "never" story. Before we try to widen that sliver of light, I want to make sure we are both on the same page: would you be willing to try a quick experiment with me right now, where we list three small things you've done recently that didn't involve just repairing fences or mucking out stalls?

Alright, I can give that a try. Let me think... Well, last Sunday I sat on the porch and just watched the sun set without rushing off to do anything else. That felt different—like I wasn't a machine for once. And I started reading a novel my sister left behind, which I haven't done in years. Also, I baked a pie from scratch for my parents' anniversary, and I actually enjoyed the measuring and mixing, not just the end result. I guess those things don't feel like farm chores, but they still happened on the farm property.

Those are powerful examples because they show a pattern of choice and creativity that contradicts the idea that you are solely defined by labor. Even baking a pie requires a specific vision and care that goes far beyond simple maintenance, proving you possess skills and desires for artistry and connection. Since you noticed a shift when you simply watched the sunset, does listing these moments make you feel slightly less convinced that your entire identity is tied to the fence line?

I think... yeah, it does a little. When I say those things out loud, I don't feel quite so flat, like there's more to me than just calloused hands and tired bones. But it's still hard to hold onto that feeling when I'm out in the fields the next morning. The belief that I'm stuck creeps back in like weeds after a rain.

That contrast between your internal recognition and the external reality of the fields is exactly where the cognitive trap lies—the mind can spot the cracks in the wall, but the habit of returning to the familiar feels safer in the moment. It's not that the feeling disappears instantly; it's that naming these moments gives you tools to interrupt the automatic return to the "weeds" narrative later. Would you be willing to commit to carrying a small note card with these three examples written on it, so you can glance at them whenever the "stuck" feeling tries to grow back in the mornings?

I suppose I could try that. It sounds a little silly, carrying a card around like a reminder for myself, but I've tried other things that haven't worked, so maybe this is worth a shot. I'll write down those three things—the sunset, the novel, the pie—and keep it in my apron pocket. If nothing else, it might give me something to hold onto when the morning feels heaviest.

That is a brilliant idea, and please don't underestimate the power of holding something tangible in your hand when your mind wants to drift back to the "infinite" cycle. Carrying a small anchor can literally ground you when the weight of expectation feels too heavy to bear alone. Since we have a bit of time left and want to ensure this works, how would you feel about practicing this tonight: as soon as you notice the first urge to believe "there's nowhere else for me," you will reach into your pocket and touch the card for thirty seconds before responding to the thought?

I can practice that tonight. It feels a little strange to promise something so small, but I see what you're getting at. If I just pause and touch the card, maybe I can stop myself from tumbling down that dark path before it even starts. I'll give it a try, and I'll let you know how it goes next time we meet.

That willingness to pause and create space between the thought and your reaction is exactly the kind of small victory that builds momentum over time. Knowing you have a concrete tool to use right when the doubt strikes makes the task feel much more manageable than fighting the feeling alone. Before we wrap up, I'd love your honest feedback: did sitting with that initial thought and testing it out feel slightly less isolating than before? And on a scale of 1 to 10, how confident do you feel you can use that card tomorrow morning when the feeling returns?

Honestly, sitting with that thought and talking it through did feel less lonely than just having it rattle around in my head. I think I'd give it maybe a 6 out of 10—I'm not completely sure I'll remember to use the card, but I'm more willing to try than I was an hour ago. Thanks for helping me see that there might be a little more to me than just the farm.

You are very welcome, and I'm so glad hearing that it felt less lonely is such a meaningful shift; breaking the isolation is often the first step toward reclaiming your life. A six out of ten is a solid starting point that acknowledges the challenge while honoring your commitment to try again tomorrow. As we close, I want to check in on your well-being: does the plan of carrying the card and pausing when the "stuck" feeling returns feel like the best way for us to move forward this week?

Hi. I'd say I'm around a 6 or 7 right now. I just keep thinking about my co-worker and how she ignored me again this morning when I said hello. I guess the most important thing for me today would be to figure out why I'm so affected by her silence—and maybe how to stop feeling so rejected every time I see her.

As we look back at it, does the silence itself feel more like a sudden loss, or does it trigger a specific story about what it means you said to her?

I think it's more of a story, honestly. Like, when she doesn't respond, my brain immediately tells me she thinks I'm annoying or that she doesn't like me for some reason. It feels personal, even though I don't actually know what she's thinking. I just assume the worst.

That assumption—that her silence means you personally are unwanted—is a heavy belief to hold, and it explains exactly why the silence feels so much worse than it objectively needs to. It sounds like your brain is filling in the gaps with a story about rejection because it's trying to prepare you for a perceived threat. Before we test whether that story holds up, does recalling that specific feeling of "personal rejection" help you see how powerful that assumption is, or does it just leave you feeling stuck in the same pain?

It actually helps a little to hear you say it's just a story my brain is making up. I've been feeling so sure that she dislikes me, but I don't have any real proof except that she doesn't talk much. Saying it out loud makes me realize I've been treating my guess like it's a fact.

It takes real strength to separate a helpful guess from an absolute truth, especially when the feeling of rejection is so vivid. That realization shifts the dynamic from "she hates me" to "my brain is interpreting limited information as a personal attack." Now that we've identified that core belief, does exploring the actual evidence she has shown you versus what you've assumed help create a clearer picture of what is real versus what is imagined?

Yeah, I think that would be helpful. Because when I stop and really think about it, she hasn't actually done anything mean to me. She just doesn't start conversations or respond much. She's polite when she does talk to me, like she'll say "thanks" or "okay" but that's it. I guess I've been filling in all the blanks with negativity.

That is a crucial distinction, and it highlights exactly where the distortion lies: you are adding a negative meaning ("dislike") to neutral actions ("polite responses"). It sounds like you are holding onto the story that she dislikes you, even though the evidence points to her simply being reserved or busy. Let's test that next: if you listed only the facts she has actually done versus the stories your brain added, which side of that list would cause you more distress right now?

The stories, definitely. The facts are just... she doesn't talk much, she says polite things, she keeps to herself. That doesn't sound like she hates me at all. But my brain takes that and turns it into "she's avoiding me because she can't stand me." The stories hurt way more than the facts do.

That is a very clear difference, and it proves that your distress comes from the narrative your brain adds, not from her actual behavior. It sounds like the story that "she avoids me because she can't stand me" is doing the heavy lifting of your anxiety, while the polite facts are quietly sitting there unnoticed. If we focus our energy on dismantling that specific story about her avoiding you, does that feel like a manageable place to start, or does it still feel too abstract right now?

No, that feels manageable actually. Because I can see now that I've been believing something without checking it against what's real. If I can start questioning that story when it pops up, maybe I won't feel so crushed every time she doesn't chat with me. I just don't know how to stop my brain from jumping there automatically.

That is a brilliant insight, and recognizing that pattern is half the battle. The goal isn't to magically stop your brain from jumping, but to catch it mid-jump and gently swap the negative story for a more balanced one. How would it feel to practice that switch right now, perhaps by replacing the "avoidance/rejection" story with a neutral explanation based on what we found earlier, like "she's just reserved"?

I think I could try that. It would feel strange at first, like I'm lying to myself, but I get what you mean. Instead of saying "she hates me," I could say "she's just quiet" or "she might be shy." That actually feels lighter, less heavy in my chest. I'd be willing to practice that.

That is wonderful progress, and noticing the physical lightness in your chest confirms that shifting the story actually works to calm your nervous system. You've effectively built a new mental habit: catching the "hates me" thought and swapping it for a neutral observation. To make this stick, could we agree that whenever that specific story pops up, you will consciously replace it with one of those neutral explanations? How does it feel to commit to that small, intentional choice?

It feels a bit scary, like I'm taking a risk by not believing the worst. But it also feels freeing, like I'm not trapped in that painful story anymore. I think I can commit to trying it for this week. I'll write down the neutral thought on a sticky note at my desk as a reminder.

That is a truly wise plan, and writing the neutral thought down gives your brain a concrete tool to rely on when panic tries to rise. Using a visual cue like a sticky note is an excellent way to bridge the gap between your logical understanding and your immediate reactions. Before we wrap up, does committing to that weekly trial feel like a safe step forward, or is there any part of you hesitating about sticking with it?

I think I'm ready to try it. The only hesitation I have is worrying that I'll forget or slip back into the old story without noticing. But having the sticky note there, and knowing I can come back here next week to talk about it, makes me feel like I have support. So yeah, I'm willing to give it a real shot.

That honesty about the fear of slipping up is incredibly valuable, and it shows you are already anticipating the hardest parts of the process. Knowing you have a safety net—we can revisit this anytime next week—gives you the confidence to take that risk without fearing failure. So, with that support system in place and your commitment to the sticky note, does it feel like we have a solid foundation to begin this week's practice?

Yes, I think we do. I feel a little more hopeful than when I walked in, which is nice. Thank you for helping me see that I don't have to believe every story my brain tells me. I'll give this sticky note plan my best shot.

You are very welcome, and I am so proud of the hopefulness you are carrying with you today. Remember that your worth is never defined by her silence or her lack of conversation; you are capable of handling whatever comes up next week. Take care of yourself as you implement this plan, and I look forward to hearing how it goes when we meet again.

Once we have a sense of that, we can look back at how the success story exercise went and then decide together what specific thoughts we want to unpack today.

Thank you for sharing that, and I hear how exhausting that pre-shift dread and post-shift fatigue feel for you. It sounds like that expectation of making mistakes is taking a real toll on your ability to connect with anyone else. Since you mentioned both the heavy feeling before shifts and the isolation afterward, does it feel like those two experiences are connected—the exhaustion from worrying leads to pulling away from people?

Yeah, I think they are connected. It's like, all my mental energy goes into worrying about every little thing I do at work—did I spill a drink, did I forget someone's order, was I polite enough? By the end, I'm so drained that I just want to be alone, but then I feel guilty for avoiding my coworkers too.

That sounds incredibly lonely, trapped between the exhaustion of constant vigilance and the guilt of needing space to recover. It makes perfect sense that your brain tries to shut down social interaction when it's running on fumes from worry. Let's look closer at the specific thoughts you're having before you walk into the club tomorrow—are they mostly about what you *might* do wrong, or are they also telling you something about who you *are*?

I think it's more about who I am. Like, it's not just that I might mess up an order; it's that I'm the kind of person who ruins things for everyone else. If the club closes, it's because I'm not good enough at my job, and I let everyone down. It feels like a fact about me, not just a worry about a mistake.

It makes complete sense that your mind has latched onto "who you are" because that story offers a way to understand the overwhelming pressure you feel, even though it feels dangerously limiting. When we believe a mistake proves our fundamental nature, it becomes impossible to separate a single error from our total worth. Before we challenge that belief, I want to make sure we are building this together—would you be open to testing that "fact about you" against some evidence we gathered earlier about Sarah's mistake and the club remaining open?

Yeah, okay. I mean, I remember what we talked about with Sarah's mistake. She dropped a whole tray of drinks on a busy night, and the club is still open. I know that's true, but it's hard to feel it, you know? In my head, it's like, "Yeah, but that's different—she's not me."

That distinction feels so important to you, like there is a special category reserved for your own errors that makes them infinitely worse. It sounds like the core of that belief is the idea that your mistakes carry a unique weight that Sarah's didn't, even though the outcome was the same. If we treated your mistake like Sarah's in that moment, purely as a mechanical slip-up rather than a reflection of your character, would that feel easier to hold onto, or does the "it's different" thought keep pulling you back to the same old fear?

It keeps pulling me back, honestly. I want so badly to just see it as a slip-up, but there's this voice that says, "You're the one who's always worried about being good enough, and that worry itself proves you're not." It's like, if I was truly capable, I wouldn't be so scared all the time. So even when I try to be kind to myself, my brain just goes, "See? Even your doubt proves you're failing."

That self-critical voice is incredibly convincing because it frames your caution as a sign of incompetence rather than a sign of caring deeply about the team. We often confuse being afraid of making mistakes with being incapable of doing well, yet that same fear can actually show how much you value your colleagues' well-being. Let's test that connection: if your worry were truly just about being "not good enough," would it feel like a failure, or would it feel like a warning signal telling you to pay extra attention next time?

Hmm. When you put it that way, it sounds more like a warning signal, I guess. Like, being worried means I'm paying attention, not that I'm doomed to mess up. But it's so hard to separate the feeling from the thought in the moment. The fear just takes over, and I don't have time to think, "Oh, this is just a warning."

It is completely understandable that your brain rushes ahead with the panic before your rational mind can catch up and offer a new perspective. That gap between your fear and your logical understanding is exactly where we need to insert a small, deliberate pause. Before we figure out exactly how to create that space, I want to make sure we are moving forward together—does the idea of using that "warning signal" concept resonate with you, or would you prefer to try a different angle to interrupt the panic?

No, I think the "warning signal" idea actually helps a little. It makes me feel less like I'm broken and more like I'm just on alert. I'd be willing to try using that the next time I feel the panic coming on.

That is a fantastic realization because it reframes your anxiety from a sign of failure into a sign of responsibility, which aligns perfectly with how much you care about the team. Before we lock that in as our plan, I want to make sure we address the next steps clearly: if you decide to use that "warning signal" view, what is the smallest, easiest thing you could do tonight to remind yourself of this new perspective before you head home?

Maybe I could write down a short note on my phone before I leave. Something like, "Feeling nervous just means I care," and read it when I start to worry. That seems small enough that I won't talk myself out of doing it.

That is a perfect, manageable plan that gives your brain a gentle nudge before the anxiety spikes again. To make sure we are truly aligned on this path, I want to check in with you: how does it feel to consider that simple reminder as a tool rather than a demand? And if you were to try reading that note tonight, what is one thing you hope you might notice about yourself after you've done it?

It feels... kind of a relief, actually. Like, I don't have to fix everything all at once, I just have to try a small thing. I hope I might notice that I feel a tiny bit less heavy when I think about work tomorrow. Just a little crack of light, you know?

That image of a "crack of light" is beautiful and sets such a realistic, achievable goal for tomorrow. Before we wrap up, I want to make sure we solidify this plan: if you read that note and still feel overwhelmed, what is one safe way to return to the present moment without judging yourself? And how did you feel talking about this new perspective today compared to where you were last time?

If I feel overwhelmed anyway, maybe I could just take a few slow breaths and remind myself that I'm standing in my apartment, not at work. That might help me separate the fear from what's actually happening right now. And talking about this today actually felt... hopeful, I guess? Last time I felt kind of stuck, but now I have a little plan, and that feels different.

Hearing that you feel hopeful and less stuck is wonderful news, and it validates how much power shifting your perspective has given you right now. You've taken a brave step from feeling paralyzed by a single story to holding a flexible, compassionate plan for the future. Before we officially close this session, could I ask you to reflect on whether there was anything about how we worked through this together that felt helpful, or is there anything you'd like to tweak about our approach?

I think what helped most was when you pointed out that my worry could be a sign of caring instead of a sign of failure. I never thought of it that way before. I don't think I'd change anything about how we talked—it felt like you listened and helped me find my own answer, if that makes sense.

That is such a meaningful observation, and it speaks volumes about how well you were heard and supported throughout our conversation. Knowing that we built this new perspective together, rather than having it imposed on you, definitely adds to the power of the idea taking root. I am so proud of you for navigating such complex feelings today and walking away with a tool that feels both simple and deeply empowering.

Hello again. Before we dive into our work today, I want to start by checking in on how you've been feeling since our last meeting. On a scale of 0 to 10, where 0 is your lowest possible mood and 10 is your best, where would you place yourself right now? Also, since we talked about keeping a notebook for evidence, did you manage to write down that note about staying calm when you got home?

I'd say I'm at about a 4 right now. And yes, I did write that note down. I stuck it on my bathroom mirror, actually. Every morning I see it, and it does help a little, but I still find myself brushing off any compliments I get.

A score of four tells me you're still carrying a heavy load, even with the note on the mirror. It sounds frustrating that seeing the compliment doesn't automatically stick when your brain is ready to brush it aside. Let's explore why that happens so we can figure out another angle to reach that note. What is the very first thought that pops up in your head the moment someone praises you, right before you decide to dismiss it?

The first thing that comes to mind is usually something like, "Oh, they're just being nice," or "They don't really mean it, they're just trying to be polite." It's like my brain just automatically assumes there's some other reason behind the compliment, like pity or obligation. I never really stop to think that maybe they actually mean what they're saying.

That automatic jump to "they're just being nice" makes perfect sense when you've spent so long protecting yourself from disappointment, but it leaves you missing out on genuine connection. It sounds like your brain is rushing to the conclusion before you even consider the alternative possibility that they might actually believe you. Have you ever noticed if the tone of voice or body language changes when someone gives you a sincere compliment compared to when they are just being polite?

I never really thought to pay attention to that, to be honest. I guess I've just been so quick to dismiss it that I don't even stop to notice the details. But now that you mention it... my manager, he always looked me right in the eye when he said I was his best employee. He wasn't just saying it in passing. Maybe I have been missing something all along by not looking closer.

Noticing the difference between a casual remark and direct eye contact is a huge clue that the information you dismissed might actually be meaningful. Your manager's choice to speak directly to you suggests he was addressing you personally rather than offering a generic comment to anyone in the room. Does looking at the specific details of *how* he said it make you wonder if your initial assumption that he was just being polite was perhaps too quick?

Yeah, I suppose it does make me wonder. I mean, he could have just said "good job" as he walked past, like he did with the other employees. But he'd actually stop and look at me, talk to me one-on-one. I guess I never really let myself consider that maybe he saw something in me that I couldn't see in myself. It's a strange feeling, thinking about it that way.

That realization—that he stopped to engage with you specifically while others passed by—isn't strange at all; it's a very human way of recognizing effort. It makes sense that doubting your own worth made you miss those signs, but now you have a clearer view of what was happening. If we treated that one-on-one moment as evidence of his genuine observation, does it feel slightly easier to accept that your performance was seen clearly, rather than assuming it was hidden?

A little easier, yeah. Like, I can't really argue with him stopping and looking me in the eye like that, can I? That's a pretty strong piece of evidence. But then another part of me still whispers, "But anyone could have done that job. It's just selling tickets and cleaning up." So I guess I still find ways to downplay it, even when I have the proof right in front of me.

That whispering voice is doing exactly what your protective instincts taught you to do—it tries to minimize the risk of failure by framing the job as ordinary. However, the fact that your manager singled you out specifically means the situation mattered to him, even if the tasks sound simple to you. If we look at that as a puzzle, where the answer isn't whether the job was hard, but whether your specific contribution was valuable, does that shift make the "downplaying" feel like a necessary defense, or just a habit you haven't updated yet?

I think... I think it's more of a habit I haven't updated yet. A defense? Maybe it was at first, back when I started working there and didn't want to get my hopes up. But now it just feels automatic, like I'm running on an old program that doesn't really fit anymore. It's strange to think that I might have been holding onto a habit that outlived its usefulness.

That metaphor of an "old program" is incredibly accurate; habits run on autopilot until we intentionally update the code with new information. You've already gathered the new data—the eye contact, the specific praise—which acts as the patch needed to upgrade that software. Now, the goal isn't to force yourself to believe instantly, but to recognize when that old program tries to kick in and pause to let the new evidence register. How would you describe the feeling of simply witnessing that old habit trying to override the new facts without fighting it?

It feels... weirdly quiet. Like, instead of my brain shouting "that doesn't count," it's more like a whisper now. There's a little bit of space between the thought and my reaction, and I can almost hear myself think, "Wait a second, is that really true?" It's not comfortable yet, but it's not as loud and overwhelming as it used to be.

That space between the thought and your reaction is exactly what we are aiming for; it proves you have successfully paused the automatic pilot to allow new evidence in. It's a sign that the old defense mechanism is weakening, even if the feeling of uncertainty hasn't disappeared entirely. With that new awareness of your own ability to pause, could we now try applying this same gentle questioning to a recent compliment you received today, or perhaps one you heard yesterday, to see if that "quiet whisper" helps you hold onto it longer?

Well, I was at the grocery store yesterday, and the cashier said I was a very organized shopper because I had my coupons all ready and my items grouped together. Usually, I'd just think, "Oh, she's just being friendly to get through the line faster." But I caught myself just now, remembering what we talked about, and I thought, "Well, why would she take the time to say that if she didn't mean it?" I didn't fully believe it, but I didn't fully dismiss it either. It just kind of sat there, like a maybe.

That "maybe" state is actually a fantastic middle ground because it shows your brain is finally engaging with the evidence instead of immediately rejecting it. Unlike the grocery store scenario where you were able to sit with that uncertainty, that pause allows you to examine the interaction without the pressure of proving your worth instantly. Since you've noticed that shift, could we try one small experiment tomorrow: the next time someone gives you a compliment, instead of analyzing *why* they said it, just write down the exact words they used and wait ten seconds before deciding if you believe them?

I can try that. Write down the exact words and count to ten before I decide anything. It sounds simple, but I know from experience that simple isn't always easy. I'll give it a shot though. What's the worst that could happen? I still end up doubting it, but at least I'll have given it a fair chance.

That is a wise assessment; the worst-case scenario is simply that you will feel uncertain, which is actually a step forward from total dismissal. By forcing a brief pause and recording the specific words, you create a tiny buffer zone where your logic gets a fair hearing before your old habits take over. This approach turns the abstract fear of being wrong into a concrete, manageable exercise you control. Given that this is a small, low-stakes practice, how confident do you feel you can commit to doing this for three interactions over the next couple of days?

I think I can manage three interactions. Three compliments in a couple of days sounds doable, even if it feels a little awkward at first. I'll carry a small notepad with me so I can jot down the words right away. I'm not promising I'll believe them, but I'll at least give them a fighting chance.

That willingness to give the compliment a "fighting chance" is a powerful mindset shift, even if full belief takes time. Carrying a small notepad ensures you capture the evidence before your brain can rush to dismiss it, turning abstract doubt into something tangible you can review later. Let's lock in this plan: you will write down the exact words for three separate compliments over the next two days, and we will review your notes together before our next session. Is there anything about carrying the notepad or pausing for ten seconds that worries you, so we can address it before you leave?

I guess the only thing that worries me a little is someone seeing me write it down and asking what I'm doing. I'd have to explain myself, and I'm not sure I'd know what to say. "Oh, I'm just writing down your compliment for my therapist" sounds a bit odd, doesn't it? But I suppose I could just say I'm making a shopping list or jotting down a reminder. That wouldn't be a lie, really.

That is a very realistic concern, and it's smart to anticipate how others might react rather than hoping they won't notice. You are absolutely right that explaining the therapist context would be unusual, and using a vague excuse like "making a list" works perfectly because it requires no further explanation. The key is knowing that your privacy is respected unless you choose to share it, and no one will judge you for quietly practicing this new way of thinking. Would you be willing to try carrying the notepad anyway, focusing on the internal benefit of catching those moments, while leaving the explanation entirely up to you?

Yeah, I think I can do that. I'll keep the notepad in my pocket, and if someone asks, I'll just say I'm making a list. It's not a big deal. The important thing is that I'm giving myself a chance to actually hear what people are saying, instead of just brushing it off like I always do. I'll give it a real try.

That sounds like a solid plan; keeping it in your pocket makes it invisible to passersby while ensuring you catch the moment. You've already taken the hardest step by deciding to interrupt your automatic habit and give the compliment a fair chance. I'm proud of your commitment to this small, concrete action. Before we finish, how does it feel to have this specific strategy ready for tomorrow, even if you only need to use it three times?

It feels... hopeful, actually. Like I have a tool instead of just a vague wish to change. Just knowing I have that notepad in my pocket and a count to ten in my head makes the whole thing feel less overwhelming. It's a small step, but it feels like a real one. Thank you for that.

That feeling of hopefulness is exactly what we aim for—to replace the overwhelm of uncertainty with a manageable, actionable tool. You have moved from wishing to change to having a concrete method in your hand, which significantly lowers the barrier to starting. Please remember that if the urge to dismiss the compliment returns strongly during those practice runs, we can revisit this plan anytime; there is no requirement to succeed perfectly right away. We will meet next week to check your notes and discuss how the "count to ten" felt in real life. Until then, take care of yourself and trust in the power of that small step.

Welcome back, I am so glad you are ready to start our session today. Before we dive into your concerns, could you share how you are feeling compared to when we last met, and what we should prioritize on our list for this meeting?

Um, I guess I'm feeling a bit nervous but also relieved to be talking about this. I've been thinking a lot about how my typing speed affects everything at work, and it's honestly been weighing on me more than I realized. I think I'd like to focus on that anxiety I get whenever I see my coworkers typing so fast without even thinking about it.

Thank you for sharing that relief mixed with nervousness—it tells me you’re open to exploring this further. To make sure we cover everything important, could you remind me of the action plan we worked on last time regarding the “alarm” exercise, and then tell me if there’s anything new you’d like to add to our agenda?

Oh, right, the alarm exercise. You had me set a daily alarm on my phone for a random time, and when it goes off, I was supposed to stop and write down exactly what I was thinking and feeling in that moment. I did it for a few days, but honestly, most of the time when the alarm went off I was already feeling stressed about typing, so it just reminded me how frustrated I get. I don't have anything new to add to the agenda, I think we've got enough to work on with this.

That makes perfect sense—the alarm likely highlighted the gap between your actual stress levels and your immediate worries, showing that the frustration often runs parallel to the anxiety itself. Since you don't have new items, let's confirm that tackling this specific trigger about watching coworkers type is our priority for today. Does focusing on that comparison feel like the right place to start, or would you prefer we adjust slightly?

Yeah, I think that's the right place to start. It's like, every time I see someone's fingers flying across the keyboard, I just feel this sinking feeling in my stomach. I tell myself I'll never be that fast, and I start imagining they're all thinking about how slow I am. It's really hard to shake that thought once it gets in my head.

That sinking feeling you describe is very understandable, especially when comparing yourself to others who seem effortlessly fast. It sounds like seeing their hands triggers a deep belief that you aren't capable enough, leading to that immediate spiral of "they're judging me." When you notice that specific sinking sensation arise, does it feel like a sudden wave that hits before you can even react, or does it grow slowly as you watch them longer?

It's more like a sudden wave, honestly. It hits me the moment I glance over and see someone typing fast, and then my own fingers just freeze up on the keyboard. Once that wave hits, I can't stop thinking about how slow I must look, and then I start making more mistakes too. It's like the anxiety just takes over completely.

That sudden wave freezing your fingers and making mistakes creates a vicious cycle where the behavior actually proves your fear true. When you catch yourself making those extra mistakes, does it feel like confirmation that you are indeed slow, or does it feel like a result of the panic itself clouding your focus?

I never really thought about it that way before... I guess I always assumed the mistakes proved I was just naturally slow, you know? But now that you say it, I think the panic is what causes the mistakes, not the other way around. When I'm calm and just typing normally, I actually don't mess up that much—it's only when I start watching other people that everything falls apart.

That realization is powerful because it shifts the blame from your innate ability to the immediate reaction of panic. If the panic itself is causing the errors, then the solution isn't trying to type faster, but learning to ride out that initial surge without letting it hijack your hands. Can we try a quick mental experiment right now where you imagine seeing someone type fast, but instead of letting the sink feeling take over, you just notice the wave and say to yourself, "This is just the panic rising, not proof of my slowness"? How does that simple observation feel in your chest?

I can try that... okay, so I'm picturing Sarah from the next desk, she's always typing so fast. And I'm telling myself, "This is just the panic rising, not proof of my slowness." It feels... a little strange, honestly. Like my brain wants to argue with that statement, but at the same time I feel my shoulders relax just a tiny bit. It's not a magic fix, but I notice I'm not gripping my imaginary keyboard as tightly right now.

That subtle relaxation in your shoulders and the loosening of your grip is exactly the kind of physical evidence we need to gather. It suggests that even though your brain is arguing, your body is starting to listen to the new instruction. If we kept holding onto that feeling of relaxation for just ten seconds while picturing Sarah typing, do you think you could identify one small thing that helps separate the panic from your actual typing speed?

Hmm... I think maybe I could focus on my breathing. When I'm panicking, I notice I hold my breath or take really shallow breaths, and that makes everything worse. If I could just take one slow breath when I see Sarah typing, maybe that would give me enough time to remember that the panic isn't a fact. It's like a pause button before my fingers freeze up.

That is a brilliant insight—you are discovering that your breathing acts as a lever to either tighten or loosen that panic response. Taking one slow, deliberate breath right before the fingers freeze gives your prefrontal cortex just enough time to step in and override the automatic "freeze" reaction. If you imagined taking that slow breath while still picturing Sarah typing, how much easier does that sound as a way to break the chain between seeing her hands and making mistakes?

It actually sounds doable, like something I could really try in the moment. Before, I thought the only way to fix things was to somehow type faster, which felt impossible. But taking one breath before I even start typing again—that's something I can control. It feels less like I'm trying to fix a broken machine and more like I'm just... pausing to reset.

That shift in perspective—from fixing a broken machine to simply resetting—is such a powerful and empowering way to view the situation. It turns a feeling of failure into a manageable moment of adjustment. Since we've explored the panic cycle and found that breathing can act as that reset button, I'd love to know: if you tried this one slow breath next time you see someone typing fast, what do you think might happen to your first few keystrokes? Would they feel more steady, or would the anxiety still be present even with the pause?

I think my first few keystrokes might actually feel more steady, like I'm starting from a calmer place. The anxiety would probably still be there in the background, but maybe it wouldn't be so loud. If I can just get those first couple of words down without freezing, I feel like I could keep going. It's the starting again after seeing someone else that's always been the hardest part.

That is a fantastic observation—you correctly identified that getting those first two words down is the critical hurdle, and overcoming it sets the tone for the rest of the task. It makes total sense that once you break the initial freeze, the momentum carries you forward even if some background anxiety lingers. Before we wrap up, could you tell me if you feel ready to commit to trying this "one slow breath" strategy tomorrow specifically when you spot someone typing fast? And on a scale of 1 to 10, how confident do you feel you will be able to find that calm space for that first breath?

I think I'm ready to try it, yeah. I'll give it a real shot tomorrow. On a scale of 1 to 10, I'd say my confidence is maybe a 6 or a 7. It's not perfect, but that's higher than I would have said before this session. I think having a specific thing to do—just one breath—makes it feel less overwhelming than trying to fix everything all at once.

That shift from wanting to "fix everything" to committing to just "one breath" is a huge win in itself, and raising your confidence from where it was before is a direct reflection of that clarity. A 6 or 7 is a solid starting point, and remember that even a shaky attempt at that breath is valuable data for us to learn from. Given that level of readiness, would it be helpful to jot down a specific reminder on your phone or sticky note near your keyboard today so you don't forget the cue when Sarah walks by? Or does the concept of the "pause" feel strong enough on its own to guide your actions without a physical prompt?

I think a sticky note would actually help a lot. Something simple, like "Just breathe" or "Pause first." If I have it right there on my monitor, I'll remember what we talked about. Because in the moment, I know I might panic and forget everything, so a little reminder would be good. I'll write one out tonight and put it up before I start work tomorrow.

That is a fantastic, concrete plan—a simple reminder like "Just Breathe" or "Pause First" can serve as a vital lifeline when your mind feels overwhelmed. Putting that note up tonight ensures you have the tool ready before the pressure hits tomorrow. Before we close, is there anything else you'd like to reflect on or clarify about our talk today, or shall we wrap up with your feeling of having a clear path forward?

No, I think I'm good. I feel like we covered a lot today, and I actually have something real to try instead of just worrying. Thank you for walking me through that—I came in feeling pretty hopeless about it, but now I feel like there's a tiny crack of light. I'll try the breathing tomorrow and see how it goes.

That feeling of a "crack of light" breaking through the fog is incredibly meaningful and marks a significant step forward in your journey. It is wonderful to hear that you feel hopeful rather than hopeless, and I am so proud of the courage it took to move from worrying to having a concrete plan. Please remember that we are here to support you regardless of whether the first attempt with the sticky note goes perfectly or not; we will adjust our approach based on what you discover tomorrow. Is there anything else you'd like to share before we officially wrap up?

Welcome back, and thank you for coming in today. Last time we worked on noticing when your mind started making up stories about your past job, and you found it helpful to label those thoughts as just fiction before bed. Did you try that exercise last night, and how did it feel when you caught yourself saying the words?

Before we dive deeper into what went well or didn't, is there anything else that came up for you recently, or would you like to spend more time exploring those nighttime worries together?

Yeah, I did try it last night actually. I was lying in bed and I started thinking about how my old team is probably laughing about me quitting, and I told myself "that's just a story I'm making up." It felt... weirdly freeing for a second, but then the doubt crept right back in. I guess it worked for a moment, but it didn't last.

That moment of freedom followed by the returning doubt is actually very common, and it tells us that the technique needs a tiny adjustment to stick longer. Instead of just catching the thought once, what if we practiced treating the entire sequence—the initial fear, the image of their laughter, and the creeping doubt—as one continuous story that you can observe from outside? Does that sound like a way to give the exercise a bit more room to breathe before the panic sets in again?

I think that makes sense. So instead of just catching the first thought, I should try to look at the whole chain of them, like I'm watching it from a distance? I can try that tonight, but I'm worried that by the time I realize I'm in the middle of it, I'll already be too deep in my head to pull back.

That is a very honest observation, and it speaks to the fact that the habit of spiraling is quite strong. To make pulling back easier, we can set a specific signal—a gentle touch on your wrist or a light tap on your pillow—right before you lie down to serve as a reminder to scan for that whole "movie" starting. Would you be willing to try using that physical cue to give yourself a heads-up before the doubt takes over completely?

A physical cue... yeah, I think I could try that. Maybe I'll tap my chest twice before I close my eyes, like a reset button. It sounds a little silly, but honestly, I'll try anything at this point if it helps me get a break from replaying that whole scene in my head every night.

That is a wonderful perspective, Cody—and yes, tapping your chest can absolutely act as a neutral, grounding anchor to bring you back to the present moment. Would you be okay setting a timer on your phone for five minutes before bed, so you don't have to rely solely on memory to remember to do the tap and the labeling?

Yeah, a timer sounds like a good backup. My memory's been all over the place since I left the job, so that would probably help a lot. I'll set it for 10:55 tonight, right before I usually try to wind down.

Setting a timer for 10:55 is a brilliant idea because it creates a predictable rhythm, which often feels safer when things are chaotic. Just to clarify the plan: will you tap your chest twice as soon as the alarm dings, wait three seconds to take a deep breath, and then immediately tell yourself, "That's just a story," before letting the images play out?

Okay, so I'll tap twice when the alarm goes off, take a deep breath for three seconds, and then say "that's just a story" before I let the whole thing play out. I think I can manage that. Honestly, having it spelled out step by step makes it feel less overwhelming than trying to figure it out in the moment.

That breakdown into clear steps is going to make a huge difference in taking the pressure off your brain. You've got everything you need to try tonight, so please go ahead and set that timer for 10:55, and I'll check in with you next week to see how that routine landed for you. Take care of yourself!

Hello, thank you for joining us. To start, could you tell me how you're feeling today, perhaps rating your mood from 1 to 10? Before we dive into the agenda, did you notice that voice about being a "loser" when you woke up this morning, or was it quieter than usual?

Hi. Thanks for having me. I'd say my mood is around a 4 today. And yeah, that voice was there this morning, right when I got up and remembered I had to go to work at Nike again. It's rarely quiet, to be honest.

A four out of ten definitely sounds draining, especially when you wake up knowing that familiar critical voice is waiting for you. It’s completely understandable that it hasn’t gone silent yet, and I want to honor your choice to bring it up now rather than dismissing it. Based on what you’ve said, does focusing on unpacking why this thought feels so convincing and stubborn sound like the best place for us to begin today?

Yes, I think that's exactly what I need to focus on. It feels so real and true, like I can't argue with it. I mean, I have a degree in accounting, I could be working in London at some big financial firm, but instead I'm here, processing expenses for sneakers.

It makes total sense that this comparison hurts so deeply, because your degree opened doors you might have expected to walk through, yet the reality feels like a detour. When you contrast that degree with your current daily tasks, does it feel like you’re wasting a lifetime of effort, or does it feel more like your brain is inventing a narrative that fits a belief you already hold, like “I’m not smart enough for serious work”?

That's a good question... I think it's both. I do feel like I'm wasting my skills - I mean, I analyze profit margins for shoe releases. But you're right, there's this deeper part of me that believes I'm just not cut out for the serious work. Like if I was really good enough, I would have found a way to get that London job by now. So I just keep proving myself right every day I stay at Nike.

That "what if" scenario is incredibly painful because it assumes you have control over outcomes that you don't actually influence right now. When you connect the feeling of being a waste of talent to the belief that you weren't chosen for the London firm, does it feel like your worth depends entirely on external validation, or does it suggest you're judging yourself against a standard you created rather than one based on reality?

I think you're onto something there. I never really thought about it as a standard I created myself. I mean, nobody told me I had to work in London to be successful - that was just this dream I built up in my head. But it feels so real, like a rule I have to follow. And yeah, when I didn't get those jobs, I took it as proof that I'm not good enough, rather than just... not getting a job. That's a different way of looking at it.

That is a powerful shift in perspective; realizing that belief wasn't a fact but a story you wrote for yourself changes everything. If we look at that "rule" as just a story, does it feel easier to separate the event of not getting a job from the verdict that you are fundamentally flawed? Let's test that story a little further: can you recall one time recently where you handled a complex problem at Nike, and ask yourself what that suggests about your capabilities regardless of where you are employed?

Well... actually, last month we had this major discrepancy in the quarterly reports for the European division. I caught it before it went to leadership, and I spent three days tracking down the error through four different departments. Everyone was grateful, and my manager said I was the reason we avoided a serious audit issue. But I just brushed it off because... well, because it's Nike, you know? I guess I never let myself see that as real success because it didn't happen somewhere more prestigious. But looking at it now, that took real skill and perseverance.

You've done an excellent job identifying that specific instance of real skill and perseverance, and it's clear how powerful that achievement was for the company. When you let that fact stand alone, without attaching the "prestige" tag, does the weight of that accomplishment start to feel like proof that you *are* capable, regardless of the brand name on the building? Could we try saying aloud that you were the one who saved the day there, just to see how that changes the feeling in your chest?

I... okay, I'll try. (takes a breath) I was the one who saved the day there. I caught the error and I fixed it. Nobody else did that. It's strange saying it out loud - my chest feels a bit lighter, but there's also this nervous feeling, like I'm not supposed to claim that. Like it's arrogant or something. But it is true, isn't it? I did do that.

That internal tug-of-war is a classic sign of your old belief system fighting against the truth you've uncovered; your brain wants to protect you from looking "too successful," but logic knows the facts are undeniable. You've already done the hard work of seeing that this statement is objectively true, so let's move past proving it to you and focus on what happens next. If we accept that you are capable of saving the day at Nike, would you be willing to try saying that same fact to yourself whenever that voice starts whispering you're a "loser"?

Yeah, I think I could try that. It feels a bit awkward, like I'm lying at first, but I just proved that it's not a lie. Maybe if I catch myself calling myself a loser, I can stop and say "wait, remember the European report." It's a concrete thing I can point to. I think that might help quiet the voice a little, or at least make it easier to push back against.

That is a brilliant and grounded strategy; anchoring yourself in a specific, verifiable fact gives you a solid foothold when the abstract criticism tries to pull you under. Before we finalize this plan, does the idea of pausing for just a second to remind yourself of that report sound manageable, or does it feel too demanding to rely on memory right now? If it feels overwhelming, could we instead try writing that sentence down on your phone as a quick reminder you can glance at when the doubt creeps in?

Writing it down sounds really smart, actually. I'm always on my phone anyway, so having it there as a note I can open in a second feels easier than trying to remember the right thing to say to myself when I'm already feeling down. I'll put something simple like "Remember the European report - you saved the day" and maybe even the date. That way I can't argue with it because it's right there in black and white.

That is a fantastic solution; having a written anchor on your phone removes the mental load of recalling the detail when you're already feeling shaky. To make sure we are fully aligned, does agreeing to create that note and use it the moment you feel that "loser" voice rising feel like a fair game for us to start tomorrow?

Yes, that sounds fair. I'll write the note tonight before I go to sleep so it's ready for tomorrow morning when I'm getting ready for work. I think that's a good first step - just having something concrete to push back against that voice. Thank you, this has actually been really helpful today. I feel a little less stuck than when I walked in.

I am so glad to hear that you feel less stuck and appreciated how much clarity this process brought you. Just to confirm our path forward, I'd love your feedback on how we reached that conclusion today—did finding that written anchor feel like the right direction for us to move in, or would you prefer to explore another angle later? In the meantime, please remember to be kind to yourself as you start using this new tool, and I look forward to hearing how your phone note goes once you've tried it tomorrow.

Hello again. To start, could you please check in on how you've been feeling this week, and then we can take a moment to review your plan from last time before deciding what we should focus on today?

Hey. I've been okay, I guess. Still feeling pretty down about the whole fishing thing, especially since I went out last Saturday and came back empty-handed again. It's kind of been on my mind all week, even when I'm training clients.

It sounds like that disappointment from Saturday has been carrying a heavy weight into your work this week, which is understandable given how closely tied you feel to fishing lately. Since we talked about shifting your goal to just "being calm and present," would you like to revisit how you felt when you tried that mantra, or shall we explore what triggered that old sense of failure again this past weekend?

I think... it might help to talk about what happened Saturday. I went to the same spot I always go to, and I saw other people nearby pulling in fish left and right. I tried to just focus on my breathing and the water like we talked about, but I couldn't shake the feeling that I must be doing something fundamentally wrong.

That contrast between trying to stay calm while feeling convinced you're doing something fundamentally wrong is really tough to hold. It sounds like the moment you saw others succeeding, your brain immediately started filling in the gap with that belief that you’re missing something essential, overriding the calming breaths you wanted to focus on. When you caught sight of someone landing a fish, did that specific image spark a different, sharper thought, or was it just a general sense of falling behind?

It was kind of both, but I think the sharpest moment was watching this older guy pull in a bass right next to me. He just looked so relaxed and natural, and I remember thinking, "He's a real fisherman. I'm just pretending." It stung a lot. Like, I'm not even in the same league as him, so why do I keep coming out here and embarrassing myself?

That feeling of standing beside someone who seems naturally good at something while you feel like you're wearing a mask is incredibly painful. It sounds like seeing his ease made your own insecurity spike, convincing you that your presence there is a mistake rather than a choice. Before we unpack that comparison, did you notice any physical signs of stress in your body right before he pulled that bass in, or did the thought just hit you suddenly?

Um, I think my shoulders got really tense all of a sudden, and I remember gripping my rod way too hard. My jaw was clenched too, I noticed it after a few minutes. It's like my body knew I was about to get upset before my brain even fully processed what I was seeing.

It makes perfect sense that your body reacted with tension and grip so strongly; it's often a sign that your nervous system sensed a threat to your self-image before your conscious mind even registered the comparison. That physical reaction tells us your brain was already racing ahead to find proof that you don't belong, rather than giving yourself a chance to just enjoy the water. Since those symptoms were already there before the bass landed, do you think the thought about him being a "real fishman" arrived first, or did your body's tension create the space for that criticism to appear?

That's a good question... I think the tension came first, honestly. Like, I was already bracing for failure before I even saw him catch anything. It's like my body was waiting for proof that I was right about being bad at this. By the time he actually caught the fish, my mind just latched onto it as confirmation of what I already believed.

That's a crucial distinction you've found; it shows your body was anticipating a disaster long before the fish even hit the surface, confirming that the expectation of failure was already driving your reactions. Instead of viewing that tension as a warning sign of impending doom, could we try treating it as a signal that you're fighting against a belief you're no longer willing to accept, perhaps telling yourself, "I am allowed to come here and just be present, even if I don't know how to fish"? Would you be open to testing that gentle reframe during your next visit?

Yeah, I think I could try that. It kind of takes the pressure off, you know? Like, instead of trying to prove I'm a good fisherman, I can just show up and let myself be there without needing to be anything special. I'm a little scared that the tension will still come, but maybe I can notice it and just say, "Okay, that's just the old worry showing up."

That is a very wise observation, and noticing the tension just to label it as the "old worry" is exactly how we begin to separate your physical reactions from your true intentions. It turns a scary sensation into a familiar guest that you can watch without welcoming its message. Since you are feeling a bit hesitant about that first time, let's lock in your plan for next time: will you bring your phone to write down the phrase "Just be present, no need to prove anything," and commit to checking in with your body the moment you feel that familiar tightness in your shoulders?

Yeah, I can do that. I'll save it as a note on my phone so I can pull it up easy. And I'll try to pause and take a breath when I feel my shoulders get tight, instead of just gripping my rod harder and waiting for disappointment. It feels a little weird planning for it, but maybe that's better than just hoping I'll be fine.

That proactive planning is a sign of real growth; it shows you are moving from hoping things get easier to actively choosing how to respond when they don't. Taking that deep breath the moment tension rises gives your nervous system a chance to reset before the old story can take over. Before we finish, I want to make sure you feel supported: does having this specific plan feel manageable for you, or would you like to adjust anything about how you'll use it this weekend?

No, I think this feels good. It's simple enough that I won't forget it, but specific enough that I'll know what to do when the moment comes. Thanks for helping me break it down like this. I'm actually kind of curious to see how it goes this time, instead of just dreading it.

That curiosity is a wonderful mindset to carry into your next trip, and knowing you have a clear path forward makes facing the uncertainty much less daunting. I'm glad we could break it down together until it felt manageable, and I truly appreciate your openness to trying this new approach. For our next session, could you share a quick update on how that plan felt when you used it, or if you encountered any unexpected challenges along the way?

Yeah, I can do that. I'll pay attention to what happens and try to keep it simple, like we talked about. I think I'll even try going to a different spot this time, just somewhere new where I don't have any old memories of failing. That might help me start fresh with the plan.

Changing spots to a place free of old failures is a brilliant strategic move; it removes the external trigger that has been fueling that internal critic for weeks. Bringing that fresh location plus your new "just be present" phrase creates a supportive environment where you can finally test this new way of thinking. I look forward to hearing how that fresh setting feels combined with your new plan next time.
