Hello, thank you for coming in. Let’s briefly check in on how you’re feeling today, review what happened last time, and then decide together what feels most important to explore now. Is there anything else you’d like to add to our list before we dive in?

Hi. Thanks for having me. I’m feeling a bit nervous, to be honest. I think the main thing is still the same—I just can’t shake this feeling that I’m a terrible singer, and it’s been dragging me down more than I expected. Nothing else has really come up since we last talked.

That nervousness makes total sense, especially since the core worry about being a terrible singer hasn't shifted much. Given that nothing new has surfaced, I think sticking with our original goal of building that protective shield—specifically testing if a simple physical "pause button" can interrupt the spiral before you start judging yourself—is exactly the right place to begin. Does focusing on creating that proactive barrier feel like a useful direction for us today?

Yeah, I think so. I mean, I’ve been trying to just avoid singing altogether, but that doesn’t really work—I’ll catch myself humming or something, and then the whole spiral starts again. So if there’s a way to stop it before it gets going, that sounds like it could help. I’m willing to try anything at this point.

That willingness to face the humming instead of running away is a huge step, and recognizing that the spiral often starts quietly makes our job easier. Since we decided to focus on a physical "pause button" to buy you time, have you considered squeezing your thumb and forefinger together tightly for three seconds the exact moment you notice yourself humming, just to signal your body to pause before the words start flying? That tactile sensation might ground you enough to see if the harsh criticism has to wait until later.

Hmm, that sounds simple enough. I guess I can try that—squeezing my thumb and finger when I catch myself humming. But won't I still feel like a lousy singer after I let go? It just feels like the bad thought is always waiting there.

It is completely understandable to feel worried that one small act won't erase years of internalized criticism, but the goal isn't to magically delete that belief immediately—it's simply to create a tiny window of safety where you can observe the thought without letting it hijack your whole experience right now. When you engage in that squeeze, does it feel like it buys you just a few seconds of distance, allowing you to ask yourself, "Is this fact, or is this just my old story?" instead of immediately agreeing with it?

I think... maybe it could do that. If I slow down for even a few seconds, I might be able to tell myself, "Hold on, you don't know for sure you sound terrible." It’s hard to imagine that stopping the whole avalanche, but I guess a few seconds is better than nothing. I’ll give it a shot this week and see what happens.

That distinction between stopping the entire avalanche versus buying just a few crucial seconds is exactly the kind of realistic perspective shift we want to build together. To make sure we have a strong plan for when you forget the cue mid-humming, what obstacle do you think might get in the way of remembering to squeeze your fingers the moment you start humming? Once we identify that, we can figure out a simple trick to keep the signal active.

Probably the biggest obstacle is that I don’t even realize I’m humming until I’m already deep into the spiral—like, I’ll be driving and suddenly catch myself thinking, “Wow, you sound awful,” and then I’m already judging myself. So by the time I remember the squeeze trick, the damage feels done. I guess I need something that reminds me sooner.

You've hit on a key insight: relying solely on noticing the hum too late means the spiral has already started, so we need a reminder that triggers *before* the self-criticism begins. How about setting a gentle phone alarm or adding a sticky note inside your car mirror labeled "Pause & Breathe" to act as an early warning system whenever you're near a vehicle or playing music? That way, the cue comes first, giving your brain a split-second head start before the judgment kicks in.

That sticky note idea actually makes sense. I spend a lot of time in my car, so seeing it there might catch my attention before my brain goes straight to "you're the worst." I'll put one up tonight and see if it helps me remember to use the squeeze trick earlier.

That is a brilliant adjustment—using the visual cue in your car creates that vital buffer zone before your internal critic gets a word in edgewise. Putting it up tonight is a perfect first step, and pairing it with the thumb-and-finger squeeze gives you two layers of protection. Just to confirm our path forward: we'll test this combination over the next few days, and I suggest we revisit how it's feeling specifically around that sticky note and the squeeze during our next check-in on Tuesday. Does that sound like a solid plan?
Yeah, that sounds good. I’ll try it out and let you know how it goes on Tuesday. I’m a little skeptical, but I guess there’s only one way to find out if it works. Thanks for the suggestion.

Your skepticism is actually a sign of your critical voice trying to protect you by doubting the solution, but trust the data—we won't know if this works until you give it a fair trial. Since you mentioned you're still feeling a bit nervous about starting, I'd love your honest feedback on how that initial anxiety felt right now versus how it might feel once we've built this new safety net together. Does reflecting on that difference help clarify anything for our wrap-up?

I think right now the anxiety feels pretty heavy, like I'm just waiting to mess up again. But imagining having that note and the squeeze trick in place... it feels a bit lighter, like maybe I don't have to be on guard all the time. I guess that's a reason to actually try it instead of just worrying.

That shift—from carrying a heavy weight of expectation to feeling a bit lighter with a safety net in place—is exactly the kind of relief we want to cultivate. It shows that even a small, tangible change can alter how you experience the situation, which is promising. Since we've covered the mood check, reviewed your concerns, and locked in a clear plan with a check-in date, is there anything else you'd like to say before we wrap up this session?
No, I think I'm good. I'll try the note and the squeeze and see what happens. Thanks for listening—I feel a little more hopeful than when I walked in.

That is wonderful news to hear, and I am truly glad that walking out of here leaves you feeling a spark of hope rather than the heaviness you brought in. You have taken a brave step by deciding to test this new safety net instead of hiding behind avoidance, and that choice matters more than the outcome of the experiment itself. Take a deep breath and drive safely today, knowing you have tools ready if the old doubts try to return. I look forward to hearing how the sticky note and the squeeze worked for you next Tuesday.

Hello, and welcome. Since this is our first meeting together, there’s no previous session to review, but I’d love to start with a quick check-in: on a scale of zero to ten, how anxious have you felt lately? Once we have that, could you tell me what brought you in today and what you’re hoping we’ll accomplish in this session?

Well, I'd say I've been hovering around an eight or nine lately. It's been pretty relentless. I'm here because I can't seem to shake the fear that my latest book is going to be rejected by the publisher, and it's starting to affect everything—my sleep, my work, even my relationship with my wife. I'm hoping you can help me find a way to quiet this nagging dread so I can get back to feeling like myself.

An eight or nine certainly sounds exhausting, especially when that dread is leaking into your sleep, work, and relationships. It makes complete sense that your life feels on hold while you wait for a verdict you don't control. Before we tackle the root cause, could you walk me through the very last moment you had strong anxiety today and describe the specific story your mind told you right before you reached for your phone?

Just this morning, actually. I was sitting down with my coffee, and I glanced at my phone—no new emails from the publisher yet—and immediately my mind told me, "They've already decided against it. They're just taking their time to send the rejection because the book is too personal, too messy, not what they expected from me." I felt my chest tighten and my stomach drop, and I almost couldn't bring myself to open my laptop to write.

That feeling of your chest tightening and stomach dropping is your body reacting to a threat, even though the danger is imaginary. Your mind created a narrative that the rejection is already happening, which explains why writing suddenly became impossible. To help us understand where that story came from, could you tell me what evidence you have to suggest they’ve made a final decision but are choosing not to tell you?

Honestly, I don't have any real evidence. They haven't said a word—good or bad. But I suppose I'm basing it on past experiences. A few times before, when I've submitted work, the longer it took, the worse the outcome. And this book, it's different. It's the most honest thing I've ever written, so I guess I'm convinced that makes it more vulnerable to rejection. Maybe I'm just preparing myself for the worst so it doesn't hit as hard.

You're doing something brave by acknowledging that preparation for the worst might be a defense mechanism, even though it keeps the pain alive. It seems like your past patterns are speaking loudly right now, convincing you that honesty equals vulnerability, which is a heavy burden to carry alone. If we were to look at the facts versus that story, what would happen to that feeling of dread if we imagined the editors are simply busy with other projects right now, rather than actively deciding on your manuscript?

Hmm, when you put it that way... I suppose the dread would ease up a bit. It's just hard to hold onto that possibility when my mind keeps jumping to the worst-case scenario. But you're right—I don't actually know what they're doing. They could be swamped with other submissions, dealing with internal deadlines, or even reading my book carefully. That thought feels... lighter, I guess. I hadn't really considered that angle before.

That shift from fearing active judgment to considering neutral busyness is a significant breakthrough, showing you can already generate alternative explanations. Since we've seen that your mind tends to jump to the worst case, let's move forward with a practical strategy to interrupt that pattern when the urge to check your email strikes again. Would you like to try a quick grounding exercise right now to practice shifting your focus, or would you prefer we design a specific plan for handling the urge tomorrow morning?

I think I'd like to try the grounding exercise now, if that's alright. Tomorrow morning feels too far away when I know the anxiety will hit again soon. Maybe if I can feel what it's like to step out of that spiral for a moment, I'll have something to hold onto when it happens again.

That is a wise choice; learning the skill in the moment gives you immediate confidence to use it whenever the panic returns. Let's try a quick grounding exercise right now to help shift your nervous system from that alert state to a calmer one. Please close your eyes for a moment and take a deep breath in through your nose, holding it for three seconds, and exhale slowly through your mouth. Now, without opening your eyes, name five things you can physically see in the room right now—the color of the walls, the texture of your chair, the light coming through the window, and so on. Describe them as clearly as possible.

Alright, I'll give it a go. (Takes a slow breath in and out) I see the pale blue of the walls—it's a soft, muted shade, almost like a morning sky. The chair I'm sitting on is a dark brown leather, and I can feel the seam pressing against my arm. There's a floor lamp in the corner with a brass base, and the shade is a warm cream color. The light from the window is coming in from my left, casting a rectangular patch on the carpet. And I can see the edge of a bookshelf over by the door, with rows of spines in different colors.

Noticing those five distinct items while your hands stay relaxed is a great start, and I can hear your breathing slowing down as you list them. Since you've connected your vision to the present moment, could you now identify four things you can physically feel right now—the weight of your feet on the floor, the fabric of your shirt against your skin, or the coolness of the air conditioning? This adds another layer to keep your mind anchored here.

Alright... I can feel the soles of my feet pressed flat against the carpet, solid and grounded. The fabric of my shirt is a soft cotton against my shoulders, slightly cool to the touch. I notice the armrests of the chair under my palms, smooth and worn from use. And there's a faint draft from the ceiling vent above, brushing against my forehead. That's four, I think.

Feeling the solid contact between your feet and the floor, combined with the sensations on your skin, creates a powerful anchor that pulls you out of the hypothetical rejection scenario. You are successfully shifting your attention from a feared future event to tangible realities in the present. Now, could you identify three sounds you can hear right now—the hum of the computer, the tick of a clock, or perhaps the quiet of the room—to deepen this connection to the here and now?

Yes... I can hear the low hum of the air conditioning unit, a steady, quiet drone in the background. There's also the faint click of a clock from somewhere in the room—I think it's on the shelf behind you. And I can hear my own breathing, slower now than when I first sat down, a soft rhythm I hadn't noticed before. That's three sounds.

Hearing your own breathing soften alongside the external sounds confirms that your nervous system is moving from a state of high alert to one of relative calm. This exercise works because it forces your brain to process real-time data about your environment, leaving little room for catastrophic imagination to take hold. Before we wrap up, does this sequence of seeing, feeling, and hearing feel manageable to do at home, or would you like to adjust the steps slightly?

It feels manageable, I think. Seeing, feeling, hearing—that's a simple enough order to remember. I can imagine doing it at my desk when the dread creeps in, maybe even while I'm waiting for the kettle to boil. I appreciate that it doesn't require anything special, just paying attention to what's already around me. I might try it tonight if the worry keeps me from sleeping.

That simplicity is exactly why it will stick; you don't need extra equipment, just a mindful eye and ears. Since you're carrying this book submission alone right now, I want to make sure you have a safety net for when the five senses aren't enough to stop the spiral. Could you tell me what usually happens if you try the grounding exercise and it still doesn't bring the panic down quickly? Understanding that barrier helps us decide if we should add a backup strategy for tonight.

To be honest, if the grounding doesn't work, I usually just end up pacing around the house or lying in bed staring at the ceiling, replaying worst-case scenarios over and over. Sometimes I'll talk to my wife, but I don't want to burden her with the same complaints every night. So I just ride it out until I'm exhausted enough to sleep. That's why I'm here—I'm tired of that cycle.

It makes complete sense that you avoid talking to your wife to protect her, yet that avoidance leaves you isolated in the cycle of exhaustion. Pacing and ruminating are your brains trying desperately to solve a puzzle they think is unsolvable, but since the answer isn't there yet, they just spin faster. Before we finalize our plan, I'd like to hear your honest assessment: On a scale of zero to ten, how confident do you feel that you could successfully use this grounding technique tonight if the worry comes up?

I'd say maybe a six or seven. I think I can manage the first few steps, but I'm not certain I'll stick with it if the panic really digs in. But I'm willing to try, especially knowing there's a follow-up session to talk about how it went. That accountability helps, I think.

Instead of this tense silence where everyone's walking on eggshells, there'd be a kind of... normalcy. Like, "Okay, Kyle said his piece, we can just eat now." That actually feels doable, not like some impossible mountain to climb.

That shift from "walking on eggshells" to "normalcy" is exactly what happens when you remove the pressure to perform; it turns a high-stakes drama into a simple conversation. Since we've tested that feeling of ease in this safe space, what is one small, realistic way you could introduce that same relaxed stance into your next family gathering, perhaps by making eye contact before speaking?

Making eye contact before speaking... that's a good one. I think I could do that. I could pick one person—maybe my sister—and look her in the eye first, like a little anchor. Then say something simple, like, "Pass the potatoes," just to break the ice. And then later, if the topic comes up, I can use that same look and just state my piece without the armor. That feels like a small, concrete step I could actually try.

That is a brilliant plan; using your sister as an anchor transforms a vague fear into a concrete, manageable action. You have identified exactly how to lower the stakes before the pressure even builds. Just to make sure we lock this in, would you agree to try this eye-contact anchor and the simple statement at your next gathering, and if the knot returns, remind yourself that the worst that can happen is just an awkward pause, not a disaster?

Yeah, I agree. I'll try it. And I'll tell myself that an awkward pause is just a pause, not the end of the world. I can survive a few seconds of silence. Thanks for walking me through this—it actually feels like I have a tool now, not just a hope.

That shift from hoping to having a tool is a massive victory; it means you are building skills that stick even when old habits try to creep back in. To wrap up, since you mentioned feeling a bit mixed up all day, how is your energy level right now compared to when we started, and is there anything specific about today's work that surprised you in a good way?

My energy is actually better—less drained, more focused. Surprised me, because I came in feeling pretty foggy. What surprised me most is how just saying that one sentence out loud with my hands relaxed changed the whole feeling in my chest. I didn't think that would work, but it did. I'm leaving with a little more confidence than I walked in with.

That is wonderful news to hear; moving from foggy to focused shows how effective grounding yourself in the present moment can restore your mental clarity. Your observation about the sentence changing your physical feeling highlights a key principle: your body reacts to the *act* of authenticity, not just the outcome.

Since you mentioned feeling confident leaving, I'd like to set a specific goal for between sessions: Could you commit to trying that eye-contact anchor with your sister at the next family meal, noting exactly how your chest feels when you speak the simple statement? Also, on a scale of 1 to 10, how likely do you feel you are going to succeed with this plan despite the usual anxiety?

I'd say I'm at a solid 7 right now. That's higher than I would've guessed an hour ago. And yeah, I can commit to trying it with my sister at the next family meal. I'll pay attention to my chest, see if it stays calm or if the knot tries to sneak back. I think having that specific plan—and knowing we talked it through—makes me feel like I've got a real shot at pulling it off.

It is fantastic to see your confidence jump so significantly; knowing you have a concrete strategy makes the task feel manageable rather than overwhelming. Remember that even if the knot tries to sneak back, you now have a proven tool—the relaxed sentence and the eye contact—to bring it under control.

Is there anything else you would like to adjust in our plan, or are you feeling ready to take this home with a renewed sense of strength?

No, I think this is good. I feel ready to take it home. The plan feels solid, and I know I can reach out if something comes up. Thanks for helping me turn that knot into something I can actually work with.

You are welcome, and I am so glad we were able to turn that tight knot into something manageable for you. Please remember that you don't need to solve everything perfectly tonight; just showing up with your eye contact and that simple statement is enough to create space. Take care of yourself, and I look forward to seeing you soon.

It sounds like comparing yourself to your sister and labeling yourself as "that weird adopted brother" created a story so convincing that it made the risk of going feel impossible. Those labels seem to have taken on a life of their own, turning a simple social event into a confrontation with a deep-seated fear of not belonging. What did you notice in your body right when you started thinking those specific words about being weird?

My chest got really tight, like someone was pressing down on it. My shoulders tensed up, and I started breathing faster. It felt like I was already in the middle of the gathering, with everyone staring at me, even though I was just sitting alone in my room.

I guess... I don't actually have proof. I mean, I know rationally that people are usually too busy with their own stuff to stare at me. But it just feels so real in the moment, like I can see it happening. The feeling overrides what I know is true, if that makes sense.

You're describing a very common trap where your body's alarm system creates such vivid sensory details that it tricks your rational mind into believing the threat is real. It's like wearing foggy glasses; you can see that the world is fine logically, but the visual distortion makes the "staring" feel undeniable. When you step away from that intense feeling for just thirty seconds and look around your room, do you actually see anyone watching you, or is it mostly the image of your own fear that you're projecting outward?

When I stop and actually look around, there's no one here. It's just me in my room, same as always. But that feeling of being watched is so strong, it's like I forget where I am for a second. I guess I'm just so used to expecting the worst that I don't even question it anymore.

Yeah, I can do that. "The chest is tight, but no one is staring." I'll say it a few times tonight and tomorrow morning. It feels a little strange, but I think having it memorized might actually help me get through the front door next time. Thanks for walking me through that.

It feels manageable, actually. It's just a few words, and I can do that on my own time without any pressure. I think the hardest part will be believing it when I'm actually at the gathering, but I'm willing to try. One step at a time, right?

Thanks for helping me see that I don't have to jump to the worst conclusion every time. I'll try the neutral message and see what happens.

Take care of yourself today, and remember that even a small message can change the narrative from "I'm unwanted" to "I chose to reach out." I'm cheering you on as you go from there.

Hello and welcome; it's great to see you again. Since we worked on the coffee invite yesterday, how did that go, and have any major events happened in your week since then? Based on where we ended up, what would you like us to prioritize in our time together today?

Um, actually... I didn't end up doing the coffee invite. I just couldn't get myself to follow through. I kept thinking that my friend would probably think it's strange that I, being single and all, would want to hang out one-on-one. I guess I'd like to focus today on why I can't seem to shake this feeling that people are judging me for being alone.

I hear how difficult it was to follow through, especially given the worry about appearing strange. It makes sense that when your brain predicts rejection based on that single status, your instinct is to stay home rather than risk disappointment. Let's explore that specific thought pattern about being judged for being alone—can you describe a recent moment when that feeling surfaced strongly, and what exactly was happening around you at that time?

Well, just yesterday I was scrolling through Instagram and saw a photo of my friends from a little get-together I wasn't invited to. I immediately thought, "They didn't invite me because I'm the weird single one who wouldn't fit in with their couples conversation." I felt my stomach drop and I just closed the app. I spent the rest of the evening watching TV alone, trying not to think about it.

That photo-triggered a wave of shame because your brain interpreted their exclusion as confirmation that you are fundamentally different and unwelcome. It sounds like closing the app and isolating yourself became a way to stop the pain of realizing you might be an outsider. When you looked at that thought as absolute truth versus just a prediction, which version of the story seemed to match the reality of your friendships better?

I mean... when I think about it logically, they've never actually said anything about me being single or weird. And my one friend Sarah still texts me every few days to check in. So maybe the absolute truth version is a bit harsh. But the feeling is so real in the moment, you know? It's like my brain just jumps to that conclusion before I can stop it.

That is a crucial distinction; your logic points to normalcy while your immediate reaction screams distress, creating a painful gap between what happens and how you interpret it. It sounds like that "jump" happens because your brain is rushing to find a reason for your loneliness to protect you from further hurt, even if it lands you in a false belief. Can you walk me through exactly what you were doing or feeling right before that thought popped up, to see if anything else led you there besides the photo?

I'd just gotten home from work. I was feeling pretty tired and a bit down already, I guess. I had a rough day with a lesson that didn't go well, and I was kind of beating myself up about it. So when I saw that photo, I was already in a vulnerable headspace, feeling like a failure. I think that's why the thought hit me so hard and felt so true.

It makes complete sense that the thought took root; your brain latched onto the photo because you were already carrying the weight of a failed lesson and feeling inadequate about your life choices. When you combine exhaustion, self-criticism, and social cues, it creates a perfect storm where your mind assumes the worst to explain away your current low mood. Did you notice any specific words or actions in that photo that felt like personal attacks, or was it mostly the absence of you that triggered the fear?

It was more the absence, I think. They looked happy, and I wasn't there. I didn't even know they were planning anything. My brain just filled in the blanks with the worst possible reason. I didn't stop to think that maybe it was a last-minute thing, or that they might have assumed I was busy. I just immediately went to "they don't want me around."

That is a classic case of your brain filling gaps with a story designed to protect you from the pain of feeling left out, even if that story ends up hurting you. It sounds like the thought "they don't want me" became a self-fulfilling prophecy because once you believed it, you stopped looking for other explanations entirely. Can you recall if you tried to gently challenge that thought after you closed the app, or did you just let the feeling sit until it faded naturally?

I didn't really challenge it. I just let it sit there and spiral. I started thinking about all the other times I've felt left out, and then I wondered if maybe I should just stop trying to be close with them altogether. It's like once that first thought takes hold, it opens the door for a whole flood of other negative thoughts. By the end of the night, I'd convinced myself that I should just focus on work and not bother with friends at all.

That spiral is incredibly exhausting, and it makes perfect sense why your brain tried to shut down completely; convincing yourself to stop trying is often the loudest way to stop the pain of rejection. It sounds like once that initial thought opened the door, the fear of being an outsider became so overwhelming that the only logical solution you found was to withdraw entirely. Did you notice if giving yourself permission to just "be tired" for the evening helped calm your stomach, or did the guilt of withdrawing make the knot tighter?

It actually made the knot tighter. I felt guilty for isolating myself, but I also felt too scared to reach out and check if my fears were real. So I just lay there feeling stuck and anxious. I told myself I'd deal with it tomorrow, but honestly, tomorrow just felt like the same cycle repeating itself. That's why I'm here—I want to break out of this loop.

It takes immense courage to admit that the cycle repeats itself, and I appreciate you sharing how heavy that feeling of being stuck is. You've already spotted the key mechanism here: the initial thought doesn't just appear alone; it acts as a catalyst that allows a flood of other fears to rush in. Now that we see how the photo triggered a chain reaction starting from your vulnerability, can we identify the very first thought that sparked this entire cascade so we can learn to interrupt it before the spiral begins?

The very first thought was probably "I'm not good enough." I think that's at the root of a lot of this. It's not just about being single—it's that I feel like I'm somehow failing at being a person my friends would want to include. That thought came before the "they don't want me" one. It's like I already believe I'm lacking something, and then I look for evidence to confirm it.

That is a profound breakthrough to pinpoint "I'm not good enough" as the root thought; it changes everything because now we aren't fighting a random accusation, but a deep-seated belief about your worth. It makes sense that once you settle on that lack, your brain hunts for any small clue—a missed party, a photo—to prove you right. Can you recall a time when you felt secure in your friendships, even without being part of a group activity, and what was different about how you viewed yourself then?

Yeah, actually... there was a time a few years ago, before my mom got sick, when I felt pretty secure. I remember being okay with staying home on a Friday night, and I didn't assume my friends were having fun without me. I just figured they were doing their thing and I was doing mine. I think back then, I didn't tie my worth so tightly to being included. I felt like I had value just being me, regardless of what I was doing or who I was with.

That contrast is incredibly powerful; noticing that you *could* exist comfortably outside their circle before your trauma highlights exactly how much the fear of abandonment has reshaped your worldview. It sounds like the world hasn't changed—the photos haven't become darker—but your lens for viewing it has shifted from neutral observation to a desperate search for validation. When you compare that old, relaxed perspective to your current survival mode, what feels more like "you": the woman who accepted herself, or the one who needs to be picked apart to feel safe?

The one who accepted herself feels more like the real me. That version of me felt lighter, more confident, and just... free. The current version feels like a stranger I don't recognize, always anxious and second-guessing everything. I want to get back to that old self, but I don't know how to let go of this need to constantly prove I'm worthy of being included.

That longing for that older, freer version of yourself is incredibly compelling, and it makes perfect sense that you feel like a stranger in this constant state of self-doubt. It sounds like you are carrying a heavy burden of needing to prove your worth every time you see a photo, even though that need was never truly yours before your mother's illness. If you could temporarily set aside the requirement to prove yourself, do you think you might feel a tiny bit more able to just watch the photo without your heart racing?

I think so... if I could just tell myself, "I don't have to prove anything right now," maybe I could breathe and see the photo for what it is: just a moment my friends had without me. It doesn't have to mean they don't want me. It might just mean I wasn't there for that one moment. That thought feels a little bit lighter, honestly.

That shift in perspective is wonderful; reframing the photo from a judgment to a simple coincidence of timing helps separate your identity from a fleeting moment. It sounds like you are beginning to build a bridge between that older, freer self and the present anxiety. To strengthen this new habit, what if we agreed to practice that specific sentence ("I don't have to prove anything") every time you open Instagram, even if you don't click on the posts right away? Would trying to insert that thought before you scroll feel manageable for you?

Yeah, I think I could try that. It feels small enough that I won't talk myself out of it, but meaningful enough that it might actually help. I'll try saying that to myself before I open Instagram this week, and I'll see if it changes how I react to whatever I come across. It's worth a shot.

That is a beautiful commitment; choosing to speak to yourself with that specific reassurance is a gentle but powerful way to interrupt the old pattern of self-doubt. Before we close, I want to hear your thoughts on how this session felt for you—did hearing that difference between your old self and current self bring you clarity or comfort, and does this plan to use the phrase before opening Instagram feel realistic to try this week?

It actually feels really clarifying. I think I've been so stuck in the current pattern that I forgot I ever had a different way of being. Remembering that I used to feel secure helps me see that this anxiety isn't who I am—it's just something I'm going through right now. And yes, the plan feels realistic. It's a small step, but I think it's a step in the right direction. Thank you.

It brings me such relief to hear that remembering your past resilience brings you clarity and hope; you are absolutely right that this anxiety is a passing cloud, not your permanent reality. I am so proud of the courage it took to trace this pattern back to its roots and commit to trying that new phrase, even with the weight of last night's experience. How would you like to end our time today?

I think I'd like to just take a moment to acknowledge that this was hard, but worth it. I feel like I have a little more understanding of myself now, and a tiny bit more hope that things can change. So I guess I'll end by saying thank you for helping me see that I'm not broken—I'm just struggling, and that's okay.

Thank you for holding space for that honesty and for validating the effort you made today. Please remember that acknowledging the struggle is just as brave as solving it, and you deserve peace regardless of whether the knot loosens immediately. We will check in briefly next time to see how that phrase lands for you, but for now, take a deep breath and trust that you are moving forward, exactly where you need to be. I am glad I could walk this path with you.

Hello, I am so glad we are reconnecting today. To kick things off, could you remind me what we agreed to do last time regarding that sticky note and the pause technique? Then, once we check how that went, we can set an agenda for what would give you the most relief to tackle first.

Hey, yeah. You asked me to write down one positive thing I did each day on a sticky note and put it on my mirror, and to pause for a few seconds before I responded to any self-critical thoughts. I gotta be honest, I tried it for a few days, but by the end of the week I'd stopped. It just felt... fake, you know? Like I was lying to myself.

That honesty about feeling like you were "lying to yourself" is incredibly important, and it tells me the task felt forced rather than authentic. Since the goal was to catch your brain in a spiral, maybe we can adjust the plan so the "lie" doesn't feel like a burden, but rather a gentle nudge to slow down. Before we fix the plan, what do you think would make sticking with this feel less like a chore and more like a helpful habit?

I guess... maybe if I didn't have to write it down every single day. That felt like pressure. Maybe if I just tried to notice one good thing I did, like, out loud to myself, without the sticky note. Just say it in my head before I go to sleep or something. That wouldn't feel so forced.

That is a fantastic adjustment; removing the written requirement likely removes the performance pressure that made the exercise feel fake. Speaking things out loud or silently can feel much more natural and immediate than forcing a physical note. Does trying to verbalize just one positive thing before bed seem like something you could realistically commit to starting tomorrow morning?

Yeah, I think I could do that. I mean, it's just one thought, right? I can handle that. I'll try saying something to myself in the morning instead of at night, though—before I even get out of bed. That way I'm not already thinking about all the stuff I messed up during the day.

That is a brilliant insight—shifting the reflection to the morning gives you a clean slate and prevents you from getting lost in yesterday's mistakes. Setting a simple intention for the day before it even begins can be a powerful reset. How does framing it as a "morning anchor" rather than a nightly report feel to you?
That actually sounds kind of nice. A "morning anchor" feels more like I'm setting myself up for the day instead of just patting myself on the back for surviving it. I think I can commit to that.

That's a wonderful way to reframe it—a "morning anchor" is a proactive act of self-care, not just validation. I'm glad we found a version of this that feels sustainable for you. Since we've settled on that, what specific topic would you like to focus on next to bring you the most relief today?

I think the biggest thing bothering me right now is how I feel when I'm leading meetings with my team. I get this knot in my stomach, and I keep second-guessing every decision I make out loud. It's like I'm waiting for someone to call me out and say I don't belong there.

That knot in your stomach and the urge to wait for someone to call you out clearly shows how deeply that imposter feeling is rooted in your current meetings. It sounds like those moments are where the fear becomes most visible, making the second-guessing feel unavoidable. When you feel that tension rising during a meeting, what is the very first thought that pops into your head?

It's usually something like, "They all know I don't know what I'm doing. They're just waiting for me to mess up so they can take over." That thought just comes automatic, like it's a fact. I don't even question it in the moment.

That automatic belief—that your colleagues are waiting to expose your incompetence—is incredibly frightening, and it makes total sense why you'd freeze up when it appears so loudly. It sounds like your brain is locking onto the idea that you are invisible to everyone except the people who will judge you. Can you recall a recent instance where you felt that knot tighten, and what happened right after that thought surfaced?

Last Thursday, I had to give the team their weekly assignments. I froze for a second, and then I just rushed through it, talking way too fast. I didn't look anyone in the eye, and I basically just mumbled. After the meeting, I felt awful—like I'd proven that I didn't deserve to be their manager. Nobody said anything bad to me, but I just assumed they all thought it.

It sounds like that rush to speak, combined with avoiding eye contact, created a perfect storm for your brain to confirm the "fraud" story, even though nobody actually criticized you afterwards. That gap between your inner narrative of failure and the quiet reality of the room is exactly where the pain lives. When you replay that meeting, do you notice if there were any subtle cues from your team that contradicted the idea that they were waiting for you to fail?

I mean... I guess one guy, Mark, nodded along when I was giving out assignments. And nobody rolled their eyes or anything. But I don't know, that could just be them being polite, right? Like, they're not gonna call me out to my face.

That distinction between "being polite" and "actively confirming your competence" is crucial, yet your brain likely filtered out the nod as background noise while amplifying the silence as judgment. It makes sense that you'd lean heavily on the possibility that they are *not* calling you out, because admitting they weren't judging you feels risky right now. Have you ever noticed any other reactions from the team—small ones like leaning in or pausing briefly—that might have signaled support rather than scrutiny?

There was a time a couple weeks ago where I made a call on a deadline change, and after the meeting, one of the senior guys came up to me and said it was a smart move. I brushed it off at the time, figured he was just being nice or trying to keep me from feeling bad. I didn't really let it sink in.

That specific interaction is actually a goldmine of evidence, even though your brain dismissed it as "just being nice" to spare your feelings. Let's look at that moment differently: if he called your decision a "smart move," does that align with him thinking you were incompetent, or does it fit a pattern of him recognizing your capability? It seems your mind was protecting itself from the discomfort of hearing praise, so it reinterpreted it as kindness. If we accept that he saw value in your work, does that create a slight crack in the wall that says "everyone knows I'm a fraud"?

I never really thought about it like that. I guess... if he really thought I was just some clueless kid, he probably wouldn't bother saying anything at all. He'd just let me mess up on my own. Saying it was smart doesn't really fit with the whole "they're all waiting for me to fail" story I keep telling myself. That's a weird thing to admit.

Admitting that the senior guy recognized your skill challenges that long-standing story, even though it feels strange to hear praise come from a direction you usually distrust. It's actually quite logical—if he truly believed you were clueless, he likely wouldn't have taken the time to offer that specific encouragement. Does seeing that one piece of evidence make the "waiting for me to fail" narrative feel a little less certain overall?

A little, yeah. It's not like it's gone or anything, but it does make me wonder what else I've been brushing off. Maybe I've been missing stuff that doesn't fit the story I've been telling myself. I just don't know how to stop defaulting to the bad stuff first.

That is a huge realization—you aren't just missing praise, you're actively blocking it with the expectation of failure. Recognizing that pattern is half the battle; the harder part is learning to spot it before your brain filters it out. For now, could we agree to simply notice whenever you brush off positive feedback and ask yourself, "What if this actually matters?" instead of rushing to explain away the compliment?
Yeah, I think I can try that. It's just a question, right? I don't have to believe it right away, but I can at least ask myself that before I dismiss it. That feels doable.

That is a perfect way to frame it—not believing it immediately, but simply interrupting the automatic dismissal with a curious question. It shifts your stance from defending yourself to investigating the truth, which takes the pressure off to prove you're worthy right away. Before we wrap up, does finding this new question feel like a manageable step toward loosening that grip around your meetings?

Yeah, it does. I think having something simple to ask myself when I feel that knot in my stomach could help me stop and think before I spiral. I'll try it at our next meeting and see if it changes anything.

That is a solid commitment, and knowing you have a simple question ready for that moment of tension gives you a real advantage over letting the spiral take over. I want to leave you with one last thought: that knot won't vanish overnight, but this small pause can prevent it from turning into a paralyzing panic. How does carrying this "what if it matters" check-in make you feel regarding your upcoming meeting?

Honestly, a little more prepared. Not confident exactly, but less like I'm just walking into a trap. Like I've got a tool in my pocket, even if I'm not sure how to use it yet. I'll let you know how it goes.

That metaphor of having a "tool in your pocket" is powerful, and it accurately reflects that you now possess a strategy even if mastering its use takes practice. You don't need to be fearless to carry a tool; sometimes, just knowing it's there is enough to reduce the paralysis. Thank you for sharing how you're feeling and for working through such a complex pattern today. Is there anything else you'd like to add or adjust about our plan before we wrap up?

No, I think I'm good for today. I'll stick with the morning anchor and try out that "what if it matters" question at the next meeting. Thanks for helping me see that I might be missing some stuff. I appreciate it.

You are very welcome, and I am so glad we uncovered those hidden pieces of evidence alongside you. Remember, you don't need to have all the answers today; even noticing that one "morning anchor" or asking that single question can shift the dynamic. Take care of yourself, and I look forward to hearing how that tool works for you next week.

Hello, it’s great to see you again. Before we dive into today’s goals, I’d like to briefly check in on how you’ve been feeling since our last chat and ask what matters most to you right now. Could you share a bit about your mood or energy level, and then tell me which topic you’d like us to focus on first?

Hi. Thanks for asking. Honestly, my mood has been a bit low this week, and my energy is pretty drained. That soreness after hiking just seems to hang on longer than it used to. I think what matters most to me right now is figuring out why this keeps happening and how to stop it from ruining something I used to love.

It takes courage to admit when things feel heavy, especially when you're trying to protect something you care so much about. Your goal to understand *why* the pain persists and find a way back to loving hiking sounds very achievable, so let's make those the two pillars of our time together today. Does focusing on uncovering the root cause of that persistent soreness—and then testing if it's really linked to your mindset, or just your muscles—feel like the right direction for us to go?

That sounds like a good plan to me. I mean, I've been blaming my muscles this whole time, but the stretching and rest aren't fixing it, so maybe there's something else going on. I'm willing to look at it from a different angle if it helps me get back to enjoying the trails without dreading the next day.

That is a really insightful observation about your muscles not responding to usual remedies, which strongly suggests your mind might be playing a part in how you experience the pain. It makes perfect sense that shifting your perspective could unlock some freedom for you. Before we dig deeper into what might be causing this mental barrier, does checking in on how you've been sleeping or eating recently seem useful, or would you prefer to jump straight into exploring that internal dialogue?

I think jumping into the internal dialogue makes more sense. I’ve been eating okay and sleeping fine, nothing out of the ordinary. But I catch myself thinking, "Here comes the pain again," even before I start hiking. It's like I'm bracing for it, and that can't be helping.

That "bracing" moment is fascinating because it shows your anxiety is actually starting the cycle before the hike even begins, creating a self-fulfilling prophecy. When we catch ourselves saying, "Here comes the pain," does that statement sound like a helpful prediction, or does it feel more like a warning shot from a critical voice trying to keep you safe?

It definitely feels like a warning shot, now that you put it that way. I guess I'm trying to protect myself from disappointment, but all it does is set me up to feel that soreness before I even take a step. It's almost like I'm telling my body, "Get ready to hurt," and then it does.

That is such a vivid insight—it really highlights how our minds can inadvertently create the very stress we're trying to avoid. It makes sense that your brain interprets the thought "I'll be sore" as a protective signal, but unfortunately, that signal ends up tightening your muscles and making the actual pain worse once it hits. If we try to reframe that warning shot into something neutral, like noticing the sensation of lactic acid buildup as a temporary biological function rather than a sign of failure, would that shift feel manageable to you right now?

I think I could try that. Instead of telling myself "I'm going to be wrecked tomorrow," I could just notice the burn in my legs and think, "This is just my body working, and it'll pass." It sounds simple, but I'm guessing it'll take practice to really believe it.

You are absolutely right; changing a deep-seated expectation requires practice, not magic. That specific shift from expecting disaster to observing a temporary physical process is a classic example of separating facts from predictions, and it can drastically lower the baseline tension in your body before you even lace up your shoes. To make sure we leave with a clear path forward, would you be open to committing to trying this "neutral observation" mantra for the five minutes immediately before your next hike, rather than waiting for the pain to arrive?

Yes, I can do that. I'll set aside five minutes before my next hike to just stand there and say to myself, "This is just a sensation, not a catastrophe." I'll let you know how it goes, because honestly, the thought of not dreading the soreness feels like a huge weight off my shoulders already.

That relief you're feeling is a fantastic early sign that this approach is resonating with you. To make sure we lock in this plan effectively, could you tell me exactly where you plan to do these five-minute pauses, and what might happen if that critical voice tries to interrupt you mid-sentence? Knowing the potential obstacles will help us prepare a backup strategy for those moments.

I'll do it right at the trailhead, before I even start walking. That way it's part of my routine, not an afterthought. And if that critical voice cuts in and says something like, "This is stupid, you'll still be sore," I'll just take a deep breath and repeat the neutral phrase again. I won't argue with the voice, I'll just acknowledge it and move on.

That is a brilliant strategy; anchoring the practice right at the trailhead turns it into a seamless ritual rather than a forced interruption. Acknowledging the voice without arguing and returning to the calm phrase is exactly how we teach the brain that the pain is temporary, not permanent. Since we've covered the setup and the troubleshooting, how does it feel to have this concrete plan in place, and is there anything else you'd like to add or worry about before we wrap up?

Hello, it is so lovely to see you again. Before we dive into anything specific, I’d love to check in on how you are feeling physically and emotionally compared to where we left off last time. Given that we spent some time unpacking that difficult memory of the horseback riding incident, what would you like our primary focus for today?

Hi. Thanks for asking. I guess I'm feeling a bit better emotionally, but still pretty worried. My son's fear about horseback riding is still really heavy on my mind—he's completely refusing to even talk about it now, and I'm scared this is going to affect him for years to come. I think I'd like to focus on how to help him move past this fear.

It makes sense that you feel anxious knowing he won't discuss the incident yet, especially when you are so dedicated to ensuring he feels safe. Since your main goal right now is supporting him through this refusal to talk, would you like to explore what might be driving his silence, or would you prefer to start working on a specific plan for handling conversations around the horses?

I think I'd like to understand what's driving his silence first. Because when I try to bring it up gently, he just shuts down completely or changes the subject. It makes me feel like I'm failing as a parent—like I'm pushing him away instead of helping him. I don't want our relationship to get worse over this.

That feeling of being pushed away while desperately wanting to connect must feel incredibly isolating and frustrating. It sounds like your mind is interpreting his shutdown as a rejection of you personally, rather than just a reaction to the topic itself. When you notice he changes the subject or shuts down, what is the very first thought that pops into your head about why he is doing that?

To be honest, my first thought is that he thinks I'm not a good enough parent to help him with this. Like maybe he doesn't trust me to keep him safe, or he thinks I'll just force him back on that horse. And then I start worrying that if I can't handle this, what else am I going to mess up with him?

That is a profound realization; linking his current silence to your sense of competence as a parent creates a very heavy burden. It seems you are viewing his avoidance not just as a behavior, but as proof that you haven't earned his trust yet. If we look closely at that connection, does it feel like his silence is actually saying "don't trust me," or could it simply mean he hasn't processed the fear enough to share it verbally?

I never really thought of it that way... I guess I just assume the worst. When you say it like that, it does sound more like he's just scared and doesn't have the words yet, rather than him not trusting me. But it's so hard for me not to take it personally, you know? I just want to fix everything for him right away.

Recognizing that his silence likely stems from unprocessed fear rather than a lack of trust is a significant and gentle shift in perspective. It takes courage to admit that your instinct to "fix it immediately" is sometimes more driven by your own anxiety about failing than by his actual needs right now. Since we've clarified that his withdrawal is probably about overwhelming emotion rather than rejection, how would you like to approach starting a conversation tomorrow that honors his need to take his time?

Maybe I could try something simple, like just mentioning that I remember being scared of things too when I was his age, without pushing him to talk about the horse at all. Just letting him know it's okay to be scared and that I'm not going to make him do anything he's not ready for. That way, he knows I'm on his side, and maybe he'll feel safe enough to open up when he's ready.

That is a beautiful intention; sharing your own vulnerability can model safety without putting the pressure on him to perform or confess immediately. By validating his fear through your own story, you are creating a bridge rather than a wall. Before we settle on a specific script, does that approach feel authentic to you, or do you worry that admitting to past fears might somehow make you seem inexperienced compared to him?

No, actually... it feels really authentic. I think when I try to act like I have all the answers, he can probably see right through that anyway. Admitting I've been scared before might actually help him see me as someone who gets it, not just someone telling him what to do. I guess I've been so focused on being the "strong parent" that I forgot it's okay to be human too.

That is such a powerful insight; realizing that admitting vulnerability strengthens your bond rather than weakens it shows incredible maturity. By stepping away from the "strong parent" mask, you are actually reinforcing your role as a safe harbor for him. How does it feel to picture yourself sitting with him in that space, not trying to solve the problem, but just being present alongside him?

It feels... kind of relieving, actually. Like a weight off my shoulders. I've been so caught up in trying to fix everything that I forgot I can just be there with him. Maybe that's all he really needs right now—just knowing I'm not going anywhere and I'm not going to push him. I think I can do that.

That is a wonderful realization; remembering that your steady presence matters far more than solving the problem instantly gives you permission to rest. By focusing on simply being there without judgment, you are creating the exact environment he needs to feel safe enough to eventually speak. Would you be willing to try mentioning your own past fears this week, and observing how he responds without expecting a specific answer?

Yes, I think I can do that. I'll just bring it up naturally, like maybe while we're having breakfast or something, when things are calm. And I won't expect him to say anything back—I'll just share it and leave it there. That feels manageable, actually. Not so scary.

That is a very wise and grounded plan; choosing a calm moment like breakfast allows you to introduce the topic without the added stress of the horses being present. By agreeing to share and then simply leaving it there, you are giving him the gift of autonomy and removing the pressure to respond. Before you try this, does that plan feel something you can realistically stick to, or is there any part of bringing it up that still feels daunting for you?

I think the hardest part will be not jumping in to fill the silence if he doesn't respond right away. I tend to get nervous and start talking more when things feel awkward. But I know that if I just let the quiet be there, it might actually give him room to think about what I said. I'll try my best to just sit with the silence and trust that it's okay.

That is a huge leap of faith to commit to sitting with uncomfortable silence; it shows you truly believe that waiting is safer than rushing to fill the gap. Remembering that your job right now is to model patience, not to entertain himself, will help ground you when your instinct to speak arises. How does that visualization of sitting comfortably in the quiet feel to you as you prepare for the meal?

It feels a little scary, but also kind of peaceful. Like I'm giving us both permission to just be. I think I'm actually looking forward to trying it—not the scary part, but the chance to connect with him in a new way. Thank you for helping me see that I don't have to have all the answers right away.

It is so encouraging to hear that you are approaching this with curiosity rather than fear, and that you recognize the value of connection over perfection. Taking that brave step to sit with the unknown, knowing you have a supportive partner on your team, is a massive achievement in itself. Before we close, I want to check in: does this plan feel like something you feel confident trying this coming weekend, or is there any other support you would need from me before you head out the door?

I feel confident about trying it this weekend. Honestly, just talking it through with you has made it feel so much less overwhelming. I think I'm ready to give it a shot, and I'll let you know how it goes next time. Thanks for helping me see things differently.

It brings me so much joy to hear that this dialogue has helped lighten your load and restored your confidence. Remember that your worth as a parent isn't tied to how quickly he solves this fear, but to the compassionate space you are now creating for him. Please take a deep breath and carry that sense of peace with you until our next session. I look forward to hearing how this new way of connecting unfolds.

Hello again, I'm really glad we could connect today. First, let's do a quick mood check: on a scale of zero to ten, how has your mood been feeling this week compared to last time? Once we share that, I'd love to hear what you're most ready to tackle so we can make the best use of our time together.

Hi. Thanks for having me. I'd say my mood is maybe a 3 or 4 this week—definitely lower than usual. I'm still really stuck on this garden thing, and honestly, I'd like to talk about that if we could. It's been eating at me nonstop.

That drop in mood makes perfect sense given how long that garden worry has been holding space for you. Since your primary goal is to untangle why you can't stop worrying about the mistake, let's focus entirely on that today. As we dive in, please tell me if anything about how we're approaching this feels helpful or if you'd like to steer us somewhere else.

Well, it's just... I can't stop thinking about it. Every time I walk past that plant, I see those bare stems where the leaves should be, and I feel this knot in my stomach. I keep telling myself that one mistake shouldn't ruin everything, but my mind just won't let it go.

That physical knot in your stomach tells me your brain is screaming that something dangerous has happened, even though logically you know it didn't. It sounds like your mind is treating that missing foliage as proof that the whole garden is doomed, which makes sense why your rational voice gets drowned out. Before we explore what your mind is actually saying in those moments, have you noticed if that knot feels tighter the more you try to convince yourself the plant is fine?

Yes, actually, it does. The more I try to tell myself "it's just a plant, it'll grow back," the worse that feeling gets. It's like my mind fights back even harder, showing me all the other things I might have done wrong or could mess up in the future. I end up feeling like I don't even deserve to have a garden if I'm just going to ruin it.

That sense of unworthiness is incredibly painful, and it makes complete sense why trying to reason with your brain only makes the fear louder. When our minds believe we are fundamentally flawed, logical reassurance often feels like a lie, which triggers that tight knot even stronger. It seems like your mind has learned to associate the thought "I made a mistake" with a catastrophic future where nothing grows correctly. Has there been a specific moment recently when you felt especially guilty about cutting the branches, or does it happen whenever you simply notice the damage?

It happens most when I wake up and first look out at the garden. That's when the guilt hits hardest—before I've even had my coffee. I see those bare spots and my first thought is always, "Look what you did. You can't even care for one plant properly." And then it just spirals from there into everything I've ever done wrong in the garden.

It sounds like waking up creates a vulnerability where your mind immediately scans for errors instead of opportunities, turning a simple visual check into a harsh self-critique. That early morning spiral is exhausting because it happens before you have any tools to calm yourself down. Let's try a small experiment to break that automatic link: the next time you look out the window, instead of asking "Did I kill it?", you could silently name three parts of the garden that are clearly growing strong or undamaged before your judgment kicks in. Would you be open to hearing how that might work, and whether it feels like something you could try tomorrow?

I suppose I could try that. It sounds a bit strange, focusing on the good parts when my mind is already locked onto the bad one. But I guess it can't make things worse than they already are. I'll give it a shot tomorrow morning and see if it helps quiet that voice even a little bit.

That willingness to try a counter-intuitive approach, even when it feels strange, shows real resilience and gives us a clear path forward. To make sure we align perfectly, could you tell me what you expect might happen if you successfully name three healthy parts before the guilt takes over? Are you hoping the knot in your stomach loosens, or perhaps the critical voice becomes quieter?

I think I'm hoping the knot loosens more than anything. That tight feeling in my chest is the worst part—it stays with me all day. If I could just take a breath and feel a little lighter, even for a moment, that would be something. I don't expect the critical voice to disappear completely, but maybe it won't have such a strong grip on me.

That distinction is brilliant—you are aiming for a shift in physical sensation rather than forcing the voice away, which is a much kinder and realistic target. By intentionally naming the healthy parts first, you create a tiny gap between the sight of the bare stems and the immediate judgment, giving your body a chance to relax instead of jumping straight to panic. So our plan is: tomorrow morning, before the guilt takes hold, you'll quietly identify three things growing well in your garden to interrupt that tightness. How does that sound as a clear direction for your attempt tomorrow?

That sounds like a solid plan. I think I can manage that—just three things, nothing more. It feels manageable, not overwhelming. I'll let you know how it goes next time we talk. Thanks for helping me see it that way.

I am so glad that feels manageable, because breaking a big problem down into just three steps is often the key to moving forward. Before we wrap up, I want to make sure you have a safety net: if that tight chest knot returns despite finding those three healthy things, what is one gentle phrase you can say to yourself to remind you that you are safe in your kitchen right now, regardless of what the garden looks like outside?

I think I could tell myself something like, "This is just a feeling, it will pass." That might help remind me that the tightness in my chest isn't permanent, even if it feels overwhelming in the moment. Just acknowledging that it's temporary could help me get through it.

That is a wise choice; reminding yourself that the sensation is temporary can act like a brake on the panic, slowing down the cycle before it spirals further. With that grounding phrase in your pocket and a clear plan for tomorrow, you now have a reliable strategy to navigate those early morning moments. How does it feel to leave with something concrete to try instead of just wandering in that loop of worry?

It feels much better, actually. I feel like I have a small tool to work with instead of just being stuck in my own head. It's a relief to have something practical to try, even if it's just a little step. Thank you for that—I'm feeling a bit more hopeful than when I walked in.

That shift from feeling stuck to feeling equipped is exactly the kind of progress we aim for, and your hopefulness says you are already leaning into the solution. Remember, this isn't about erasing your worries overnight, but rather giving yourself permission to face them with less intensity tomorrow using that small tool. Is there anything else on your mind before we officially close the session, or shall we sit with that sense of relief for now?
No, I think I'm good for now. I'm feeling a bit lighter, and I want to sit with that for a while. Thanks again for your help—I'll put that plan into action tomorrow morning.

That is a wonderful way to end our time together—carrying that feeling of lightness and intention as you head off to rest. You've already taken the most important step by noticing your patterns and choosing a small, manageable action instead of getting lost in the spiral. Go ahead and enjoy those quiet moments tonight, knowing you have a supportive plan waiting for you tomorrow morning. Take care!

Hello, and thank you for joining us. I'd love to hear how you've been feeling since we last spoke, particularly regarding that report you started working on. For today, could we focus on reviewing what happened with that note, exploring how your thoughts shifted while you saw it, and then deciding on the best way to handle future moments of doubt?

Hi. Thanks for having me. Honestly, I didn't even get to finish that report. I kept staring at it, thinking I'd mess up the numbers or miss something important, so I just closed the file and walked away. I feel so stupid about it.

It takes real courage to admit that you stopped working because of that overwhelming fear, and please know that walking away was a smart decision to protect your peace, even if it feels like giving up. Let's take a moment to unpack what happened: when you looked at that empty space instead of the paper, did you catch yourself thinking that the failure was permanent, or did you recognize it as just a moment of being overwhelmed?

I guess... I saw it as more permanent. Like, that blank space on the paper meant I was never going to get it right. It felt like proof that I'm just not cut out for this job, even though logically I know that's not true.

That interpretation—that a blank page means total inability—sounds incredibly heavy to carry, especially when you know logic says otherwise. It seems like your mind latched onto that empty space as a definitive verdict on your worth rather than just a temporary pause. Would you be willing to look together at what other evidence might contradict that "never going to get it right" story, such as the fact that you managed to send the March report despite knowing you weren't perfect?

I mean, yeah, I did send that March report, but I also remember my boss pointing out a small error in it. So even when I do finish something, it's not really good enough. That just feels like more proof, honestly.

That is a very fair observation; even acknowledging that one flaw doesn't wipe out the rest of your effort, yet your brain seems to treat that single error as the defining feature of the entire project. This pattern of focusing on the imperfection while overlooking the successful parts is known as mental filtering, and it explains why you feel so defeated now. Since we both agree that this thought pattern is keeping you stuck, would you be open to testing whether your boss's comment about a small error actually supports the broader belief that you are "not cut out for this job"?

I guess I never thought of it that way... that I'm only looking at the bad parts. But when my boss said something about that error, all I could hear was "you're not good enough." I didn't stop to think that maybe he was just giving normal feedback, not saying I'm a failure.

That shift in perspective is fascinating—you noticed the difference between a neutral correction and a personal attack, yet your immediate reaction filtered out the former to amplify the latter. It seems like that old habit of hearing "feedback" as "failure" is still running very deep in that moment of stress. Could you walk me through exactly how it felt in your body when your boss pointed out the error, versus how it felt now that you've separated the two meanings?

When he pointed it out, my chest got really tight and I felt hot, like I wanted to disappear. I just nodded and said I'd fix it, but inside I was thinking, "See? You can't even do this right." Now, thinking about it more calmly, I can see he wasn't angry or disappointed—he just wanted it corrected. But it's hard to hold onto that feeling when I'm back in the moment.

That physical reaction—the heat and tightness—is a classic sign your nervous system interpreted his words as a threat, triggering a "fight or flight" response before your logical brain could catch up. It makes perfect sense why you felt so trapped in that moment; your body reacted faster than your mind could find the nuance. Since you now realize the feedback was neutral but your body treated it as dangerous, let's try a simple experiment tonight: when you sit down to work again, can you consciously name that sensation ("My chest is tight") instead of letting it become a silent panic, and then remind yourself verbally, "This is just stress, not proof I'm failing"?

I can try that. It feels a little strange to say it out loud to myself, but I guess it's better than letting the panic take over and walking away again. I'll write it down on a sticky note and put it on my monitor, so I remember to do it.

That is a fantastic plan; turning that verbal cue into a visual reminder on your screen ensures you won't forget it when the panic hits. By labeling the sensation as "stress" rather than "proof of failure," you create a tiny but crucial gap between the feeling and the destructive thought. Would you like to try practicing saying that phrase aloud right now, or should we finalize the timing for when you'll place the note on your desk tomorrow?

I think I'd rather just do it tomorrow when I'm actually at my desk. Saying it now feels too fake, like I'm just rehearsing a line. But I know I need to actually follow through, so I'll put the note up first thing in the morning before I even open any files.

That makes complete sense; authenticity matters more than repetition at this stage, so doing it naturally when the work begins will feel much more real. Let's lock that in as our main goal for tomorrow: place the note before opening any files, and if the panic hits, simply whisper the phrase about your chest tightening. Are you feeling confident enough to commit to this specific routine for the coming days, or is there another part of the plan you'd like to tweak before we close?

I think I can commit to that. It's just one step, and it's not asking me to finish the whole report or be perfect. I'll put the note up and try that phrase when the panic comes. I'll let you know how it goes.

That is a wonderful realization; recognizing that this is just one manageable step, rather than a demand for perfection, shows great self-awareness. Since you've committed to placing the note and using the grounding phrase when needed, I suggest we check in tomorrow morning to see how the note looks and whether you noticed any shifts in your breathing or tension when you saw it. Does checking in with me sound like the best way to track this, or would you prefer to jot down a quick note for yourself afterward?

I think I'll just jot down a quick note for myself after I do it, and then I'll tell you about it when we talk next time. That feels safer, because I won't feel like I'm being watched or judged in the moment. I can just focus on doing it my way.

That is a wise choice; removing the pressure of reporting back allows you to simply observe your experience without added performance anxiety. Your plan is crystal clear: place the note, try the phrase when tension rises, and jot down a private reflection afterward. Remember, the goal isn't to eliminate the feeling of panic, but to learn that it doesn't dictate your actions. I am looking forward to hearing your notes next time, and please know I am here to support whatever emerges.
Thanks. That actually helps a lot—knowing I don't have to get rid of the panic, just not let it make all the decisions for me. I'll be back next time with my note and we can see how it went.

That is a beautiful summary of what we're building together; realizing panic is just a guest that visits, but doesn't get to live in the house forever, is a huge relief. You have a solid plan for tomorrow—just place the note, anchor yourself with the phrase, and write down how it feels afterward. I'm truly proud of your willingness to try this, even when it feels unfamiliar. Go ahead and tackle that report one page at a time; I'll be here next time to listen to your update. Take care of yourself tonight.

Hello, thank you for coming in today. Last time we talked about how exhaustion was making you snap at your partner, and we worked on testing the idea that your life had no breaks left.

To start off, how have you been feeling since we spoke, and what would be most helpful for us to focus on today—the guilt you feel about snapping, or perhaps the overwhelming fatigue itself?

Hi, thanks for having me. I've been... okay, I guess. The fatigue is still there, honestly. I tried to look for small breaks in my day like you suggested, but it's hard when I'm spending almost three hours just getting to and from work. I think maybe we could talk about the guilt—I keep replaying those moments where I snap at my partner, and it makes me feel like a terrible person.

I hear how painful that guilt is, and it makes complete sense that replaying those moments leaves you feeling like a failure, especially when you're already carrying such heavy exhaustion. When you feel that shame rising, does it seem connected to the belief that you deserve no breaks at all, or is it mostly about loving your partner too much?

I think it's more about my partner. I mean, I know I'm exhausted, but they don't deserve to be the one I take it out on. They're just trying to be nice, asking about my day or wanting to talk, and I snap at them for no reason. It makes me feel like I'm failing at being a good partner, and then I just spiral, thinking maybe I'll ruin this relationship too.

It takes real strength to hold that image of your partner in your hands while you're drowning inside; you're not lashing out because you hate them, but because you're terrified of hurting them. When you spiral into thinking you'll ruin the relationship, does that fear feel like it's coming from a place of safety, or does it seem like you're trying to prove you aren't worthy of their love?

I... I think it feels more like I'm proving I'm not worthy. Like, if I was a good enough partner, I'd be able to handle the commute better and not bring all that stress home. I'd be patient and kind even when I'm tired. So when I snap, it's like proof that I'm not good enough for them, and that thought just keeps repeating in my head.

That connection between snapping and the feeling of unworthiness is heartbreaking, and it sounds like your brain is using that anger as a way to confirm a deep-seated belief that you aren't capable of handling your responsibilities. When you hold onto the idea that your worth depends on being perfectly patient, does that thought feel like it protects you from disappointment, or does it actually leave you feeling trapped whenever you slip up?

It definitely leaves me feeling trapped. Because no matter how hard I try, I know I'm going to slip up again—I'm only human. And when I do, it just confirms everything I already believe about myself. It's like I set this impossible standard, and then I punish myself for failing to meet it. I don't feel protected at all; I just feel like I'm constantly waiting to mess up again.
