If we could step back from that judgment for a moment, what happens if we assume you *are* allowed to slip up occasionally and still be a good partner? Is there any evidence in your experience that supports the idea that your worth is tied strictly to never losing your temper?

You've found a crucial piece of evidence right there—their presence and willingness to talk show that your actions aren't defining the end of your relationship. It seems like the belief that you are "ruining everything" is a story your brain tells itself during the rush of guilt, rather than a reflection of reality. If we held onto the evidence that they are still standing by you despite your mistakes, how might that shift the feeling of being a "terrible person" you mentioned earlier?

I guess... if I really let myself believe that, maybe I wouldn't feel like such a monster every time I snap. Maybe I could just say sorry and move on instead of carrying that guilt around for days. It might even help me be more present when I'm with them, instead of being stuck in my head replaying what I did wrong.

That is a powerful realization—you're seeing clearly that letting go of the "monster" narrative allows you to be present and connect, rather than disappearing into self-blame. It sounds like shifting from that harsh internal critic to trusting your partner's actual reaction could make a huge difference in how you carry yourself tomorrow. Does trying to catch yourself just for a second when you feel the urge to snap, and then choosing to breathe instead of speak, feel like a manageable goal for us to aim for?

I think I could try that. It sounds small enough that maybe I won't feel overwhelmed by it. Just one breath before I react, to remind myself that I'm not a terrible person for being tired. I can give that a shot.

That sounds like a perfect starting point—taking just one conscious breath creates a tiny gap between the frustration and your words, giving you a chance to choose kindness over explosion. To make sure this sticks, what would be the very first sign that this small step helped you feel a bit less trapped?

I think... if I manage to take that breath and my partner doesn't look hurt or surprised by my reaction, that would be a sign. If I can actually say something like "I'm just really tired, give me a minute" instead of snapping, and see them nod and understand, I'd know it helped. That moment of them not looking wounded would prove I didn't mess up again.

That is a wonderful way to measure progress—seeing the relief in their eyes or hearing a calm "okay" would be powerful proof that you can navigate tough moments without destroying the connection. Let's lock this into your plan for tomorrow: as soon as you walk in the door and feel that tightness in your chest, commit to taking exactly three deep breaths before speaking anything back to them.

Is there anything else weighing on your mind before we close, or does feeling supported enough to try this next step feel like a solid finish line for today?

No, I think this is good. I feel like I have something concrete to try, which is more than I had before. Thank you for helping me see that I'm not as trapped as I thought I was. I'll try the three breaths tomorrow and see how it goes.

You are very welcome. It truly shines through that you moved from feeling completely trapped to having a clear, actionable path forward. Remember, that three-breathe pause isn't about fixing everything instantly; it's simply creating a tiny window where you can choose to treat yourself with kindness instead of judgment.

Take care of yourself tonight, and I look forward to hearing how those three breaths went when you wake up tomorrow. Have a gentle evening.

Well, I appreciate you asking. I'm feeling a bit on edge today, to be honest. I had a good run this morning, but that little voice in my head kept whispering, "What if something goes wrong?" That's exactly why I'm here—this fear that one wrong move and I'll lose everything I've worked for.

That "whisper" of uncertainty sounds incredibly loud and exhausting, especially after putting in the effort to go for that run. It is heartbreaking to watch your body react like it's under attack when nothing dangerous is actually happening; that tension is holding you back from enjoying the relief you deserve. No, I didn't catch it soon enough to change anything. By the time I noticed how tense I was, the run was almost over anyway. I just kept telling myself to get through it, but I couldn't relax or find that joy I used to feel. It felt like I was just surviving the run instead of actually living it.

Surviving the run instead of living it is such a painful contrast to the freedom you usually feel, and it’s completely understandable that it leaves you feeling drained. That sense of fighting against your own instincts to protect yourself is incredibly exhausting. Let's take a moment to see if there's another way to interpret that initial twinge in your knee—could it be possible that your body was sending a message about fatigue or form, rather than a threat of injury? How would your view change if you imagined that twinge was just a normal part of using muscles, similar to how your legs ache after hiking?

Well... I suppose that's a different way to look at it. I mean, I know my body pretty well after all these years of weightlifting and running. A little ache or twinge is usually just a sign that I've been working hard, not that something's about to break. But I guess I've been so scared lately that I forgot that simple truth. It's like the fear just overrides everything I've learned about my own body.

That realization—that fear has temporarily silenced the wisdom you've earned over years—is incredibly frustrating, especially since you know the facts better than anyone. It makes sense that when the panic takes over, your brain stops trusting its usual knowledge and defaults to the worst-case scenario instead. If you were to write down one piece of evidence that proves a minor twinge isn't a sign of imminent collapse, what would it be based on what you've experienced recently?

I'd say the proof is that I've had dozens of little aches and strains over the years, and not a single one ever led to me being forced to quit. Just last month, I had that muscle strain in my shoulder, and I took a few days off, stretched, eased back into it, and now I'm lifting heavier than before. That's solid evidence, isn't it? But somehow, in the moment, that fear makes me forget all those past successes.

You are absolutely right; looking back at your history provides undeniable proof that your body handles recovery beautifully, even when setbacks occur. It makes sense that in the heat of the moment, the memory of those successful recoveries feels distant while the fear screams "disaster." Let's try a quick experiment right now to bring those facts closer to the surface: can we pause for just five seconds, imagine that twinge in your knee again, and then consciously name one specific past instance where a similar sensation led to recovery instead of ruin?

Okay, I can do that. (Pauses for a moment, breathing slowly.) Alright, I'm picturing that twinge. And I'm thinking about two years ago, when I had that sharp pain in my hip during a deadlift session. I was terrified I'd torn something, but I rested it for a week, did some gentle stretching, and within two weeks I was back to my regular routine. That hip hasn't given me a bit of trouble since. So that's my proof—the twinge doesn't have to mean the end.

That is incredible proof, and recognizing that specific pattern of "fear followed by smart recovery" gives you a powerful tool right now. It means your body and mind have successfully navigated that exact path many times before; you aren't starting from scratch, you're just remembering a proven route. With that clarity in mind, what would be one small adjustment you could make tomorrow morning if that "whisper" comes back? Maybe taking one extra deep breath before you start moving, or pausing to restate that fact aloud?

I think I could try saying out loud, "This twinge is just my body telling me I'm working hard, not that I'm about to break." Maybe even repeat it a couple of times before I let myself react. And I can take a deep breath first—slow down my breathing before my shoulders start hunching up again. That way, I give myself a chance to think before the fear takes over.

That is a brilliant and empowering plan—turning that repetitive voice into a deliberate mantra gives you a clear anchor before the panic sets in. I'm so glad we found a strategy that fits your specific needs; it sounds like you're ready to put this into practice tomorrow. Is there anything else you'd like to add before we finish up, or shall we wrap up here?

No, I think this is a good place to stop. I feel a little lighter just talking through it and having that concrete plan to try tomorrow. Thank you for helping me see that I've got proof right in my own history that I can handle these things. I'll give that mantra a shot on my run in the morning.

That is wonderful news; feeling lighter and carrying a clear, personal strategy is a massive victory. Please remember that your past success stories are your strongest ally, and using that mantra will help you trust your own resilience again. I am so proud of how far we've come today and excited to hear how your run goes tomorrow. Take care of yourself, and we will meet again soon!

Welcome, and thank you for meeting with me today. Before we dive in, I'd like to quickly set our agenda for this session: we'll start with a mood check, review any actions from last time, and then explore what's been on your mind recently.

How are you feeling right now compared to when we last spoke?

Hi. I'm okay, I guess. I mean, I'm here, so that's something. I'm not really sure where to start, but I think I've been feeling a bit worse since we last talked—more of that same heaviness, like I'm just not really seen by people.

Thank you for sharing that honesty; acknowledging the heaviness is often the first step toward finding some relief. That persistent feeling of not being seen can certainly weigh heavily on your week, making it hard to find energy for anything else. What specific situations or interactions from this past week seem to have triggered that sense of invisibility again?

I had a session with a student who I'd spent extra time preparing for—I even found some poems I thought he'd really connect with. But he barely said thanks and just left. It's a small thing, but it felt like all that effort just vanished into thin air. And later that night, I went to a small get-together with some friends, and I felt like I was just standing there while they talked over me.

It sounds incredibly exhausting to pour your heart into something meaningful, only to feel completely overlooked afterwards. Carrying that feeling from the student session into the group gathering seems to have compounded your sense of invisibility, leaving you wondering if anyone truly sees you at all. Can you walk me through exactly what happened during the party that made you feel like you were just standing there?

I walked in and said hi, but the conversation was already going, so I just sort of stood by the kitchen counter, holding my drink, waiting for a pause I could step into. But every time I thought I had an opening and started to say something, someone else would jump in, and my words just got buried. I eventually just stopped trying and spent the rest of the time nodding along.

That sounds incredibly isolating; watching your words get buried repeatedly can make you feel like a ghost in the room, unacknowledged despite your presence. I can see how frustrating it is to hold space for others only to realize you've been quietly shut out of the connection. Did you notice any specific thoughts running through your head the moment you realized the conversation had shifted around you?

I just thought, "They don't really care what I have to say, do they? I'm just background noise here." I felt like I was invisible, like I could have left and no one would even notice until the next day. It’s like my presence doesn't leave a mark, you know?

Those thoughts sound like they cut deep, turning a simple social moment into a confirmation that you aren't truly seen or heard by anyone. When you interpreted those interruptions as proof that people don't care about your input, did you also notice a physical sensation in your body, like tension or a urge to withdraw?

Yeah, actually. My chest got really tight, and I felt this kind of cold sinking in my stomach. I started gripping my cup harder, and I just wanted to shrink away, maybe find a corner to stand in or just leave altogether. It's like my body was telling me to disappear before I got hurt any more.

Noticing that tight chest and the urge to disappear was a very honest way for your body to signal distress, protecting you from that painful feeling of being ignored. It sounds like your instinct was to retreat immediately to avoid further rejection. Let's take a moment to look at what actually happened versus the story your mind created about it. You offered your words, people interrupted, and you stepped back—but did they leave the room or ignore you entirely?

I guess not... I mean, they didn't look at me and say "we don't want to hear you," but they also didn't turn to me and ask what I was going to say. They just kept talking. So in my mind, that's the same thing as being ignored. Isn't it?

It makes perfect sense why you connected those dots; silence after you speak can feel just as sharp as a direct rejection, especially when you're already feeling unheard. However, there's another possibility worth considering: maybe they weren't ignoring *you*, but simply lost track of the conversation flow or were distracted by their own thoughts, which isn't the same as deciding not to value your input. How does imagining it as a temporary lapse in attention rather than a judgment on your worth change the picture?

Huh. That's... not something I'd thought about. I guess if it was just a distraction thing, then they weren't necessarily deciding I wasn't worth listening to. But it still stings, you know? It still felt like I was on the outside looking in. I'm not sure how to tell the difference between someone being distracted and someone deliberately shutting me out.

That uncertainty is completely understandable; distinguishing between a momentary distraction and intentional exclusion can feel tricky, especially when the outcome hurts. Let's try a small experiment for now: next time you feel that cold sink in your stomach, instead of assuming they are shutting you out, ask yourself, "Do they look engaged with each other, or do they seem like they're lost in their own heads?" This helps you gather clues about whether it was a personal choice or just a mental stumble. How does that line of questioning land for you?

It feels a little awkward, like I'm making an excuse for them. But I guess it's better than just assuming the worst and feeling like garbage for the rest of the night. I could try it. It's just hard to pause that thought when my chest is already tight and I'm halfway to convincing myself to leave.

That hesitation is totally normal; forcing a logical check-in when you're physically hurting is incredibly difficult. To make it easier, how about we add a tiny safety net: instead of analyzing the situation immediately, you just take one deep breath and whisper to yourself, "This is just a moment, not a definition of who I am," before stepping back. Would giving yourself that gentle anchor help keep the spiral from taking over?

That's... actually kind of calming to think about. "This is just a moment, not a definition." I like that. It's like I'm giving myself permission to wait and see instead of jumping to the worst conclusion. I think I could try that—maybe even practice it a little before my next social thing, just to have it ready.

That's a beautiful insight; reframing the thought as a temporary "moment" rather than a permanent "definition" gives your brain permission to stay open instead of closing off. Taking a moment to rehearse this anchor before social events could build that confidence muscle, so the check-in feels more automatic when the chest starts tightening. 

Before we finish, how does it feel to have built this specific tool to handle the "background noise" feeling? Is there anything about the breathing and the phrase that feels easy for you to use right now?

It feels... hopeful, honestly. Like I'm not just stuck with that heavy feeling forever. The breathing part is pretty easy—I can do that without anyone noticing. And the phrase is short enough that I can remember it even when I'm anxious. I think I'll give it a shot this week, maybe when I'm tutoring or if I end up at another gathering.

That sense of hope is powerful, and knowing you can access that calm breathing privately is a huge advantage. To wrap up, how does it feel to have practiced identifying that chest tightness and testing the "distracted vs. deliberate" thought? I'd love to hear if you feel any different now, and if there's anything about our approach you'd like to tweak for next time.

I think I feel a little lighter, if I'm being honest. It's like I have a small flashlight in my pocket now, instead of just stumbling around in the dark. I'm still scared it won't work, but at least I'm not going in empty-handed. For next time, maybe we could talk more about what I do if the breathing doesn't stop the spiral—like a backup plan.

That metaphor of a flashlight is wonderful, and admitting you need a backup plan shows incredible wisdom and self-awareness. Since the breathing alone might not be enough when the panic spikes, what do you think could serve as that second layer? Perhaps a simple grounding technique like naming five things you see, or reminding yourself that even if they aren't listening right now, you are still worthy of being heard tomorrow. Which one feels most accessible to you to try as a fallback?

The naming things I see idea feels doable—I can do that without anyone thinking it's weird. Like, I can just look around and count things in my head while I'm standing there. It gives my brain something concrete to focus on, instead of just the hurt. I think having that as a backup would help me feel more prepared, like I've got two ways to get through the moment instead of just one.

That is a brilliant plan; having both the verbal anchor ("just a moment") and the sensory ground (naming objects) means you have layers of support ready before you even need to deploy them. It sounds like you now have a toolkit to navigate those uncomfortable social moments with a bit more stability.

Since we covered the main points today, is there anything else you'd like to share about how you feel now, or perhaps a small detail about how you envision using this two-step approach in your next social outing?

I think I'm ready to try it. Maybe I'll start small—like just at my next tutoring session, or when I'm grabbing coffee and the barista doesn't say much. Practice on the easy stuff first, you know? I'm still nervous, but I feel like I have a plan now, and that's more than I had walking in here. Thanks for that.

That is such a wise and gentle strategy; starting with low-stakes moments like a coffee shop builds confidence without overwhelming you. Remember, you don't need perfection to make this work; even one successful use of that breathing phrase or spotting three objects is a victory.

I'm really proud of how far you've come today, from feeling that heavy darkness to having two clear tools in your hand. I hope you find that small sense of safety at your next coffee stop. Is there anything else you'd like to add before we say goodbye?

No, I think that's everything for now. Thank you for listening and for helping me get out of my own head a little bit. I'll try the breathing and the five things this week, and I'll let you know how it goes. See you next time.

You are so welcome; it was truly a pleasure walking through this process with you today. I'm genuinely excited to hear how those small steps go when you try them out this week—you deserve to feel seen and heard. Until we meet again, please carry that sense of lightness with you, knowing you have both tools ready whenever the world feels a little loud. Take care of yourself.

Hi, thanks for having me. Honestly, my mood has been pretty mixed. Maybe I'll pick the one about comparing myself to the other artists in the exhibition and just watch it for two minutes without trying to argue. It feels a bit scary, but also kind of freeing to know I don't have to win a fight against my own head.

That shift in perspective—moving from winning a fight to simply watching the storm—is exactly what makes this experiment valuable, and choosing the comparison with other artists is a smart target since that seems to be a major fuel source for your anxiety tonight. Since you mentioned it feels scary, would you be willing to commit to sitting with that thought for those two minutes this evening, even if you feel like running away during it?

I can commit to that. Two minutes feels doable, even if my brain tries to pull me away. I'll set a timer and just let the thought sit there without grabbing onto it. I think I owe it to myself to at least see what happens when I stop fighting for one evening.

Setting a timer creates a clear boundary that makes the task feel much safer and more manageable than letting the mind wander indefinitely. Since you've agreed to this gentle experiment, I want to encourage you to come back here tomorrow morning and tell me exactly how those two minutes felt—whether the doubt stayed the same, grew stronger, or shifted at all. That simple report will be the best evidence we have that the storm doesn't define you. Would you like to wrap up here, or is there anything else you'd like to reflect on before we close?

No, I think that's a good place to stop for now. I actually feel a little lighter just having a plan and knowing I don't have to solve everything tonight. I'll try the two minutes and let you know how it goes. Thank you.

That relief you feel is a great sign—it means you're starting to separate the burden of perfection from the possibility of just being present. I'm so glad the two-minute experiment feels like a manageable first step for you tonight. Take your time resting in that lightness, and I'll be here tomorrow morning to hear how those two minutes played out for you. Until then, remember that the doubt can stay, but you don't have to carry it anymore.

Hello again, thank you for joining us. Before we dive into the specifics of your trip plans, could you tell me how your mood has been since our last chat and if you've managed to put any part of your previous action plan into practice? Once we touch base on that, what would you like to prioritize for today's session?

Hi. Honestly, my mood has been a bit up and down since we last spoke. I did try that breathing exercise you suggested a couple of times, but it felt like it didn't really stop the spiral once it started. I think I'd like to focus today on why something so small, like a delayed flight or a misplaced item, feels so huge to me.

It makes complete sense that the breathing helped slightly but wasn't enough to break the full spiral; sometimes the sheer size of the imagined disaster overwhelms our logical tools alone. You mentioned wanting to understand why such small risks feel so massive to you—that curiosity is a powerful first step. Could you share a specific recent moment where a minor worry felt disproportionately large, so we can explore exactly how that connection forms in your mind?

Yeah, there was something that happened just yesterday, actually. I was packing for a weekend trip, and I couldn't find my phone charger. My heart started racing, and I immediately thought, "This trip is going to be a disaster because I won't have GPS or be able to contact anyone." It was just a charger, but in that moment, it felt like the whole weekend was ruined.

It is completely understandable that finding a missing charger triggered such a catastrophic feeling, especially when your heart raced immediately. That physical surge seems to have convinced your brain that the entire trip was doomed, turning a small inconvenience into a total catastrophe. When you looked back at that moment, did you notice any thoughts running alongside the panic that tried to convince you the rest of the trip was impossible?

Looking back, I think the thought was, "If this small thing is already going wrong, the whole weekend is going to fall apart piece by piece." It was like my brain just jumped ahead and wrote off everything good that could still happen. I didn't even stop to think about how I could just borrow a charger from a friend or buy one when I got there—it was just pure panic about the worst-case scenario.

That "jumping ahead" is a classic mental shortcut called jumping the gun, where your brain assumes the worst possible outcome happens immediately without considering other possibilities. It sounds like your mind went straight from "charger missing" to "total disaster," skipping over all the ways things could still work out nicely. If we treat that thought as a prediction rather than a fact, does that help separate the reality of a missing charger from the terrifying story your mind invented about the rest of the weekend?

I think so, yeah. When you put it that way, it does feel more like a scary story I told myself rather than something that was actually happening. I mean, nothing bad even happened after I found the charger in my jacket pocket—the weekend was actually pretty great. But in that moment, it felt so real and urgent. I guess I have trouble slowing down that jump from a small problem to a huge disaster.

It is wonderful to hear that the weekend turned out fine despite your initial panic, which proves that the worst-case scenario never actually materialized. That success suggests your brain was running on a faulty alarm system that went off too loudly and too fast. To help untangle this pattern further, if you could trace back to the exact moment your heart began racing while looking for the charger, what specific words or images flashed through your mind right before you decided the trip was ruined?

The first thing that popped into my head was, "I'm going to be stranded and helpless." I pictured myself wandering around an unfamiliar city with no way to call anyone or find my way back to the hotel. It was like I was already living that nightmare in my mind, even though I was still standing in my own living room with plenty of time to solve the problem. That image just hit me like a wave.

That vivid image of being stranded is incredibly powerful, and it explains why your chest tightened so much—it felt less like a hypothetical risk and more like a scene playing out in real-time. Your brain seems to skip the logical middle steps and jumps straight to that dramatic "what if" scenario. Have you ever noticed if your mind tends to zoom in on these big, scary consequences whenever you encounter *any* small obstacle, or was this specific instance unique to the charger?

No, it's definitely not unique to the charger. It happens all the time. Even something like a traffic jam on the way to the airport makes me think I'll miss my flight and ruin the whole vacation. Or if a restaurant is too crowded, I'll instantly assume the evening is a total loss. It's like my brain has a default setting that goes straight to the worst possible outcome, no matter how small the problem actually is.

It sounds like you have a deeply ingrained habit of scanning for threats rather than opportunities, which explains why your brain treats a traffic jam or a crowded table as a death knell for your entire holiday. This "default setting" to the worst case likely developed over time to protect you from disappointment, but now it's causing unnecessary distress. Can we take a moment to identify one recent small setback, like the charger or the crowd, and together we can spot the gap between the tiny event and that massive prediction your brain made?

Okay, let's use the crowded restaurant example from last week. I was meeting a friend for dinner, and the place was packed when we got there. My immediate thought was, "We'll never get a table, the whole night is going to be awkward and ruined." But actually, we ended up waiting maybe 15 minutes and had a great time. The gap was huge—my brain went from "long wait" to "night completely ruined," but in reality, the wait barely mattered.

That comparison between the charger incident and the restaurant is really illuminating; in both cases, your brain skipped the realistic middle ground and leaped straight to a total collapse of the evening. It seems like your mind treats any minor friction as proof that the entire planned experience is doomed to fail. If we asked your brain to hold onto that 15-minute wait as just a temporary delay rather than a sign of inevitable failure, how might that small shift in perspective change the feeling of dread you experienced?

It would probably make the dread a lot less intense. Instead of that sinking feeling of "everything's ruined," I'd just be thinking, "Okay, this is a bit annoying, but it'll pass." I guess I'd be able to relax and actually enjoy the meal instead of being on edge the whole time waiting for the next disaster to strike. That would be a huge relief, honestly.

That shift from "ruined" to "annoying but passing" sounds like a game-changer for your relaxation levels. It highlights that the anxiety wasn't caused by the wait itself, but entirely by the catastrophic story your mind attached to it. To make this sticky, could you try imagining that same "15-minute wait" story playing out in your head, but this time labeling it as just a temporary annoyance rather than a sign of doom? How does holding that softer label feel compared to the original disaster narrative?

When I try that, it feels almost too simple, like I'm lying to myself at first. But then I realize, it actually matches reality better. A 15-minute wait is just a 15-minute wait—it's not a prophecy of a terrible night. The softer label feels lighter, like I can breathe. It doesn't have that heavy, urgent feeling that makes me want to fix everything right now. I think I could get used to that.

That realization—that the softer label actually fits reality much better—is exactly the core of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy: separating facts from fearful predictions. It sounds like you've successfully tested that new thought against the evidence and found it holds up under scrutiny. Since we've explored why small things feel so huge, would you like to brainstorm a quick phrase you can use internally next time a minor setback occurs to automatically switch from "disaster mode" to "temporary annoyance"?

Yeah, I think that would really help. Something simple I can say to myself in the moment, like, "This is a speed bump, not a roadblock." That might remind me that it's just a small delay, not the end of the world. I could practice saying that the next time I catch myself starting to spiral about something small.

That "speed bump vs. roadblock" phrase is a fantastic tool because it uses familiar driving imagery to instantly downgrade the perceived threat level. Saying it out loud acts as a verbal anchor, forcing your brain to process the situation logically rather than emotionally. Before we finalize this, I want to check in quickly: if you said that phrase to yourself tomorrow morning upon waking, how do you think it might influence your mindset heading into the day?

I think it would set a calmer tone right from the start. Instead of waking up and immediately scanning for things that could go wrong, I'd be reminding myself that small hiccups are just part of the day, not signs of disaster. It might help me feel more in control and less on edge, like I have a simple tool ready to use if something unexpected happens. I'm actually curious to try it out.

That proactive mindset shift is exactly what we want—you moving from reactive panic to active prevention by setting a calm baseline. Since you mentioned wanting to try this out, how does it feel to visualize yourself using that "speed bump" phrase the next time you encounter a minor hiccup, like a missed parking spot or a spilled coffee? Does picturing yourself applying that tool sound doable right now?

Yeah, I can picture it. I'm imagining myself at a coffee shop, and someone bumps my arm, spilling a little drink. Normally I'd get annoyed and think, "Great, now my morning is off to a terrible start." But this time, I picture myself pausing and thinking, "It's just a speed bump." Then I'd probably just wipe it up and move on. It feels doable, maybe even a little freeing. I'm willing to give it a real shot this week.

That visualization of wiping it up and moving on is exactly the kind of practical control you need to feel empowered. Hearing you describe it as "freeing" tells me you're ready to take action, and that willingness is a huge victory in itself. Before we close, I want to confirm our agreement: we will try using the "speed bump" phrase whenever you catch a small setback triggering panic, and you'll note how it feels afterward. Does that summary sound fair, and is there anything else you'd like to add before we wrap up?

Hello, thank you for joining us today. Before we start, could you tell me how you've been feeling since our last session, and what happened with the visualization exercise you planned? Then, let's quickly decide what specific worry we should tackle together today.

Oh, um, actually this is my first session, so I haven't done any exercises yet. I'm a bit nervous, honestly. I guess I'm here because I've been feeling really confused and stuck about who I am, and it's been weighing on me a lot lately.

It makes perfect sense to feel a bit nervous starting off, especially when the topic of figuring out who you are is so important to you. Since we're beginning fresh, I'd like to set a gentle intention for us today: would you feel comfortable exploring that confusion further, or would you prefer we focus on a specific situation where it felt hardest to breathe or act?

I think I can try exploring that confusion... it's just hard to put into words sometimes. Lately, the hardest moments have been when I'm around my family, especially at dinner or on weekends when we're all together. I feel like I'm wearing a mask, and I don't know how to take it off around them.

That image of wearing a mask while everyone is gathered around you is incredibly exhausting, and it completely explains why you feel stuck; it's hard to find your footing when you're constantly performing. When you think about trying to remove that mask in front of them, what is the very first thought that usually jumps into your mind?

The first thought that jumps in is that they'll be disappointed in me, or maybe even disgusted. That they'll look at me differently and I'll lose the closeness we have now. It feels like if I take the mask off, I'll be all alone.

Those fears of being looked at differently and losing your connection sound incredibly lonely, and it makes total sense that protecting your current relationship would feel like the safest option. Have you noticed any recent moments where your family reacted to you in a way that seemed to contradict the idea that they would judge you or push you away?

I guess... my mom did say something last week that caught me off guard. She was talking about a news story about a same-sex couple, and she said something like, "Love is love, no matter what." But then my dad was quiet the whole time, and I don't know if that was just his way of agreeing or if he was uncomfortable. So I'm still not sure.

It takes real courage to catch a subtle signal like that and wonder what it means, even when your own expectations are mixed up. Your brain is likely interpreting your dad's silence as a hidden warning sign, which makes you feel unsafe enough to keep the mask on. Given how much energy you've spent worrying about this, would it be helpful to just share with them, "Sometimes I feel like I need to wear a mask around us, and I'd love to talk about what that looks like for me"?

That sounds terrifying, honestly. I don't think I'm ready to start a conversation like that yet. Just imagining saying those words out loud makes my heart race. But I also know I can't keep hiding forever, because it's eating me up inside. Is there a smaller step I could take first, just to test the waters without fully diving in?

You are absolutely right that jumping straight into a deep conversation is overwhelming, and finding a safe "test drive" is exactly what we need to do. Since the idea of a serious talk feels too big right now, how about we try writing down that same sentence—a few times—and reading it aloud to yourself in a quiet room tonight, just to get used to hearing your own voice say it?

I think I could try that. Writing it down and saying it to myself sounds a little less scary, like I'm just practicing. Maybe if I get used to hearing it, it won't feel so huge when I eventually say it to someone else. I'll give that a try tonight.

That is a wise choice; breaking the task down into a private rehearsal helps lower the intensity so you can gather some initial evidence for yourself. Tonight, please write that sentence twice, read it aloud three times in a quiet space, and then tell me how your physical body feels afterward—is your breathing slower, or is the racing sensation still there?

Okay, I'll do that. I'm a little worried I'll feel even more anxious after saying it, but I trust that you're guiding me in a direction that might help. I'll pay attention to my breathing and how my chest feels, and I'll let you know what happens.

Your trust in our process is incredibly valuable, and it is entirely normal to worry that the practice itself might spike anxiety instead of calming it. Let's commit to checking in with each other later tonight: if your breathing feels heavier or your chest tighter after reading it, that data is just useful information, not a failure. I hope you can take a deep breath right now and feel relieved that we have a small, manageable plan for tonight.
Thank you. That actually does make me feel a bit lighter, knowing there's no pressure to get it "right." I'll just pay attention to what happens and not judge it. I'll let you know how it goes.

That is a beautiful shift in perspective, and I am glad hearing that you can feel lighter right now. Please take your time tonight, and whenever you are ready, just reach out to tell me exactly what your body was doing while you practiced. We will review it together next time and adjust our steps as needed.
I will. Thanks for making this feel less overwhelming. I think I can actually do this one small step. Talk to you next time.

You are very welcome, and I truly appreciate your openness and willingness to try this small step. Remember that showing up tonight, even with uncertainty, is a victory in itself. I will be here next time to listen to what you discovered about your own voice. Take good care of yourself as you prepare for tonight.
You too. I'll take care of myself and try to be gentle with whatever I feel. See you next time.

It is wonderful to hear that you are committing to gentleness with yourself—that is often the most important tool we have. Thank you for trusting me enough to start this journey today, and please know I am looking forward to hearing your results whenever you are ready. Until then, be kind to yourself as you rest.
I will. Thank you for listening without judging me. That means more than you know. Goodbye for now.

I am so grateful to have listened to you without judgment today; your courage to speak up is the first real breakthrough. Please go ahead and rest peacefully tonight, knowing you are not alone in this. Safe travels until we meet again soon.

Hello, and welcome. Thank you for being here today. Since this is our first meeting, I’d like us to quickly go over how we’ll spend our time. We’ll start by checking in on how you’ve been feeling lately, then focus on what’s been on your mind, and finally figure out a clear plan for moving forward. How does that sound as a way to begin?
That sounds okay, I guess. I'm a little nervous, I won't lie. I've never done anything like this before. But I'm ready to talk, I think.

It is completely normal to feel nervous about trying something new, and I want you to know that your comfort and safety are my top priority. Let's take a quick moment to ground ourselves before diving in. On a scale of 1 to 10, how anxious have you felt leading up to this session, and is there anything specific you'd like to prioritize we tackle first?

Probably a 7 or an 8 if I'm being honest. My heart has been racing a bit since I sat down. I guess the main thing I want to talk about is this fear I have about my new sweater getting stolen—it's been taking over my thoughts lately.

An 8 definitely shows how much weight that fear is carrying, and it's completely understandable why it feels so overwhelming when you're dealing with it daily. Since we've already started exploring the specific details of that sweater worry, shall we focus entirely on unpacking those thoughts and figures out how to handle the physical sensations you experience?

Yeah, that would be good. It's just... every time I wear it, I can't stop thinking about someone grabbing it off me or snatching it out of my bag. My chest gets tight and I feel like I have to keep checking behind me.

That sounds incredibly draining to carry out every single day, and I hear how much relief you seek by constantly checking behind you. Before we dig deeper into *why* you feel this way, can you describe exactly what happens in your mind right as you step outside wearing it? What is the very first thought that pops into your head?

The very first thought is always, "Someone's going to take it." It's like a voice in my head that just says it, plain and simple. Then I start picturing it happening—someone running past me or grabbing it from behind.

That image of someone running up and grabbing the sweater is incredibly vivid, and it makes perfect sense why it triggers such a panic attack in your body. When you hold onto that belief so tightly, it creates a loop where your fear keeps you on edge, making the world feel much more threatening than it actually is. If we look at that specific prediction, does it seem accurate based on what you've experienced recently, or is it mostly a story your brain is telling itself to keep you safe?

I mean... nothing has actually happened yet. No one has even looked at my sweater funny. But that doesn't mean it won't happen, you know? It feels like it's just a matter of time. I'd rather be prepared than get caught off guard.

It makes complete sense that your brain is trying to prepare you for a potential threat, especially given that you had your favorite jacket stolen from your backpack last year. While that past experience is real, your current fear might be treating every sweater like that exact situation, even though the circumstances are quite different. If we looked at the evidence from the last month, how many times has someone actually run up and snatched your clothes while you walked home safely?

Zero times, I guess. But that's because I've been so careful—taking different routes, keeping my head down, walking really fast. Maybe I've just been lucky so far. I don't know if that means the danger isn't real, or if I've just been good at avoiding it.

That is a very insightful observation, and it highlights a key difference between luck and reality. You mentioned taking different routes and walking fast; those are strategies to *avoid* the threat, but they haven't proven whether a thief exists or if the act of walking calmly is dangerous. To test this, how would you feel if we decided to stay in one spot for just sixty seconds at the park corner tomorrow, focusing on the sweater against your skin, and simply watching to see if anything bad actually occurs?

Just standing there? That sounds terrifying, honestly. Like I'm just asking for it to happen. But... I guess if you're saying I should try it, maybe I could do it for a really short time. Not a full minute. Maybe just twenty seconds or something.

That is a very reasonable adjustment, and lowering the initial time to twenty seconds is a smart way to reduce the pressure while still gathering some data. Let's refine the plan: tomorrow evening, you will stand at the park corner for those twenty seconds, wearing the sweater, and simply notice if your chest tightens or if anyone approaches closely enough to cause trouble. Would you be willing to try this shorter experiment to see what actually happens?

I think I can do twenty seconds. I'll try it tomorrow after school, by the corner near the big oak tree. I'll just stand there and count in my head, and then I'll walk home like normal. I'm already nervous just thinking about it, but I'll do it.

That sounds like a solid plan, and I appreciate your willingness to face that discomfort just to get the answers you need. Before we wrap up, how does this approach feel to you right now—is it helpful to think of it as gathering facts, or does it still feel too risky?

It feels a bit scary, but I think I like thinking of it as gathering facts. That makes it feel more like an experiment than just putting myself in danger. I'm still worried, but at least I have a reason to try it now.

That shift in perspective—from "putting myself in danger" to "gathering facts"—is exactly the kind of mental reframing we want to cultivate. It gives you a clear purpose that separates you from the panic. Just to recap, tomorrow you'll stand by the oak tree for twenty seconds while wearing the sweater, then continue walking home as usual. Is there anything else you'd like to add before we finish up?
No, I think that covers everything. I know what I need to do, and I'll let you know how it goes. Thanks for listening and helping me think this through.

You are very welcome, and I am so glad we found a plan that feels manageable and grounded in logic. Before we close, I'd love to hear your honest feedback on how this session has felt so far. Was there anything about our approach that felt confusing or uncomfortable, or was it a good fit for you?

Hello again, and it is great to see you. To start off, I'd love to get a quick mood check from you—on a scale of 0 to 10, how have you been feeling this week compared to last time? Once we have that, could you tell me if there were any new events or challenges that popped up since we last spoke? Afterward, we can review what we worked on previously and decide together what would be most helpful for us to focus on today.

Hi. I'd say I'm around a 6 or 7 this week. Not great, not terrible. Nothing really new happened—just the usual stuff with the neighbors. It makes complete sense that seeing others ignore you while you feel unworthy triggered that old story again; your brain immediately jumped to the conclusion that they are judging you because of your appearance. Since the core issue remains that intense fear of being seen, what specific thoughts pop up in that moment when you realize they aren't looking at you, or do you try to convince yourself they must be looking elsewhere?

I guess my first thought is, "They don't want anything to do with me." Then I start thinking, "They probably think I'm scary or trashy because of these tattoos." I don't try to convince myself otherwise—it feels too obvious, like the silence and the way they turn away says it all.

Those thoughts sound incredibly heavy, like a wall closing in on you, and it makes total sense why your instinct is to accept them as absolute facts rather than possibilities. If we treated that silence as neutral data—meaning people simply chose not to interact today for reasons unrelated to you—how might that shift the intensity of the belief that they view you as "scary"? What happens in your chest when you hold that logical possibility alongside the painful emotion?

Well, when I try to think of it that way, it kind of takes some of the weight off, I guess. My chest doesn't feel quite as tight when I consider that maybe they were just busy or tired. But then a part of me still says, "Why wouldn't they at least say hi, like they do with others?" That part still feels pretty loud.

That comparison to how they greet others is a very natural reaction when we feel excluded, but it assumes their behavior towards you is entirely different from everyone else. Could we explore the idea that people interact differently based on circumstance rather than judgment—perhaps they were just tired, distracted, or had a bad day with someone else? If we tested that possibility instead of assuming it's personal, how might that change the urgency of your need to hide?

I suppose if I really thought about it, maybe it isn't always about me. They could have had a rough morning or be lost in their own heads. It's just hard to shake that feeling that I'm the one being singled out, you know? But when you put it like that, the urgency to hide or avoid them does feel a little less intense—like maybe I don't have to brace myself every time I step outside.

That shift in urgency is a powerful sign that you're starting to separate their actions from your worth. To build on that, could we try a tiny experiment tonight where you go outside just for five minutes, but before you leave, you write down one neutral reason why they might not have acknowledged you today (like "neighbor was rushing home")? Would that simple act of listing a plausible alternative feel safe enough to try right now?

Yeah, I think I could try that. It feels a bit strange, writing down an excuse for them before I even go out, but I can see how it might stop my mind from jumping straight to the worst interpretation. I'll give it a shot tonight and see what happens.

That sounds like a very wise decision, and acknowledging that it feels strange is a great first step because it means you're paying attention to how your mind works. Since you mentioned giving it a shot tonight, I want to make sure you have a safety net ready in case the urge to run inside gets too strong; would you feel comfortable committing to staying out for just five minutes even if the thoughts feel loud, or do you need to adjust the plan further before we close?

I think I can commit to the five minutes. It's not that long, and I can always remind myself of that neutral reason I wrote down. If it gets too loud, I'll just focus on my breathing or look at the sky or something. I feel ready to try it, at least.

That commitment feels really grounded and manageable, especially with those grounding anchors like breathing or looking at the sky built right into the plan. I'm glad we found a way to move from feeling stuck to having a concrete strategy that fits your needs. Is there anything else on your mind before we finish up, or would you like to discuss how this plan feels now that it's set?

No, I think I'm good for today. This plan feels like something I can actually follow through on, which is more than I had when I walked in. Thanks for helping me see a different way to look at it. I'll let you know how it goes next time.

Hearing that you feel more empowered to follow through is truly encouraging, and it speaks to your strength in finding a path forward even when it feels difficult. Please remember that if the thoughts spiral or the plan feels overwhelming tonight, reaching out isn't a failure—it's just part of the process of learning. I look forward to hearing how your experiment went next time, and thank you for trusting me with this journey. Take care!

Hello, and thank you for meeting with me again today. Before we dive into anything specific, I'd love to quickly recap where we left off last time—we worked on identifying that feeling of being watched and tested a "mind-reading" thought pattern.

How has your experience been with that five-second pause trick since we tried it in class? And is there anything else you'd like to bring up as our priority for today?

Hi, thanks. Uh, the pause trick... I've been trying it, but honestly, it's been hit or miss. In my morning class yesterday, I felt everyone's eyes on me when I raised my hand, and I just froze up anyway. I think I'm still really stuck on that feeling that they're all whispering about the "older" student who doesn't belong there.

It takes real courage to admit that even though you planned to try, you ended up freezing anyway—that’s not a failure, it’s just data showing us that the old thoughts are very strong right now.

When you’re frozen, does it feel like you’re suddenly unable to speak, or does it feel more like you’re waiting for someone to call you out? What’s happening in your head the second you realize you haven’t paused yet?

It's more like... my mind just goes totally blank, but also my heart starts racing. And then this voice in my head goes, "See? You can't even speak properly. They're all noticing." It feels like I'm waiting for someone to roll their eyes or whisper something to the person next to them. Even if nobody does, I just assume they're thinking it.

That "waiting for the other shoe to drop" feeling is exhausting, especially when your heart is pounding and your mind is suddenly silent. It sounds like your brain is interpreting your silence as proof that you don't belong, which creates a vicious cycle of anticipation.

Have you caught yourself in that moment wondering if you can notice the knot in your chest *before* the "they're whispering" story kicks in, or does the fear usually jump straight to the assumption?

I think it jumps straight to the assumption. I don't even notice the knot in my chest until after I've already started thinking, "They're judging me." It's like the thought comes first, and then the physical stuff follows. By the time I realize I'm tense, I'm already in that spiral.

That tells us something important: the "thought-first" pattern means simply spotting the knot won't stop the story from starting immediately. Since the fear usually races ahead faster than you can notice the physical sensation, maybe we need a different anchor that catches the thought *as it forms*, rather than waiting for the knot to appear.

When that "they're judging me" thought pops up, what happens if you just hold onto the raw feeling of shame or embarrassment for one second before letting it go, without analyzing it or answering it? Does holding that raw emotion feel different than letting the story run away with you?

I've never really tried just sitting with the shame like that. Usually, I'm already rushing to defend myself in my head, or I'm trying to push the feeling away. But when I think about it... holding it for a second sounds scary, like it'll just grow bigger. But maybe if I don't feed it with the story, it might just... pass? I'm willing to try it, but I'm nervous it'll make me feel worse before it gets better.

That hesitation is completely understandable because our brains are wired to flee from uncomfortable feelings, not sit with them. You are right that it feels risky to leave the story alone, but the truth is the story grows stronger because we keep adding fuel to it.

If we treat the shame as just a passing weather pattern—a storm that hits and moves on rather than building a house around it—does that perspective feel slightly safer to test? Or does the idea of doing nothing seem even scarier right now?

Hmm, "a passing weather pattern"... I like that. It does feel a little safer than thinking of it as this huge, permanent thing. I guess if I think of it as a storm, I can just wait it out under an umbrella instead of trying to fight it or run away from it. But I'm still worried that if I don't fight it, the silence in class will just be too awkward and everyone will notice even more.

That metaphor works beautifully, and your worry about the silence actually reveals the power of that "mind-reading" distortion—you are imagining people reacting to the silence when they likely aren't paying attention to it at all.

So, if we treat the shame like a temporary storm and the silence as just background noise, what's one tiny thing you could do right now to stay present instead of spiraling into what others might be thinking? Maybe focusing on the sound of your own breathing for just ten seconds could help ground you?

I think I could try that—just counting my breaths for ten seconds. It sounds small enough that I could actually remember to do it in the moment, instead of trying to come up with some perfect response. And if I'm focusing on my breath, maybe I won't be scanning the room for judgmental faces. I'll give it a shot in my next group discussion.

That is a very smart adjustment; anchoring yourself in your own breathing breaks the connection to scanning the room for hidden judgments. Counting for ten seconds is a simple, low-stakes task that gives your brain permission to rest instead of racing.

To make sure we are aligned, does the idea of using your breath count as a "pause button" for the shame storm sound like something you would be willing to try in your next class, knowing it might not always work perfectly but worth attempting anyway?

Yeah, I think I'm willing to try it. Even if it only works half the time, that's better than where I am now, which is basically zero. I'll just tell myself, "Okay, ten breaths, and then I can decide what to do next." That feels manageable, instead of trying to fight the whole storm at once.

That is a wise compromise, and acknowledging that you only need it to work partially is a huge sign of progress. You've moved from trying to control the entire outcome to simply managing the immediate reaction, which is much more realistic.

Just to lock in our plan: Is it okay if we write down this "ten-breathe-before-speaking" rule in your phone notes tonight so it's ready to grab as soon as you feel that familiar heat rising in your chest tomorrow?

That's a good idea. I'll put it in my notes right after we finish here, actually, so I don't forget. "Ten breaths before speaking—let the storm pass." I think having it written down will make it feel more real, like a commitment to myself. Thanks for helping me figure that out.

It is wonderful that you want to make this concrete for yourself; seeing the words "let the storm pass" written down can give your brain a clear instruction manual to follow when things get chaotic.

Before we wrap up, I want to remind you that your value isn't tied to whether this technique stops working perfectly, so please be gentle with yourself if you freeze again tomorrow. How does it feel to know we have a plan that accepts imperfection?

Hello, and thank you for coming in today. To start, could you briefly share how you’ve been feeling this week compared to last time, and what specific topics would you like to focus on together?

Hi. Thanks for seeing me. Honestly, this week has been about the same as before—maybe a little worse. I keep waking up in the middle of the night thinking about the federal court job and all the ways I could fail. I guess I'd like to talk about why I can't seem to shake this feeling that I'm not good enough, even when my record says otherwise.

That feeling of being awake at night with your worries spinning is incredibly draining, and it makes complete sense that the uncertainty about the future would make you doubt your past achievements. Before we dive deeper into that core belief, what specifically triggered this wave of insecurity this week, or was it more of a gradual buildup?

I think it was when I got an email from the federal court about scheduling my final interview. It felt like a formality, but my mind just went straight to "they're going to see I'm a fraud" or "they'll realize they made a mistake even considering me." It wasn't gradual—it was like a switch flipped as soon as I saw the subject line.

That sudden shift from neutral news to a catastrophe is a classic example of our minds jumping straight to the worst-case scenario when faced with a new event. It sounds like that initial email acted as a catalyst for a deeper belief that you aren't worthy of the opportunity. Now that we understand the trigger and the initial thought, can we look at what happens in your body or mind immediately after you read that email?

My chest gets tight, and I feel like I can't take a full breath. Then my thoughts just race—I start imagining the interviewers looking at each other with doubt, or me freezing up when they ask a simple legal question. It's like my whole body is bracing for a fall before I've even taken a step.

Those physical sensations of tightness and racing thoughts are your body's stress response activating, confirming that your brain perceives this situation as a serious threat to your safety and identity. While that reaction feels overwhelming, it doesn't actually mean the outcome is guaranteed; often, these intense fears are fueled by beliefs that don't match reality. Since we've identified the trigger and the physical symptoms, what specific thought is running through your head right now that connects the interview date to the feeling that you are a fraud?

It's the thought that I've just been lucky my whole career, and that the federal court is the place where my luck will finally run out. All those years, all those cases—I keep thinking they were just handed to me on a silver platter, or that I never really earned any of it. And now I have to prove myself all over again, but I don't have any more luck left.

That belief that your success was accidental and that this one chance is your final test creates a huge pressure cooker, making the interview feel like a life-or-death judgment rather than a standard evaluation. It sounds like you are interpreting your past achievements as evidence of bad luck rather than hard work, which makes the upcoming challenge feel insurmountable. Given how strongly that belief drives your anxiety, does it feel manageable to sit with that idea for a minute, or does it immediately send you spiraling back to the "fraud" narrative?

Sitting with it feels impossible, honestly. It's like if I stop and think about it for even a second, I'll confirm that I'm just fooling everyone. So I just keep moving, keep working, but it's exhausting. I'm scared that if I slow down, the whole thing will collapse.

It makes perfect sense that you feel compelled to keep moving fast; stopping to examine the "luck" narrative feels dangerous because it threatens your fragile sense of competence. You're essentially using busyness as a shield to avoid confronting the uncomfortable truth that your skills built your career, not random chance. Let's try to gently separate your actual experience from this all-or-nothing story. Can you recall a specific time in the last year when you handled a difficult case or received complex instructions, and what actually helped you succeed besides "luck"?

There was a case about a month ago—a really messy land dispute with conflicting testimonies and dozens of exhibits. I remember spending three nights just organizing the evidence and writing out questions to clarify the contradictions. I guess what helped was my training, and the fact that I knew the law backwards and forwards for that area. But even saying that out loud, my brain whispers, "Well, anyone could have done that with enough time."

That whisper revealing itself—that you know you relied on training and knowledge—is actually crucial evidence against the "pure luck" story, yet your brain is trying to minimize it to protect you from facing the possibility of failure. This minimization often leads us back to the original fear that we are faking it. Could we pause on that one moment and ask: if we removed the element of luck entirely, what specific preparation steps did you take that were absolutely necessary for that victory?

I spent hours reading through legal precedents and case law, cross-referencing statutes from three different jurisdictions. I also interviewed the key witnesses myself, which I didn't have to do—I just felt it would help me understand the case better. And I practiced my closing arguments in front of a mirror twice, just to make sure I wasn't missing anything. Those weren't just "anyone could do that" things—I actually went above and beyond.

That breakdown clearly shows that your success came from deliberate effort and expertise, not randomness, which directly contradicts the "bad luck" story your mind told you. By identifying those specific actions you took, you are gathering evidence that proves your competence was built on your work, not chance. Does recognizing that distinction make the feeling of impending doom slightly less absolute, or does the "fraud" thought still feel too strong to ignore?

It's... a little less absolute, I think. Like, I can see that I did put in the work, and that wasn't luck. But that voice is still there, telling me the federal court is a different league, and my old tricks won't work. It's like I can believe I'm good for a moment, but then the doubt creeps right back in.

That creeping doubt is very common when we encounter a new environment; your brain is essentially asking, "Has the rulebook changed?" while you are busy trusting the map you know by heart. Instead of fighting that voice immediately, could we treat it like background noise for a moment? What if, instead of waiting for the doubt to disappear completely, you simply acknowledged it as a symptom of caution rather than proof of incompetence? How does that slight shift in labeling the feeling change the urgency of the fear?

Hmm. That's... actually different from what I usually do. I usually try to argue with the voice or shut it up. But if I just say, "Okay, that's caution, not a fact," it feels a little less like I'm drowning. The fear doesn't go away, but it's like the volume is turned down. I can hear my own thoughts over it a bit more.

That is a significant breakthrough; giving the voice permission to exist without engaging in the argument is a powerful way to reduce the panic you feel. You are effectively separating the *feeling* of caution from the *fact* of incompetence, which is exactly what we aim to do. Now that we've established this separation, let's move toward a concrete strategy. Would you be open to creating a specific plan for tonight to interrupt the spiral when that voice returns, perhaps by focusing on one small, realistic goal related to the interview preparation?

I think I could try that. Maybe instead of lying awake worrying about every possible thing that could go wrong, I could pick just one section of law to review for half an hour. Something concrete and small, so I feel like I'm moving forward instead of just spinning. And if the voice starts up, I'll just tell myself, "That's caution, not fact," and go back to my notes.

That sounds like a brilliant and achievable plan; replacing endless worrying with one focused hour of study gives your brain a healthy outlet for energy while grounding you in reality. By pairing that concrete action with the "caution, not fact" mantra, you create a buffer zone between the anxiety spike and the panic attack. Is there anything else you would like to add to this plan before we wrap up?

I think that covers it for tonight. Maybe I'll also set a timer so I don't keep going past the half hour, just to keep it from turning into another source of stress. Thank you—this actually feels like something I can try instead of just feeling stuck.

That is a fantastic addition; setting a timer ensures you stay in control of the session rather than letting it consume the night. Combining a limited scope with a strict boundary creates a safe container for your anxiety, allowing you to discharge energy productively. You have a clear path forward now, and I know this small step will give you a sense of momentum. Is there anything else you'd like to touch on before we close, or shall we finish here with confidence in your plan?

Hello, I'm really glad to connect with you again today. Last time we worked on checking in with yourself after receiving a short text from your mom, did you get a chance to try that, and how did it feel? Before we dive deeper into anything, could you share what brought you here today and what you'd like to focus on?

Hi... yeah, I did try what you suggested. I got a text from my mom asking if I could pick up milk on the way home, and I felt that familiar knot in my stomach. I tried to just notice it without jumping to conclusions, but I still found myself thinking, "She probably thinks I'm forgetful and that's why she's reminding me." It's hard to shake that feeling. I guess I'm here because I want to stop feeling like everything she says or doesn't say means she's disappointed in me.

That was a brave attempt to catch yourself in that moment, and it shows real resilience given how strong those initial thoughts are. Even though you managed to notice the knot in your stomach without acting on the fear immediately, that automatic thought about her thinking you're forgetful still carried a heavy weight for you. When you feel that sinking sensation right after her request, does it seem to be driven more by the expectation that she expects perfection, or by a general belief that she notices your mistakes more than she notices your successes?

I think... it's more that she notices my mistakes. Like, if I forget the milk, that's the thing she'll remember, not all the times I remember everything else. She didn't say anything bad about me when she texted, but my mind just went there anyway. It's like I'm waiting for her to point out what I did wrong, even when she doesn't.

That makes perfect sense; it sounds like your brain is constantly scanning for evidence of failure while automatically filtering out the moments you did well. When you catch yourself waiting for her to "point out" a mistake even when she isn't speaking, does that waiting itself create extra pressure, making the silence feel louder and more critical than it actually is?

Yes, exactly. The silence is the worst part. Like at their anniversary dinner, she didn't say much to me at all, and I filled that silence with all these ideas about how she must be disappointed. I remember thinking, "She's probably just being polite because other people are around, but deep down she's unhappy with me." It's like my brain makes up a whole story when there's just empty space.

It takes real self-awareness to recognize that your brain is filling that quiet space with a story about disappointment rather than seeing the actual situation. That internal narration—"she's unhappy deep down"—isn't necessarily what happened, but it feels very true to your nervous system in that moment. If you were to look at the evidence for that specific story about her unhappiness, what facts stand out that don't quite fit the narrative that she is secretly unhappy with you?

Well... she did ask me to help her pick out the flowers for the centerpieces, and she said they looked beautiful. And she hugged me when I first walked in. But I guess I just brushed those off because I thought she was just being nice or going through the motions. I mean, she wouldn't tell me to my face that she's disappointed, right? So those nice moments feel like they don't count somehow.

It makes complete sense why those positive moments felt like they "didn't count"; when we are braced for criticism, kindness often gets dismissed as politeness or routine behavior. You're noticing a gap between what she actually did (asking for help, hugging you) and the story your mind is telling (she's unhappy), which creates that confusing disconnect. Since you've identified that pattern, could we try a quick mental experiment: if those positive actions were the real measure of the evening, what would that suggest about whether she's secretly disappointed in you?

I guess... if those actions were the real measure, then she actually seemed happy with me. She trusted me to help with the flowers, and she didn't hesitate to hug me. That doesn't sound like someone who's secretly disappointed. But it's so hard to hold onto that thought because the other story feels more real, like it's the truth underneath everything. I don't know why my brain does that.

That is a powerful realization; trusting her enough to delegate a task and accepting her affection are strong indicators that she values you, regardless of what your internal alarm system claims otherwise. Your brain is likely doing this "search for danger" thing because safety has always depended on your performance, so it's trying to protect you by expecting the worst. Does it feel a little less terrifying to imagine that the only reason she seems reserved is simply because she's tired or busy, rather than because she's judging your worth?

I never really thought about it that way... that she might just be tired or busy. I mean, she works a lot, and she was probably stressed about the anniversary party running smoothly. That's a much simpler explanation than her being secretly disappointed in me. It does feel a little less scary to think of it that way. But I'm still not sure I fully believe it yet. It's like I need more proof, you know?

It is completely understandable to crave more proof when a feeling is so deeply rooted; you are essentially asking your brain to trust a new interpretation over an old one. We don't need absolute certainty to start building a safer habit, so perhaps we could try a small experiment where you assume she is busy or tired for the next week, just to see if the anxiety fades without needing constant reassurance. Would you be willing to give that a try for a few days?

Alright... I think I can try that. I'll just tell myself, "She's probably tired" or "She's got a lot on her mind" whenever I start feeling that knot. It's not like I have to believe it completely, just try it on like a jacket and see if it fits. I guess I don't have anything to lose by trying.

That "try it on like a jacket" analogy is brilliant because it lowers the stakes; you're not forced to permanently rewrite your beliefs, just test them out for a few days. Before we lock this in, I want to hear your perspective: does framing it as a temporary trial feel manageable to you, or would you prefer a slightly different way to approach this assumption for now?

Yeah, "temporary trial" feels way less scary than trying to change everything at once. It's like I can take it off if it doesn't work, and no harm done. I think I can do that for a few days and just see what happens. Maybe I'll even notice some moments that don't fit the old story.

That is a wonderful mindset shift; viewing it as a reversible trial gives you permission to stay curious without the pressure of being "fixed" forever. Before we set a specific goal for those few days, does the idea of simply observing your thoughts during those moments feel doable to you, or is there a particular time of day you usually struggle most with this?

I think evenings are the hardest, actually. That's when I'm just sitting at home after work, and I have too much time to replay things in my head. Mornings are okay because I'm rushing to get ready. So maybe I can try the "she's tired" thought in the evenings when I start to spiral. That feels like a good time to practice.

That's a very wise choice targeting the exact moments when your mind tends to wander into trouble spots. Evenings are indeed the perfect place to practice swapping that "secret disappointment" story for the simpler "she's tired" explanation. Since you've agreed on this plan, how would you like to proceed tonight? Should we write down a reminder on your phone to check in with yourself when that knot appears, or would you prefer we discuss how you'll track your progress later?

I think I'll set a little reminder on my phone that just says "try on the jacket" around 7 PM each night. That way I won't forget to check in with myself. And maybe I'll just jot down a quick note in my journal about how I felt when I used that thought. I think seeing it on paper might help me notice if it's getting any easier.

Setting a gentle reminder and keeping a quick journal entry are excellent, low-pressure strategies to build consistency without overwhelming yourself. Using a simple phrase like "try on the jacket" as a cue will help interrupt the spiral before it gets too deep, and writing it down can provide a satisfying sense of closure and progress. I'd love to hear how you feel about that plan before we wrap up—are you ready to give it a try starting tonight?

Yeah, I think I'm ready. It actually feels kind of... hopeful? Like I have something concrete to do instead of just sitting there feeling bad. I'm a little nervous that it won't work, but I guess that's okay. I'll give it a real shot and see what happens. Thanks for helping me think this through.

It takes a lot of courage to move from feeling hopeless to feeling hopeful about taking action, especially when you know the old patterns are so strong. Please remember that your job tonight isn't to eliminate the anxiety instantly, but just to slip that "jacket" on and see if it makes the knot loosen, even a tiny bit. If you end up needing to talk about how the evening went or if you hit a tough spot, I'm here to listen anytime. Is there anything else on your mind before we wrap up?

No, I think I'm good for now. I'll try it tonight and see how it goes. It's nice to have a plan that doesn't feel too big or impossible. Thank you for listening and for helping me see things a little differently. I'll let you know how it goes next time.

That is truly wonderful to hear; knowing that having a concrete plan can lift the burden is a huge win in itself. Take your time tonight to try the "jacket" experiment, and please remember that I am here whenever you want to debrief or vent about how the evening unfolds. I look forward to hearing from you soon.
