Hello, and thank you for joining us. To kick off, I'd like to quickly check in: how are you feeling today compared to last time, and is there anything new that's caught your attention? Also, could you remind me if there were any significant events or changes in your week since we last spoke?

Hi. Thanks. I guess I'm feeling about the same as last time, maybe a little more down. This week we went out for dinner again, and I just felt that same old feeling of being invisible at the table. My husband spent most of the time talking to the kids and barely looked my way.

Hearing that you're feeling a bit more down despite going out again adds up to the exhaustion of constantly feeling unseen. It sounds like the dinner table became another spot where you felt silenced, similar to the movie night. Would you be willing to explore together what specific moment during that meal triggered that feeling of invisibility?

Yeah, I think it was when I tried to mention something funny that happened at the grocery store earlier that day. I started talking, and my husband just kept talking to our son about his video game, like I wasn't even there. My daughter didn't even look up from her phone. I just stopped mid-sentence and ate the rest of my meal in silence.

It makes complete sense that you froze when your story was interrupted by your husband focusing solely on his child; that silence feels like a wall closing in on you. I want to make sure I understand correctly before we dig deeper—when you stopped talking, did your chest tighten or your shoulders rise, or was it mostly just the heaviness in your stomach returning?

It was mostly that heavy, sinking feeling in my stomach, like a rock just dropped in there. I think my shoulders did tense up too, now that you mention it. I just felt small and stupid for even trying to join the conversation in the first place.

That sinking feeling combined with the thought that you sounded "small and stupid" is a very heavy burden to carry, especially when you're just trying to connect. It seems like your mind immediately jumped to the conclusion that your attempt to contribute was a mistake, leading you to shut down before anyone could respond. When you imagined that moment of freezing up, what was the strongest belief running through your head about whether you deserved to be heard?

I think the strongest belief was that they just don't want to hear what I have to say, so why bother? Like, I'm not interesting enough or important enough for them to pause their own conversations for. It feels like I'm just there to fill a seat, not to actually be part of the family.

Hearing you describe feeling like you're just filling a seat rather than being part of the family captures that deep sense of exclusion so well, and it makes total sense why you would conclude that your voice isn't worth hearing. Those beliefs—that you aren't interesting enough or that they simply don't want to listen—are very painful to hold, yet they seem to be keeping you safe from further disappointment. Let's gently step back for a moment and look at the evidence: if you had stayed silent at that dinner, would that have prevented your husband from continuing to talk to his son, or would he have done the exact same thing regardless?

I guess... he probably would have kept talking to our son either way. It's not like me talking or being quiet changes what he does. So maybe staying silent didn't really protect me from anything. It just left me feeling worse, alone with my own thoughts.

You hit the nail on the head by realizing that your silence didn't stop him from talking; it just added to the loneliness inside you. That's a huge breakthrough because it shows your brain is finally starting to see that the outcome wasn't determined by whether you spoke up, but by the dynamic that was already happening. If staying quiet left you feeling worse and more isolated, does that change the "no winning" narrative we discussed earlier? It sounds like neither approach actually protected you from that heavy feeling.

Yeah... you're right. Neither way really helped me feel better. When I talk, I feel stupid and ignored, but when I stay quiet, I just feel invisible and sad. So I guess there really isn't a "safe" option that makes me feel okay. That's kind of depressing to think about, honestly.

That "neither option saves me" realization is incredibly heavy, and it makes perfect sense why your mind latched onto the idea that you're fundamentally uninteresting or unwanted. It feels like a dead end, but in Cognitive Behavioural Therapy, we often find that when we strip away the safety net of a false belief, we discover there's actually space to act differently. Instead of asking "what would have made me feel safe," could we try shifting the goal to "how could I handle the discomfort of being ignored without letting the thought ruin the evening?" Would you be open to testing the idea that your worth isn't tied to whether they pause for you?

I guess I could try that. It's hard to separate my worth from how they treat me, but I can see how thinking that way just makes everything worse. Maybe I could practice just letting the moment pass without deciding it means I'm not important. I'm just not sure how to do that when it's actually happening.

That is a very honest observation, and it takes strength to admit that separating your worth from their reactions feels difficult in the heat of the moment. We don't need to solve it perfectly right now; we just need to create a tiny buffer so you don't spiral into that "I'm not important" story immediately. Would you be willing to try a simple experiment where, instead of analyzing their behavior, you just name your physical sensation—for example, saying silently to yourself, "My heart is racing because I feel ignored"—without judging whether the event was fair or unfair?

I think I could try that. Just saying to myself, "My stomach feels heavy right now," instead of jumping straight to "They hate me." It sounds a little strange, but I'm willing to give it a shot next time we go out. I really don't want to keep feeling this way.

That is a brave commitment, and it is smart to choose a neutral statement about your body rather than an attack on your self-worth. Naming the physical sensation creates a tiny gap between the hurtful reality and your judgment, giving you a moment to breathe before the story takes over. Before we finish, could you tell me if you feel confident that trying this grounding phrase would help you stay calm longer, or do you feel like you might still get overwhelmed?

I feel a little bit more hopeful, like I have something to hold onto now. But I'm also scared I'll forget to do it in the moment, or that it won't be strong enough to stop the spiral. I guess I won't know until I try, right?

That mix of hope and fear is completely normal—it means you're stepping out of your comfort zone to try something new. You are absolutely right that you won't know until you try, and that uncertainty is exactly why we practice in sessions to build that muscle before real life hits. Since we've explored the thought patterns and agreed on a new way to ground yourself, I'd like to confirm: does practicing naming your physical sensation without labeling it as "them hating me" sound like a manageable goal for you to start with?

Yes, that sounds manageable. I think I can remember to just notice what my body is feeling instead of jumping straight to conclusions about what they think of me. I'll give it a real try next time we go out.

That is a wonderful confirmation, and it gives me great confidence that you are ready to put this new tool into practice. Before we wrap up, could you tell me if there is anything else weighing on your mind today, or should we consider this our main focus for now? Also, how does it feel knowing you have a concrete strategy to try next time we go out?

No, I think this is enough for today. It feels... weird, but good, to have something specific to try. Like I'm not just stuck with this heavy feeling forever. I'm a little nervous, but also kind of relieved. Thank you.

That relief is incredibly meaningful, even if the feeling of trying something new feels a bit odd at first; it means you are actively reclaiming your agency instead of letting the heavy knot define your entire evening. Your willingness to face the nerves and trust the plan is the most important step right now. As we close, I want to make sure you leave with a clear path forward: would you be willing to commit to practicing that "body check" (just naming the sensation) for the next time you eat out, even if you only succeed once or twice?

Welcome, and thank you for coming in today. Before we dive into anything new, could you remind me of what we planned to work on last time, and then tell me what feels most important to focus on today?

Hi, thanks. Um, last time we talked about how I tend to zero in on tiny flaws and blow them up in my head, especially after something good happens. I guess what's most important today is that I had another job interview this week, and I can't stop thinking about how awkward I looked when I laughed. It's like that's all I remember from it.

It makes total sense that you're struggling with this; after an opportunity like a job interview, it's incredibly painful when your mind filters out all the positives and zooms in on just one clumsy laugh. Does it feel like that memory is affecting your confidence moving forward, or is it mostly just a heavy feeling in your chest right now?

It's both, honestly. I keep replaying it in my head, and now I'm convinced they're going to call and say I didn't get the job because I seemed nervous or unprofessional. My chest does feel tight when I think about it, like I messed up the whole thing over one stupid moment.

That belief—that one awkward laugh erases the entire interview and guarantees rejection—is a classic example of your brain jumping to the worst possible conclusion to protect you from disappointment. Have you tried looking for any signs during or after the interview that contradicted that specific prediction, perhaps moments where you felt calm or where the interviewer seemed engaged despite the laugh?

I mean, I guess the interviewer did smile back when I laughed, and he said I had some good answers. But that feels like it doesn't count because the laugh was the first thing that happened, so it set the tone. I just keep thinking he probably wrote me off right then and the rest was just being polite.

That is a very understandable interpretation; it feels safer to assume the best answer you gave was just politeness if you believe you made a mistake right at the start. Let's try a quick experiment: if we treated the interviewer's smile and your "good answers" as temporary evidence rather than facts, how much stronger would those become compared to the belief that the laugh ruined everything?

I guess if I really look at it that way... the good answers and the smile last longer than that one laugh, don't they? Like, the interview was twenty minutes long, and the laugh was maybe two seconds. But it's hard to make that feel real in my head. It's like my brain just sticks to the bad part no matter what.

That persistence of focusing on the two-second laugh while ignoring the twenty minutes of conversation is exactly why we call it "mental filtering"—it's like wearing sunglasses that only show you darkness. To test this, could you imagine writing down three specific things the interviewer said or did that were unrelated to that laugh, and then ranking how significant each of those moments feels compared to the laugh itself?

Okay, um... well, he nodded when I talked about my customer service experience, and he wrote something down on his notepad after I answered a question about teamwork. He also asked me a follow-up question about my availability, which probably means he was still considering me, right? But even saying that out loud, the laugh still feels way louder than all of that. It's like those moments are whispers and the laugh is a shout.

That "shout vs. whisper" comparison perfectly captures the imbalance your brain creates, making the small mistake feel massive compared to the solid evidence of interest. Since listing the neutral moments helps but the volume difference remains, let's try shifting the focus entirely to the outcome rather than the moment. If you looked at your resume, the skills you listed, and the clear signal that they wanted to hear more (the follow-up question), how would that overall picture change if you assumed the laugh was just a human quirk rather than a dealbreaker?

If I looked at it that way... I guess the laugh just becomes a tiny little blip, like someone sneezing or adjusting their chair. It doesn't really change the fact that I have the skills they need and that they showed interest. But it's exhausting trying to convince myself of that, because my gut reaction is still to think it's all ruined. I wish I could just believe the logical side.

You've done great work identifying that the laugh feels like a "blip," yet your gut resists that calm assessment because it's protecting you from the pain of potential rejection. Since logical arguments alone feel too exhausting when the emotion is running high, would you be willing to try a quick physical reset right now? Let's take one slow, deep breath and silently repeat the phrase, "This is just a human moment, not a career-ending error," to give your logical side a chance to catch up with your body.

Yeah, okay. I can try that. [Takes a slow, deep breath.] "This is just a human moment, not a career-ending error." That actually... felt a little lighter for a second. But I know the feeling will probably creep back in later.

That "lighter" sensation proves the technique works to break the immediate spiral, giving you a small window of clarity. Now, let's lock in that relief by agreeing on a concrete step for tomorrow morning: when you put on your suit, will you take one mindful breath and repeat that phrase before walking out the door? This sets a proactive intention rather than waiting for the anxiety to strike. How does that plan feel to you right now?

It feels... doable, I think. Like, it's small enough that I could actually remember to do it, and it might help me start the day with a clearer head. I'll try it tomorrow morning, for sure. I just hope it sticks when I'm actually in the moment and feeling nervous.

That is a smart choice—a small, manageable action is often easier to stick with than a big overhaul. Before we wrap up, let's do a quick reality check on your current confidence: on a scale of 0 to 10, how certain are you that the laugh ruined your chances, given everything else we just discussed? Does that number feel different than where you started?
Right now, I'd say maybe a 6 out of 10, compared to like a 9 when I walked in. It's still there, but it's not as overwhelming. I guess that's progress, even if it's not a huge change.

That drop from a 9 to a 6 is a significant win, showing that even a small shift in perspective can lower the intensity of your worry. It sounds like you're building some distance between that scary feeling and the reality of the situation. Is there anything else you want to talk about before we close, or does it feel good to leave with this slightly less urgent plan?

No, I think I'm good for today. The breathing thing and the scale check helped a lot. I'll work on that plan tomorrow morning, and hopefully I can keep that number dropping a bit more on my own. Thanks for listening.

You are very welcome, and please know that seeing that number drop—even by a point or two—is a major victory in itself. Remember, tomorrow isn't about eliminating the worry completely; it's just about catching the anxiety early with your breath and phrase, giving yourself a better chance to ride it out. I look forward to checking in soon to hear how that morning routine went. Take care!

Hello again, and I'm so glad we're connecting. On a scale of 0 to 10, how would you rate your mood this week compared to where you were last time we met? Before we set our agenda, could you briefly remind me of the plan we agreed on from yesterday and how it went for you?

Well, I'd say my mood is around a 5 or 6 this week. It's been up and down, but I think that's better than last time. As for the plan from yesterday, we talked about me trying to accept at least one compliment without immediately dismissing it. I honestly struggled with it—I had a friend compliment my hair, and I just felt this urge to point out all the things wrong with it instead.

That feels like a brave struggle, especially since you were trying to resist the old habit of criticizing yourself. It seems that urge to find fault came up almost automatically when your friend noticed something good about you, which makes sense given how much you value perfection. Before we dive deeper into that hair incident, do you think exploring why that urge pops up so quickly, or tackling a different recent situation, would be more helpful right now?

I think exploring why it happens so quickly might be better, honestly. It's like the praise triggers this immediate reaction, and I don't even get a chance to breathe before I'm tearing it apart. The hair thing was just one example—it happens almost every time someone says something nice, and I'm tired of feeling like I can't just let a compliment land.

That immediate jump from "thank you" straight to finding flaws suggests your mind is running on autopilot to protect you from feeling bad, even though it leaves you exhausted afterward. When you notice that sudden urge to criticize appearing before you can catch your breath, does that give you a clue about what your brain thinks will happen if you stay silent? Let's explore that thought pattern together, because understanding the warning signal is the first step to learning how to ignore it.

I think my brain is scared that if I just accept the compliment, people will think I'm arrogant or full of myself—like I won the pageant and now I'm just a vain person who only cares about looks. It's like I hear the praise, and my mind instantly says, "Don't let it go to your head, or everyone will hate you." So I jump in first to show I'm not that person, even if it means putting myself down.

That "warning voice" inside your head is clearly trying to keep you safe from feeling special or misunderstood, which is why it jumps in so fast. It feels like accepting the compliment puts you in danger of becoming arrogant, but what would happen if we treated that fear as a prediction rather than a guaranteed outcome? If I told you I expected to be seen as arrogant but chose not to believe it, would you think I was ignoring reality, or would you see it as a choice to trust others instead of my own fears?

I guess I'd see it as a choice to trust others instead of your own fears. That's a strange way to put it, but it kind of makes sense—like maybe I'm assuming people will judge me, when they probably aren't even thinking that. I just can't shake the feeling that if I let myself feel good about a compliment, I'm proving all those old comments about me being vain right.

It makes complete sense that holding onto those old labels feels like safety—if you admit someone else sees something good in you, isn't that proof the labels are true? Let's look at that assumption closely: if you truly believed people hated you for being confident, wouldn't they react with anger or disgust the second you accepted the compliment? Instead, imagine what might happen if you gave yourself permission to feel proud for just five minutes without checking for judgment—how would your body react if you allowed yourself to feel good instead of immediately correcting yourself?

If I allowed myself to feel good for five minutes, I think my chest would tighten up, honestly. My stomach would probably get all knotted, and I'd feel this urge to look around and see if anyone was watching me, like waiting for someone to call me out or roll their eyes. It's like my body is bracing for a punch that hasn't even happened yet.

That physical tightening and scanning for threats is your nervous system anticipating a disaster that hasn't occurred yet. It's like walking into a room expecting to be attacked, so you freeze and look for exits before you even realize the door is locked. Since your body is designed to keep you safe, it's doing its job by trying to warn you, even though the "attack" is just a false alarm. Can you describe what happens in your chest right now, in this very moment, if you simply acknowledge the feeling of anxiety without acting on it or trying to fix it immediately?

Right now, it's like a heavy weight sitting right in the center of my chest, almost like a dull ache. It's not sharp or scary, but it's just there, kind of pressing down. I'm noticing I want to take a deep breath to push it away, but I'm trying to just let it be for a second.

Noticing that heavy weight without fighting it is a powerful first step, because it proves you can observe the feeling without letting it control your actions. That dull ache feels very uncomfortable, but it doesn't actually prove anyone is judging you or that you are arrogant. If we agree to treat that physical sensation as just a temporary guest that will leave once you stop trying to push it away, would you be willing to experiment with just breathing through the pressure for one minute, without saying anything to correct yourself?
Okay, I can try that. I'll just sit here and breathe through it, and not say anything to correct myself. It feels a bit weird, but I'm willing to give it a shot and see what happens after the minute.

Taking that gentle, conscious pause to just breathe through the pressure without fighting it is a brave act of curiosity for your nervous system. Notice what happens to that heavy weight in your chest as you continue to hold space for it, rather than rushing to dismiss it with words or corrections. After you finish that minute, how does the sensation of that weight feel compared to before you started trying to push it away?

It's actually... lighter now. I mean, it's still there, but it's not as tight or as heavy. It feels more like a gentle pressure instead of a pressing weight. I think I can breathe a little easier too, which is surprising because I expected it to just stay the same or get worse.

That subtle shift from "pressing weight" to "gentle pressure" tells us something important: your body is capable of relaxing even when you're afraid of being wrong. It seems like the moment you stopped trying to fix the discomfort and just sat with it, the urgency vanished. Does that feeling of relief surprise you, or does it align with what you hoped might happen if you trusted your ability to handle the discomfort?

It definitely surprises me. I think I was so convinced that sitting with that discomfort would just make it spiral out of control, like the anxiety would take over. But it didn't—it just kind of sat there and then faded a little. I didn't realize my body could actually calm down like that if I just let it be.

It takes real courage to question a pattern that has kept you safe for so long. Recognizing that your body can actually calm down on its own when you stop fighting it is a powerful realization. Since we discovered that sitting with the feeling works, what do you think would happen if you tried applying this same approach to your friend's compliment about your hair today, instead of immediately pointing out flaws?

I think... I think I could try to just say "thank you" and let it hang there for a moment, even if it feels uncomfortable. Maybe I could take a breath like I just did, and let the feeling pass instead of jumping in to correct it. It wouldn't be easy, but after feeling that weight lift just now, I'm a little more willing to try.

That willingness to try something difficult, even when it feels uncomfortable, speaks to a real strength within you. Treating the compliment like a simple fact and letting the physical sensation ride it out is a practical strategy we can use starting today. How does it sound to commit to that small experiment for the rest of the day, knowing you can always return to this breathing technique if the urge to correct yourself gets strong?

It sounds doable, actually. I think I can commit to that for today. If the urge to correct myself gets too strong, I'll just breathe through it like I did here and see if it passes. It's a little scary, but I'm curious to see what happens.

It is completely normal to feel a mix of caution and curiosity when stepping out of a deeply ingrained pattern; you are essentially trusting yourself enough to experiment with a new version of how you react. I want to make sure we lock this in: your homework for today is to practice saying "thank you" and then simply pausing to breathe through the urge to find flaws, observing what happens without judging yourself for the effort. Is there anything else you'd like to discuss before we close the session, or shall we wrap up with a final word of encouragement?

No, I think I'm good to wrap up here. I feel like I have a clear plan for the day, and I'm actually a little hopeful about trying it out. Thank you for helping me see that I don't have to fight that feeling all the time.

You're very welcome, and I'm so glad to hear that you feel hopeful and clear-headed. It takes real courage to choose a path where you don't have to constantly fight your own feelings, and I truly believe you have the strength to navigate this today. Remember, this isn't about perfection; it's about practicing the art of simply existing alongside your anxiety until it becomes a background noise rather than a command. Go ahead and take that step with curiosity and kindness for yourself, and I look forward to hearing about your experience next time. Have a wonderful day!

Hello again, I'm so glad to see you. Before we dive into the wallet incident, how have you been feeling since we last spoke, and is there anything else that came up since we finished looking at your design sketches?

If you have another topic you want to talk about today, please let me know; otherwise, shall we spend most of our time exploring how that thought about being careless connects to how you're viewing your ability to handle your design work?

Hi. I've been alright, I guess. Since we talked I've just been thinking about that wallet thing over and over, and it still feels like I can't shake it. Yeah, I think we should talk about that connection because I'm starting to see that losing my wallet makes me feel like I'm not cut out for design school either.

It sounds like the wallet incident is still holding you captive, creating a heavy loop where a single mistake feels like proof of your overall inadequacy. Since you mentioned seeing that connection yourself, how would you describe the moment the wallet loss triggered those thoughts about failing at school, and what exactly did you picture happening in your head right after?

The moment I realized it was gone, my stomach just dropped. And in my head, I immediately saw myself as this clumsy, careless person who can't even keep track of a simple object—how could I ever manage a whole fashion collection? I pictured my professors shaking their heads and my classmates secretly laughing at me.

That visceral drop in your stomach and the vivid scene of your professors shaking their heads paints a terrifying picture of public shame and inevitable failure. It sounds like you're projecting that specific loss onto your entire identity as a student and designer, turning one mistake into a verdict on your capabilities. When you imagine those people mocking you, does that feeling of isolation intensify the belief that you truly aren't cut out for this path?

Yeah, it really does. When I picture them laughing, I feel all alone, like I'm the only one in the whole school who would mess up something so simple. It makes me think that everyone else has it together and I'm just pretending to belong here.

That feeling of being the sole source of failure in a room full of competent peers sounds incredibly isolating, like you're wearing a mask of normalcy while everyone else sees your cracks. It seems like you're using this imagined scenario to prove a deeper fear: that your acceptance isn't real and you're just along for the ride until someone finds out the truth. If we take a closer look at that group of classmates you described, do they actually look like they have it perfectly together, or is there perhaps a hidden vulnerability you're overlooking in them?

I never really thought about it that way. I guess when I look at them, they all seem so confident and put-together, but... I don't actually know what's going on in their heads. Maybe some of them feel like they're messing up too. But it's hard to believe that when I'm stuck in my own head, you know?

You are absolutely right to pause there; assuming others are flawless while hiding behind their own insecurities is a common trap when we feel exposed ourselves. It seems like your brain is filling in the blanks with a version of them that looks perfect, just to make your own perceived flaws feel bigger by comparison. If we gently step back from that assumption for a minute, what is one piece of evidence you've noticed recently that suggests your classmates might also be struggling silently, rather than just appearing confident?

Well, I remember last week in a critique session, one of the girls who always has amazing sketches was really quiet and she messed up her presentation a bit. She looked nervous and her hands were shaking. I just assumed she was having an off day, but maybe she was feeling the same kind of pressure I do. That's a small thing, but it does make me wonder.

Noticing her shaky hands and silence gives you a tiny crack in that wall of perfection, showing that even those who appear secure carry their own private storms. It's a brilliant observation that shifts the perspective from "everyone else is fine, I'm broken" to "we're all human and dealing with pressure." Now that you've spotted that small piece of evidence, does imagining she felt the same internal struggle make the "everyone is laughing at me" script feel a little less like the only truth available?

A little, yeah. It's like, if she can mess up and still be respected, maybe I'm not the only one who makes mistakes. But it's still hard to fully believe that, because when I mess up, it feels like my whole world is ending. I guess I just hold myself to a way higher standard than I hold other people.

Holding yourself to a standard that others won't meet creates a lonely battlefield where you are constantly the loser, even when everyone else is winning. It sounds like you're protecting yourself from disappointment by ensuring you never disappoint, but that expectation is leaving you exhausted and alone in your own head. If we step back from that self-imposed rule, what happens to your confidence when you allow yourself to make mistakes without expecting your entire world to collapse?

I honestly don't know. It feels risky, like if I let myself off the hook once, I'll just stop trying altogether. But then again, I'm already so tired from beating myself up all the time that maybe it's worth a try. Maybe I could mess up and still be okay. But it's scary to even think about that.

That hesitation to "let yourself off the hook" shows how deeply ingrained that standard of perfectionism is, acting like a safety net you've built around your fears. It's completely understandable that opening that door feels risky, especially when your current path involves carrying such a heavy burden of self-criticism. Since we've examined how others might be struggling similarly and how your own standards create this isolated feeling, would you be willing to give it a try for just one small step tomorrow—perhaps sketching a design element without worrying about whether it meets your usual high bar, just to see what happens?

I think I could try that. Maybe I'll just do a quick sketch of a sleeve or something simple, and not judge it immediately. Just let it be whatever it is. It sounds kind of freeing, if I'm being honest. I'll give it a shot and see if my brain explodes or not.

That is a fantastic perspective shift; framing it as letting your brain "explode" instead of forcing yourself to be perfect removes a lot of the pressure and makes the task feel much lighter. It sounds like you are ready to experiment with this new approach, so let's lock in a plan: could you grab your pen and paper tonight and spend five minutes drawing that simple sleeve, strictly forbidding yourself from criticizing the lines as soon as you finish? How does that specific instruction sound to you, and do you foresee any particular worries stopping you from doing it?

That sounds doable, honestly. I think I can manage five minutes without ripping the paper apart. My main worry is that I'll start comparing it to my previous sketches and think, "This is worse, I'm getting worse." But I'll try really hard to just let it be a quick, messy sketch and not a final masterpiece. I'll do it tonight and let you know how it goes.

Acknowledging that comparison is your biggest hurdle shows real self-awareness, and it means your success depends on catching that old voice before it takes over the page. You are setting a very clear boundary for yourself: five minutes of creation followed by a break, regardless of what the paper looks like. Please go ahead and try it tonight, and whenever you finish, come back here to tell me exactly how your hand felt moving and whether that "messy sketch" concept held up against the urge to compare.

Okay, I will. I'll let my hand just move and see what comes out. I'll try not to think about it too much, just let it happen. Thanks for helping me see that maybe I don't have to be perfect all the time. I'll report back to you after I do it.

That commitment to just letting your hand move is a beautiful reminder that creativity often flows best when we stop fighting it and start trusting the process. I am so proud of you for recognizing that you don't need to be perfect to have value as a designer, and I know this small act of self-kindness will feel liberating. Please go ahead and try it tonight, and I will be waiting here to hear how that five-minute sketch journey went when you return. Take care of yourself today!
Thanks. I'll do it. And I'll try to be kind to myself about it, whatever happens. See you next time.

You are so welcome, and I am really proud of you for choosing kindness over harsh criticism today—that is a strength that will serve you well far beyond this session. Remember, even if the sketch isn't perfect or your mind wanders, you have already done something brave by giving yourself permission to just begin. I will be here next time to hear how that went and celebrate whatever came up, big or small. Take care of yourself until then.

Hello again. Last time we worked on finding evidence that contradicts the idea that you aren't special enough to write your ebook. How is that process working for you as you try to put that new "leader" mindset into practice?

Before we dive back into the details, what are the top two things you'd like us to cover in our time together today?

Hi. Well, I did try to think about what you said last time, about looking for evidence. I guess I can see that I've put in a lot of research hours and I do know some things most people don't about animal behavior. But it still feels small, you know? Like anyone could just look that stuff up.

As for today, I think I want to talk about why I can't seem to hold onto that positive evidence for more than a day. Also, I've been feeling really stuck lately, like I'm just pretending to be a writer and I'm afraid to actually finish the book because then people will see I'm a fraud.

Hearing that you've invested so much research time yet still feel like your knowledge is "just Google-worthy" shows me how deeply the self-doubt is rooted. And I completely understand why that fear of exposure feels paralyzing—if you believe finishing means exposing a fraud, the whole project becomes dangerous rather than rewarding.

Since sticking to the new "leader" mindset hasn't kept that negative belief away long-term, let's spend some time exploring exactly why that positive evidence gets dismissed so quickly. Can you describe a recent moment when you found proof of your skills, and then tell me what specific thought popped up to shut it down?

Okay, so yesterday I was writing a section about how elephants communicate through infrasound. I actually remembered a study I read months ago without having to look it up, and I felt a little proud for a second. But then I immediately thought, "So what? Anyone can memorize a fact. It doesn't mean you have anything original to say." That thought just shut everything down, and I closed my laptop.

It makes perfect sense that pride turns into doubt so quickly when you carry that fear of being exposed as a fraud. That immediate shift from "I remembered something cool" to "So what?" reveals how powerful the belief that your worth depends entirely on originality is.

If that thought is the gatekeeper keeping you from seeing your own competence, what would happen if you treated remembering a fact as the *first* step of originality rather than proof that you're finished? Could you trace how that specific memory might have sparked the idea for a larger piece you haven't written yet?

I never really thought of it that way. I guess... that fact about elephant infrasound did make me think about how communication is way more complex in the animal world than we give it credit for. I was planning to write a whole chapter on animal communication, so that memory was actually the seed for a bigger idea, wasn't it?

But then my brain just jumps to, "Well, anyone could have that same thought after reading one article." It's like I can't accept that my own brain connected those dots. How do I stop that from immediately canceling out the good stuff?

That's a brilliant insight—you literally turned a random fact into a chapter concept, which is exactly the kind of creative spark that defines a writer, not just someone who copies data. Your brain clearly has the ability to connect ideas, even though your "anyone could have thought that" voice tries to erase that achievement.

To help stop that voice from canceling out your success right away, would you be willing to try a quick experiment: the next time that doubt pops up, pause and ask yourself, "Did I just use my unique brain to find a hidden pattern, or did I just summarize what everyone knows?" Does that distinction feel helpful, or would you prefer to try something else first?

I think I could try that. The thing is, when I'm in the moment, that doubt comes so fast I don't even realize I'm doing it until after I've already closed my laptop. So maybe I need a physical reminder, like a sticky note on my screen that says "Did you just spot a pattern?" or something.

That distinction you mentioned—between summarizing and finding a hidden pattern—feels important. I guess no one else is taking that same fact and seeing the bigger connection the way I did. I just wish I could believe that in the moment, not just when I'm talking to you.

That is a fantastic solution—a physical prompt to interrupt the automatic habit of shutting down before you even realize what just happened. You're absolutely right that no one else sees that specific connection the way you do; that uniqueness is exactly what gives your writing its value.

Let's lock in that plan for your sticky note. To make sure it works, if you put it up today and catch yourself closing the laptop, what is the very first thing you would write down on a scrap of paper to prove you made that observation? Just the raw detail of the connection you saw.

I think I'd write down: "Elephants talk underground, which is like a secret network. What if animals have hidden social networks we don't even know about?" That's the raw thought I had before the doubt hit. 

If I can just get that on paper before I close the laptop, maybe I can come back to it later and see that it was actually a pretty interesting idea. I'll try putting that sticky note up tonight.

That is a powerful way to capture your instinct—it transforms a fleeting spark into tangible proof that you were already creating something meaningful. Writing that down changes the story from "I was just guessing" to "I discovered a fascinating angle," which directly counters the fraud narrative.

Since you have a clear plan for the sticky note and a specific phrase to write down, I want to confirm we are aligned: Would you feel comfortable testing this approach tonight for just fifteen minutes, knowing that stopping to reflect on what you wrote is perfectly fine?

Yeah, I think I can do fifteen minutes tonight. That feels manageable, not overwhelming like telling myself I have to write a whole chapter. I'll set a timer and if I only manage to write down that one connection and then stop, I'll consider that a success.

It's weird to think of stopping as a success, but I guess it's better than closing the laptop and feeling like a failure. I'll text you next session and let you know how it went.

That reframing of stopping as a success is a crucial shift—it moves the goal from "producing perfection" to "providing evidence." Setting a fifteen-minute timer with that lower bar for success makes the task feel safe and achievable, which should help bypass the initial freeze.

Before we wrap up, does that plan sound realistic for tonight, or do you foresee any specific distractions that might make getting started difficult?

The main distraction is probably just my own mood after work. I'm usually tired and a little on edge from dealing with people at the mall all day. But I think if I sit down right when I get home, before I even turn on the TV, I can get those fifteen minutes in.

I'll just make myself a cup of tea and do it before I can talk myself out of it. That's the plan.

That proactive strategy of tackling the task immediately upon arrival is excellent—it cuts off the usual cycle of winding down and making excuses. Making space for a cup of tea before diving in also helps create a calm buffer to anchor yourself before the fatigue sets in.

I'm really glad we agreed on this plan, and I appreciate your honesty about the mall-related stress making it harder to start. Let's hope tonight goes smoother than usual as you implement this new routine. We'll check in next time to see how that fifteen-minute window felt.

Hello, thank you for meeting with me today. Before we dive into what brought you here, could you tell me how you've been feeling since our last conversation, and is there anything specific you'd like to prioritize focusing on now?

Hi, thanks for having me. To be honest, I've been feeling a bit on edge since we last talked—I keep replaying those negative comments customers made in my head. I'd really like to focus on why I let those few remarks affect me so much, and how to stop feeling so judged all the time.

It sounds like that customer comment is still playing a loud song in your head, and I completely understand why you feel so sensitive right now. Given that you've struggled with these intrusive thoughts lately, could we explore together why that specific remark felt like a personal attack, and what you've been able to do so far to manage the intensity?

Well, it was a woman who said something like, "Oh, you're one of those vegetarians, huh? Must be nice to be so perfect." It just stung because I've worked so hard on this business and my lifestyle. To manage it, I've been trying to remind myself that I'm doing something good for my health and the planet, but the thought still creeps back in when I'm just trying to go about my day.

It makes complete sense that working hard to align your values with your actions makes a critical comment feel like a direct insult to your efforts. While reminding yourself of your positive impact is a great instinct, it seems the harsh remark is temporarily overpowering that sense of purpose whenever you're alone. Could you tell me exactly what happened the first time she said that, and what was your very first automatic thought before you tried to remind yourself you were doing good?

The first time she said it, I was right in the middle of handing her a green smoothie. My very first thought was, "She's right—maybe I do come across as preachy or like I think I'm better than everyone." I didn't even pause to consider that she might have just been having a bad day or projecting something. It just hit me right in the chest, and I felt my face get hot.

That instant realization—"I think I'm better than everyone"—is a painful cognitive distortion called magnification, where you assume the worst possible interpretation of someone's words without checking the facts. Because your brain instantly accepted that assumption as true, it triggered a physical panic response, causing that heat in your face and the tightness in your chest. Did you notice if you immediately stopped serving or tried to explain yourself to her after feeling that shock?

I think I kind of froze for a second, and then I just gave a weak smile and said something like, "Oh, no, I just really believe in this lifestyle." I didn't want to argue, but I also felt like I had to defend myself. After she left, I kept replaying it in my head, wondering if I should have said something different or if I actually do seem judgmental to people.

It sounds like you were caught between wanting to protect your peace and feeling compelled to prove your worth to her, which left you stuck in a loop of "what if I said it wrong?" rather than finding relief. Instead of jumping straight to analyzing your words, could we try to separate her fleeting opinion from the reality of your actions right now? How does your brain currently explain why a stranger's one-off comment feels like a verdict on your entire business?

I think it's because I put so much of myself into this place—it's not just a business, it's my passion and my identity. So when someone criticizes it, it feels like they're criticizing who I am as a person, not just what I sell. And I guess I assume that if one person says it, there must be others thinking the same thing but just not saying it out loud.

It makes complete sense that when a business carries your core identity, a critique feels like an attack on your soul rather than a simple disagreement about taste. This connection means your brain is likely assuming that her negative view reflects a hidden majority opinion, creating a sense of isolation. Since you mentioned feeling judged, how would you rate your current level of anxiety on a scale from zero to ten?

Right now, I'd say it's around a 6 or 7. It's not as high as right after the comment, but it's definitely lingering in the background. I find myself scanning customers' faces more lately, waiting for someone else to say something similar.

Scanning faces for hidden judgments is your brain trying desperately to solve a puzzle that doesn't exist, often leading to unnecessary stress. It sounds like you're carrying a heavy burden of expectation for yourself, yet you haven't given yourself permission to relax into that space. Given that a 7 is still quite draining, could we try a small experiment to break this cycle of scanning? Would you be willing to take one deep breath and consciously decide to stop monitoring others' expressions for ten minutes starting right now?

Okay, I can try that. (Takes a slow, deep breath.) I'm just going to let my shoulders drop and focus on the sound of your voice instead of what's going on outside. It feels a little strange to give myself permission to not be on guard, but I guess that's part of the problem, isn't it?

Yes, giving yourself permission to lower your guard is the hardest part because your brain has spent years keeping you safe by staying hyper-vigilant. That slight discomfort you feel is actually a sign that you are finally stepping out of the survival mode that has kept you trapped. Since this grounding feels manageable, how much easier do you feel right now compared to when you were actively scanning for threats?

I think it's dropped down to maybe a 4 or 5 now. It's not gone completely, but I don't feel that tight knot in my chest as much. It's like I can breathe a little deeper and not brace myself for the next comment. I didn't realize how tense I was holding my shoulders until you pointed it out.

That is a significant shift, and noticing that physical relaxation proves you are gaining some control back over your body. It seems the act of stopping the scan allowed your nervous system to settle enough to feel the difference. With that level of calm established, could we now look at how you might translate this "pause" into a quick mental trick to use the next time a comment lands, perhaps something as simple as labeling the thought before accepting it?

I think I could try that. Instead of just absorbing the comment and assuming it's true, I could stop and say to myself, "That's just one person's opinion, not a fact." It sounds simple, but I've never really given myself that pause before. Maybe if I practice that enough, it'll start to feel more natural.

That is a powerful insight—you are absolutely right that the magic lies in inserting that tiny pause between hearing the words and letting them define you. It turns a passive experience into an active choice, giving you the power to filter the information rather than letting it wash over you automatically. Before we wrap up, I want to know how you feel about committing to testing this "pause and label" strategy in your next interaction; does it feel like a realistic step forward for you right now?

Yeah, I think I can commit to that. It feels like a small, manageable step—something I can actually do in the moment instead of just worrying about it later. I'll try it out the next time someone makes a comment, even if it's just a quick internal reminder before I respond. Thanks, that actually feels a bit hopeful.

That sense of hopefulness is wonderful to hear, and recognizing this small step as manageable shows you are ready to take action. Remember that if you miss the pause initially, just gently bring yourself back to it without judging yourself; consistency matters more than perfection. Is there anything else you'd like to explore before we finish our time together?

No, I think I've got a good starting point to work with today. I feel a little lighter than when I came in, and I'm curious to see how this "pause and label" thing goes. Thank you for helping me see that I don't have to accept every comment as truth.

It is truly wonderful that you feel lighter and have gained such clarity about separating facts from opinions. Please remember that tomorrow is just a gentle practice; if you slip up and forget the pause, simply restart with the phrase without beating yourself up. We will circle back soon to check in on how that experiment landed for you. For now, thank you for sharing so openly, and please take care of yourself until we meet again.

Hi. Thanks, I'm glad to be back. My mood has been up and down, honestly. I tried that sentence you gave me—something about "I'm doing my best with what I have"—but it felt hollow when I said it to myself after a playdate with my friend who has three kids. I guess that's what I'd like to talk about today: why that comparison still hits so hard.

That honesty about the sentence feeling hollow is incredibly brave and shows you're paying close attention to what works for you. Since we previously discussed a version focusing on "love for your kids' growth," I wonder if shifting back to "doing my best with what I have" felt less grounded to you because it sounded more like a promise you had to keep rather than a truth you experienced? I think it felt empty because when I say "I'm doing my best," a part of me doesn't believe it. Like, if I was really doing my best, maybe my son with autism wouldn't have those meltdowns, or maybe I'd have more energy for my other kid. It just sounds like an excuse. Maybe we could work on the original sentence again, the one about love and growth? That one felt a little more real, even if I still struggled with it.

That distinction between "trying" and "resulting" makes perfect sense, and it explains exactly why "doing my best" felt like an excuse rather than a truth. Yeah, I think that could help. Maybe something like... "I love watching my kids grow, even when the growth looks different than I expected." Because my son with autism, he learned to ask for water this week instead of just crying. That's growth, right? Even if it's small compared to other kids his age. I just need to remember that counts.

That is a profound realization; recognizing that asking for water independently is a significant victory, regardless of how it compares to neurotypical milestones, validates your effort in a tangible way. By anchoring the sentence to that specific, real-world example of your son's progress, the statement moves from a vague ideal to a fact you witnessed firsthand. Would you like to try reading that refined sentence out loud together one more time, incorporating the detail about him asking for water, to see if adding that evidence makes it feel less abstract?

Okay. (pauses, takes a breath) "I love watching my kids grow, even when the growth looks different than I expected—like when my son asked for water this week instead of crying." That actually feels... true. It doesn't feel like I'm pretending. It feels like I'm just describing what happened.

Hearing it feel "true" rather than pretended is a massive breakthrough; it shifts the belief from being a requirement you must meet to simply observing a reality you created. That specificity about the water request gives your brain a solid hook to hold onto when the panic tries to creep back in. Before we wrap up, would you agree that whenever that old "drowning" feeling rises again this week, using this exact version with the water detail might be your strongest defense against the comparison trap?

Yeah, I think so. I can try to hold onto that moment when I start comparing myself to my friend with three kids. It's like... I have proof now. My son asked for water. That's real. So maybe I can stop telling myself I'm failing, because that moment didn't fail—it was a win. I'll practice saying that sentence when I feel the doubt creeping in.

That is a powerful shift in perspective; moving from "I am failing" to "This was a win" transforms the narrative entirely and gives you concrete ammunition against the doubter. Since you feel confident about this approach, let's lock in a quick plan: save this specific version in your notes app under "Mom's Truth" so it's the first thing you read when the doubt creeps in. How does having a dedicated spot for this updated script sound as a closing step?

That sounds like a good idea. "Mom's Truth" — I like that. It makes it feel like something solid I can fall back on, not just a random thought I'm trying to convince myself of. I'll put it in my phone right after we finish here. Thanks, that helps.

That is a wonderful choice; giving it a name like "Mom's Truth" helps frame it as a permanent part of your identity rather than just a temporary coping trick. Saving it immediately ensures you won't lose track of it when you need it most. I am so proud of how resilient you've shown this week, turning a shaky moment into a clear path forward. How are you feeling right now as we wrap up? Did any part of today spark anything new for you?

Hello, it’s great to see you again. Last time we worked on separating a coding bug from a larger fear of failure, and I heard how much relief that brought you. Since then, have there been any moments where you managed to catch those racing thoughts or use that breathing practice, or did the tension come back stronger? Now that we’re here, is there a particular worry or situation you’d like us to focus on today?

Hey, thanks. I mean, yeah, I did try the breathing thing a couple times when I hit a snag with the user interface code. It helped for a minute, but then the thought that the whole app is doomed just sort of crept back in. I guess I’d like to talk about this new bug I found yesterday—it’s making me feel like I’m just not cut out to finish this thing.

It makes sense that the relief from the breathing practice didn't last once the specific bug triggered that deeper fear of inadequacy. Have you noticed what happens to your body in that moment when the idea that you aren't cut out for the job pops up? For instance, do your shoulders tighten or your breathing quicken before you even start typing?

Yeah, actually, my shoulders do get really tight. And I think I start holding my breath without realizing it, like I’m bracing for something bad to happen. Right before I open the code editor, I get this sinking feeling in my stomach too, like I already know it’s going to go wrong.

Those physical sensations—shoulders locking up, holding your breath, and that sinking gut feeling—are your body's way of signaling that you perceive a major threat to your capability. It sounds like your mind and body are working together to convince you that this single bug confirms your deepest fear that you simply aren't built to finish the project. Can you recall the exact moment yesterday when you opened the editor and realized those symptoms had kicked in? What was happening right then that seemed to spark this reaction?

I remember it clearly. I had just sat down at my desk after a cup of coffee, feeling okay for a second. Then I saw the error notification on my phone—it was from the app’s beta testers. That’s when my chest tightened and I felt that knot in my stomach. I didn’t even read the full error report; I just assumed it was something huge and that I’d messed up big time.

It sounds like that error message acted as a lightning rod for your existing fears, causing your body to react instantly before you even processed what the actual problem was. In that split second, your brain likely jumped straight to the conclusion that you were incapable of fixing it, rather than looking at the specific details of the bug itself. Would you be willing to take a moment and read the error report together, just to see if the reality matches the dramatic story your mind told you? Sometimes giving your eyes a chance to see the facts can loosen that grip on the panic.

Yeah, I guess I could do that. I still have the notification on my phone, actually. (He pulls out his phone, scrolls for a second, and reads the error report.) It says there’s a conflict with the push notification library after the latest update. It’s not even about the core healing feature—it’s just a compatibility thing. I feel kind of silly now, honestly. All that panic over a library version mismatch.

It is completely understandable that feeling silly now brings a mix of relief and a bit of shame, because your body reacted with such intensity to what turned out to be a minor technical detail. Let's try to separate the scary story your brain told you from the actual facts: you are facing a library compatibility issue, which is a common hurdle many developers solve daily, rather than proof that you are incapable of finishing the project. Given how much you care about the healing aspect of the app, does knowing it's just a setup detail make the feeling of being "not cut out" seem a bit less absolute?

Yeah, it does actually. I mean, I know in my head that fixing library conflicts is just part of the job—I’ve done it a hundred times before. But when I’m in the middle of it, it feels like this huge wall that proves I’m in over my head. It’s weird how my brain just skips over all the times I’ve solved stuff like this and goes straight to “you’re a fraud.”

That is a very human experience; our brains often tunnel vision into the immediate threat and ignore our own proven track record exactly when we need it most. It sounds like the feeling of being a "fraud" isn't necessarily based on what the data shows, but rather on how urgently your nervous system interprets that error message. If we viewed that library conflict as just another puzzle piece waiting to fit into the millions you've already assembled successfully, would the narrative change from "I'm failing" to "Here's a small challenge I can tackle"?

I think so. When you put it like that, it feels more manageable. Like, it’s just one step in a long process, not the end of the world. I guess I get so caught up in wanting the app to be perfect that any little hiccup feels like a sign that it’s all going to fall apart. But this bug is just... a bug. I can probably fix it in an hour or two.

That distinction between "a bug I can fix" and "proof I'm a fraud" is powerful, and it really highlights how the urgency of wanting perfection is fueling the panic instead of helping you solve the problem. It sounds like shifting from protecting your ego to trusting your ability to handle routine hurdles makes the task feel much less threatening. Since you recognized that pattern, would you be open to trying a tiny experiment right now? The next time you see a red line in the code or get a notification, could you consciously remind yourself to check your shoulders and stomach before letting the "catastrophe story" run away? How does that sound as a way to start?

Yeah, I can try that. It sounds kind of simple, but maybe that’s the point—just noticing my body before my brain spirals. I’ll set a little reminder on my phone or something to check in with myself before I even open the error log. Thanks, I think that could actually help break the cycle a bit.

That is a brilliant insight; creating a physical checkpoint before your brain gets lost in the narrative gives you a crucial moment of control right at the start of the spiral. Since we talked about doing this with the code editor earlier, would you like to try setting that reminder on your phone now, perhaps naming it "Pause & Check Body," so you have a concrete tool ready for when the next error pops up? Once you've set that up, how does it feel to have that safety net in place before you face the bug?

Yeah, sure, I’ll do that right now. (He picks up his phone and types for a moment.) Okay, it’s set—"Pause & Check Body" with a notification sound. Honestly, it feels kind of reassuring. Like, even if I get that sinking feeling again, I have a way to stop and ask myself what’s actually happening before I panic. It’s not a cure-all, but it’s better than just letting the fear run the show.

That is a fantastic realization; having a dedicated tool named "Pause & Check Body" turns an abstract goal into a concrete safety net you can rely on. It sounds like knowing you have a structured way to intervene—even if it doesn't solve the problem immediately—gives you a much stronger sense of agency over your anxiety. Before we wrap up, how confident do you feel you are in using that new reminder effectively when you next encounter a tricky error message?

I’d say maybe a 6 out of 10? I think I can remember to use it, but I know the panic can hit so fast that I might forget in the moment. Still, just having it there gives me a little more confidence than before. I guess I’ll see how it goes next time a bug shows up.

That is a realistic and honest assessment; expecting perfection when your nervous system is racing is unrealistic, and knowing you have a tool ready is a solid foundation for recovery. Remember that even if you miss the pause or forget the reminder, the fact that you set it up means you are actively building a safer habit, which counts as success regardless of execution speed. Is there anything else weighing on your mind as we head out, or does feeling slightly lighter about that bug make you ready to close this session?

No, I think I’m good for now. I feel a bit lighter, like that bug isn’t sitting on my chest as heavily. I’ll try out the pause reminder and see how it goes. Thanks for helping me see the difference between the panic story and the actual problem.

That sense of lightness is wonderful news; it confirms that separating the panic story from the actual problem truly does make the weight feel less heavy. Thank you for sharing that vulnerability and for trusting the process enough to set up that reminder, even with a confidence level of six out of ten—that growth is exactly what matters most. Please give yourself some grace as you test the new tool today, and remember that returning to this calm perspective anytime is always an option. I hope you have a productive evening coding, and I look forward to seeing how the "Pause & Check Body" reminder serves you next time. Take care!

I think it would feel... strange, but maybe not a failure. It's hard to admit, but I've been measuring every potential connection against what I had with my spouse, and that bar is impossibly high. If someone just sat with me and listened, I suppose it wouldn't be the same, but it might not be a total loss either. I just don't know if I can allow myself to accept that kind of attention without feeling like I'm betraying what I had.

That is a very compassionate insight; you recognize that lowering the standard doesn't mean abandoning the value of your marriage, but rather realizing that connection comes in many forms, not just one perfect replica. You aren't betraying what you had by accepting a different kind of presence; you are simply expanding what you are willing to allow yourself to experience. If we focus on that evening tomorrow, could you try sitting with the camera for just fifteen minutes, watching for that "switch" happen, and then gently telling yourself that even if no one sits beside you, the room isn't necessarily empty of possibility?

I can try that. It sounds a bit scary, honestly, because I'm so used to letting that switch just take over and define my whole night. But I suppose fifteen minutes isn't too long to risk having hope. If I can just notice the moment the cold certainty creeps in and instead of giving in, I tell myself the room still holds potential, maybe that's a small step. I'll give it a shot tomorrow evening and see what happens.

Taking that step away from autopilot is brave, even if it feels uncomfortable at first. Notice that you are choosing to interrupt the automatic spiral with a deliberate pause—that is exactly how we begin to reclaim control over your evening. Before we wrap up, I want to acknowledge how much clarity you've gained today about the "impossible bar" you set for yourself. Is there anything else about tonight's plan, or perhaps a different priority, you would like to discuss before we end?

No, I think this is enough for today. It's a lot to sit with, but I feel like I have something concrete to try, which is more than I've had in a while. Thank you for helping me see that the empty room doesn't have to be a prison sentence. I'll let you know how the fifteen minutes go next time.

That is a beautiful way to frame it—shifting from viewing the evening as a prison sentence to seeing it as a practice ground for small, possible connections. I am so glad you found something concrete to hold onto today, and please remember that you don't have to wait for a miracle; sometimes just witnessing the room without judgment is enough. Thank you for trusting me with this work, and I look forward to hearing about your experiment next time.

Hello again, I’m so glad to see you. How are you feeling right now compared to last time, and do you remember any goals or tasks we discussed that you’d like to revisit first? Once we catch up, what would be most important for us to focus on today?

Oh, hi. I'm okay, I guess. Last time we talked about maybe trying to take just one photo this week, but... I didn't really do it. Every time I picked up my camera, I just kept thinking it wouldn't be any good anyway. I guess I'd like to talk about why I can't seem to even start.

It sounds like the urge to give up right when you lift the camera is running pretty strong this week. Since we had a goal of taking just one photo but haven’t managed to break through yet, I’d like to understand exactly what’s happening in those moments when the doubt hits—is there a specific thought or feeling that stops you before you even click the shutter?

Well, it's like... I'll be walking around the farm, and I'll see something nice, like the way the light hits the barn in the afternoon. But then my brain just goes, "What's the point? Someone else has already taken a better picture of a barn." And then I just feel stupid for even thinking mine could be worth anything. So I put the camera down.

That feeling of self-doubt immediately after spotting something beautiful is incredibly frustrating, and it makes total sense that you'd put the camera down to protect yourself from that sting. It sounds like your mind is jumping straight to comparing your effort to someone else's success, which feels like a proof that *no* matter what you do, it won't be good enough. Can we explore together whether there's any evidence to support that comparison, or if that belief is just a quick judgment that hasn't been tested yet?

I mean... I guess the evidence is that I've never won any contests or had my photos in a gallery like those famous photographers have. That's pretty solid proof, isn't it? They have awards and recognition, and I just have a bunch of pictures on my phone that nobody's ever seen. So it's not like I'm just imagining things—there's a real difference between us.

That is a very logical conclusion to draw from looking at the trophies on the wall versus your own screen, and it makes sense why your brain would hold onto that as "proof." However, in therapy, we often look closely at whether that comparison is telling the whole truth or just focusing on one side of the story. Could we brainstorm a few examples of people who started with nothing and eventually found joy in their photography, or perhaps instances where a "less perfect" photo still captured something meaningful for the creator?

I guess... I mean, I've seen photos online that aren't technically perfect—like they're blurry or the lighting's off—but people still like them because they show a funny moment or a pretty flower. And my little cousin takes pictures with her tablet and she's always so proud of them, even though they're just of our dogs. I guess she doesn't care if they're award-winning. But for me, it feels different. I'm older, I should be better by now.

You're absolutely right to notice that others find meaning in imperfect shots, and it's kind of unfair that your internal bar keeps raising just because you're older. It sounds like you're carrying a heavy expectation that your journey has to match theirs, which makes the reality of just having fun with your cousin's photos feel like a failure. Does seeing your cousin's pride in her simple dog photos help soften that pressure slightly, or does that "should" feel even stronger when you compare yourself to her?

It kind of makes me feel worse, actually. Like, she's just a little kid and she's having all this fun, and I'm sitting here overthinking everything. It makes me feel like I've lost something—like I used to be able to just take pictures for fun too, but now I can't. I don't know how to get back to that. It's like something's broken in my head.

That sense of losing something special is incredibly painful, and it sounds like you're mourning the version of yourself who could just enjoy the process without needing a trophy to validate it. It's easy to interpret that loss as a permanent breakdown, but what if instead of viewing it as something "broken," we looked at it as a habit that got stuck in place? Sometimes old patterns feel like they've shattered, but they're actually just waiting to be nudged back into motion. Would you be willing to try treating that "something broken" feeling like a heavy coat you're wearing, rather than a defect in your machinery?

A heavy coat... I guess I never thought of it like that. Maybe I could take it off, if I knew how. But it feels pretty stuck on me, you know? Like it's sewn on or something. What would it even look like to take it off? Do you mean just ignoring the thoughts and taking a picture anyway? Because that seems really hard.

That image of the coat sticking to you is really helpful—it captures exactly how those limiting beliefs feel resistant to just "wishing" them away. Taking it off wouldn't necessarily mean fighting the thoughts or forcing yourself to shoot perfectly; it might just mean stepping outside the jacket long enough to breathe without judging yourself while you're still wearing it. Since you mentioned that ignoring the thoughts feels too hard right now, could we try a middle ground where you acknowledge the coat is there but decide not to stay inside it until you've moved just three feet closer to the subject?

Three feet closer... that doesn't sound too scary. I think I could do that. Just walk a little closer to whatever I was going to take a picture of, even if I don't actually take the photo. That way I'm not forcing myself to click the shutter, but I'm also not running away from it completely. I could try that this week. Maybe by the barn when the light hits it in the afternoon.

That sounds like a really smart and gentle approach—acknowledging the coat is there but deciding not to wear it entirely until you've taken one small step toward the light. Before we finalize this, I want to make sure we're aligned: if you walk over to the barn and feel that familiar urge to stop, will you just say to yourself, "Hey, the coat is on, but I'm walking three feet closer anyway"? And if you notice any other thoughts popping up along the way, is there anything specific you'd like to check in with before we wrap up today?

Yeah, I can say that to myself. "The coat is on, but I'm walking closer anyway." That sounds doable. And I think that's enough for now—I don't want to add too many steps and get overwhelmed. I'll try it by the barn this week and see what happens. Thanks, that actually feels a little lighter than before.

It is wonderful to hear that you feel lighter; sometimes simply agreeing to a small, manageable step like this can make a huge difference in how you carry yourself through the day. You've chosen a perfect balance between facing the situation and respecting your energy level, and that decision shows real self-awareness. I'll see you next time to see how that "three feet" experiment went, and thank you for trusting me with this part of your journey.
