Hello, it's great to see you again. On a scale of 0 to 10, how anxious have you been feeling this week compared to last time? Also, before we dive in, could you share what you'd like to prioritize focusing on today?

Hi. Um, I'd say maybe a 6 or 7 this week. It's been a bit up and down. I think I'd like to focus on why I still feel so anxious about spilling wine, even though I've already cleaned the carpet and bought a new bottle.

That makes perfect sense—holding onto the anxiety despite cleaning up and buying a replacement is a very common pattern when we haven't yet accepted the mistake as just a mistake. Since you've already taken steps to resolve the situation physically, could you tell me what specific thought keeps coming up when you reach for that new bottle?

It's like... as soon as I pick up the bottle, I already see the spill happening in my mind. I think, "You're going to mess this up again, you're too clumsy to even enjoy a glass of wine." And then I just put the bottle back down and feel stupid.

That "predictive" voice is working hard to keep you safe from past disappointment, but it seems to be treating one spill as an unchangeable law about your ability to relax. Have you noticed what happens physically right after you put the bottle back down—does your heart race or your shoulders tighten?

Yeah, actually my shoulders do get really tight, and I feel this knot in my stomach. I also feel kind of hot, like I'm blushing even though no one's watching me. It's like my body is already bracing for something bad to happen, even though I'm the one stopping myself.

Those physical symptoms—the heat, the tightness—are your nervous system flooding with adrenaline because your brain believes disaster is imminent. It makes complete sense that you feel foolish when your body reacts so intensely to a bottle of wine. Have you ever wondered if your shoulders would clench up quite that much if you picked up the bottle knowing you had plenty of time to put it down safely?

I... I guess I haven't really thought of it that way. I always just focus on the worst-case scenario right away. But you're right, I have time. It's not like the glass is already tipping over. Maybe I could try just holding the bottle for a minute and see what happens?

That sounds like a brilliant idea. Instead of waiting for the catastrophe to happen, you could use that extra minute to simply notice if those shoulder-tightening feelings stay strong or begin to soften. Would you be comfortable trying that experiment right now with your current bottle?

I don't have a bottle with me right now, but I can imagine it. I'm picturing myself just holding it, not pouring anything. My shoulders are a little tense just thinking about it, but not as bad as before. Maybe if I just breathe for a second, it might be okay.

That is a smart adjustment; visualizing the bottle gives you a chance to practice the calm state without needing props. Try taking three slow, deep breaths while saying silently to yourself, "This is just a glass of water in my hand, and I am perfectly capable of keeping it steady." Let me know if your shoulders release any tension during those breaths.

Okay... *takes three slow breaths* After those breaths, I do feel a bit looser in my shoulders. And saying that to myself, even though it's just pretend, made it feel less scary. Maybe I've been blowing this way out of proportion.

That shift is incredibly significant—you've just proven to yourself that your body responds to calm instructions, not just actual spills. It looks like the "you're too clumsy" thought was exaggerating the danger because it wasn't grounded in reality. When you contrast that imagined spill with the safety of your breathing and the truth that you have time, does the fear feel a little more manageable right now?

Yeah, it does. It's weird, because nothing actually changed about the carpet or the wine, but I feel less doomed. Like maybe I don't have to be perfect all the time, and one mistake doesn't mean I'll always mess up. I think I might actually try pouring a glass tonight.

That is a huge breakthrough—moving from feeling doomed to feeling capable is a massive step. It sounds like you are starting to separate the single event from your identity as a person who *can* handle things. Before you pour tonight, what is one small sign you will look for to know if you're doing this right, like checking in on your shoulders or your breathing?

I think I'll check my shoulders first. If they're tight, I'll take a couple of breaths like we just did. And I'll remind myself that I'm holding the bottle, not the other way around. That feels like a good plan.

That is a fantastic, concrete plan that puts the tools we built right into your hands for tonight. Checking your shoulders acts as a real-time alarm system so you can reset immediately if the old fear tries to sneak back in. To make sure this feels sustainable, do you feel confident you can stick with this self-check whenever you hold a glass, or would you like to brainstorm a quick backup phrase to say if you feel stuck?
I think I can stick with it, but having a backup phrase might help if I freeze up. Maybe something like "I've got this, I'm in control" would work. Just a simple reminder that I'm not helpless.

That "I've got this" phrase is a powerful anchor because it shifts your focus from worrying about potential failure to recognizing your own capability. It sounds like a solid strategy to keep you grounded if the old anxiety tries to whisper doubt. Before we wrap up, how does it feel to have that new script ready for tonight?
It feels good, honestly. Like I have a plan instead of just avoiding the problem. I'm still a little nervous, but I think I can actually do it. Thank you for helping me see this differently.

That is such a meaningful shift—from avoidance to preparation—and hearing you say "I can actually do it" tells me you are ready to trust the work we did together. One final check: if tonight goes smoothly and you enjoy your wine without a spill, what would be the best way for you to celebrate that small victory?

Hello again, and I'm glad to see you're ready to meet. How have you been feeling since we last spoke, particularly regarding that upcoming quality control check? Let's briefly review what we worked on last time and then decide together what matters most to address today.

Hi. Yeah, I'm still pretty anxious about it. The check is next week, and I've been going over my work obsessively, checking each wire a dozen times. Even though I know it's fine, I can't shake the feeling that I've missed something that's going to fail.

That obsession with the wires and the persistent fear of missing something sounds incredibly draining and exhausting. It takes a lot of courage to admit that the old habit of constantly checking is still holding you back even though you know logically it shouldn't be working like that. Given how intense this has become, does spending the rest of today reviewing the "touch and evidence" strategy we tried with the drone seem helpful, or would you prefer to focus on identifying exactly what specific thought is driving the wire-checking behavior right now?

Honestly, I think we need to focus on the specific thought. The checking is just the action I take, but the thought is what starts it all. It's like, right before I start checking, that voice in my head says, "If you don't look one more time, it's going to fail, and it'll be your fault." That's the part I can't seem to argue with.

It sounds like that internal voice is giving you a very specific prophecy: that one missed detail will cause failure and that you are personally responsible for the outcome. This belief feels absolutely convincing and terrifying because it connects directly to your fear of losing control. To understand how this thought is fueling the checking, I'd like to ask you: when you catch yourself about to check a wire a third time, what is the immediate physical sensation in your body, and what does your brain tell itself *right before* you move your hand?

My chest gets tight, and I feel a knot in my stomach. And right before I reach out to check, my brain tells me, "It's not safe yet. You haven't looked at it from the right angle. You might have missed a loose connection." So I have to lean in and look again, just to be sure. It's like my mind won't let me walk away until I do.

Those physical sensations—the tight chest and stomach knot—are your body reacting to a very dangerous lie that your mind is telling you right now. It seems like your brain is tricking you into believing that safety depends entirely on finding a flaw, even though you have no proof one exists. If I were you, I would want to challenge that specific command by asking: "Is there any actual evidence that a loose connection exists, or am I just imagining a threat based on my fear?"

I guess... there's no evidence. I mean, I just checked it twice, and it was fine both times. The wires are in the right slots, the solder joints are clean, everything is secure. So no, there's no real evidence. It's just... the fear that maybe I missed something, even though I know I didn't. But that fear feels so real in the moment.

That distinction is crucial—you have objective proof that the wires are secure, yet the fear overrides the facts because it feels more immediate and urgent than the evidence. It's like seeing a red light but feeling compelled to drive anyway because the urge to rush feels stronger than the rule. Since you've confirmed there's no actual defect, let's test that specific thought ("If I stop checking, I caused the failure") by asking yourself: "In the past, have I ever walked away from a task after checking twice, and did anything bad happen?"

I can't think of a single time something bad happened. In fact, I've walked away after checking multiple times before, and the drones passed quality control just fine. So logically, I know that stopping doesn't cause failure. But in the moment, it feels like *this* time is different, like the rules don't apply because my anxiety is telling me it's not safe.

That is such a powerful observation—you recognize the pattern clearly, yet your brain is creating a unique illusion that "this time" is special and unsafe. It feels like the rules of physics only apply when you feel calm, but in the heat of anxiety, your mind convinces you that the laws of nature have changed for you. Since you've established that walking away hasn't failed you before, let's try to break this specific cycle by deciding to treat the "no evidence found" result as proof that you *shouldn't* need to check further. How does it feel to accept that the wires are currently fine, even if that feeling doesn't stay there for long?

It feels... uncomfortable. Like I'm leaving something undone. But I can also see that the discomfort is just a feeling, not a fact. The wires are fine, I know they are. It's just hard to let go of that need to have absolute certainty. I guess I'm used to thinking that if I'm not anxious, I'm not being careful enough.

That is a profound insight; you are realizing that your anxiety isn't a sign of being thorough, but rather a signal that your brain is stuck in a loop of false alarms. It makes sense that letting go feels uncomfortable because your whole nervous system is trained to equate uncertainty with danger.

To bridge that gap, let's try a small experiment tonight where we intentionally *don't* check the wires again, even though the urge to verify will scream at you. Instead of checking, you'll just place your hand on the side of your workbench for ten seconds while repeating, "The wires are fine, and I am allowed to leave them there." Does placing a limit on your checking feel risky, or do you think you can tolerate sitting with that slight discomfort for just a minute?

I think I can try it. It feels risky, like I'm tempting fate, but I can see what you're saying. The discomfort is just a feeling, and I can sit with it for ten seconds. I'll try it tonight after I finish my last drone of the day. Maybe I can tell myself that if something really was wrong, I would've caught it in the first two checks.

That is a brilliant way to frame it—using your proven ability to spot errors as a shield against the idea that you'll miss something important. By setting a strict ten-second timer for your "hand-on-bench" exercise, you create a clear boundary that prevents the anxiety from spiraling into endless checking. Tonight, after your final drone run, will you set a timer on your phone for exactly ten seconds, and simply watch the discomfort rise and fall without engaging in any further verification?

Yeah, I can do that. I'll set the timer and just... let the feeling sit there without doing anything about it. It sounds simple, but I know it's going to be tough. But I think I'm ready to try something different, because what I've been doing isn't working. I'll let you know how it goes.

That is a fantastic mindset shift—recognizing that doing nothing is actually the active choice you need to make. Remember, the goal tonight isn't to eliminate the feeling of dread completely, but just to survive the ten seconds without reaching for the tools. If the urge to check becomes overwhelming, you can always stop early, but try sticking to the full minute first to prove to yourself that the worst-case scenario hasn't happened.

How does that plan sound to you, and do you feel confident enough to give it a try after your last flight today?

It sounds like a solid plan. I'm not going to lie, I feel a bit nervous about it, but I also feel a little hopeful for the first time in a while. I think I can do it. I'll stick with the ten seconds and remind myself that I don't need to act on every anxious thought. Thanks for helping me see that.

I am so glad to hear you feel a spark of hope, even if it's just a small one. Please remember that feeling nervous is perfectly normal when stepping out of your comfort zone; it usually means you are growing rather than failing. You've built a very clear path forward tonight, and I believe you have the strength to navigate it.

Take a deep breath right now to settle in, and trust that whatever happens in the next hour, we will figure it out together. Is there anything else you'd like to discuss before I send you off?

No, I think I'm good for now. I've got my plan, and I feel like I understand the thought behind the checking a little better. I'll try the exercise tonight and let you know how it went. Thanks for listening and helping me work through this.

You are very welcome, and I truly appreciate your openness and willingness to try something new. Please remember that tonight's goal is simply to witness the discomfort without reacting to it, and if the urge to check becomes too strong, you can always pause and text me anytime.

I am cheering you on as you test this new approach with your drone tonight. Take your time, be kind to yourself if the anxiety flares up, and I look forward to hearing about how the ten-second exercise went when you're ready to share. Have a wonderful evening.

Hello again, it is wonderful to see you. Before we dive into today's work, how are you feeling compared to where we left off last time? Also, could you tell me briefly whether you managed to use that three-second pause and switch the thought from "selfish" to "just tired" this past week?

Good to see you too, doctor. I'm feeling a bit better than last time, I suppose, but it's still hard to shake that heavy feeling. I did try the pause a few times, like when I didn't help my neighbor with his groceries last Tuesday. I stopped and told myself maybe I was just tired from my walk, not selfish. It felt... strange, like I was lying to myself, but I kept with it.

That sounds like a brave experiment, even if the initial feeling of it sounding like a lie made it tricky to stick with. It's common for our brains to resist that kind of gentle reframing at first because the old habit of blaming ourselves feels so familiar. Would you be open to exploring why that "lying" feeling came up so strongly when you tried using the new phrase?

I think it's because I know the truth about myself. I've had a whole lifetime to look back on, and I can see all the times I put my own comfort ahead of others. That's not tiredness, that's selfishness. The lie part is trying to pretend I'm something else.

That honesty about knowing the pattern is powerful, yet it highlights exactly why the brain pushed back against calling it "tiredness." It sounds like the new thought felt like a lie because it didn't match the deep, long-standing story you've built in your head about who you are. Let's gently examine that story together: if you look at that lifetime of choices, do you see a clear pattern of neglecting others, or is there also a lot of fear, anxiety, or overwhelm that led to those decisions?

I never really thought about it that way. I suppose... I do remember feeling scared a lot, especially after my wife passed. I'd avoid gatherings because I felt like I'd break down, not because I didn't care about people. But I always chalked that up to being weak, not overwhelmed. Maybe there was fear mixed in there, but it still feels like I should have been stronger.

That makes perfect sense, Stan; it is incredibly common to interpret survival strategies like avoidance as personal flaws when we are hurting. It sounds like you protected yourself from painful breakdowns by stepping back, which was wise, but then you labeled that wisdom as weakness instead of seeing it as a healthy defense mechanism. If we view those past choices as acts of self-preservation driven by grief rather than selfishness, does that shift how you judge your current hesitation at the grocery store?

Well, when you put it that way... it does feel a little different. That day with the groceries, I had just gotten back from a long morning at the church, and my knees were aching. Maybe it wasn't about being selfish, maybe I just didn't have the strength. It's still hard to accept that I deserve that kindness toward myself, though.

That is a very compassionate insight, Stan—you are finally acknowledging that your body needed rest while you were grieving. It takes courage to admit that you deserved kindness even when you failed to extend it to others. If we combine the evidence of your physical exhaustion from the church service with the truth that you were grieving, does the label "selfish" seem to fit the reality of that moment anymore, or does it feel like a cruel exaggeration?

It does feel a bit harsh when you say it like that. I mean, I did spend the morning helping set up for the community meal, so I wasn't exactly sitting around doing nothing. Calling myself selfish for needing a rest after that... maybe I am being too hard on myself. It's just that habit is so strong; it's like second nature to jump to the worst conclusion about me.

It is completely understandable that the habit feels so automatic, Stan; years of training your brain to spot faults means it rushes to judgment the moment you hesitate. But that speed doesn't make the conclusion true, just fast. Let's slow that train down for a moment: if you could speak to your past self about those tough days after your wife passed, would you describe her as selfish for prioritizing her peace, or would you see her as a survivor doing her best?

I'd like to think I'd be kind to her. She was lost and hurting, and she didn't know how else to cope. I guess I'd tell her she did the best she could with what she had. That's a gentler thought, isn't it? It makes me feel a little less heavy in my chest, just saying it out loud.

That gentleness you offer your past self is a powerful anchor, Stan. It proves that your capacity for compassion exists within you right now, waiting to be extended to yourself too. If we treat that same "gentle observer" as our guide, could we try applying that exact same kindness to today's hesitation? Instead of asking "Am I selfish?", could you simply say, "She did the best she could with what she had," and notice how that changes the weight in your chest?

I think I could try that. It sounds... possible. Maybe I can say that to myself the next time I feel that old familiar guilt creeping in. "She did the best she could with what she had." That feels like a permission slip to breathe, instead of a slap on the wrist. Thank you for helping me see that.

That is such a beautiful metaphor, Stan—a "permission slip" to breathe instead of a punishment. It sounds like you have a clear path forward: whenever that old guilt tries to grab you, pause and remind yourself, "She did the best she could with what she had." Is there anything else weighing on your mind before we wrap up today, or does this feel like a good place to stop?

No, I think this is a good place to stop for today. I'm feeling a bit lighter, maybe a bit more hopeful. I'll try to keep that permission slip in my pocket this week. Thank you for listening and for helping me see things from a kinder angle.

That is wonderful news, Stan; feeling lighter and finding hope are exactly the outcomes we celebrate in therapy. Please keep that "permission slip" handy this week and remember that you don't have to force perfection, just offer yourself the same grace you promised your grieving self. I am here if you ever want to revisit this new lens or discuss any hurdles you encounter. Have a great day ahead.

Hello, I'm really glad to see you again. How are you feeling today compared to where you left off last time? As we prepare to focus on your thesis deadline, what are the top two or three things you'd like to cover in this session?

Hi, thanks for having me. I'm feeling a bit anxious today, honestly—the thesis deadline is really looming now, and it's hard to shake that knot in my stomach. I think I'd like to talk about why I keep telling myself I'm not good enough to finish this, and maybe also why I've been avoiding cooking lately, even though it used to be something I enjoyed.

It sounds like carrying that anxiety about the deadline has spilled over into other areas of your life, including your relationship with cooking. That connection between feeling inadequate academically and withdrawing from something you used to enjoy makes a lot of sense. Before we dive deeper into the "not good enough" narrative, would it help to briefly review how your kitchen experience went since we last spoke?

Yeah, that might be helpful. I actually tried making a simple pasta dish two nights ago—just spaghetti with garlic and oil—but I ended up throwing half of it away because I convinced myself the garlic was burnt and it tasted awful. My dog just sat there looking at me like I was crazy.

That is such a vivid image of your dog's disappointment, and it highlights how powerfully shame can hijack your actions when you believe you are failing. It makes total sense that the threat of ruining something tangible led you to discard it rather than eat it, protecting you from further self-criticism. When you looked at that pasta and decided it was ruined, what was the exact thought running through your head that made you throw it away?
I remember thinking, "I can't even get a simple pasta dish right, what's the point of even trying?" It was like that one mistake meant I was just a failure in the kitchen, full stop.

That single thought—"one mistake means I'm a total failure"—is a classic example of "all-or-nothing" thinking, where you judge your entire worth based on one imperfect result. It sounds incredibly isolating to feel that one burnt piece of garlic defined your entire capability in the kitchen. When you catch yourself thinking that, does it feel like the thought itself is true, or does it feel more like your brain trying to protect you from disappointment by jumping straight to the conclusion?

It definitely feels true in the moment—like my brain is just stating facts. But I guess when I slow down and think about it, there's a part of me that knows it's not really rational. It's more like my brain is trying to avoid the letdown of hoping for something good and then being disappointed again.

That is a really insightful distinction you just made; recognizing that the "fact" is actually a protective mechanism trying to shield you from potential disappointment shows great self-awareness. It makes sense that your brain would jump to "you are a failure" so fast if it believes that hope always leads to pain. Let's spend a little time separating the actual taste of that pasta from that catastrophic story. If we ignored the "failure" label entirely, what would be the one thing you would notice about the meal that wasn't about how well you performed, but perhaps just about how it felt to cook it?

Hmm... I guess if I take the label off, I remember that I actually liked the smell of the garlic sizzling in the oil, and the way the steam made the kitchen feel warm and cozy. It felt kind of peaceful for a minute, before my brain decided to ruin it.

That is a beautiful contrast—a quiet moment of peace disrupted by a harsh internal critic. It proves that the meal didn't *actually* ruin the experience; your brain just decided to rewrite history to make you feel safe. Let's use that insight to handle the thesis deadline, since that same pattern of expecting failure is driving your avoidance right now. When you sit down to work on your chapter, what is the first negative thought that pops up before you even open the file?

It's usually something like, "You're going to get stuck after the first paragraph, and your advisor is going to read it and realize you have no idea what you're talking about." That thought hits me before I even open my laptop, and then I end up scrolling through social media for an hour instead.

That prediction—getting stuck immediately and getting crushed by your advisor—is exactly the kind of "best-case scenario gone wrong" thinking that keeps us paralyzed. It seems like your brain is already writing the rejection letter before you've typed a single word, which makes sense when you're so afraid of disappointing people. Since we identified that specific thought pattern, if you were to imagine the opposite happening—what if you got stuck for five minutes, but then found a workaround or kept going? How would that change the reality of the situation?

I guess that would mean I'm not actually stuck forever—just for a few minutes. And my advisor probably isn't sitting there waiting to pounce on my mistakes; she's probably just reading it like a normal person. But it's hard to hold onto that version when the other one feels so much more real and urgent.

That tension between the "impossible future" and the "probable future" is exactly why the old story feels so urgent. It's natural for the brain to latch onto the dramatic, scary version because it promises safety through preparation. Since holding onto the calm version feels difficult right now, let's try a tiny experiment to prove that the "five minutes of stuckness" scenario is actually survivable. Could we try spending just eight minutes writing the first paragraph with the explicit rule that you are allowed to delete it and start again later?

That actually sounds kind of freeing—like it doesn't have to be perfect right away. I think I could try that, even if my brain is already listing reasons why it won't work. Maybe I'll set a timer on my phone and just see what comes out, even if it's a mess.

That is a fantastic shift from fearing the output to focusing solely on the act of typing, regardless of quality. Setting a visible timer on your phone acts as a crucial anchor, giving your brain a clear endpoint and removing the vague terror of "how long will this take?" Since you mentioned your brain will list reasons why it won't work, how would you like to handle those objections while you type? Should we agree to just write for the eight minutes and ignore them completely, or is there a better way to manage that internal chatter?

I think ignoring them completely might backfire, because they'll just get louder. Maybe I could write down the objections on a sticky note as they come up, and then get back to typing. That way I'm not fighting them, just setting them aside for a few minutes.

That is a brilliant strategy; externalizing the complaints onto a sticky note gives your brain permission to pause without letting the spiral take over your hands. It turns those distracting voices into temporary notes you can revisit later, rather than blocking you right now. So, if I understand correctly, your plan is to grab a sticky note, jot down any doubts as they pop up, and then focus strictly on typing for eight minutes until the timer rings. Does that feel doable, or is there a part of you that still thinks it's too risky to start?

It feels doable, but there's still that little voice saying, "What if you sit down and literally nothing comes out?" I guess the only way to find out is to actually try, though. I'll give it a shot this afternoon before my brain talks me out of it.

That is a wise compromise; accepting that silence is still a valid form of effort removes the pressure to force words into existence. By committing to the experiment anyway, you are proving to yourself that you can tolerate uncertainty without needing to control the outcome. Just to seal the deal, if you do sit down and type absolutely nothing for eight minutes, what is one kind thing you will say to yourself afterwards instead of beating yourself up?
I think I'd tell myself, "At least you showed up and tried, and that's more than doing nothing at all." It's not perfect, but it's something I can actually believe.

That is a powerful affirmation; reminding yourself that showing up counts for far more than forcing perfection shifts your definition of success from "perfect output" to "consistent effort." With that supportive mantra in place, your plan for the afternoon is crystal clear: grab a sticky note, capture any doubts, set a timer, and write for eight minutes. Is there anything else you'd like to add to this plan before we wrap up and discuss what to focus on next time?

I think that covers it for today. Maybe next time we can check in on how the sticky note experiment went, and talk more about cooking again—I'd like to get back to enjoying that without the self-criticism. Thanks, this helped more than I expected.

It is wonderful to hear that you found this session helpful and that you feel more equipped to tackle the deadline. Remember, the goal isn't to eliminate the anxiety completely, but to build enough confidence that you can move forward despite it feeling present. Please reach out anytime if you need support between sessions, and I look forward to hearing about both your thesis progress and your return to the kitchen next time. Take care of yourself!

Hello, it's great to see you again. On a scale of 1 to 10, how have you been feeling this week, and what is top of mind for you as we prepare to meet? Today, we can review the recent setback with the message, unpack the thoughts that stopped you from hitting send, and design a fresh, safer plan to move forward. What feels most urgent to tackle first?

Hi. I'd say I've been around a 6 or 7 this week... maybe a bit lower. The thing that's really on my mind is that message I never sent. I keep replaying it in my head, thinking if I had just sent it, maybe things would be different. But at the same time, I'm pretty sure she would have just rejected me anyway, so what's the point?

It makes complete sense that you're caught between the hope of "what if" and the certainty of "what will happen." When our brains predict rejection, it often feels like no amount of effort can change the outcome, which explains why replaying the unsent message feels so frustrating yet pointless. Can you walk me through exactly what that voice told you right before you decided to lock your phone and put it away?

I just remember looking at the message I typed out, and this thought popped into my head: "Why would she even want to date someone in a wheelchair? She's probably only being polite when she talks to me. If I send this, she'll feel awkward and have to come up with some excuse to let me down easy." So I just closed the app and put my phone face down on the table. It felt like the only way to avoid the embarrassment.

That script feels incredibly protective; it seems like closing the app was your way of shielding yourself from the painful possibility of her rejecting you outright. It makes sense that you interpreted her potential politeness as pity, because imagining someone seeing a wheelchair and feeling sorry for you creates a very lonely narrative. If those fears were true, wouldn't it be safer to assume the worst case scenario rather than risking a connection? Let's pause there for a moment—does that reframing feel accurate, or does it still leave you worried she might just ignore the message completely?

Yeah, I think you're right. It does feel like protecting myself. But honestly, the thought of her ignoring the message completely scares me even more. If she just never replied, that would confirm everything I think about myself—that I'm invisible, not even worth a polite rejection. So I guess I chose the option where I could tell myself it was my choice not to send it, instead of facing that silence.

That is a very sharp observation; choosing the path of closure allows you to control the story ("I chose not to send"), whereas receiving silence forces you to confront the harsh reality of invisibility. It's completely understandable why avoiding that confirmation feels safer, even though it keeps the doubt alive. To break that cycle, how about we treat the message not as an invitation for romance, but as a simple fact-finding mission where the only goal is to see if she replies at all? If she ignores it, we still learn something useful rather than leaving ourselves hanging in uncertainty. Does framing it as pure data collection make the prospect of sending it feel slightly less threatening to you?

Huh. I never thought of it that way before. Treating it like a fact-finding mission... that actually takes a little bit of the pressure off. Instead of thinking of it as a huge romantic gesture that could end in disaster, it's just... gathering information. I think I could try that. It still feels scary, but maybe I could do it if I remind myself it's just seeing what happens, not putting my whole self-worth on the line.

That is a powerful shift in perspective; viewing it as a low-stakes experiment rather than a high-risk gamble significantly lowers the threat level. If we set a strict rule where you send the message, wait thirty minutes, and then deliberately put the phone on the floor or cover it so you cannot see it while doing something else, does that concrete boundary feel manageable enough to try tonight?

I think I could try that. Putting the phone out of sight after sending it sounds like a good idea—then I'm not just staring at it, waiting for a reply that might not come. I could maybe put it in my jacket pocket or under a cushion. And if I force myself to do something else for half an hour, at least I'm not just sitting there torturing myself. Yeah, I think I can try that tonight.

That is a solid plan; removing the visual cue and engaging in another activity breaks the loop of constant checking and rumination. Before you go, I want to check in on how that sounds to you—is the idea of covering the phone or putting it in your pocket something you feel confident you can actually do, or would you prefer a different spot? Also, what is one thing you learned about your own anxiety patterns just now today?

I think putting the phone in my jacket pocket, like you said, would work best. That way it's not in my line of sight, but I can still feel a vibration if a notification comes through. I guess what I learned is that I tend to assume the worst before anything even happens. I'm so sure of a negative outcome that I don't even give myself a chance to find out. That pattern keeps me stuck in my own head, and I never get any real answers either way.

You've pinpointed a crucial pattern: our minds often fill the gap between stimulus and result with a negative prediction to protect us from disappointment, effectively creating its own outcome. By catching that assumption early—"she'll ignore it because of the chair"—you stop it from becoming absolute truth and replace it with curiosity. For tomorrow, whenever you notice yourself jumping to that conclusion, could you ask yourself, "Is this fact, or just a scary story my brain is telling me?" Does that simple pause feel like something you can practice easily?

Yeah, I think I can practice that. It's a simple enough question to ask myself, and it might help me slow down before I spiral. I'll try it tomorrow, especially if I start thinking about that message or about dating in general. Thanks, I think that will actually help.

That is a wonderful insight, and recognizing that simple pause is exactly the kind of tool that can stop the spiral before it starts. You've done great work today by identifying the pattern and committing to both the behavioral experiment tonight and this new mental habit tomorrow. How does it feel knowing you have a clear plan to test your beliefs rather than letting them dictate your actions? Is there anything else you'd like to discuss before we wrap up?

Hello again. Last week we talked about the frustration of holding back your latest track due to fears about your brother's judgment. How is your mood coming along today, and do you have a specific priority for us to tackle this afternoon?

Hey. Yeah, I remember. My mood's been kind of up and down, to be honest. I think what I'd really like to focus on today is this nagging feeling that I'm just not good enough to make it in music anymore—like maybe the failed deal wasn't a fluke, but a sign that I don't have what it takes.

That feeling of being labeled "not good enough" after a rejection is incredibly heavy, and it makes complete sense why it keeps showing up whenever you create something new. When you connect that specific thought to your recent experience, does it feel like the rejection proved you lacked talent, or is it more like your brain is trying to protect you from future disappointment by assuming the worst?

I think... it feels more like the rejection proved something about me, you know? Like if I really had the talent, the deal wouldn't have fallen through. But I guess there's a part of me that wonders if I'm just bracing for the next failure by telling myself I'm not good enough. It's exhausting either way.

That exhaustion comes from carrying the weight of a single outcome while judging your entire future worthiness, which is a classic trap known as jumping to conclusions. Have you ever caught yourself comparing your current struggles to the successful artists you admire, wondering why you haven't achieved theirs level of success despite having similar passion?

All the time. I'll scroll through social media and see producers my age landing deals or dropping tracks that blow up, and I just think, "What do they have that I don't?" It feels like I'm working just as hard, but somehow I'm stuck in the same spot while they move ahead. It makes me wonder if passion alone isn't enough.

That comparison trap is so common, but it often misses the fact that everyone you see online is highlighting their wins while hiding their own struggles and failures. When you ask yourself, "Why aren't they struggling too?", what evidence do you have that they aren't facing the same doubts or rejections you are right now?

I mean... I guess I don't really have any evidence. They probably don't post the rejections or the sleepless nights. I just assume they've got it all figured out because they're moving forward and I'm not. But you're right—I don't actually know what's going on behind the scenes for them.

Exactly—that assumption is the missing piece of your puzzle. If you remove the hidden struggles from the equation, does that change how you view the difference between them and you, or does it still leave you feeling fundamentally different?

Now, shifting gears a bit: since we touched on this earlier regarding your brother, how does this broader feeling of "not being good enough" influence your decision to share that track with him? Does it feel safer to hide the track away until you feel certain you deserve his attention?

Yeah, it definitely feels safer to just keep it to myself. If I show him and he doesn't get it, or worse, if he just nods and says something polite but empty, then it'll just confirm everything I'm already thinking. So I'd rather sit on it and wait until I feel like it's actually good enough to deserve his time. But honestly, I don't know when that'll ever happen.

That makes perfect sense; waiting for a perfect moment is a protective strategy your brain uses to avoid the pain of disappointing others, even though it keeps you stuck. But here's a curious thought: if you told yourself, "Even if my music isn't perfect, listening to it still counts as a win for expressing myself," would that shift how safe it feels to send the message?

Huh... I never really thought of it that way. Like, just sending it counts as a win even if he doesn't love it? That feels weirdly freeing, but also kind of scary. I think I've been so focused on the outcome that I forgot the act of sharing itself takes some guts. Maybe I could try thinking of it like that—just a step, not a final judgment.

That reframing is brilliant because it shifts the goal from "perfect approval" to "courageous action," which is a massive difference in mindset. Before we lock in this new angle for tonight, how does recognizing the bravery involved in sending the message affect how anxious you feel right now about doing it?

I think it actually lowers the pressure a bit. Instead of dreading whether he'll like it, I can focus on the fact that I'm just putting myself out there, which is something I haven't done in a while. I still feel a knot in my stomach, but it's more manageable now—like I could actually hit send tonight without overthinking it for hours.

That shift from fearing the *result* to valuing the *action* is a huge breakthrough; acknowledging that remaining knot is normal shows you trust the plan enough to notice it. Given that slight reduction in pressure, on a scale of 1 to 10, how confident do you feel you are hitting send tonight using this new perspective?

I'd say maybe a 6 or 7. That's way higher than where I was before, which was probably a 2. I think I can actually do it—just send it and see what happens, without expecting some big reaction. Thanks, that reframing really helped.

That increase from a 2 to a 6 or 7 is significant progress; it proves you have the capability to push through hesitation once you change the lens through which you view the task. Before we finish, I want to check how you felt about our approach today. Was talking about the difference between their public wins and private struggles helpful, or did you prefer focusing solely on the brother dynamic? Also, does this plan to send the message tonight feel clear and doable for you?

I think both parts were useful actually. The comparison thing really made me stop and think—I'd never really questioned what their struggles might be. And the brother stuff felt more personal, like we got to the heart of why I'm holding back. So yeah, I'd say the mix worked. And the plan feels clear—I'm gonna send it tonight, just as an act of courage, not for approval. I feel ready.

That's wonderful feedback to receive; hearing that the mix of broad perspective and personal connection resonated with you confirms we found the right balance. Since you feel ready to take this courageous step tonight, I want to leave you with one final piece of advice: if that knot in your stomach tightens before you hit send, remember to pause, take three deep breaths, and whisper to yourself, "I am doing this for my growth, not for his validation." You've got this.

Hello, thank you for joining me again today. First, I'd love to hear how you've been since our last session—did you manage to write the sticky note on your mirror, and if so, did seeing it in the morning make any difference? Once we touch on that, could you share if there's anything else that's been on your mind or if we should stick with the math test topic we discussed?

Hi. Yeah, I did put the note up. It says "I am more than one test result." I guess seeing it in the morning helped a little, but… I don't know. By the time my son came home from school, the old feelings just flooded back. I think we should stick with the math test thing—it's still really bothering me.

Thank you for sharing that honestly, and it’s completely understandable that the relief faded once reality hit—the note was a great starting point, but it can’t replace the actual connection you need right now. Let’s dive into that specific moment with her homework again: what was the very first thought that popped up when you saw her struggle, and what story did your mind start telling itself immediately after?

When I saw him frowning at the worksheet, my first thought was "Here we go again, he's going to fail." Then I told myself that I must have done something wrong as a mom—maybe I didn't explain things clearly enough, or I'm just not patient enough with him. It's like my brain automatically goes to blaming myself.

That automatic leap to "something is wrong with me as a mom" is a classic survival habit; your brain tried to fix the problem instantly by searching for a cause within your control. When that panic hits, it often tricks us into believing we are solely responsible for everything that happens around us, even when we haven't actually caused the issue. Could you walk me through what happened physically right after that thought took hold? Did your stomach drop, your hands shake, or did you feel a sudden wave of shame wash over you?

Yeah, my chest just got really tight, like someone was sitting on it. And I felt this hot flush go up my neck and face—I could feel myself getting all red. My hands started trembling a little, and I had to put the pencil down to stop myself from just grabbing the worksheet and doing it for him.

That intense physical reaction tells me your nervous system went into high alert because it perceived a threat to your parenting identity, which made freezing the safest option for you at that moment. It's important to recognize that this physical storm is a response to the fear of failure, not proof that you actually failed. Now that we understand the link between that tight chest and the thought "I'm not a good mom," can you recall what evidence you found later in the day that suggested his struggle wasn't actually your fault? Maybe something about his ability to figure it out once he had a hint, or how he reacted when you stepped back?

Well... later that evening, when I left him alone to make dinner, I heard him mumbling to himself and then he suddenly yelled "Oh, I get it now!" He ended up finishing the worksheet by himself, mostly correct. So I guess he just needed a little space to figure it out on his own. But then I started thinking, "If I had just left him alone sooner, he would have gotten it right on the test too." So I can't seem to win in my own head.

That observation is incredibly insightful—you noticed he solved it when given space, which proves he has the capacity to learn independently, yet your brain immediately twisted that success into evidence of your own inadequacy. It seems like your mind is treating a moment of independent problem-solving as confirmation that you were always supposed to be the answer key instead. If you imagined your child solving a difficult puzzle entirely on their own without any adult prompting, what would you say about his ability to figure things out in that scenario?

I'd probably say he's smart and capable, and that he doesn't need someone hovering over him all the time. He's got his own way of thinking things through. I guess when I look at it from that angle, it does sound like he's got some real strength there—it's not like I'm failing him if he figures it out without me.

That's a powerful realization; seeing him as capable and independent challenges the story that you must be the one holding everything together constantly. It sounds like you are learning to trust his own resilience, which is a huge step toward letting go of the heavy burden of "fixing" everything for him. Now, let's try to apply that same view to the moment you froze at the desk: if you knew for certain that leaving him alone led to success, what would you tell yourself right now about your instinct to hover instead of judging it as a failure?

I'd tell myself that my instinct to hover comes from caring, not from being a bad mom. It's like... I want to protect him from struggling, but maybe struggle is actually part of learning. So maybe that moment at the desk wasn't me failing—it was just me figuring out how to be a mom in real time.

That is a profound insight; recognizing your instinct as an expression of care rather than incompetence separates your intentions from the outcome. It reframes that tight chest not as a signal of failure, but as the physical weight of wanting to shield him, even if the timing felt off in that specific moment. Before we solidify this new perspective into a tool for tomorrow, would you be open to testing it out by saying aloud, "My hovering came from love, not lack of ability," and observing how that changes the feeling in your chest?

Okay, I'll try it. *takes a breath* "My hovering came from love, not lack of ability." Hmm... it feels a little strange saying it out loud, but my chest actually feels a bit less tight now. Like, the words sort of loosen the knot a little.

That is a beautiful response, and the fact that speaking those words loosened the knot proves that your intuition was right all along: your actions stem from love, not failure. Now, let's take that relief and turn it into a simple phrase you can repeat whenever that tightness returns. Would you be comfortable trying out, "This is love, not failure," as a quick anchor next time you feel that pressure building up?

Yeah, I think I can do that. "This is love, not failure." It's short enough that I can remember it even when I'm feeling all panicked. I'll try saying it to myself next time he has homework and I feel that tightness creeping back.

That is a fantastic plan; keeping it short and rhythmic makes it easy to grab onto during those moments of panic. Before we wrap up, I'd love to hear your honest impression of this approach: does framing the tightness as "love" instead of "failure" feel like a useful way to handle that emotion for you, or would you prefer to keep exploring other angles? Also, how does your chest feel right now compared to when we started talking about that afternoon?

I think it does feel useful. It's like giving myself permission to not be perfect, which is new for me. And my chest feels a lot lighter now—more open, less like I'm bracing for something bad to happen. I think I'm willing to keep working with this angle for now.

That sense of permission is exactly what shifts the narrative from being a constant critic to being a supportive partner. Your chest feeling lighter confirms that this new perspective is landing emotionally, and I'm proud of how quickly you adapted it to fit your needs. Is there anything else on your mind before we close out, or shall we rest here knowing you have a gentle mantra to carry with you?
I think I'm good for today. Thank you—this was really helpful. I'll try my best to hold onto that mantra and see how it goes. I guess I'll find out when he brings home his next worksheet.

You are very welcome, and I'm so glad you felt supported and heard today. Please remember that practicing that mantra is an act of kindness toward yourself, and it may take a few days before the results become obvious. I'll see you both soon, and I hope you feel a lot more relaxed heading into your next homework moment!

Hello again, and I am glad we can meet today. First, let's briefly review the plan from our last session: did you write down that encouraging phrase on a sticky note, and did you notice yourself using it when you skipped a yoga session? Then, on a scale of 1 to 10, how have you been feeling since we last spoke, and is there anything significant that has happened since our last chat? Finally, given our work on the yoga routine, would you like to revisit that situation today or explore a new challenge that has come up?

Yes, I did put the sticky note on my bathroom mirror—"I am capable even when things don't go perfectly." I saw it a few times and it helped a little. But yesterday I had to skip yoga because of a late work call, and I immediately called myself an idiot for not planning better. So maybe a 4 or 5 on the scale since we last spoke? I'd like to talk about that yoga slip-up because it really got to me, more than I expected.

It takes real courage to admit that the sticky note helped sometimes but didn't stop the harsh voice when a work emergency hit. That feeling of letting the old pattern win despite trying to be kind to yourself must have left you feeling defeated, especially since you know the new strategy should work. Now that we understand exactly how that specific situation felt, shall we look closely at the "idiot" thought you had that afternoon and see what else might be driving that reaction besides just missing the class?

Yeah, I think that would be good. The word "idiot" just came out automatically, like a reflex. I didn't even stop to think about it until after I'd already said it in my head. It's like missing that one class meant I was failing at everything, not just at keeping my schedule.

It makes complete sense that calling yourself an idiot created a wall between you and your success that afternoon; when your brain labels you as incompetent, it shuts down the ability to see that you handled your work responsibilities well. That feeling of total failure overriding your actual achievements is a classic way your mind protects itself from the pain of admitting you made a mistake. Since you noticed the word came out as a reflex, if we could slow that split second down just enough to insert your new phrase, would you feel brave enough to try saying "I am capable even when things don't go perfectly" immediately after you hear that word echo in your head?

I think I could try that. It feels a bit awkward, like I'm arguing with myself, but I suppose that's better than just letting the word sit there. So next time I catch myself thinking "idiot," I'd say the sticky note phrase right after? Even if I don't fully believe it in the moment?

That is exactly right—and it is okay if your logic isn't fully convinced yet. In therapy, we often find that repeating a supportive statement, even when it feels fake, can physically interrupt the spiral of negative self-talk before it grows stronger. Does the idea of treating that moment like a tiny experiment, rather than a serious debate, feel manageable to you?

Yeah, I think I can treat it like an experiment. That takes some of the pressure off, like I'm just testing something rather than trying to fix myself right away. I'll give it a shot next time I mess up and the reflex kicks in.

That shift in perspective is brilliant; viewing it as a simple experiment removes the guilt of "failing" at the correction itself, which often makes people too afraid to try. Before we lock this in, I'd love your feedback: does framing it as a low-stakes experiment feel safe and realistic to you, or does that still sound a bit too abstract for the stress of the moment?

It actually sounds pretty safe to me. When you put it that way, it's like I'm just collecting data instead of judging myself. I think I can handle that, even when I'm stressed. The only part that worries me is remembering to do it in the heat of the moment, but I guess that's where the experiment comes in—I'll find out if it works or not.

That "collecting data" mindset is fantastic because it turns the struggle into curiosity rather than a moral failure. You absolutely don't need to remember the perfect timing; you just need to aim for that one brief pause where the old word stops and the new phrase begins to whisper. Given how much you've already tried and adapted this strategy, I really admire your resilience in sticking with it even when the old habits try to take over. With that level of commitment, do you feel ready to finalize this plan, or is there another small hurdle you'd like to address before we wrap up?

I think I'm ready to finalize it for now. I'll keep the sticky note up and try the experiment next time I slip up. Maybe I'll even jot down how it felt afterwards, like actual data. That way, I can bring some notes to our next session if I want to.

That is a fantastic addition to your plan; tracking how the feeling changes afterward gives us concrete proof that the harsh thought loses its power over time. You are building a strong foundation here by combining a physical reminder with a mental experiment and a method for gathering evidence. Is there anything specific about carrying this forward that worries you, or are you confident you'll have a moment to reflect on the results before our next meeting?

I'm a little worried that I'll forget to do the experiment entirely if I'm really stressed or tired. But I think having the sticky note there will help jog my memory. And yeah, I'll definitely have time to reflect before we meet again. I'm curious to see what I notice.

That worry is completely understandable, and it shows you are anticipating potential obstacles rather than ignoring them. Remember that the sticky note serves as your external anchor when your internal battery is low; seeing those words on the mirror is often enough to trigger a pause even if you can't elaborate immediately. How does knowing you have that visual backup make you feel about trying to recall the exercise during high stress?

It makes me feel more secure, actually. Like even if my brain goes blank, there's that reminder staring back at me. I can just read it and take a breath before I start beating myself up. So I think I'm good to go with this plan and see how it plays out.

That security you're feeling is a huge step forward; having a reliable external anchor means you won't be relying solely on your memory or willpower when you're overwhelmed. You've built a solid safety net with the sticky note and a clear way to track your progress, which will give you confidence going into the next challenge. Thank you for trusting me with this process and for being so willing to try this new approach even when it feels difficult. Let's take care of each other, and I look forward to hearing how that experiment goes when you face the next slip-up.

Hello again. How are you feeling right now compared to last time, and is there anything specific you’d like to prioritize for our session today?

Hey. I guess I'm feeling okay, a little nervous still. I've been thinking a lot about what we talked about last time, and I think I'd like to dive deeper into why my name bothers me so much. It feels like it's been on my mind even more this week.

That’s great that you’re reflecting on it; exploring the roots behind the name issue can definitely bring clarity. Since that seems to be the main priority, shall we spend some time unpacking those underlying thoughts, and is there anything else you’d like to touch on while we do that?

Yeah, I think that's all I really want to focus on today. It's just... whenever I hear "Nick," I feel like it's so plain, you know? Like, there's nothing special about it, and that makes me feel like there's nothing special about me either. I don't know, it just feels like I'm stuck with this label that screams "average."

That connection between your name and feeling "average" is really heavy to carry, and it makes total sense that it would keep coming up. When you say you feel stuck with a label that defines you, what specific moments in your day recently triggered that thought the strongest?

Probably when I was at a party last weekend. I had to introduce myself to this group of new people, and I just felt this pit in my stomach. I said "I'm Nick," and I could practically hear how boring it sounded compared to everyone else's names. It's like the word just hung in the air, and I immediately felt smaller.

That physical sensation of shrinking and hearing your name hang in the air sounds incredibly isolating. It seems like that moment confirmed your fear that being named "Nick" means you are inherently unremarkable. Can we explore together whether that feeling of being "smaller" was a direct reflection of how the others reacted, or if it was mostly driven by what you were expecting them to think?

I think... it was mostly what I was expecting them to think. I mean, no one said anything rude or even looked at me funny. But in my head, I was already filling in the blanks. I just assumed they were thinking, "Oh, another Nick, how original." It's like I can't help but predict the worst reaction, even when there's no evidence for it.

That is a powerful realization, Nick; your brain was racing ahead to fill in a story before anyone had even given you a chance to speak. It sounds like the gap between what happened (no rude comments) and what you predicted (judgment) created that intense pressure. If we look at that party scene, what was the very first thing you noticed or heard once you finished introducing yourself?

One of the guys just smiled and said, "Hey Nick, nice to meet you," and then asked where I was from. It was totally normal. But in the moment, that just felt like people being polite, y'know? Like they were just going through the motions after hearing such a boring name. Even now, it's hard to shake that feeling that they were just being nice.

It makes complete sense that those polite words felt hollow because your expectation of judgment was so loud that you couldn't hear the kindness underneath. That mismatch between your internal narrative ("they're just being nice") and reality ("they are genuinely friendly") is exactly what fuels that shame cycle. Let's look closer at that interaction: if you had told yourself beforehand, "Even if he thinks my name is common, he probably still finds me interesting anyway," how would that slight shift in mindset have changed how you received his smile?

Hmm... I guess if I had thought that, I wouldn't have spent the rest of the night replaying the introduction in my head. I probably would have just relaxed and talked to them without overthinking every word. Maybe I would have even cracked a joke or something. But I didn't give myself that chance; I was already convinced they saw me as forgettable.

That is a crucial distinction, Nick; giving yourself permission to relax and perhaps even crack a joke would have broken the loop of replaying the introduction. It sounds like holding onto the belief that your name equals forgettability left you with no room to engage naturally. Before we solidify a new approach for next time, does it feel helpful to treat your name as just a label people use, rather than a summary of who you are?

Yeah, I think that could help. It's hard to separate the two, but I never really thought of my name as just a label before. It always felt like the whole package. If I could just see it as a word people use to get my attention, maybe I wouldn't feel so defined by it. That might be a good thing to keep in mind when I start spiraling about it.

That is a really useful perspective shift, Nick; seeing the name merely as a tool for attention rather than a definition of your worth gives you more control over how you feel. Before we finalize this, do you feel ready to try applying this new lens—the idea that your name is just a label—in a low-stakes social setting soon, or would you prefer to talk about any other barriers holding you back?

I think I'm ready to try it. Maybe I can start with just ordering coffee or something simple, where I only have to say my name once. If it feels okay, maybe I can work up to a bigger group. But I'm a little scared I'll just slip back into the old thoughts without realizing it.

That is a smart, gradual step; starting with a coffee order keeps the stakes low while still practicing the new lens. To help you catch yourself slipping back into old thoughts, how would it feel if you prepared a quick mental script beforehand, like telling yourself, "My name is just a word, and the person listening cares about the person behind it"?

That actually sounds doable. I like the idea of having a little script ready—it gives me something to hold onto when my mind starts racing. I'll try it next time I grab coffee and see how it feels. Thanks, I think I'm starting to see a way out of this, even if it's just a small step.

I am so glad to hear that you are finding a sense of hope and clarity. Having a small script to anchor yourself is a powerful tool, and taking that first step with coffee is perfectly manageable. Before we wrap up, is there anything else about your feelings or the plan you'd like to add, or shall we go ahead and close our session here?
